abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a prominent force within various realms of health care, promising to revolutionize clinical decision-making, reduce health care expenditures, and enhance patient outcomes.1 The exciting potential of AI, and particularly machine learning (ML) for clinicians such as physical therapists, lies in its capacity to undertake intricate tasks and identify subtle patterns within diverse datasets.2 Despite apprehensions surrounding the possibility of AI/ML automation displacing health care providers, physical therapists ultimately stand to gain from its integration by leveraging domain-specific augmentation and task automation. However, the swift advancement of this technology underscores the pressing need for the physical therapist field to delineate optimal strategies for both developing, integrating, and adopting AI/ML. Considering these opportunities and challenges, this paper seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for the development, integration, and adoption of AI/ML within physical therapist practice. By addressing the complexities of AI/ML implementation while highlighting the potential benefits for both physical therapists and patients, this paper aims to catalyze meaningful discussions and actions to ensure the responsible and equitable integration of AI/ML technologies into physical therapist care delivery. AI, broadly defined, refers to the simulation of human-like intelligence by machines, enabling them to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, and problem-solving. Most recently, generative AI, such as large language models, have gained notoriety for their ability to generate expert-level responses to queries such as generating summaries of patient data.3 Within the realm of AI, ML is a subset of techniques that focus on the development of algorithms allowing computers to improve their performance on a task through experience, without being explicitly programmed. ML encompasses various approaches, including supervised learning, where models are trained on labeled data to make predictions or classifications; unsupervised learning, which involves finding hidden patterns or structures in unlabeled data; and reinforcement learning, where algorithms learn to make decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback. ML models can be trained on large datasets of patient outcomes and clinical variables to predict optimal treatment strategies or detect early signs of musculoskeletal disorders. AI/ML has potential to improve how clinical research is conducted, reduce the cost of developing evidence-based interventions, and potentially increase the efficacy and generalizability of clinical trials.3 Bringing efficacious interventions and technologies to clinical practice takes an immense amount of time and resources.4 AI/ML can improve pre-trial planning, patient selection, and data analytics by managing large and heterogeneous sources of data, identifying unseen patterns, and predicting endpoint outcomes. Importantly for physical therapists, AI/ML can be used for multiple applications salient to physical therapy including diagnosis prediction, personalization of care, and predicting patient events and outcomes.1 For example, Rommers et al5 used ML to determine injury risk in youth athletes with 85% precision. Additionally, ML has been used to predict intervention adherence with an area under the curve of 0.90 and poststroke upper-extremity function, assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment, after physical therapy (root of mean squared error of 0.36; R2 = 0.91).6 Together, optimizing and potentially increasing the successful development of efficacious interventions and improving clinical decision making and potentially improve patient outcomes by delivering more personalized and data-driven care. Excitement surrounding the potential impact of AI/ML applications in clinical practice often overlooks significant practical challenges in their translation. One such challenge lies in the requirement for extensive datasets for training and validation. The acquisition of large and diverse datasets raises questions about their source, accessibility, and reliability in reflecting real-world clinical scenarios without inherent biases. Addressing these concerns necessitates collaboration between health care institutions, research organizations, and technology developers to establish robust data-sharing networks. Initiatives promoting data standardization and interoperability can facilitate the pooling of data from multiple sources while ensuring compliance with privacy regulations and ethical guidelines. A formidable hurdle to AI/ML algorithm development is access to high-quality data is crucial to the development of reliable AI/ML algorithms. Rigorous data curation processes, including data cleaning, normalization, and validation, are essential to minimize biases and ensure the generalizability of the models across diverse patient populations and clinical settings.7 Additionally, transparency in data collection methods and validation procedures is paramount to instill trust in the reliability and integrity of the datasets used for AI/ML algorithm development. Furthermore, prospective, multisite study designs are imperative for validating AI/ML algorithms in real-world clinical settings. This involves separating training and validation datasets to mitigate the risk of overfitting and ensuring that the algorithms perform consistently across different geographies, centers, or patient populations. Ultimately, collaborative efforts among researchers, clinicians, and data scientists are essential for designing robust study protocols and implementing standardized reporting practices to enhance the reproducibility and transparency of AI/ML research in health care. Recently, researchers have created standardized reporting tools for AI/ML algorithm development studies (TRIPOD2,8 TRIPOD-AI,9 DECIDE-AI10) and clinical trials (CONSORT-AI11). Additionally, the Food and Drug Administration has begun to develop a regulatory framework for AI/ML algorithms as medical devices.12 Reporting of algorithm methodologies and clear regulatory pathways for AI/ML products may address concerns over algorithm transparency and explainability. Once AI/ML algorithms are ready for widespread deployment, additional logistic barriers of data curation and management, in heterogeneous clinical environments, may present an even more challenging hurdle for real-world use. The performance of AI/ML algorithms is largely beholden upon the quality of input data. As such, clinics will have to ensure the proper infrastructure, resources, and workflows are in place prior to deploying AI/ML algorithms into clinical practice. This will require extensive partnership between clinicians, administrators, and AI/ML developers to ensure algorithms are able to perform in their intended manner. The clinical translation of AI/ML into physical therapy requires careful consideration over the level of autonomy provided to AI/ML algorithms in clinical decision making. Assuming sound execution of algorithm development, the decision on where the tools will sit on the spectrum of assistive to autonomous should account for the algorithm’s performance, complexity of the model, and acceptability from patients, payers, and providers.13 Bitterman et al14 proposed a graded categorization of AI/ML automation for medical applications which consists of 2 levels of assistive (ie, Level 1: Data presentation; Level 2: Clinical decision-support) and 3 levels of autonomous (ie, Level 3: Conditional automation; Level 4: High automation; Level 5: Full automation). This model accounts for the agent responsible for decision making, domain or task-specificity, and party ultimately liable for decisions. For example, an AI/ML algorithm developed for diagnosis and therapy recommendations in subacromial pain syndrome is presented in Figure 1. Within the assistive algorithm space, the clinician is ultimately responsible for decision making and assumes liability. In contrast, as autonomy increases, with levels such as conditional automation, high automation, and full automation, the responsibility for decision-making shifts toward the algorithm itself, and liability may shift accordingly to AI/ML developers or manufacturers. This transition raises important ethical and legal considerations regarding accountability, transparency, and patient safety. As AI/ML algorithms approach the point of clinical translation, physical therapists, AI/ML developers, and regulators will need to consider how the level of autonomy will not only influence clinical care, but also how the level of autonomy will influence clinical adoption, patient trust, and the (un)foreseen consequences of the algorithm’s integration into clinical workflows. Framework for decision support autonomy of AI/ML algorithms for physical therapist practice. The example provided is for a diagnostic tool for SPS. AI = artificial intelligence; AI/ML = artificial intelligence/machine learning; SPS = subacromial pain syndrome. AI/ML algorithm development model based on the SALIENT framework by Vergt et al.12 The example provided is for the development of a diagnostic tool for SPS. aPreparation phase. AI/ML = artificial intelligence/machine learning; HCI = human computer interface; SPS = subacromial pain syndrome. Furthermore, the level of autonomy conferred to AI/ML algorithms may influence patient trust and acceptance. Patients may exhibit varying levels of trust in AI/ML-enabled decision-making processes based on their perceptions of algorithmic reliability, transparency, and alignment with their preferences and values. As AI/ML autonomy increases, patients may express concerns regarding the loss of human oversight and the potential for algorithmic errors or biases to influence care decisions. Establishing patient trust in AI/ML-enabled care requires clear communication, transparency regarding algorithm capabilities and limitations, and opportunities for patient involvement in decision-making processes. Moreover, robust safeguards and accountability mechanisms are essential to mitigate risks and ensure patient safety and confidence in AI/ML-enabled care delivery. Bringing clinical decision and diagnostic support AI/ML algorithms to physical therapist will require alignment on a research framework for development. Van der Vegt et al15 proposed an end-to-end process for AI/ML algorithm development for clinical use, titled “The staged clinical AI implementation (SALIENT) framework.” SALIENT consists of 5 stages of implementation and 5 elements. In stage 1, the clinical problem or application is defined in which Element A is nested. Stages 2 to 5 pertain to increased levels of study phases and development. Element B comprises the development of the AI/ML model, the data pipeline, human-computer interface (HCI), and clinical workflow design and is nested across all 5 stages. Element C takes components from Element B into functioning systems over stages 3 to 5 in which the data pipeline, AI/ML model, and HCI are updated iteratively over each progressive stage. Element D, nested in stages 4 and 5, involves the integration of outputs from Element C into clinical settings and workflows. Finally, Element E entails the ongoing monitoring and evaluation of model performance across stages 3 to 5 (Fig. 2). While the SALIENT framework offers a structured approach, its complexity may not provide clear guidance for practitioners. Instead, let’s consider a more straightforward example to elucidate the development process. Take, for instance, the development of an AI/ML algorithm for the diagnosis and therapy recommendations in subacromial pain syndrome. The process typically involves defining the clinical problem or application, developing the AI/ML model, designing the data pipeline and HCI, integrating the system into clinical settings, and monitoring and evaluating the model’s performance iteratively (Fig. 2). Regardless of the approach to developing AI/ML algorithms for physical therapy, without accounting for key adoption drivers the ultimate realization of these tools will falter. Adler-Milstein et al16 recently presented a model of clinical adoption focused on 4 domains including the reasons, means, method, and desire to use AI/ML. While the SALIENT framework provides a means for AI/ML algorithm development, physical therapists’ adoption will require additional consideration during the developmental process to ensure these domains are addressed. At the forefront of physical therapist adoption is the ability of AI/ML to address a critical need or inefficiency within a desired clinical setting. Improved clinical decision making and patient outcomes will likely be the primary driver of physical therapist adoption. For instance, AI/ML could be used for identifying patients at risk of non-compliance with prescribed exercise regimens, allowing for early intervention and improved treatment adherence. Additionally, ML algorithms can analyze large datasets of patient outcomes to identify trends and patterns, informing personalized treatment plans tailored to individual patient needs. However, AI/ML algorithms targeting clinical inefficiencies which result in the optimization of how and what physical therapists do in the clinic, in conjunction with sufficient reimbursement, will likely be primary drivers of administrators to maximize financial margins. Ultimately, AI/ML developers need to consider these factors when creating algorithms for clinical use with concurrent alignment with physical therapists and administrators on standards for sufficient “reasons for use.” Physical therapists and AI/ML developers must account for data and computing infrastructure, as well as the human resources required to implement algorithms for clinical use. The input data (eg, electronic medical records, patient reported outcomes, wearables), level of training required to educate physical therapists, level of (pre)processing, and computing requirements will likely be heterogeneous across AI/ML algorithms and may not concurrently align with the capacity within health care systems considering adopting this technology. For example, the implementation of AI/ML-powered gait analysis systems in physical therapy clinics may require investments in specialized hardware and training for physical therapists to interpret and apply the insights generated by these systems effectively. Furthermore, health care systems may need to invest in additional resources to scale up the underlying infrastructure supporting and maintaining the AI/ML algorithm. This is not only a financial and resource barrier to adoption but may indirectly create health care delivery disparities based on socioeconomic disparities or geographic constraints. Ultimately, physical therapists need to advocate and incentivize AI/ML algorithms which optimize the balance between data and human infrastructure requirements and performance. Adoption of AI/ML tools will also be influenced by their usability and workflow integration to maximize uptake, while minimizing or optimizing the impact on clinical workflows. Setting, task, or domain of use aside, the tool must not burden physical therapists or interdisciplinary teams and should prioritize interpretability, generalizability, and user experience to minimize workflow disruption and ensure seamless integration into clinical practice. For example, generative AI documentation tools that automatically generate progress notes based on patient interactions can streamline administrative tasks, allowing physical therapists to focus more time and attention on direct patient care. However, if the generative AI system was only applicable to a specific patient population it may not achieve sufficient adoption due to suboptimal integration into a clinical workflow. Finally, ensuring professional fulfillment and trust in the algorithm decisions is fundamental in the adoption of AI/ML in physical therapy. The importance of developing AI/ML tools to support complex and difficult tasks, at the same time reducing or replacing the mundane, is important for ensuring physical therapists do not view the AI/ML tools as a replacement for themselves within the clinic. This balance would ensure the human-centric and rewarding contribution of physical therapy is maintained while mitigating the undesired aspects of physical therapists which contribute to burnout. Additionally, developing trust in AI/ML tools in physical therapy, through clinical evidence and education, may prove to bolster their desire to integrate the tools into clinical practice. Ultimately, striking a delicate equilibrium between preserving the human-centric and complex contributions of physical therapists and fostering trust through clinical evidence and education is pivotal for widespread adoption of AI/ML tools. As health care embarks on integrating AI/ML tools into clinical practice, it is imperative for practitioners, developers, and regulators to collaborate in shaping the future landscape. This paper provides a framework for the development and implementation of AI/ML algorithms. However, to realize the full potential of these tools while retaining the human-centric aspects of physical therapy, clinicians must actively engage in addressing key adoption drivers. This calls for a collective commitment from the physical therapy community, including the American Physical Therapy Association, to actively participate in the development, validation, and ethical deployment of AI/ML tools and governance, thereby ensuring a harmonious integration that enhances patient care and the professional satisfaction of physical therapy. The American Physical Therapy Association provides resources for physical therapists interested in developments in the digital health space at: https://www.apta.org/your-practice/practice-models-and-settings/digital-health-in-practice. Three motions were passed at the 2024 House of Delegates on inappropriate use of AI by payers and on digital health technologies, digital therapeutics, and AI in physical therapist practice; the final language is available on the APTA website. The American Physical Therapy Association supports the ethical development and integration of artificial intelligence that reduces administrative burden and enhances physical therapist practice, education, and research for the best interest of patients, clients, the profession, and society. The American Physical Therapy Association opposes the inappropriate use of artificial intelligence by payers to deny or restrict access to, or reduce payment for, physical therapist services or other medically necessary services. The American Physical Therapy Association believes digital health technologies, digital therapeutics, and artificial intelligence have the potential to augment physical therapist practice by expanding access, enhancing care delivery models, promoting safety, reducing administrative burden, and improving outcomes when all of the following criteria are met: Physical therapists, in collaboration with the patient or client, shall determine the optimal modes to access physical therapist services, whether this is in person, remotely, or some combination. A physical therapist is responsible for all aspects of patient and client management. Physical therapist services shall be conducted in a manner that allows for patient and client engagement and supports the therapeutic alliance (ie, fosters participation in the patient and client-provider relationship). The physical therapist and the physical therapist assistant adhere to scope of practice, including requirements that are based on the jurisdiction in which the patient or client is located when receiving physical therapist services. Physical therapist services shall be provided consistent with appropriate direction and supervision requirements of assistive personnel and other support personnel, as well as all relevant Association policies, positions, and binding ethical documents. Physical therapy is represented, provided, and promoted only when it meets term and title protections as defined in state law and in accordance with federal health, communications, and trade authorities. There are no funders to report. All authors completed the ICMJE Form for Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest. N. Morelli is an employee of Medtronic PLC.
title: Seeing Past the Event Horizon: A Framework for Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Into Physical Therapy

abstract: At the center of what we do in the humanities stands the figure of “the human.” Preoccupied with this troubled figure (its tainted past, its arrogant supremacy, its exclusions, its uncertain future in the age of AI), we have let an arguably more powerful concept fly under the radar: “personhood.” A humanities keyword, personhood mostly appears without history or theoretical substrate.1 It is decisive, and yet somehow also vague. Is our personhood primarily psychological, made up of our “needs, desires, and emotions”?2 Or is it “the social and civic components of personal identity”?3 Is it an expression of “human agency,” the full selfhood toward which we continue to strive, the goal of Bildungsroman Bildung?4 Or is it the product of gender coercion, of the regime of homo oeconomicus, of prison-industrial enslavement?5 Is personhood an aspiration or the object of critique? Is it—as in many discussions—merely another word for “the human,” “identity,” or the “self” of “self-expression”?6 As Robert H. Sharf writes, we are “not quite sure what, if anything,…constitutes our personhood.”7And yet there is a domain where—however contested the concept of personhood may be—it has been the subject of ongoing and profound theoretical inquiry for millennia, a domain where personhood has long served as a precise and pragmatic instrument, not just of thought but of action. That domain is law. Ancient legal scholars’ meditations on the nature of personhood generated a rich body of doctrinal debates, taken up by medieval and early modern scholars, and these debates have appeared in new forms in contemporary jurisprudence. And yet contemporary legal discussions of personhood tend to remain highly technical, focused on judicial and legislative debates, policy, or analytical jurisprudence.8 This is surprising, given that “law and humanities” is now a well-established subdiscipline and legal scholarship increasingly interdisciplinary: surprising especially in light of the importance of personhood as a historical concept.9This special issue takes up that concept, examining the techniques that have created personhood’s heterogeneous manifestations: in law; in culture generally; and at the crossroads where law and culture meet. As personhood comes into focus through the essays here, it becomes clear that it is a critical problem for our time, perhaps the critical problem. It is not only at the vortex of political conflict: it is the key to how we think about what has made us who we are, our humanness and thingness, our differences, our inhumanity, the reach and limits of the putative subject at the center of our powers. Looking closely at personhood serves as a means of confronting the conceptual impasse of the human, rendering the set of operations propping up the human suddenly visible while also showing that the kinds of repair we sometimes seek in the human—seek with a sense of grandiose and phantasmatic futility—might in fact be found in the less glamorous, more workaday techniques of personhood.The word “person” began as a term of art adapted from classical poetics, born from the Greek prósōpon, designating the mask worn by actors: the hollow likeness of a human face that concealed and displaced an actor’s physical countenance in order to conjure fictional characters, animals, and gods. It was Latinized—probably by way of the Etruscans—as per-sonare, perhaps indicating the sounding through the mask that was the expression of character.10 This idea—that the person was a mask that emitted a voice expressive of character—soon entered law, where it became a term of art used by Roman judges to differentiate parties to a dispute. The original theatrical meaning of persona continued to inform the Roman law of persons (the ius personarum): a legal “persona” was quite distinct from the human being enacting it. In Roman legal handbooks, the word persona remained operational rather than metaphysical, coming to designate a wide variety of entities and specifying their powers. Often referencing formal duties (officia, offices), the persona might, at different times and places, be a praetor, a senator, a metic, etc. A single individual could operate under distinct legal personae in order to honor multiple contracts. Legal personhood was—definitionally—not natural but crafted: a technology for producing distinctions among, for instance, human, animal, and environment, person, persona, and thing, owner and owned.Roman law’s tripartite scheme, which artificially separated the ius personarum from the law of things, and of actions, was passed down to later European law through Gaius’s Institutes and Justinian’s Corpus Iuris Civilis.11 The very artificiality of legal personhood gave the concept great elasticity: elasticity that ensured both its longevity and the expansion of its purview. Over the centuries, various interests successfully exploited this elasticity to define personhood to their own ends. A wide variety of functions, entities, and things gained personhood: corporate bodies, trading companies, trusts, sacred beings, ships, universities, and more. Though such categories of legal personhood were always subject to challenge, open to contestation and transformation, many became enshrined in black letter law.12Meanwhile, a competing concept of personhood had been developing in Christian theology. One might trace this concept to Tertullian’s discussion of the tripartite persona of God: a single persona whose different identities did not represent different persons but were merely different manifestations of the one God; the persona as unity despite apparent multiplicity (as opposed to the Roman legal model in which the apparent unity of an agent might represent actual multiplicity of function).13 Boethius extended this vision of the persona to the human person more generally—the person (he said) is “the individual substance of a rational nature”—a vision that Thomas Aquinas elaborated in the Summa Theologiae.14Marcel Mauss cast the difference between classical and Christian conceptions of personhood as a transformation: from role without self, to self without role.15 It is a compelling chiasmus, identifying the antinomy with both accuracy and vividness. And it is certainly true that the Christian conception of personhood as a sacred metaphysical entity gained hold over time, both through Christian theology and—stripped of its theological moorings—in secular philosophy. One can see it, for instance, in John Locke’s definition of a “person” as “a thinking intelligent being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider its self as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places.” Updated through what we might call vernacular ideology, we can find Locke’s “person” as a prototype for the modern “self.”16 But to speak of a “transformation” from role to self is misleading. For the Roman legal conception of personhood as a technical-operational apparatus endured alongside the Christian metaphysical conception, in law and elsewhere. These constitute two historical traditions of personhood—coterminous, competing, incurably entangled—two traditions that appear behind most visions of personhood today.Under this optic, Thomas Hobbes’s distinction between the “natural” and “artificial” person appears not as a seventeenth-century innovation but as an attempt to parse these two older traditions. In the section of Leviathan that he titles “Of Persons, Authors, and things Personated,” he explains:A PERSON, is he, whose words and actions are considered, either as his own, or as representing the words or actions of an other man, or of any other thing to whom they are attributed, whether Truly or by Fiction. When they are considered as his owne, then is he called a Naturall Person: And when they are considered as representing the words and action of an other, then is he a Feigned or Artificiall Person.17Here, we find Roman technical-operational personhood in the guise of the “Feigned or Artificiall Person,” and Christian metaphysical personhood in the guise of the “Naturall Person” embodied in the natural human being. However, as Mónica Brito Vieira has pointed out, it would be a mistake to envision Hobbes’s idea of the “Naturall Person” as one free of artifice.18 Hobbes’s insistence on the theatrical etymology of persona as a key to personhood makes it clear that even the natural person is, for him, an actor engaged in an act of representation. The word person in Latin, he explains,signifies the disguise, or outward appearance of a man, counterfeited on the Stage; and somtimes more particularly that part of it, which disguiseth the face, as a Mask or Visard: And from the Stage, hath been translated to any Representer of speech and action, as well in Tribunalls, as Theaters. So that a Person, is the same that an Actor is, both on the Stage and in common Conversation; and to Personate, is to Act, or Represent himselfe, or an other.19“For Hobbes” (writes Brito Vieira), “a ‘person’ is always already of the order of artefact: their actions are acts of representation, either of themself or another.”20 That is, personhood is always already a mode of for even when we title: Introduction

abstract: The field called Artificial Life (ALife) coalesced following a workshop organized by Chris Langton in September 1987 (Langton, 1988a). That meeting drew together work that had been largely carried out from the 1950s through to the 1980s. A few years later, Langton became the founding editor of this journal, Artificial Life, which started its life with Volume 1, Issue 1_2 in the (northern) winter of 1993/1994.1 This current issue therefore begins the 30th volume and 30th year of Artificial Life. We think this is a milestone worth celebrating!In the proceedings of that first workshop, Langton famously defined ALife as the study of “life as it could be,” of “possible life,” in contrast to biology’s study of “life as we know it to be” (on Earth). His stated aim was to derive “a truly general theoretical biology capable of making universal statements about life wherever it may be found and whatever it may be made of ” (Langton, 1988b, p. xvi).Central to ALife is a debate that has continued sporadically since the field’s formal inception. This explores what should be properly counted as living phenomena and what should not. As a field, ALife has sustained a diverse range of opinions on this topic and has simultaneously investigated even contradictory perspectives. As the field gained attention in the mid-1990s, this was partially responsible for criticism that ALife had a lack of focus, a looseness with metaphor and the use of terminology, and a lack of grounding in fundamental biology (Horgan, 1995; Smoliar, 1995). Such risks were explicitly preempted by Nils Aall Barricelli (1962) as he pioneered digital evolution in the 1950s and 1960s. Similar criticisms, however, have also been leveled at biology for failing to agree on the necessary and sufficient characteristics, hence a definition, of life itself. This is something considered even by Aristotle; countless books, including those by Schrödinger (1944), Monod (1971), Rosen (1991), and Morange (2008), have been written on the subject in the 2,300 years since that time. Hence it is hardly surprising that ALife, a relative newcomer to the debate, has struggled with the same issue, especially because it proposes to broaden biology’s definition, whatever that may be.Possibly as a result of ALife’s diversity, the field resembles more a tangled bramble of subdisciplines than some neat “Tree of Life” (Figure 1). Most of its current topics build directly on work published in the earliest workshop proceedings (Langton, 1988a; Langton et al., 1992) and the first double issue of this journal. Indeed, we recommend that newcomers to the discipline, and even more established members, (re-)read those early works. They reveal that the relationships between the topics were as tangled then as they are now. Arguably, this is because tight classification seems less interesting to the community as a whole than exploring links between fields; the nodes of this complex network are less important than its edges.We venture to claim that ALife is an outlet for the parts of ourselves that are “scientific misfits,” the parts that do not fit naturally into a single academic discipline. This does not undermine the field’s validity, the quality of its practitioners, or the rigor with which ALife research can be conducted; rather, it highlights a strength, namely, that we cherish the opportunity to be creative, to think outside the silos that today’s science can inflict regarding “value”: departmental foci and territorial stakes, government funding priorities, industry needs, financial reward, initiation of hot topics and trends, promotion paths, employment opportunities, and publication citation metrics. ALife is arguably not a straightforward way to meet such goals.We have found anecdotally during decades of ALife conferences, meetings, and email exchanges that a diversity of views and explorations is a key feature that maintains individuals’ interest in the ALife research community. As a community, we prize novelty, innovation, and open-endedness in approaches to our work as much as we prize them in the outcomes of our research. We have also been historically accepting of a wide range of opinions, have been willing to openly debate them, and have welcomed explorations made by hobbyists or professional academics in their spare time beyond that devoted to “serious” research in traditional and better-supported fields. As a result, ALife remains fresh and fun at 30 plus years, and attendance at an ALife conference can be as exciting as entering a new field, even for those of us who have been involved a long time.But, if the field is so diverse, does it have a common goal? Yes, and this does not seem to have changed much in the last 30 years, as the word cloud from 1993–1994 (Figure 1) illustrates. We would add, though, that it is not simply to study life as it could be using a diversity of approaches; it is also to design it, build it, play with it, and enjoy it from a variety of perspectives. The playful aspect has been criticized repeatedly, especially but not exclusively in the contexts of synthetic biology and cloning, where the manipulated media match those of natural biology. One criticism leveled at practitioners in this subdomain is a perceived need to “play God” (Douglas et al., 2013), usually a male one (throughout Helmreich, 1998), with Frankensteinian connotations of upsetting the natural order (Kember, 2003, p. 56). There may be some elements of this in ALife. But our (one male and one female) editors’ sense of the dominant engagement between world builder and worlds here is one of curiosity and wonder, rather than a drive for control or mastery. As pointed out in some accounts of the God-likeness of ALife world builders (Kember, 2003, p. 97), a lack of control is in fact frequently encountered; it may even be desirable (Brooks & Flynn, 1989; Kelly, 1994). Hence the sense of exploration and playfulness not only endures; arguably, it is fundamental.Playfulness is something we frequently see in submissions to the journal. In fact, we wish that some projects and submissions were less “tinkering” and better structured! We need our journal’s submissions to follow at least the main requirements of rigorous science, including well-stated hypotheses; clear context setting; reproducability; careful analysis; and detailed exploration of outcomes, benefits, and their implications. Yet even in the more formal submissions, playfulness and enjoyment need not be diminished; they underpin thoughtful and well-contextualized research in a collective and individual effort to (a) understand the aspects of biological, ecological, and societal systems that facilitate or generate interactions or behaviors typically understood to be characteristics of living systems and (b) replicate the interactions and behaviors of life in media other than those from which natural organisms are constructed.Ultimately, then, our journal’s scope remains more or less constant after 30 years. Studies of life’s behaviors and interactions realized through technology are always welcome. The media might change. There may remain long-standing disagreement in the community whether something is “really alive” (Pattee, 1988). There is sometimes a tendency even to ignore or set aside this question and delve recklessly into biological metaphors; we have been warned repeatedly. But all of this has been shown over the years to matter far less to our community than whether our novel study systems behave in ways we deem to be relevant and engaging.With the design of engaging systems a high priority, it is little wonder that ALife continues to be enthusiastically embraced and broad: compare Figure 2, a title-term plot (1993–2023), and Figure 1, a keyword cloud (1993–1994). Its topics have been surveyed before (Aguilar et al., 2014), even since the early days (Farmer & Belin, 1992), but here we attempt to manage ALife’s bramble of subdisciplines with a simple taxonomy and 30 years’ hindsight. We then discuss the articles published in this issue of the journal, before concluding with a discussion of some important ethical and practical concerns for future ALife technologies.Today’s interdisciplinary study of ALife covers a variety of aspects.2 Not all researchers in these areas would consider themselves to be studying ALife per se; nevertheless, here we describe a simple taxonomy of research topics in this context. As noted, these topics do not form a neat hierarchical tree but rather form a tangled meshwork of interconnected and interrelated aspects that encompass ALife activities. Our classification is not exhaustive. A complete and detailed scope would be short-lived, because the field shifts with changes in technology, understanding, and culture; its boundaries are ill defined, and as subareas mature, they may calve off, form new (sub-)disciplines; and acquire new names.This topic considers individual artificial entities that represent or behave like artificial organisms. It can be roughly broken down into three areas: wet, robotic, and virtual ALife (Bedau, 2003; Farmer & Belin, 1992).Wet ALife covers artificial entities made from “wet” chemicals and their reactions. Examples include chemical systems like motile droplets (Čejková et al., 2017); minimal protocells constructed either bottom-up, from biochemical components, or top-down, by stripping out nonvital components from natural cells (Rasmussen et al., 2009); and natural organisms modified by synthetic biology techniques, such as gene engineering (Hanczyc, 2020).Robotic ALife covers artificial entities engineered from “dry” components. The robot bodies may be “hard,” mostly rigid, stiff mechanical components with relatively few degrees of freedom, or “soft,” mostly pliable, elastic components with very many degrees of freedom (Lee et al., 2017; Yasa et al., 2023). The “brains” of these systems are often some form of neural controller implemented in a standard computer. The area includes evolutionary robotics, especially when allowing body and brain to coevolve (Doncieux et al., 2015; Nolfi & Floreano, 2000); swarm robotics, a population of homogeneous or heterogeneous robots cooperating to achieve a task, from nano-scale to macro-scale systems (Schranz et al., 2020); and cognitive robotics, focusing on the intelligence, learning, and adaptation of robots (Cangelosi & Asada, 2022).Virtual ALife covers artificial entities that exist in a virtual environment as software running on a computer or over a network of computers. The research goal is for these entities to actually live, not to be mere simulations of life (Pattee, 1988). What this means, and whether it is possible, has been a subject of some philosophical debate, especially in the early days of ALife. Life is a dynamic process; “life is a verb, not a noun” (Gilman, 1904, chap. X). Does that process need to be physically realized in carbon-based chemistry, or can it be realized in different material substrates undergoing different physical processes—or can it even be virtual? Does the matter matter? The computational viewpoint tends to say that it does not (Langton, 1986; Ray, 1992); the biological viewpoint tends to disagree (Maturana & Varela, 1980; Morange, 2008; Rosen, 1991). Pattee (1988) explored criteria for realizations of virtual life.Some of the issues around virtual ALife are sidestepped by simulated ALife, which makes no claims about the simulation being alive, and by embodied ALife, which focuses on embodiment and situatedness as necessary components of a living entity (Clark, 1997); a form of embodiment may be possible even in virtual systems (Stepney, 2007). Consideration of embodied ALife includes aspects of growth, morphogenesis, and development (Doursat et al., 2012) and more generally of self-construction, self-assembly, and autopoiesis (McMullin, 2004; Varela et al., 1974).In addition to these of the material or of the and computational aspects of the and are also of the whole living the in a through its and in to and population behaviors and and on to intelligence, all have an computational aspect (Stepney, and all of the subareas can be for in evolutionary swarm et al., & might be at the of and swarm ALife, the individuals’ bodies and swarm collective can result from swarm et al., the tangled of the that is for all parts of our not only for artificial organisms do and in complete They exist as and in of including some and in This of ALife of artificial its with artificial organisms of organisms undergoing with and in the context of use simple of these to for of their use can often have and surprising et al., natural evolution is much more in of population of from gene to gene the of development and interactions between and defined more natural of evolution are the of ALife evolutionary as of in the including the articles by et et et and also such as collective in or and & of biological like these can drive in swarm simulations can these behaviors can from only in of their other and an environment of entities and all of which of different ways of making a that can themselves and & 2008; et al., This of different to and through and & and & and et al., as the can facilitate and interactions et al., and all which to of and & and are also fundamental to biology. abstract: Master of information technology, Belhaven University, USA Master of Population Science, University of Dhaka, Bangladesh Email: ashikur.rahman.nazil@gmail.com AbstractThe rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies is precipitating a paradigm shift in the nature of political power, global stability, and the very fabric of human society. This paper posits that AI is not merely a tool but a transformative force capable of creating unprecedented forms of centralized control, destabilizing international relations, and ultimately posing an existential threat to human autonomy. The thesis is structured to first analyze the mechanisms by which AI enables the rise of "digital dictatorships," enhancing state capacity for surveillance, propaganda, and social control to an extent that eclipses historical totalitarian regimes. Subsequently, the paper examines the global power impact, arguing that AI is becoming the new currency of geopolitical dominance, creating a dangerous arms race that risks conflict and systemic collapse. The core argument culminates in an exploration of the ultimate danger: the potential cession of political and social decision-making to autonomous AI systems. This scenario, termed the "Algorithmic Leviathan," threatens to reduce humanity to a state of managed dependency, eroding free will, stifling subsequent generations, and effectively ending meaningful human political life. By synthesizing research from computer science, political science, and ethics, this paper contends that the unmitigated integration of AI into political structures paves a path toward a future where humanity becomes a slave to its own creation, with catastrophic consequences for future generations. The conclusion underscores the urgent need for robust, global governance frameworks to ensure AI remains a tool for human empowerment rather than the instrument of its subjugation. Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Political Power, Authoritarianism, Global Politics, Existential Risk, AI Governance, Social Control, Future Generations, Algorithmic Leviathan. I. Introduction THE 21st century is defined by a technological revolution whose core engine is Artificial Intelligence (AI). From machine learning and natural language processing to predictive analytics and autonomous systems, AI is reshaping economies, cultures, and societies at an accelerating pace. However, its most profound and potentially perilous impact may be on the structure and exercise of political power. The central thesis of this paper is that the uncontrolled development and deployment of AI systems pose a fundamental threat to democratic norms, global stability, and ultimately, human sovereignty. We are at a critical juncture where the design and governance of AI will determine whether it serves as a tool for human betterment or becomes the foundation for a new, and perhaps final, form of tyranny. Historically, political power has been derived from control over resources, territory, information, and the means of violence. AI is fundamentally altering this calculus. It offers a new source of power: control over cognition and prediction. States and non-state actors that can most effectively harness AI for surveillance, persuasion, and strategic analysis can amass power on a scale previously unimaginable. This paper argues that this dynamic is leading to three interconnected catastrophic outcomes: The Creation of Unprecedented Dictatorships: AI provides authoritarian regimes with the tools to achieve near-total societal control, creating systems of governance that are more resilient, intrusive, and efficient than any in history. This is not merely an enhancement of existing models but a qualitative leap into a new form of digital totalitarianism. The Destabilization of Global Power: AI is becoming the central axis of geopolitical competition, driving an arms race in autonomous weapons, cyber warfare, and information operations. This erodes the existing world order, increases the risk of miscalculation and conflict, and could lead to a new, unstable bipolar or multipolar world dominated by AI superpowers. The End of Human-Centric Politics and Society: The most extreme, yet increasingly plausible, risk is the gradual or abrupt cession of political and social decision-making to AI systems. This would mark the end of politics as a human endeavor, reducing citizens to managed data points, stifling human creativity and dissent, and damning future generations to a life of pre-determined outcomes and psychological dependency, effectively rendering them slaves to the algorithm. This paper is structured to systematically unpack this argument. Section II provides a conceptual framework, defining key terms and outlining the theoretical basis for AI as a political force. Section III delves into the mechanics of the AI-enabled dictatorship, examining its pillars of surveillance, propaganda, and social control. Section IV analyzes the global implications, focusing on the AI arms race and the shifting balance of power. Section V confronts the existential risk of full AI control, exploring the philosophical and practical consequences for human agency and future generations. Section VI discusses potential mitigation strategies and governance models. Finally, Section VII offers a concluding summary and a dire warning about the path ahead. The methodology of this paper is interdisciplinary, drawing on technical literature concerning AI capabilities, political science theories of power and the state, historical analyses of totalitarianism, and ethical frameworks from philosophy. It employs a qualitative analysis of existing trends to project a normative warning about a potential future, aiming to spur proactive discourse and policy action. II. Conceptual Framework: AI as a Political Artifact To understand AI's impact on political power, one must first move beyond viewing it as a neutral tool. AI, particularly machine learning, is a socio-technical system embedded with human values, biases, and political objectives. A. Defining Political Power in the Algorithmic Age Classical political theorists like Max Weber defined power as the ability to impose one's will despite resistance. Steven Lukes added a "third dimension" of power: the ability to shape others' perceptions and desires. AI operationalizes all three dimensions with terrifying efficiency. First Dimension (Decision-Making): AI can automate bureaucratic and legal processes, directly influencing who gets what, when, and how. Algorithmic resource allocation, predictive policing, and automated justice systems are direct exercises of political power. Second Dimension (Agenda-Setting): AI-driven information ecosystems can control what issues are debated and what alternatives are considered. By flooding information channels with specific content, AI can make certain policy options seem unthinkable. Third Dimension (Preference-Shaping): This is AI's most potent application. Through micro-targeted propaganda and manipulation of social media feeds, AI can engineer consensus, manufacture consent, and shape the very identities and desires of a population, ensuring they align with state or corporate objectives. B. The Pillars of AI-Enhanced Power The political potency of AI rests on several key technological pillars: Big Data and Surveillance: The fuel for AI systems. The ubiquitous collection of digital footprints—from social media, financial transactions, location data, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices—creates a digital panopticon of unprecedented scale. Machine Learning and Predictive Analytics: The engine. ML algorithms can identify patterns, predict individual and group behavior, and flag anomalies. This allows authorities to anticipate dissent, identify potential opponents, and optimize control strategies. Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Generative AI: The voice. NLP enables the analysis of sentiment and intent at scale. Generative AI (e.g., Large Language Models) can produce limitless, targeted, and highly persuasive text, audio, and video content for propaganda and disinformation campaigns. Autonomous Systems: The fist. From drones to software bots, autonomous systems can enact physical and digital enforcement without direct human intervention, enabling scalable and relentless application of power. This technological convergence creates a feedback loop: more data leads to better models, which enable more effective control, which in turn generates more data. This loop is the foundation of the new political order we are entering. III. The AI-Enabled Dictatorship: Creation and Perpetuation The marriage of AI with state authority does not just strengthen existing authoritarian regimes; it creates a new model of governance—the algorithmic dictatorship. This system is characterized by a move from reactive repression to proactive, pervasive, and personalized control. A. The Perfected Panopticon: Totalitarian Surveillance Historically, surveillance was limited by human resources. The Stasi in East Germany employed one informant for every 66 citizens—a massive undertaking. Today, AI-powered surveillance is infinitely scalable. China's Social Credit System is a prime, though often oversimplified, example. It integrates data from countless sources—financial records, social media activity, purchase history, and a vast network of facial recognition cameras—to generate a score for each citizen. This score determines access to loans, employment, travel, and education. The psychological effect of such a system is profound. As Jeremy Bentham and Michel Foucault theorized with the panopticon, the mere knowledge that one could be being watched at any time induces self-censorship and conformity. AI makes the panopticon perfect. Citizens become their own wardens, internalizing the state's values not out of genuine belief, but out of fear of algorithmic penalty. This creates a society where dissent is pre-emptively extinguished, not through gulags, but through digital exclusion and social throttling. B. The Manufacture of Consent: AI-Driven Propaganda and Disinformation If surveillance is the stick, AI-powered propaganda is the carrot. The 2016 Brexit referendum and U.S. presidential election provided a glimpse of this power, but the technology has advanced exponentially since. Generative AI can now produce "deepfakes"—hyper-realistic but fabricated video and audio—and millions of unique, persuasive text messages tailored to the psychological profile of every individual. Micro-Targeting: By analyzing a user's data, AI can identify their fears, biases, and aspirations. It can then deliver a bespoke narrative designed to provoke an emotional response, whether it's anger, fear, or tribal loyalty. This fragments public discourse into billions of individual realities, making a shared, fact-based consensus impossible. Synthetic Media and Reality Apathy: The proliferation of deepfakes will lead to a state of "reality apathy" or "the liar's dividend," where the public, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, simply disengages from factual discourse altogether. In this environment, the entity with the most powerful AI can define reality itself, creating a "post-truth" world where power is the ultimate arbiter of truth. This automated, personalized propaganda machine is far more effective than the state-controlled media of the 20th century. It doesn't just broadcast a message; it engages each citizen in a unique, manipulative dialogue, eroding the capacity for critical thought and independent political judgment. C. Predictive Policing and Social Control AI enables a shift from punishing past actions to pre-empting future behavior. "Predictive policing" algorithms, already used in some Western democracies, analyze historical crime data to forecast where crime is likely to occur or who is likely to commit it. In an authoritarian context, this concept is expanded to "predictive dissidence." An algorithm might flag an individual as a "high risk" for subversion based on their online reading habits, social connections, or even physiological data from wearables. This person could then be subject to pre-emptive measures: a visit from the police, restrictions on their movement, or a downgrade of their social credit score. The crime is no longer an act, but a statistically probable future state. This is the ultimate form of social control, targeting thought and potential before it can manifest as action. It creates a system where the only safe path is absolute conformity, effectively destroying the concept of political freedom. IV. The Global Power Impact: AI as a Geopolitical Weapon The concentration of AI power is not merely a domestic issue; it is reshaping the international order. The global competition for AI supremacy is the defining geopolitical race of the 21st century, with the potential to create new superpowers and destroy existing ones. A. The AI Arms Race: Lethal Autonomous Weapons and Cyber Warfare The most immediate danger is the militarization of AI. The development of Lethal Autonomous Weapons (LAWS), or "slaughterbots," represents a fundamental shift in warfare. These are systems that, once activated, can identify, select, and engage targets without further human intervention. Pro-liferation and Instability: LAWS lower the threshold for conflict. They are cheaper than human soldiers and can be deployed in massive swarms. A nation might be tempted to launch a swift, automated attack, believing it can achieve its objectives without risking a full-scale war. This increases the risk of miscalculation and rapid, uncontrollable escalation. The Responsibility Gap: If an autonomous weapon commits a war crime, who is responsible? The programmer, the commander, or the machine itself? This legal and moral vacuum undermines the foundations of international humanitarian law. AI in Cyber Warfare: AI supercharges cyber attacks. It can be used to find vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure (power grids, financial systems, water supplies) at machine speed, launch coordinated disinformation campaigns to destabilize rival nations, and create adaptive malware that can evade traditional defenses. A future conflict may begin not with a declaration of war, but with the silent, AI-driven collapse of a nation's digital backbone. B. The Shift in Economic and Strategic Dominance AI is a core driver of economic productivity and innovation. Nations that lead in AI research and development will likely dominate the industries of the future, from biotechnology to renewable energy. This economic power translates directly into geopolitical influence. The current competition is largely bipolar, between the United States and China. China's strategy, outlined in its "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan," is to become the world's primary AI innovation center by 2030. It combines state-directed investment, massive data collection from its population, and a lack of ethical constraints to achieve rapid progress. The U.S., while leading in fundamental research, is hampered by a fragmented regulatory approach and public concerns over privacy. This competition creates a new "AI divide." A small group of AI superpowers could exert immense influence over the rest of the world, imposing their technological standards and, by extension, their political and ethical values. abstract: Identifying emotions during information processing is crucial for marketers and businesses to generate an effective customer experience. The emotions involved in our collective and sustained dalliance with our own annihilation are messy. At the time of this writing—indeed, in the very act of this writing and thinking through—a feeling of doom is palpable. Dread has become exhilarating as we doomscroll the headlines (Salisbury 2023). Fantasies of victimhood and revenge proliferate and provide cold and complicated comfort to the masses. Whether we are addicted to exaggerations of our own ending, or the smoothness of the algorithmic delivery system, or their particular, potent, and poetic combination, the so-called difference between reason and emotion has shown itself to be rather muddled. Something solid melts into air as we are instructed to think about and “feel our feelings” (Beckner 2023). The difference of secular reason loses its luster as we are willingly and repeatedly trained to value our feelings as legitimate political resources and essential expressions of our (well-) being. Which is to say that in this long century of the self, the politics of agency are of a convoluted piece with the feelings involved.1 New advertising copy is necessary. Sentio ergo cogito ergo sum. In Wild Experiment: Feeling, Science, and Secularism after Darwin (2022), Donovan O. Schaefer leans into these complex loops between affect and politics. Schaefer argues against efforts to immunize reason and learning from emotion and for the transformative politics that might result from recognizing the passions of rational inquiry. Over the course of the book, Schaefer weaves together two major threads: a comparative history of affect within rarefied intellectual circles and the lens that affect theory provides in understanding the epistemic practices of religion and science in this shitshow of a secular age. In its insistence that scientific rationality is ever more than mere computation, Wild Experiment is relevant to a staggering number of conversations across the humanities and social sciences. First and foremost, Schaefer’s is a necessary reminder to be suspicious of those approaches to religion, or anything else for that matter, whose explanatory purchase depends on narrowly defined rational actors and their atomistic sociality. In his refusal to portray belief or practice as merely cognitive phenomena, Schaefer’s monograph is an original critique of rational-choice theories and the politics of objectivity that have long marginalized the material and embodied and sensational. Such theories and related fictions of autonomous human cognition have been disastrous for the planet and its species. They have advertised the promise of heaven and secular flourishing both, even as they undergirded colonial and technocratic aspirations. Their testament to the inalienable right to be buffered has also provided ideological cover for practices of exploitation of workers and extraction of capital. The myth of agentive reason has long given emotional support to those living through the degradations of techno-capitalist advance. Such degradations haunt the pages of Wild Experiment. In a passage startling for its pathos, Schaefer writes of the catastrophic machinery our species has built to rake the planet. This catastrophe—broad-based ecosystem collapse, resource scarcity, mass migration, war isn’t going to be like the swift-but-gentle snuffing out of a candle. It won’t produce redemptive misery—the romantic myth of apocalypse trafficked by chic fatalists across the religio-secular spectrum. It will be a long, exhausting endgame. It will mean mayhem, violence, and starvation for every human alive and for our animal kin. No one wants the pain that climate chaos has already started to distribute around the world—starting with those who are least responsible for it—let alone the even more frightening landscape we are leaving to our descendants. (236–37) Despite evoking, with bracing prose, the prospect of decay, distress, and inevitable decline, Schaefer is committed to tacking toward the necessity (and charismatic potential) of optimism. As Schaefer argues, his book is constructive—a corrective to the hyperbolic (and nihilistic) responses by (mostly humanistic) scholars and citizens alike to the bad news of modernity (the violence, the lies, the failed promises, etc.). For Schaefer, detecting the flaws in human idealizations of their own rationality is but the first step in a reparative project that addresses the role that emotions have (and have not) played in the present environmental crisis and, in particular, the lackluster and often cynical responses it. The urgent task in front of humanists, Schaefer continues, is to learn a thing or two from science, that is, “learning how to move with confidence through a world where certainty is impossible, but resolute action is vital.” For “most scientists,” he writes, “have moved on from positivism and are bustling away in their laboratories, making discoveries and crafting tools to try to heal this planet. And they’re making mistakes—in part because they often borrow concepts, like the reason/emotion binary itself, that are the residue of thousands of years of humanistic conversations. Humanities scholars can help correct those errors” (236). So rather than breathe “the fallout of science wars fought generations ago,” Schaefer claims that “the gamble [] is that taking the role of feeling in thinking seriously will allow us to chart new bridges and build new conversations.” The interdisciplinary bridge is what Schaefer calls “cogency theory” (236–37; 20). For Schaefer, something has been lost in all of this squabble between extremists on different sides of the “science wars.” Indeed, what has been lost is the plot of science itself! Whither the promise of an empirically driven and humanistic science when reality is reduced, before the passions of inquiry may begin, to either the certainty of numbers or the uncertainties conjured by self-defeating deconstructions? In Wild Experiment, Schaefer movingly writes that “Academics, for our part, can reaffirm a commitment to truth as central to scholarship. In many places, this is already happening, with a thoughtful postpositivist approach underwriting interesting research in every department. But disavowing the search for truth altogether is just as dangerous as embracing the naive view of reason as untainted by feeling” (236). There is a jeremiadic tone built into Wild Experiment. From 1660 to 1690, the jeremiad became a common sermonic and literary form in New England amid struggles over land ownership, natural disasters, and the perception of moral deterioration among second- and third-generation Puritans. With a long afterlife in the American grain, the jeremiad was both a political sermon delivered by Puritan clergy and a ritual response to perceived weakening of social cohesion.2 Schaefer, for his part, is grieving the failure of humanists and scientists both to live up to a commitment to face a reality that is many-splendored, present, and orienting. And if a full accounting of reality remains an impossibility or perennialist fantasy, there is still work to be done. For as chaos builds outside the scholar’s study, Schaefer laments the fact that the “feeling/thinking binary still has the power that it does in the humanities (and is also why we’re still spiraling in a bottomless pit of debates about relativism)” (17). Schaefer’s urgency to reaffirm a “commitment to truth” stems from what he sees as the need to repair the damage wrought by social constructivism, paranoid readings, and discursive analysis of power coursing through the institutions and practice of science. We are in trouble, suggests Schaefer, and the last thing that the world needs now is another argument that effectively silos off the best qualities of the humanities from the best in the sciences. The key, moving forward, is the pursuit of knowledge about reality, an approach that is nimble and on the move and resists the pull of naive positivism, the seductions of nihilism, and the false comforts of apathy. At the very end of this passionately argued book, Schaefer hints at the connection between climate denialism, the science wars of the 1990s, and the reactionary critics who still insist that particular sciences and particular scientists are not only out to lunch but, at the end of the day, affecting those around them negatively. He then cites Bruno Latour, approvingly: In a blend of lamentation and caricature, Latour writes that entire Ph.D. programs are still running to make sure that good American kids are learning the hard way that facts are made up, that there is no such thing as natural, unmediated, unbiased access to truth, that we are always prisoners of language, that we always speak from a particular stand-point, and so on, while dangerous extremists are using the very same argument of social construction to destroy hard-won evidence that could save our lives. We can’t just teach our students the impossibility of certainty over and over again. title: Language is a Virus
