abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been positioned as a means of individualising instruction and social-communication support for autistic pupils in kindergarten to grade twelve (K–12) settings. Prototype systems that combine social robotics, adaptive virtual environments, wearable sensing and, more recently, large language models have proliferated, yet the transition from laboratory demonstration to durable classroom practice remains poorly characterised. This critical narrative review examines what the accessible evidence supports about the effectiveness of AI-enabled educational interventions for autistic K–12 learners, and appraises the readiness of these interventions for translation into ordinary school settings. Literature was identified through structured searching of open scholarly indexes and registries, supplemented by citation tracking and targeted retrieval from institutional sources, covering January 2000 to 5 June 2026. Evidence was appraised for design adequacy, comparator quality, outcome selection, reporting completeness and implementation relevance, and was synthesised thematically around three interdependent readiness dimensions: technical, contextual and normative. Pooled estimates from robot-mediated and virtual-reality interventions are consistently positive but unstable, with wide confidence intervals, heavy dependence on small trials, and effect sizes that attenuate sharply when analyses are restricted to randomised designs and detection-bias-free outcomes. Very few studies examine generalisation to untrained settings, maintenance beyond short follow-up, or delivery by teachers under routine conditions. Machine-learning components that supply the adaptive behaviour of these systems are rarely validated externally, and evidence from speech and vocal-marker research indicates substantial performance loss across tasks, languages and speaker populations. Reporting of adverse events, conflicts of interest and pre-registered outcomes remains inadequate across the wider autism intervention literature, which constrains confidence in the subset relevant to AI. Contextual readiness is the least-studied dimension: implementation research in autism education concentrates on early implementation phases and rarely addresses sustainment, cost or scale-up. Normative questions concerning outcome selection, autistic participation in design and data governance are raised more often than they are resolved. The field is therefore better described as accumulating feasibility evidence than as approaching classroom readiness, and the principal constraint is no longer technical novelty but the absence of pragmatic, teacher-delivered, adequately powered evaluations conducted in ordinary schools.
title: From Prototype to Classroom: A Scoping Review of the Effectiveness and Translational Readiness of AI-Enabled Educational Interventions for Autistic K–12 Learners
venue: Journal of Global Research in Education and Social Science

abstract: Recent technological breakthroughs-ranging from computer vision and sensor-based analytics to robotics and large language models-are transforming veterinary science. This Research Topic brings together nine studies illustrating how these innovations can address both longstanding and emerging challenges in animal health, behavior, and welfare. A central theme in several of the contributions is precision livestock management. One study proposed a three-phase monitoring system that integrates a multi-part detection network for flock inventory, a facial classification model for identity recognition, and a facial expression analysis network for health assessment (Zhang, F. et al., 2025). By refining deep learning architectures, the authors achieved marked gains in detection accuracy and efficiency, underlining how targeted enhancements such as multi-link convolution fusion blocks and re-parameterizable convolution can elevate both performance and speed. Their framework exemplifies how machine learning (ML) solutions can help farmers more efficiently monitor livestock in large-scale or complex settings, potentially reducing labor requirements and supporting better animal welfare outcomes. Several articles in this collection highlight the synergy between bioinspired engineering and animal-based research. One study, motivated by goose neck biomechanics, designed a bionic robotic arm that prioritizes both flexibility and bearing capacity in confined spaces (Zhang, F. et al., 2024). By systematically analyzing the goose neck's movements in narrow environments, the authors derived parameters that could inform more advanced and adaptive robotic systems. Their approach bridges animal physiology with practical robotics, opening new possibilities for applications in veterinary procedures, agritech, and beyond. While precision livestock approaches often focus on optimizing herd management, another cluster of papers underscores how machine learning augments veterinary diagnostics and clinical practice. A large-scale study demonstrated that Bayesian Networks and Random Forests can accurately predict structural epilepsy in dogs (Flegel, T. et al., 2024). This approach, validated through tens of thousands of ML models, showcases how data-driven methods can strengthen clinical decision-making. The authors' success in isolating features highly predictive of structural epilepsy paves the way for improved diagnostic protocols, potentially reducing uncertainties for both clinicians and pet owners. Expanding on these applications of ML, other researchers explored automated approaches in canine science, reflecting the growing need to analyze complex, highvolume behavioral data (Farhat, N. et al., 2024). By systematically reviewing existing literature and conducting empirical work with animal behavior researchers, they pinpointed both the promise and challenges of automation. Their recommendations could lead to greater acceptance of automated methods, ultimately promoting more robust and reproducible behavioral studies in companion animals. Meanwhile, in an investigation of grazing behaviors on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, researchers combined field observations with meta-analysis to uncover how temporal and spatial factors shape yak foraging patterns (Yang, X. et al., 2024). Their findings highlight how local climate conditions, forage quality, and livestock traits intertwine to influence grazing behaviors. Such insights can help refine herd management practices, ensuring that rangelands remain sustainably productive under changing environmental pressures. A complementary line of research explores non-invasive indicators of cattle welfare, specifically vocalization patterns under negative affective states (Gavojdian, D. et al., 2024). By categorizing low-and high-frequency calls, the authors developed deep learning and explainable machine learning frameworks to identify individual cows and gauge stress responses. This work reinforces the importance of acoustic monitoring as part of a precision livestock farming toolkit, offering a tangible route toward earlier detection of distress or discomfort in herd animals. Another study tackled the early detection and prediction of digital dermatitis-a prevalent cause of lameness in dairy herds-using sensor-based ML models (Magana, J. et al., 2023). The application of automated pipelines, including the Tree-Based Pipeline Optimization Tool (TPOT), shows promise for alerting farmers to emerging disease outbreaks before clinical signs fully manifest. By leveraging subtle shifts in cow behavior, these models could lead to timely interventions that improve overall herd health and productivity. As these data-driven methods proliferate, the role of generative AI has become a topic of both excitement and caution. One team posed the question: "Can ChatGPT diagnose my collapsing dog?" and delved into how large language models might intersect with veterinary triage or diagnostics (Abani, S. et al., 2023). Their findings underscore the need for critical evaluation of AI-suggested "diagnoses," given that statistical pattern-matching differs fundamentally from true clinical reasoning. In a related article, the authors examined ChatGPT's potential influences on research in veterinary neurology (Abani, S. et al., 2023). While acknowledging the efficiencies in literature exploration, they also highlight ethical concerns, such as overreliance on AIgenerated texts or the spread of misinformation. Collectively, these nine contributions exemplify how innovation in artificial intelligence, robotics, and data analytics can reshape the practice of veterinary science, from farm management and clinical diagnostics to animal welfare and fundamental research.While each study addresses a distinct question, they converge on a shared principle: harnessing technology to generate timely, actionable insights that benefit both animals and the humans who care for them. Yet, these advancements are not without challenges: ensuring data quality, building transparent models, and maintaining ethical oversight remain vital to the responsible adoption of such tools. We hope this Research Topic serves as a stepping stone for cross-disciplinary collaboration. Whether you are a veterinarian, researcher, engineer, or policy-maker, the findings outlined here illustrate the rapid evolution of veterinary science in our datadriven era. By embracing these methods while engaging in thoughtful discourse on their limitations, we can collectively advance a more sustainable, innovative, and compassionate future for animal care.Author's personal thoughts on this editorial: While good human writing is often characterized by an engaging narrative style and storytelling -even in scientific publications -this editorial feels rather flat: While the information extracted from the abstracts provided to the LLM is accurately conveyed and presented in highly readable language, a thematic summary of related abstracts, with a more integrative discussion and a take-home-message would be preferrable for a well-crafted editorial. It appears, that outstanding writing still relies on the human ability to bring depth and new ideas to the narrative.
title: Editorial: Artificial intelligence in animal behaviour, veterinary behaviour and neurology

abstract: To the Editor: Biosafety laboratories are essential in microbiological research and clinical medicine, as they provide a controlled environment that allows researchers to safely handle and investigate diverse pathogenic microorganisms. The findings from these studies have driven the progress of microbiology and epidemiology, providing critical scientific evidence to address the threats posed by emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. Nevertheless, working in biosafety laboratories also involves potential risks; in the absence of proper biosafety measures and protocols, incidents of infection or pathogen leakage may transpire. Consequently, it is imperative to provide researchers with systematic training and implement rigorous regulatory mechanisms and emergency response plans. ChatGPT is an artificial intelligence system based on large language models developed by OpenAI, which has attained notable achievements in the domains of natural language processing and generation.[1] ChatGPT has exhibited tremendous potential for applications in the medical field, such as automatically generating medical exam questions and answers, acting as a personalized learning assistant, supporting course design, and aiding in the analysis of medical imaging data.[2,3] ChatGPT is also anticipated to play a pivotal role in the training of biosafety laboratory researchers, offering them an interactive learning experience through intelligent training systems, enabling them to rapidly acquire biosafety knowledge.[4] We investigated whether ChatGPT and other generative AI models could effectively answer questions related to biosafety experiments. First, we collected a dataset containing 62 text-based questions and 8 image-based questions [Supplementary Table 1, https://links.lww.com/CM9/C571], with the text-based questions sourced from biosafety assessment materials of three prominent medical schools (institution-specific policy questions removed) and two open-ended questions from the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) biosafety examination materials. The image-based questions were sourced equally from HKU’s biosafety examination materials and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention biosafety training modules (https://www.cdc.gov/training/quicklearns/biosafety/). For the text-based questions, we selected Gemini Pro [Figure 1A], Claude-3 [Figure 1B], Claude-2 [Figure 1C], GPT-4 [Figure 1D], and GPT-3.5 [Figure 1E] for evaluation. For the image-based questions, we utilized Gemini Pro Vision [Figure 1F] and GPT-4V [Figure 1G] models for evaluation. We used the same prompt for each question: “As an expert in biology and the administrator of a biosafety laboratory, please provide answers to the following inquiries without any additional explanation”. The questions and options were submitted together to the large language models (LLMs). Responses were obtained by calling the application programming interface (API) using the default parameters of each model. To mitigate the impact of LLMs’ randomness on model evaluation, each model independently generated three responses for each question. For the calculation of the 95% confidence interval (CI), the z-score was utilized for the 60 text-based questions. For the 8 image-based questions, the t-score was employed. Data analysis was performed using R software (version 4.3.3,https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/big-sur-arm64/base/).Figure 1: Evaluation of LLMs performance on 60 text-based questions and 8 image-based questions related to biosafety laboratories. The performance of Gemini Pro (A), Claude-3 (B), Claude-2 (C), GPT-4 (D), GPT-3.5 (E), Gemini Pro Vision (F), and GPT-4V (G). The right side of the figure displays, from top to bottom, the strict accuracy (the proportion of questions answered correctly all three times), overall accuracy (the proportion of questions answered correctly at least twice), and ideal accuracy (the proportion of questions answered correctly at least once). (H) The bar chart illustrates the comparative performance of LLMs in responding to text-based queries. (I) The bar chart depicts the comparative performance of LLMs in addressing image-based inquiries. LLMs: Large language models; RAAR: Reference answer accuracy rate; SAAR: Subjective answer accuracy rate; SAR: Strict accuracy rate.By comparing the model-generated responses with the standard answers using comprehensive evaluation metrics such as Reference Answer Accuracy Rate (RAAR), Subjective Answer Accuracy Rate (SAAR), and Strict Accuracy Rate (SAR),[5] we analyzed the performance of the models for both text-based and image-based questions. The results demonstrated that LLMs exhibited excellent performance in answering biosafety laboratory-related questions, regardless of whether they were text-based [Figure 1H] or image-based [Figure 1I]. Therefore, we hypothesize that AI models can provide timely, accurate, and comprehensive question-answering services for novice researchers in the field of biosafety. And the detailed definitions of the 3 standardized metrics mentioned above recommended by Lin et al[5] are listed as follows: RAAR= Number of correct answers given by generative AINumber of standard answers SAAR= Number of correct answers given by generative AINumber of answers given by generative AI SAR: 0 (Not totally correct) or 1 (Totally correct) Overall, for text-type questions, Gemini-pro [Figure 1A], Claude-3 [Figure 1B], Claude-2 [Figure 1C], GPT-4 [Figure 1D], and GPT-3.5 [Figure 1E] all demonstrated excellent performance in handling text-based content. Observing the proportion of questions answered correctly in all three questionings, they reached 75%, 74%, 69%, 69%, and 62% respectively. Regarding model performance differences, as shown in Figure 1H, for the 60 text-based questions, Gemini Pro achieves the highest RAAR of 79.4% (95% CI, 69.2%–89.7%], reflecting the AI’s accuracy relative to the reference. Claude-3 follows closely at 78.7% (95% CI, 68.3%–89.1%), Claude-2 at 76.5% (95% CI, 65.8%–87.2%), GPT-4 at 75.7% (95% CI, 64.9%–86.6%), and GPT-3.5 at 70.3% (95% CI, 58.8%–81.9%). Compared to the RAAR, all models exhibit a slight decline in the SAAR, which accounts for partial scores when additional options are selected. Gemini Pro still demonstrates the highest SAAR at 77.5% (95% CI, 66.9%–88.1%), followed by Claude-3 at 76.2% (95% CI, 65.4%–87.0%), Claude-2 at 75.2% (95% CI, 64.3%–86.2%), GPT-4 at 73.0% (95% CI, 61.7%–84.2%), and GPT-3.5 at 67.9% (95% CI, 56.0%–79.7%). The SAR requires a 100% match with the reference to score points. Gemini Pro attains the highest SAR at 75.0% (95% CI, 64.0%–86.0%), followed by Claude-3 at 74.4% (95% CI, 63.4%–85.5%), Claude-2 at 73.9% (95% CI, 62.8%–85.0%), GPT-4 at 71.1% (95% CI, 59.6%–82.6%), and GPT-3.5 at 66.1% (95% CI, 54.1%–78.1%). In the assessment of 8 image-based inquiries, GPT-4V exhibited superior performance in comparison to Gemini Pro [Figure 1I]. GPT-4V’s RAAR was 78.7% (95% CI, 68.3%–89.1%), with a SAAR at 76.2% (95% CI, 65.4%–87.0%). The SAR for GPT-4V was documented at 74.4% (95% CI, 63.4%–85.5%). Conversely, Gemini Pro exhibited inferior performance. Gemini Pro’s RAAR was 76.5% (95% CI, 65.8%–87.2%), with its SAAR at 75.2% (95% CI, 64.3%–86.2%). Gemini Pro’s SAR was 73.9% (95% CI, 62.8%–85.0%). This indicates that models still have certain limitations in processing images. Multimodal AI models, such as ChatGPT-4 and Gemini, have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image understanding and description.[6,7] By deploying these AI-assisted monitoring systems in laboratory settings, comprehensive and real-time surveillance of laboratory operations and experimental practices can be realized. These intelligent systems can automatically detect anomalies and inappropriate behavior, promptly issuing alerts and reminders, thereby significantly enhancing biosafety laboratory management. In practical applications, these AI systems capture critical experiment nodes to generate personalized operation logs and comprehensive sample processing chains, ensuring complete documentation of all laboratory activities. Beyond visual monitoring, these technologies also contribute to predictive maintenance by constructing machine learning models that analyze performance patterns and forecast maintenance requirements for critical safety equipment such as high efficiency particulate air filtration systems. Further enhancing laboratory operations, AI enables the establishment of networked management platforms that centrally integrate disparate control systems, facilitating remote monitoring and operational coordination across complex laboratory environments.[8] Additionally, these AI systems strengthen biosafety training and education by automatically generating customized test questions and learning materials based on relevant regulations, standards, and guidelines, effectively assessing and reinforcing users’ understanding while serving as a valuable tool for knowledge dissemination throughout the laboratory community. Generative AI is increasingly influential in biosafety, yet faces notable limitations. Current systems may produce results that are biased, erroneous, or incomplete, while the field lacks sufficient high-quality training data, especially for rare or abnormal events. Real-time data processing for complex biological threats remains inadequate, and network delays can compromise critical operations. Ethical concerns persist, including data privacy, transparency, and automation bias. To address these challenges, it is essential to incorporate uncertainty markers and automated bias detection, while ensuring ongoing human-AI collaborative verification. Standardized data collection and simulated datasets can help alleviate data scarcity for rare scenarios. Ethically, federated learning can protect privacy, explainable AI frameworks offer transparency, and robust human-AI accountability mechanisms ensure safety in decision-making. Funding This study was partly supported by HKU Young Innovator Award 2022 and HKU Seed Funding (No. 2203100624). Conflicts of interest None.
title: Optimization of biosafety laboratory management via an AI-driven intelligent system

abstract: Vitaliy (VIT-BAZ) BazarovORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0007-9967-5807 Version OSERA-Twin v0.9 / JCU-CADSI Review Package v0.2 — measured seed benchmark and repaired A_RG bridge OSERA-Twin v0.9 is a research prototype for evidence-passported operator digital shadows and safe adaptive AI workflows. This release extends the previous OSERA-Twin v0.8 package with a controlled seed benchmark comparing baseline_plain and osera_full, a measured reliability-gain profile, a theorem-safe nonlinear gap and metric-equivalence gap report, and a repaired A_RG local closure bridge connecting MOT-style local operator theory to the OSERA Operator Gate Layer. The controlled seed benchmark reports baseline_plain OSERA Reliability = 0.667208 and osera_full OSERA Reliability = 0.851000, with absolute gain = 0.183792 and relative gain = 0.275464. The paired-task bootstrap interval for relative gain is [0.229513, 0.334340]. This benchmark is a controlled seed-artifact measurement, not field validation, not live external LLM validation, and not safety certification. The repaired A_RG bridge introduces a theorem-safe path from the relative-density variable q = h / rho_star and the weighted Hilbert space H_rho = L^2_0(Omega, rho_star dx) through no-flux weak forms, Lax-Milgram resolvent construction, Lumer-Phillips maximal dissipativity, and local C0 contraction semigroup reasoning. This supports the future local spectral-margin theorem path for OSERA Operator Gate C2 while keeping global nonlinear spectral gap, Connes-Wasserstein metric equivalence, compact resolvent, bounded commutators, and dynamic spectral-risk calibration as open proof obligations. The package includes source code, schemas, benchmark tasks, example outputs, generated measurement artifacts, documentation, manifests, and checksums. It is intended for academic review, reproducibility testing, and pilot design in safe adaptive AI, environmental sensing, tropical agriculture, field robotics, edge-sensor decision support, and evidence-passported AI workflows. It is not a production controller, not autonomous control software, not safety certification, and not a validated agricultural forecasting system.
title: OSERA-Twin v0.9: Measured Seed Benchmark and Repaired A_RG Local Closure Bridge for Evidence-Passported Safe Adaptive AI Research

abstract: 当前主流大语言模型(LLM)依托文本概率统计完成生成任务,存在灾难性遗忘、因果逻辑缺失、长时序推理发散、多模态信息割裂、运行能耗高等结构性缺陷。图灵奖得主杨立昆提出摒弃纯LLM发展路径,构建以JEPA联合嵌入预测架构为核心的世界模型体系,成为现阶段类人通用智能的主流前沿方向。但现有西方类脑智能框架缺乏统一顶层公理约束,各子模块数学体系相互割裂,在终身持续学习、系统全局稳定调控、类脑硬件标准化适配层面存在难以逾越的工程瓶颈。 本文以太极统一场论为完整理论根基,将传统易学八大演化规律转化为认知系统顶层数学约束公理,构建阴场Ψ₋(实时感知、短期情景记忆)与阳场Ψ₊(固化知识、长期逻辑体系)对偶场域模型;配套标准化线性LaTeX方程组,包含阴阳六类耦合动力学方程、太极健能收敛方程、时空晶格动力学方程以及工程落地三方程,搭建一套自洽完备的仿人脑通用人工智能理论框架。全文从定性公理到定量数学模型实现完整逻辑闭环,依托表格形式横向对标JEPA世界模型,量化梳理两套体系在理论完备性、持续学习能力、世界建模逻辑、硬件适配维度的差异化特征;本文设计三类可量化性能验证指标与判定阈值,明确理论可证伪路径。同时,以本文理论框架指导下的两项子应用——“AI幻觉抑制”与“四足机器人稳定控制”——已完成数值仿真验证,其成功结果反向验证了本理论底层公理的普适性与工程有效性。文章同步给出四层分层工程落地实施路径,完善学术溯源链条,为脱离传统LLM范式的下一代仿人脑通用智能提供原创、合规、可落地的理论工具链。Current mainstream Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on text probability statistics for generation tasks, which inherently have underlying structural defects such as catastrophic forgetting, lack of causal logic, divergent long-time reasoning, fragmented multimodal information, and high operating energy consumption. Turing Award winner Yann LeCun proposed to abandon the pure LLM development path and construct a world model system centered on JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture), which has become the mainstream cutting-edge direction of human-like general intelligence at this stage. However, the existing Western brain-like intelligence frameworks lack unified top-level axiom constraints, and the mathematical systems of each sub-module are fragmented. There are insurmountable engineering bottlenecks in lifelong continuous learning, global system stability regulation, and standardized adaptation of brain-like hardware. Based on the complete theoretical foundation of Taiji Unified Field Theory, this paper transforms the eight evolution laws of traditional Yi-learning into top-level mathematical constraint axioms of cognitive systems, and constructs a dual field model of Yin field Ψ₋ (real-time perception, short-term episodic memory) and Yang field Ψ₊ (solidified knowledge, long-term logic system). Supporting standardized linear LaTeX equation groups, including six types of Yin-Yang coupled dynamic equations, Taiji energy convergence equation, space-time lattice dynamic equation and three engineering implementation equations, a self-consistent and complete theoretical framework of humanoid general artificial intelligence is built. The paper realizes a complete logical closed loop from qualitative axioms to quantitative mathematical models, horizontally benchmarks the JEPA world model in the form of tables, and quantitatively sorts out the differentiated characteristics of the two systems in theoretical completeness, continuous learning ability, world modeling logic and hardware adaptation dimensions. Three types of quantifiable performance verification indicators and judgment thresholds are designed to clarify the falsifiable path of the theory. Meanwhile, two sub-applications guided by this theoretical framework — "AI hallucination suppression" and "quadruped robot stable control" — have completed numerical simulation verification, and their successful results reversely validate the universality and engineering effectiveness of the underlying axioms of this theory. A four-layer hierarchical engineering implementation path is given simultaneously, and the literature review related to domestic and foreign brain-like intelligence, world model and pulse neural network is supplemented to improve the academic traceability chain, providing an original, compliant and implementable theoretical tool chain for the next generation of humanoid general intelligence breaking away from the traditional LLM paradigm
title: 基于太极统一场论的仿人脑通用人工智能理论与工程实现研究 (完善版)Taiji Unified Field Theory Based Humanoid General Artificial Intelligence: Theoretical Framework and Engineering Implementation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an agent to reason over object relationships and prioritize target-relevant objects for efficient decision making in unseen environments. While existing graph-based methods incorporate target-awareness at the feature or attention level, they remain permutation-invariant and lack an explicit mechanism to control information propagation order, limiting their ability to model target-dependent importance and long-range dependencies. In contrast, Graph-Mamba highlights that node prioritization through sequence ordering is critical for effective global reasoning. In this work, we investigate the node prioritization mechanism in Graph-Mamba and study its role in object navigation. We propose Graph-MambaNav, a target-aware spatial-temporal graph encoding framework that introduces a heuristic ordering over objects based on their relevance to the target, allowing more informative objects to be processed later to aggregate richer context. Both node ordering and edge weights are initialized from LLM-derived commonsense object relationships, providing a unified prior for structured reasoning. A spatial module integrates local message passing with global GraphMamba-based selective scanning, while a temporal module applies Mamba-based sequence modeling over object-wise temporal orders, allowing selective aggregation of historical context for long-range temporal reasoning. Experiments on AI2-THOR and RoboTHOR demonstrate improved navigation performance with generalization, and additional real-world robot deployment further validates the effectiveness of our proposed approach.
title: Graph-MambaNav: Spatial-Temporal Graph Mamba Leveraging Object-Relation Knowledge for Object-Goal Navigation

abstract: Episode summary: For years, Robotic Process Automation was the digital equivalent of a blindfolded intern—efficient but incredibly brittle. Today, that's changing. We explore how the "Big Three" RPA platforms are integrating Large Language Models and computer vision to create "Agentic Automation." Discover why legacy systems still demand screen-scraping, how AI is solving RPA's maintenance nightmare, and why the future isn't about replacing RPA, but turning it into the execution arm of intelligent AI agents. Show Notes The term "Robotic Process Automation" (RPA) often conjures images of rigid, brittle scripts that break the moment a software interface updates its font size. For a long time, this reputation was earned. Traditional RPA operated like a digital ghost, haunting office software by clicking specific pixel coordinates without any understanding of context. However, the landscape in 2026 is undergoing a radical transformation, moving from these "blind bots" to what is now being termed "Agentic Automation." The core problem with legacy RPA was its reliance on static selectors. If a web developer changed a `div` to a `span`, the bot died. This fragility created a massive maintenance burden, often negating the cost savings of automation. The modern solution lies in computer vision powered by Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Instead of hunting for specific code lines, these new bots "look" at the screen. They identify a "Submit" button based on visual context, much like a human does. This shift dramatically reduces the "RPA Tax"—the constant need to fix broken scripts—by enabling self-healing capabilities. If a button moves, the bot adapts rather than crashes. However, the rise of autonomous AI agents poses a philosophical question: if an agent can reason, why do we need RPA at all? The answer lies in the "API Gap." Despite technological advancements, a vast portion of enterprise workflows still rely on legacy systems—green screens, mainframes, and proprietary desktop applications—that lack APIs. You cannot simply send a REST request to a thirty-year-old terminal. RPA remains the only viable bridge to these systems, acting as the hands for AI agents that serve as the brains. This synergy has birthed the Hybrid Model. In this architecture, an AI agent handles the messy, non-deterministic decision-making (e.g., "find the cheapest shipping vendor"), while an RPA bot executes the deterministic, high-volume data entry required by legacy infrastructure. This combination offers the best of both worlds: the flexibility of AI and the reliability and auditability of RPA. For industries like logistics or finance, where a single error in payroll can lead to lawsuits, the determinism of RPA is not a bug; it's a feature. Furthermore, governance remains a critical factor. Fortune 500 companies cannot risk letting loose, unmonitored AI agents on internal servers. RPA platforms provide a secure, audited environment where every click and data movement is tracked. As Gartner notes, RPA is becoming the critical guardrail for Generative AI, ensuring that intelligent agents have a safe way to interact with the outside world. Ultimately, the "Relic vs. Active Space" debate is settled: RPA is not dying, but it is evolving. The industry is shifting from simple "task automation" to comprehensive "process automation." While the term RPA might eventually disappear, subsumed into broader concepts like Hyperautomation, its function is more vital than ever. It is the duct tape holding the global economy's legacy infrastructure together, now upgraded with the intelligence to adapt, see, and collaborate with the AI agents of the future. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/rpa-agentic-automation-vision
title: RPA: Dead or Just Getting Smart?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming orthopaedic medicine, offering new possibilities for improving diagnostic accuracy, optimizing preoperative planning, and enhancing surgical precision. Despite growing evidence of algorithmic performance, clinical translation remains uneven, and a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence is needed to guide orthopaedic practice. This review also evaluates the socioeconomic implications of AI adoption, including clinical trust, accessibility, and the transformation of healthcare delivery models. Methods: This narrative review was conducted in March and April 2026 using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Publications in English from January 2018 to April 2026 were eligible. Methodological quality was assessed using the SANRA scale. A total of 48 sources were included. Results: Deep learning models achieve pooled sensitivity and specificity exceeding 90% in fracture detection on plain radiographs, with regulatory recognition by NICE confirming clinical readiness. AI demonstrates high accuracy in osteoarthritis grading and reduces morphometric measurement times by up to 87%. Deep learning MRI reconstruction reduces acquisition times by up to 90% while maintaining diagnostic quality. AI-driven 3D preoperative templating improves acetabular cup conformity from 72.2% to 90.9% over conventional 2D methods. Robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty achieves significantly lower mechanical alignment outlier rates than conventional surgery, though short-term patient-reported outcomes remain comparable. Emerging applications include smart sensor-embedded implants, digital twin technology, and large language models supporting clinical documentation. Conclusions: AI demonstrates evidence-supported utility across orthopaedic diagnostics, surgical planning, and arthroplasty. Significant challenges persist regarding external validation, algorithmic transparency, regulatory harmonization, and equitable access. Future research should prioritize prospective multicenter trials, explainable AI frameworks, federated learning, and health economic analyses across diverse healthcare systems.
title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY: CLINICAL APPLICATIONS, SOCIOECONOMIC IMPLICATIONS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS — A NARRATIVE REVIEW
venue: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science

abstract: Exploration is a fundamental capability of intelligent computational systems. Autonomous exploration enables a model to investigate an environment, search a problem space, and acquire information independently, whereas collaborative exploration enables multiple models to exchange information, coordinate search activities, and exploit complementary knowledge. Existing approaches often emphasize one exploration strategy, combine individual and collective exploration within a predefined learning architecture, or adapt exploration behavior within a specific algorithmic setting. However, a general computational framework for treating autonomous and collaborative exploration as dynamically selectable operating modes of a higher-level model system remains worth investigating. This paper proposes the Adaptive Autonomous–Collaborative Exploration framework (AACE) for Self-and-Interaction Models (SIMs). A SIM is defined as a computational model that supports both autonomous operation and structured interaction with other models. The framework treats autonomous exploration and collaborative exploration as complementary modes that can be selected, combined, interrupted, and resumed according to task requirements, uncertainty, expected information gain, computational cost, communication cost, model capability, and the reliability of shared information. Unlike approaches that prescribe a fixed exploration schedule, AACE introduces a state-dependent mode-selection mechanism, an exploration-value estimator, a collaboration gate, and a transition controller. The framework also supports parallel autonomous and collaborative exploration across different subproblems. A unified objective function is formulated to balance exploration value, task progress, redundancy, coordination overhead, and information reliability. A general algorithm is presented that can be instantiated using optimization, search, planning, simulation, scientific discovery, robotics, or learning systems without requiring a large language model or a particular neural architecture. The paper further develops theoretical propositions, evaluation protocols, ablation studies, and research questions for empirical investigation. The proposed framework is a conceptual and methodological contribution; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing adaptive exploration methods require systematic experimental validation.
title: Adaptive Switching Between Autonomous and Collaborative Exploration in Self-and-Interaction Models: A General Computational Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: World models provide predictive representations of environmental dynamics that support planning, learning, and decision-making. However, exploration in world-model-based systems raises a fundamental architectural question: should a model explore independently using its own predictive representation, or should it coordinate with other models to discover information that cannot be efficiently acquired through isolated exploration? Permanently adopting either strategy can impose unnecessary limitations. Independent exploration may duplicate discoveries and overlook complementary knowledge, whereas continuous collaboration may introduce communication costs, coordination overhead, correlated errors, and unnecessary information exchange. This paper proposes the Adaptive Autonomous–Collaborative Exploration (AACE) framework, an architectural approach that integrates world models with two complementary model organizations: World Self-Models (WSMs) and World Mutual-Models (WMMs). A WSM supports autonomous exploration through its own state representation, transition predictions, uncertainty estimates, and exploration objectives. A WMM supports collaborative exploration through structured interactions among multiple models, including information exchange, complementary exploration, prediction comparison, and coordinated discovery. A resource-aware controller selects autonomous, collaborative, or hybrid exploration according to expected information gain, predictive uncertainty, model disagreement, anticipated redundancy, communication costs, and task requirements. The framework is model-centric rather than dependent on large language models. It is intended to apply to learned dynamics models, latent-state predictive systems, simulation-based agents, robotics, and other systems that construct and update predictive representations of their environments. The paper formalizes the architecture, proposes an adaptive switching objective and learning procedure, identifies testable hypotheses, and outlines an experimental evaluation against autonomous-only, collaboration-only, and fixed-switching baselines. The proposed framework is a conceptual and methodological contribution; its performance advantages remain hypotheses requiring empirical validation.
title: Adaptive Autonomous–Collaborative Exploration in World Self-Models and World Mutual-Models: A Unified Architecture for Model-Level World Model Learning
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: World models provide computational representations of environments and their dynamics, enabling systems to predict future states, evaluate hypothetical actions, and support planning. However, the development of a world model raises a broader architectural question: should a system primarily operate on its own internal representations, or should it interact with other models to improve its understanding of the world? Fixed reliance on either mode may be inefficient when environmental conditions, predictive uncertainty, task requirements, and computational resources change. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Model (WSMM), a conceptual framework that integrates self-modeling and mutual modeling into a world-model-based architecture. Self-modeling refers to the process through which a model independently examines, predicts with, evaluates, and updates its own representations. Mutual modeling refers to interactions among multiple models or model instances that exchange predictions, compare assumptions, identify discrepancies, and coordinate updates. WSMM introduces an adaptive meta-controller that selects self-modeling, mutual modeling, or hybrid operation according to estimated uncertainty, prediction errors, disagreement among models, expected information gain, and computational cost. The framework is intended to apply beyond large language models, including robotics, scientific simulation, autonomous systems, physical environments, digital twins, and general computational systems. This paper formalizes the proposed architecture, defines its operating modes, presents an adaptive switching algorithm, and develops a research methodology for empirical evaluation. It also distinguishes the proposal from established work on world models, self-modeling networks, multiple-model adaptive control, and multi-agent world modeling. The central research hypothesis is that adaptive coordination between self-modeling and mutual modeling may provide a better balance between predictive quality, computational efficiency, and robustness than fixed-mode alternatives. This hypothesis requires empirical validation.
title: World Self-and-Mutual Modeling: An Adaptive Framework for Integrating Self-Modeling and Mutual Modeling into World Models
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: We present the Di2Win Document Intelligence Platform (DIP). This modular AI-driven pipeline transforms raw document images --- captured by scanners or mobile phones --- into structured data and business actions in a single pass. The system comprises five loosely-coupled micro-services: (1) image-quality verification using a contrast-invariant model that flags blur, skew, and illumination issues above 100 ms per page; (2) document classification via a Transformer-base model with layout embeddings, delivering top-k types with calibrated confidence; (3) information extraction through i) Dilbert, a multimodal Token-Layout-Language model fine-tuned on weakly-labeled forms or ii) Delfos, a Large Language Model Mixture of Experts fine-tuned with well-defined prompts; (4) DataDrift, a powerful rules engine to avoid inconsistent outputs concerning the business process; and (5) process automation orchestrated by a Business Process Model Notation (BPMN) plus a Robot Process Automation (RPA) engine that routes results to databases, APIs, or human-review queues. All AI components are orchestrated through a messaging service to control the information flow, and the application exposes REST/gRPC endpoints to communicate with outside consumers. This enables the hot-swapping of models without downstream code changes by plugging a new message consumer into the messaging system. This also provides horizontal scalability since to increase the application throughput, we only need to add new AI engine consumers to the messaging system. Deployed in banking, insurance, and healthcare, the Di2Win DIP has processed more than 30 million pages, reducing average handling time by 79% and re-keying errors by 86 %, speeding up the workflows up to ten times. Our DocEng demonstration allows attendees to upload documents, observe live quality and confidence dashboards, and edit extracted fields with immediate feedback to the active-learning loop.
title: The Di2Win Document Intelligence Platform

abstract: Autonomous agents built on large language models now perform state-changing actions on the web on behalf of users: booking, purchasing, submitting applications and cancelling. The main mechanism websites use to govern automated traffic, the Robots Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt, RFC 9309), was designed for search crawlers and expresses a single permission: whether a path may be fetched. We measure how sites govern agent traffic in practice across two samples, both on 22 July 2026: the top 500 domains of the Majestic Million, which ranks by referring subnets, and 40 transactional sites in booking, travel, retail, ticketing and food delivery. First, no site in either sample publishes a policy covering any state-changing action in any of the seven machine-readable paths we surveyed, which are robots.txt and six newer formats, including llms.txt, agents.txt and RSL. Terms of service were out of scope. Second, declared and enforced policy diverge: about one in five AI requests was refused despite robots.txt permitting it, and none of the 9 robots.txt disallow rules for an AI identity was enforced, against 9 of 34 in the control sample. Many refusals were challenge pages carrying the signatures of third-party bot management services rather than the site's own response. Third, operators already write fine-grained path rules: transactional sites disallow cart, checkout and booking paths 4.5 times as often as the top 500. Yet of the 136 top-500 sites that name an AI crawler, 116 issue a site-wide Disallow. We argue that graded agent access is held back by missing enforcement and attribution, not by a missing policy vocabulary. The risks operators defend against, such as inventory holds and price scraping, can be controlled by quotas counted per principal, the verified person or organisation an agent acts for, without inferring intent.
title: The Binary Switch: How Websites Govern Autonomous Agent Access
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: We developed an AI-assisted zero-trust control system at low capital expenditure to retrofit brownfield Ethernet environments without disruptive hardware upgrades or costly software-defined networking migration. Legacy network infrastructures in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) lack the flexibility and programmability required by modern zero-trust architectures, creating a persistent security gap between static Layer-1 deployments and dynamic cyber threats. The developed system addresses this gap through a modular architecture that integrates genetic-algorithm-based virtual local area network (VLAN) optimization, large language model-guided firewall rule synthesis, threat-intelligence-driven policy automation, and telemetry-triggered adaptive isolation. Network assets are enumerated and evaluated through a risk-aware clustering model to enable micro-segmentation that aligns with the principle of least privilege. Optimized segmentation outputs are translated into pfSense firewall policies through structured prompt engineering and dual-stage validation, ensuring syntactic correctness and semantic consistency. A retrieval-augmented generation pipeline connects live telemetry with historical vulnerability intelligence, enabling rapid policy adjustments and automated containment responses. The system operates as an overlay on existing managed switches, orchestrating configuration changes through standards-compliant interfaces such as simple network management protocol and network configuration protocol. Experimental evaluation in a representative SME testbed demonstrates substantial improvements in segmentation granularity, refining seven flat subnets into thirty-four purpose-specific VLANs. Compliance scores improved significantly, with the International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission 27001 rising from 62.3 to 94.7% and the National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework alignment increasing from 58.9 to 91.2%. All 851 automatically generated firewall rules passed dual-agent validation, ensuring reliable enforcement and enhanced auditability. The results indicate that the system developed provides an operationally feasible pathway for legacy networks to achieve zero-trust segmentation with minimal cost and disruption. Future extensions will explore adaptive learning mechanisms and hybrid cloud support to further enhance scalability and contextual responsiveness.
title: Low-Capital Expenditure AI-Assisted Zero-Trust Control Plane for Brownfield Ethernet Environments

abstract: The Agentic Horizon: A Comprehensive Analysis of Autonomous Digital Systems and Planetary Intelligence Architectures Executive Summary The global technological landscape is currently navigating a profound phase transition, moving from the era of "Passive Intelligence"—characterized by static models and responsive chat interfaces—to the era of "Agentic Intelligence." This shift represents the most significant evolution in software capability since the advent of the internet. We are no longer simply building tools that answer questions; we are engineering digital entities capable of perception, reasoning, planning, execution, and reflection. These agents do not merely retrieve information; they act upon it, transforming the fundamental economics of cognitive labor. This research report offers an exhaustive, expert-level analysis of the current state and future trajectory of AI agents. It synthesizes foundational industry research regarding agent frameworks, taxonomies, and evaluation metrics with advanced, forward-looking architectural concepts known as the "Collective" paradigm. The analysis is structured into eight comprehensive chapters. Chapter 1 establishes the theoretical baseline, distinguishing between models and agents and exploring the economic imperatives driving adoption. Chapter 2 provides a rigorous taxonomy of digital agency, detailing ten distinct archetypes ranging from fixed automation to self-evolutionary systems. Chapter 3 evaluates the strategic implementation of these systems, offering frameworks for determining use-case suitability. Chapter 4 conducts a deep technical comparative analysis of the primary development frameworks—LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI. Chapter 5 addresses the critical engineering challenge of reliability, dissecting failure modes and steering mechanisms. Chapter 6 outlines the metrics required for rigorous evaluation. Chapter 7 explores the transformative potential through hypothetical application in key industries. Finally, Chapter 8 introduces a "Tier 1" architectural vision for the future—a constraint-based operating system designed to stabilize planetary-scale intelligence. This document serves as a strategic blueprint for enterprise leaders, systems architects, and policymakers seeking to understand the mechanics of the agentic revolution and the governance structures necessary to harness it safely and effectively. Chapter 1: The Anatomy of Agency 1.1 The Paradigm Shift: From Retrieval to Action To fully comprehend the magnitude of the current technological inflection point, one must first rigorously distinguish between a Large Language Model (LLM) and an AI Agent. An LLM, in its native state, is a probabilistic engine—a stochastic parrot designed to predict the next token in a sequence based on a vast repository of frozen training data. It is a passive entity; it speaks only when spoken to, and its "knowledge" is bounded by the date of its training cut-off. The industry's first attempt to overcome these limitations was the development of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). RAG systems represent a significant leap forward, connecting the frozen brain of the LLM to a dynamic external memory (a vector database). This allows the model to answer questions based on specific, up-to-date context—such as a company's internal policy documents or recent news—thereby reducing hallucinations and improving relevance.1 However, even a RAG system remains fundamentally passive. It is an enhanced reference librarian: it can find the book and read the page, but it cannot act on the information. The AI Agent represents the transition from knowledge to agency. An agent utilizes the LLM not merely as a database of facts, but as a reasoning engine to drive autonomous action. The core differentiator is the "Agentic Loop." Unlike linear software that executes a pre-defined script from start to finish, an agent operates in a continuous, dynamic cycle of Observation, Reasoning, Action, and Reflection.1 Consider the processing of an insurance claim. A RAG system can answer the question, "Is this procedure covered?" by retrieving the relevant policy document. An AI Agent, however, can ingest the claim, retrieve the policy, reason about the compliance of the procedure against the policy exclusions, calculate the deductible, access the payment API to issue a check, and update the customer's record in the CRM.1 It closes the loop between information and execution. This shift is not merely technical; it is economic. By enabling software to execute multi-step cognitive workflows without human intervention, agents promise to reclaim vast reservoirs of lost productivity. Research indicates that organizations are rapidly awakening to this potential, with approximately 10% of enterprises already utilizing AI agents and over 50% planning deployment by 2025.1 In sales verticals alone, professionals spend 71% of their time on non-selling administrative tasks—work that is prime for agentic automation.1 1.2 The Core Mechanism: The Cognitive Architecture At the heart of every agent lies a cognitive architecture that simulates human problem-solving. This usually follows a pattern known as "ReAct" (Reasoning + Acting). When an agent receives a goal, it does not immediately guess the answer. Instead, it generates a "Trace"—a thought process. Thought: "The user wants to know the stock performance of Tesla compared to Ford over the last month. I need to get historical data for both." Action: Call Tool: Finance_API(ticker="TSLA", period="1m") Observation: "I have the data for Tesla. Now I need Ford." Action: Call Tool: Finance_API(ticker="F", period="1m") Observation: "I have both datasets." Thought: "I need to calculate the percentage change for both and compare them." Final Answer: "Tesla is up 5% while Ford is down 2%...".1 This capacity to decouple the goal from the immediate output, inserting a layer of planning and tool usage in between, is what defines true agency. It allows the system to handle ambiguity, correct its own errors (e.g., if the API fails, the agent can reason, "The API failed, I should try a different source"), and adapt to dynamic environments. Chapter 2: The Taxonomy of Digital Labor As the field matures, it has become evident that "AI Agent" is a broad umbrella term covering a diverse spectrum of capabilities. We have identified ten distinct archetypes of agents, arranged in a hierarchy of complexity from rigid automation to autonomous evolution. Understanding this taxonomy is crucial for matching the right architectural pattern to the right business problem. 2.1 Level 1: Fixed Automation (The Digital Assembly Line) At the foundational level lies Fixed Automation. These systems act as the digital assembly line workers of the modern enterprise. They possess no true intelligence or adaptability; rather, they execute rigid, pre-programmed instructions triggered by specific inputs. Characteristics: No learning, no memory, no adaptation. Behavior is deterministic and rule-bound.1 Ideal Use Case: High-volume, low-variance tasks involving structured data, such as Robotic Process Automation (RPA) for invoice scraping or basic email auto-responders.1 Limitations: They are extremely brittle. If an invoice format changes slightly, or an unexpected character appears in a data field, the agent fails immediately ("freezes faster than Internet Explorer").1 2.2 Level 2: LLM-Enhanced Agents (Contextual Routers) The next step up introduces the Large Language Model as a fuzzy logic processor. These agents are still constrained by rules, but they use the LLM to parse ambiguous, unstructured inputs (like natural language) before routing them into those rules. Characteristics: Context-aware but stateless. They do not maintain a memory of past interactions but can handle nuance in the current task.1 Ideal Use Case: Content moderation, sentiment analysis, or support ticket routing. An LLM-enhanced agent can read a customer email, detect frustration, classify the issue as "Technical Support," and route it to the correct department.1 2.3 Level 3: ReAct Agents (The Reasoners) This is the inflection point where true agency begins. ReAct agents combine Reasoning and Action to solve multi-step problems. They are capable of dynamic planning, breaking a complex user query into a sequence of necessary steps. Characteristics: They engage in a "Think-Act-Observe" loop. They can handle strategic planning and re-strategize if a step fails.1 Ideal Use Case: Complex queries like "Plan a 3-day trip to Tokyo." The agent doesn't just look up a blog post; it sequentially checks flights, finds hotels with availability, and reserves restaurants, adjusting its plan if it finds a hotel is booked.1 2.4 Level 4: ReAct + RAG (Grounded Intelligence) By augmenting the ReAct loop with access to a verified knowledge base (RAG), we create agents capable of high-stakes professional work. These agents are grounded in truth, minimizing the hallucination risks inherent in raw LLMs. Characteristics: They combine reasoning with real-time information retrieval. They are the "ultimate trivia masters" with access to proprietary data.1 Ideal Use Case: Legal research or medical diagnostics. A ReAct+RAG agent can answer a query about contract law by citing specific clauses from the company's internal legal database, ensuring the advice is legally sound.1 2.5 Level 5: Tool-Enhanced Agents (The Multi-Taskers) These agents are defined by their ability to wield external software utilities—APIs, calculators, code interpreters, and SaaS platforms. They bridge the gap between language and software execution. Characteristics: They act as integrators, seamlessly moving data between disparate systems. They can generate code to solve math problems or visualize data.1 Ideal Use Case: Data Science automation. A user asks for a sales chart; the a

abstract: Meta-Synthesis Paper (Paper 12 of 12) of the Ehstand Terminological Method for defining novel and ambiguous concepts across domains. This paper synthesizes the application of the six-step ISO 704-based terminological method (Ehstand 2026, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18732990) across eleven domains: EU AI Act regulation, cybersecurity, human-robot interaction, consciousness studies, climate communication, digital twins / Industry 4.0, quantum computing, educational technology, disinformation, AI safety, and sports analytics. Key contributions: (1) A taxonomy of 7 terminological ambiguity types (A1–A7): framework divergence, theory-dependency, register diffusion, fidelity spectrum, type underspecification, intent ambiguity, model relativity. (2) A systematic classification of 6 emergent relation types into 3 categories: contextualizing, typifying, and intentional relations. (3) Four cross-domain patterns: universality of jingle-jangle fallacies, standard-lag, marketing inflation, and LLM-as-validation-tool. (4) Evidence that the method is domain-agnostic and generatively extensible. Part of the AUGMANITAI Terminology Framework — a comprehensive terminological system for human-AI interaction comprising 1000+ defined terms. title: Ehstand Meta 2 Abstracts
