abstract: Language-model inference can delay emergency supervision, but cancellation alone cannot provide an immediate physical response. HERA (Hierarchical Event-driven Reflex Architecture) separates a measurement-driven deterministic local action from language-service scheduling, with biological inspiration limited to temporal separation and local feedback. A fixed 1472-trial campaign evaluated canonical-command scheduling, simulated actuator faults and live integration. Across three workloads, the mean validated-command latency was 0.486-0.512 s with preemption, 1.476-11.101 s with single-lane FIFO and 0.543-0.575 s with two-slot serving. The original detector identified all 544 complete faults but missed all 160 half-strength faults. A separately frozen 560-trial follow-up evaluated a sustained effort-discrepancy warning without changing control. On the same 160 new half-strength trajectories, the original detector again missed every fault, whereas the warning detected all faults with mean delays of 161.0 and 155.5 ms of simulated time in clean and noisy conditions. No false onset occurred in 2400 simulated robot-seconds of new healthy exposure. This addresses conditional detection sensitivity, not improved physical recovery. In the original campaign, local support reduced the mean upright deficit but worsened some paired cases and reduced terminal speed; every physical trial met the fixed-horizon safety criterion. All 96 normal integrated supervisory commands completed 50-step holds and returned to local fallback, and local action persisted under injected transport failure. Because supervision reaffirmed the existing support array, these results establish neither additional LLM physical benefit nor general diagnosis or hardware safety.
title: HERA: Bioinspired Separation of Local Fault Response and Language-Model Scheduling in Simulated Quadruped Control

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded across organic synthesis, from choosing disconnections to predicting products, conditions and yields, and from selecting experiments to controlling automated platforms. Yet performance at one computational layer does not necessarily translate into reliable synthetic practice. This critical narrative review evaluates AI for organic synthesis as an integrated decision stack rather than as a collection of isolated benchmark tasks. Literature published from 1 January 2010 to 10 July 2026 was searched across multidisciplinary, biomedical, engineering and scholarly indexing sources, with seminal earlier work retained when needed for context. The evidence indicates that AI has matured most convincingly in bounded inference problems where large reaction corpora provide close precedents: single-step retrosynthesis, major-product prediction, reaction classification and local optimisation. Multi-step planning has also progressed through combinations of learned policies and graph or tree search. However, benchmark success remains only an imperfect proxy for chemical utility because commonly used datasets over-represent successful reactions, incompletely encode conditions and work-up, contain duplicated or closely related chemistry, and often favour random splits that reward interpolation. Yield and selectivity prediction are particularly sensitive to dataset design and out-of-distribution shifts. Closed-loop optimisation and robotic synthesis provide stronger evidence of practical value because predictions are tested experimentally, but published demonstrations remain narrower in reaction scope, hardware compatibility and scale than the breadth implied by general AI benchmarks. Large language models and tool-using agents improve orchestration and natural-language access, while introducing additional risks of overconfidence, hidden tool failures and poorly calibrated reasoning. The most defensible near-term model is therefore augmented synthesis: machine-generated options, uncertainty-aware prioritisation, structured experimental execution and expert oversight. Progress towards trustworthy autonomy will depend less on marginal benchmark accuracy than on provenance-rich reaction data, realistic prospective evaluation, uncertainty propagation across the full synthesis stack, machine-readable procedures, and explicit validation of route feasibility, robustness, safety and reproducibility.
title: Artificial Intelligence for Organic Synthesis: From Retrosynthetic Planning to Reaction Prediction and Experimental Decision-Making
venue: Book Publisher International (a part of SCIENCEDOMAIN International)

abstract: Introduction: Visual grounding aims to localize target objects in images based on given textual descriptions, with broad applications in fields such as autonomous driving and human-robot interaction. However, existing visual grounding models still face three major challenges: (1) Most prior works employ separate encoders to process images and text independently, which enlarges the semantic gap between visual and textual features; (2) The use of large-language models leads to excessive parameters, making deployment on lightweight devices difficult; (3) Single-level cross-modal attention mechanisms are insufficient for fully capturing interactive information across modalities. Methods: To address these issues, this paper proposes a Task-aware Liquid Cross-modal Network (TLCN), which consists of four key modules: a Feature Extraction Module (FEM), a Liquid Fusion Module (LFM), a Task-aware Cross-modal Refinement Module (TCRM), and a Multilevel Grounding Module (MGM). Specifically, the FEM utilizes textual features to guide the extraction of visual features, thereby reducing the feature gap. The LFM employs Liquid Neural Networks (LNNs) to capture temporal dependencies and significantly reduce model parameters. Furthermore, the TCRM deepens textual representation via a second-level attention mechanism, while designed Conv-Trans Blocks (CTBs) are applied to image data to extract deeper visual features. Additionally, a similarity loss function based on KL divergence is introduced to optimize the cross-modal alignment. Results: The proposed model is extensively evaluated on three widely-used public benchmarks: RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg. Moreover, a specialized text localization task is designed for further evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that the TLCN achieves superior performance across all evaluated datasets and tasks. Discussion: The superior performance of TLCN validates the effectiveness of its structural designs: text-guided visual extraction successfully bridges the semantic gap, the introduction of LNNs effectively reduces parameter counts for lightweight deployment, and the second-level attention with CTBs sufficiently captures deep cross-modal interactions. These findings suggest that TLCN provides a promising, efficient, and lightweight solution for visual grounding and related localization tasks.
title: Task-aware cross-modal refinement and liquid fusion for text-visual grounding

abstract: Human spaceflight is entering a renewed period of expansion beyond low Earth orbit (LEO), with cislunar stations, lunar surface outposts, Mars-transit habitats, and commercial LEO destinations being developed in parallel. These systems will operate under conditions that differ substantially from terrestrial facilities and from current LEO operations: life-support processes must run in tightly coupled loops; power, thermal, and consumable margins are constrained; dust, radiation, and partial gravity affect hardware and crew performance; resupply is limited; and real-time ground support becomes increasingly unavailable with distance from Earth. As a result, future habitats will require artificial intelligence (AI) as a decision-support, monitoring, planning, control, and robotic-assistance layer that can operate within explicit authority and assurance boundaries. This review presents a PRISMA-guided systematic mapping of AI for long-duration space habitat operations. From 259 eligible sources published between 2016 and 2026, we construct a 246-record quantitative evidence-mapping corpus and code each record by habitat category, operational function, AI method family, lifecycle phase, validation environment, NASA Technology Readiness Level (TRL), and ECSS E1--E4 mission-execution autonomy level. The results show rapid but uneven growth. We found that 76% of the quantitative corpus was published in 2020 or later, and the substantive-AI subset spans classical machine learning, symbolic reasoning, constraint-based planning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and large language models. However, most flight heritage remains concentrated in LEO and ISS-related systems, while cislunar, deep-space, planetary-surface, and analog habitat applications remain stronger in concepts, simulations, and demonstrations than in operational deployments. The maturity analysis further shows a gap between high-autonomy concepts and high-TRL habitat-resident learning-enabled systems. We synthesize these findings into a layered conceptual reference architecture, a four-stage human--AI teaming pathway, and a research roadmap for moving from research-grade autonomy toward operationally trustworthy AI for long-duration human spaceflight.
title: Toward AI-Enabled Space Habitats: A Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence for Long-Duration Habitat Operations

abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental dynamics that support prediction, simulation, planning, and decision-making. However, learning within a world model and learning through interactions among multiple world models are often treated as separate design choices. Independent adaptation can preserve model-specific knowledge and reduce communication overhead, whereas collaborative adaptation can facilitate knowledge transfer, error correction, and the identification of shared environmental regularities. Neither mode is universally optimal across all tasks, environments, and stages of learning. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for adaptive learning and collaborative adaptive learning between World Self-Models and World Mutual-Models. The framework distinguishes autonomous model adaptation from inter-model collaborative adaptation and introduces a dynamic switching mechanism that selects between these modes according to predictive uncertainty, model disagreement, learning progress, environmental change, expected collaboration benefit, and coordination cost. Rather than requiring continuous collaboration or permanent isolation, the framework treats learning mode selection as a sequential decision problem. A world model can independently update its internal dynamics, selectively request information from other world models, incorporate externally obtained evidence, or return to autonomous learning when collaboration is unnecessary or counterproductive. The proposed architecture includes model-specific state representations, predictive dynamics, uncertainty estimation, collaborative information exchange, adaptive mode selection, and feedback-based evaluation. A formal objective is developed to balance predictive performance, adaptation speed, robustness, knowledge diversity, and computational efficiency. The paper also proposes implementation procedures, research hypotheses, comparative baselines, evaluation metrics, and ablation studies. The framework is intended for model-based reinforcement learning, embodied agents, robotic systems, and other environments in which multiple predictive world models learn related or interacting dynamics. It does not require large language models as its fundamental computational substrate. The proposed framework is a research design rather than an empirically validated algorithm; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing adaptive multi-agent world-model methods require systematic experimental investigation.
title: Adaptive Learning and Collaborative Adaptive Learning Between World Self-Models and World Mutual-Models: A Dynamic Switching Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Purpose This survey aims to examine the paradigm shift from predictive, assistive artificial intelligence (AI) to agentic AI in healthcare. Agentic AI refers to systems capable of perceiving, reasoning, planning and acting with adaptive autonomy, enabling more proactive and intelligent decision-making within complex healthcare environments. It establishes a clear conceptual foundation, systematically maps key application domains and identifies the governance, ethical and regulatory requirements necessary for the safe, responsible and effective adoption of agentic AI in healthcare systems. Design/methodology/approach A structured review (2017–2025) was conducted across major academic databases using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria focused on autonomy, proactivity, adaptability and explainability. Findings were organized into a taxonomy contrasting passive and agentic AI, with analysis of enabling technologies, including reinforcement learning, multi-agent systems, large language models and digital twins, alongside ethical, safety and regulatory considerations. Findings Agentic AI is evolving from intelligent assistants to autonomous collaborators in diagnostics, treatment planning, surgical robotics, remote monitoring, hospital operations, patient engagement and public health. Benefits include earlier detection, individualized therapies, reduced clinician workload and improved system efficiency. Challenges remain regarding reliability, transparency, bias, privacy, accountability and workflow integration, requiring safeguards such as explainability, human-in-the-loop oversight, auditing and post-deployment monitoring. Research limitations/implications Evidence remains concentrated in pilots and simulations, highlighting the need for large-scale validation, interoperability, adaptive autonomy, fairness-aware learning and resource-efficient deployment. Practical implications The taxonomy provides guidance to developers, academia and regulators on designing and governing agentic AI solutions aligned with clinical standards. Social implications Responsible adoption can expand healthcare access, improve outcomes and reduce inefficiencies, while poor governance risks deepening inequities and eroding trust. Originality/value This work is among the first comprehensive surveys of agentic AI in healthcare. It defines what makes AI agentic, integrates applications with enabling technologies and links them to ethical and governance frameworks, reframing healthcare AI from prediction to action.
title: From prediction to action: a comprehensive survey on agentic AI in healthcare, foundation, application and challenges

abstract: B³D-HPA V3.52 Upgrade Introduction Version 3.52: From Lab Prototype to Production-Ready Photonic Computing Architecture V3.52 represents a major architectural evolution that elevates the B³D-HPA platform from an experimental photonic prototype to a mature, industry-ready volumetric computing framework. This update establishes full engineering closure across physical mechanisms, optical control systems, and high-dimensional instruction orchestration, enabling stable, scalable, and repeatable operation for real-world AGI and LLM workloads. Key architectural advancements include: - All-Cold Dual-Wavelength Pumping A shift to cold-write and cold-erase optical excitation eliminates thermal stress, material damage, and structural drift associated with conventional femtosecond laser processing, enabling sub-micron positional stability and long-term volumetric integrity. - Metastable Non-Excitation Invariance A redefined physical principle for non-volatile yet fully erasable photonic state retention, establishing reliable logic-layer behavior without relying on destructive material modification. - Cross-Hybrid 3D Writing Mechanism A unified writing scheme combining high-throughput area-source full-layer deposition and SLM-based high-precision local refinement. This architecture simultaneously resolves SNR degradation and throughput bottlenecks in traditional 3D optical addressing. - Closed-Loop HDI-IC Orchestration Integration of the High-Dimensional Information Instruction Compiler (HDI-IC) creates an end-to-end control loop connecting high-level AI computational graphs to real-time wavefront modulation, pump control, and photodetector readout. - EDA-Compatible Design Methodology A standardized, parameterized simulation and verification flow compatible with mainstream electronic design automation tools, enabling full digital twin validation of the 3D photonic medium across the entire development cycle. Executive Vision V3.52 breaks through the fundamental limits of silicon-centric computing by delivering a thermally stable, erasable, high-density volumetric photonic processor. By moving beyond material ablation toward precise energy-level locking, the architecture achieves unprecedented stability, parallelism, and energy efficiency for next-generation AGI inference. This release establishes a practical pathway to post-Moore computing, solving the longstanding challenges of high throughput, high precision, and high stability in 3D optical computing. It enables a neutral, blank-silica medium for on-device model injection and true data sovereignty, defining a scalable, low-power foundation for the age of artificial general intelligence. Technical Brief: HDI-OIS (High-dimensional Information Orthogonal Instruction Set) A Universal High-Dimensional Instruction Framework for 3D Photonic Computing and AGI Inference 1. Core Concept HDI-OIS is an architectural framework designed to treat the intrinsic physical dimensions of light—Phase, Polarization, Wavelength, and Spatial Mode—as a unified, orthogonal instruction space. Unlike traditional architectures that rely on serialized binary state transitions, HDI-OIS utilizes the high-dimensional degrees of freedom available in 3D photonic lattices (such as the B³D-HPA architecture) to perform parallel semantic transformations directly within the wave-field. 2. The LLM-Native Architecture HDI-OIS is purposefully engineered to align with the mathematical structure of Large Language Models (LLMs): Direct Vector Mapping: HDI-OIS maps high-dimensional embedding tensors onto coherent wave-fronts. By utilizing Orthogonal Phase Space, complex vector operations are represented as simultaneous physical states, minimizing the need for data decomposition and reducing computational latency to the limits of light propagation. Passive Inference Primitives: The architecture utilizes Optical Phase Interference as a fundamental primitive for relational computations. Within the 3D photonic medium, operations such as "Attention" are realized through the natural convergence and interference of orthogonal signal modes, enabling a transition from active logic-gate switching to passive physical evolution. Spectral-Spatial Concurrency: By leveraging Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) and Spatial Mode Orthogonality, HDI-OIS enables a high-density, concurrent execution environment. Multiple semantic streams can co-exist within the same physical volume without interference, providing a sustainable trajectory for scaling model context and complexity. 3. Theoretical Significance The introduction of HDI-OIS marks a shift in computational theory: from "Calculating Logic" to "Designing Fields." It provides a formal language to describe how information can be encoded, processed, and collapsed within a 3D physical substrate. By aligning the physics of the hardware with the topology of the neural network, HDI-OIS offers a high-efficiency path for the future of AGI inference. Update Highlights for B³D‑HPA v3.51 Core Addendum: Semantic Navigation & Physical Hash Localization 4. Semantic Navigation Sketching & Physical Hash Localization: V3.51 introduces a revolutionary hybrid addressing-routing paradigm that fundamentally bypasses the "computational inversion" bottleneck. Semantic Navigation Sketches: Instead of calculating exhaustive pixel-level phase maps, the SLM Physical Compiler generates high-level "navigation sketches" based on program intent. These sketches define the global potential field and heuristic gradients within the 3D medium. Physical Hash Anchor Localization: These sketches are dynamically bound to the "Physical Hash Anchors" (rare-earth ion clusters) identified via PHAT (Physical Hash Address Table). By locking logical nodes to these unique physical fingerprints, the architecture achieves deterministic logic execution within a disordered medium. The Result: The system effectively performs "semantic-to-physical" mapping. The SLM provides the "intent" (the sketch), the anchors provide the "coordinates," and the A*-Recursive Self-Guiding mechanism provides the "execution" (pathfinding). This ensures that trillions of optical paths collapse into precise logical answers without the need for high-overhead digital pre-simulation.
title: A Continuous-Field Photonic Chip Architecture: 3D In-Memory Computing with Dynamic Weight Modulation via PHAT

abstract: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly transitioning from isolated software tools to enterprise-grade actors embedded in complex socio-technical organizations. Yet no existingframework jointly formalizes their cognitive dynamics, computational architecture, and organizational governance within a single coherent model. This paper presents Unified Agent Dynamics (UAD), a three-layer socio-technical framework that models enterprise AI agents as entities evolving across a CognitiveLayer (LC), a Computational Layer (LP ), and an Organizational Layer (LO). The core technical contribution is a canonical form dynamics equation, dF dt = Gint(F) + Genv(F,E) + Gctrl(F,C), that generalizes classical agent architectures, control systems, and LLM-based orchestration frameworks by making governance an intrinsic component of agent dynamics rather than an external afterthought. Building on this formalization, we derive three governance-specific theoretical properties: (i) a critical governance threshold μc beyond which enforcement intensity destabilizes agent behavior via a Hopf bifurcation; (ii) a stratification property showing that heterogeneous enterprise MAS self-organize into hierarchical layers predictable from the spectral clustering of theinteraction matrix; and (iii) a complexity ceiling Cmax adapt/(λsα) that governance-enforced optimal control cannot exceed—and whose violation is both necessary and sufficient for governance failure. We introduce a five-type enterprise agent taxonomy (Agent as Application, Service, Employee, Physical Twin, Human Twin), a lifecycle finite state machine, and a simulation study with parameter sweeps and topology comparisons that validate the theoretical properties. Explicit falsifiability conditions are stated to distinguish UAD from unfalsifiable conceptual frameworks.
title: Unified Agent Dynamics: A Multi-Layer Socio-Technical Framework for Enterprise AI Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, dynamics, and potential future outcomes, supporting prediction, planning, and decision-making. However, a general architectural question remains: how should a system organize its reasoning process when independent reasoning and collaborative reasoning offer different benefits under changing conditions? Independent reasoning can reduce communication overhead, preserve model autonomy, and enable efficient local inference. Collaborative reasoning can improve coverage, expose disagreements, combine complementary representations, and support the resolution of complex or uncertain situations. Neither mode is universally optimal. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for adaptive reasoning and collaborative reasoning between Self-and-Interaction Models within a World-Model architecture. The framework distinguishes three architectural components: a world model representing environmental dynamics, self-models maintaining internally organized representations and reasoning processes, and interaction models representing relationships, information exchange, and coordination among self-models. A mode-selection mechanism determines whether reasoning should proceed through an individual self-model, through coordinated interaction among multiple models, or through a hybrid process combining both modes. Mode selection is formulated as a sequential decision problem involving expected reasoning quality, uncertainty, computational cost, communication overhead, model disagreement, and the consequences of error. The framework does not assume that the underlying models are large language models, nor does it require a fixed multi-agent implementation. It can be instantiated using symbolic models, probabilistic models, learned dynamics models, model-based control systems, or heterogeneous computational components. This paper defines the architecture, formalizes the switching mechanism, describes a reasoning lifecycle, and develops propositions and an experimental protocol for future validation. Its central hypothesis is that reasoning performance may improve when the system selects its reasoning mode according to task conditions rather than relying permanently on independent reasoning or permanent collaboration. The proposed framework is a conceptual research contribution, and its comparative advantages remain to be established empirically.
title: Adaptive Reasoning and Collaborative Reasoning between Self-and-Interaction Models within a World-Model Architecture: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Mode Switching
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Preliminary Mathematical Research Note (v0.1.0)Author: TerminusAkivili中文标题:Kimi Delta Attention 中的潜在召回脆弱性:条件化动力学分析Can a recurrent memory state contain information about future recall failure that is absent from its current answer? This research note develops a conditional dynamical analysis of latent recall fragility in controlled Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). It specifies the future input law, prediction horizon and terminal failure event; constructs reachable core states with identical current margins and norms but different future failure probabilities; derives exact finite-horizon risk and a geometric criterion for additional state information in an exogenous linear-Gaussian submodel; and computes a norm-constrained intervention preserving the current readout. For independent random updates, augmented-state recursions yield exact first and second moments and one-sided risk bounds. Counterexamples distinguish moment prediction from probability identification and show why temporal dependence cannot be ignored. An explicit sign-error bridge describes what would be needed to connect a local proxy to whole-model failure.The archive contains the full mathematical note, proofs, source references, validation code, original results, and a pre-publication rerun. All supplied assertions passed; the stochastic checks use 200,000 trajectories for each of two initial states. No pretrained language model or LLM benchmark was run. These results concern controlled systems under stated assumptions; naturally occurring mechanisms, calibration and generalization in trained models remain open empirical questions.This version records TerminusAkivili’s specific research formulation, constructions, derivations and reproducible calculations for academic attribution and a citable public disclosure. Established KDA architecture, observability, linear-system and probability tools retain their cited attribution. Please cite this DOI when using or extending these materials.Report and data: CC BY 4.0. Validation code: MIT License. Copyright (C) 2026 TerminusAkivili.
title: Latent Recall Fragility in Kimi Delta Attention: A Conditional Dynamical Analysis
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly visible in digitally mediated environments, raising important questions about how users express emotional reactions to perceived AI presence. While prior research has frequently examined AI acceptance, trust, and behavioral outcomes, less is known about how different forms of AI perception are reflected in large-scale user-generated discourse. This study investigates the relationship between multidimensional AI perception, emotional expression, trust-related discourse, and purchase-related discourse in naturalistic online environments. Methods: A large-scale dataset consisting of 2,326,781 cleaned YouTube comments collected from 8,947 videos and 5,176 channels was analyzed. AI perception was operationalized through six categories: automation perception, robotic communication style, scriptedness, lack of authenticity, perceived artificiality, and uncanny valley perception. The analytical pipeline combined LLM-assisted weak supervision, transformer-based classification, manual validation, sentiment analysis, and statistical association tests to examine emotional expression and discourse patterns across AI perception categories. Results: AI perception was highly prevalent throughout the dataset and was strongly associated with negative emotional expression. Comments containing AI perception cues exhibited substantially higher levels of negative sentiment than comments without such cues. Emotional expression varied meaningfully across AI perception categories, with robotic communication style, lack of authenticity, automation perception, and uncanny valley perception showing the highest levels of negative expression. In contrast, trust-related discourse and purchase-related discourse remained rare across the corpus and displayed only limited differentiation across AI perception conditions. These findings indicate that emotional expression is considerably more visible and differentiated than explicit behavioral discourse in AI-related user comments. Discussion: The findings support a pattern of expressive decoupling, whereby perceived AI presence is strongly reflected in emotional expression while explicit trust-related and purchase-related discourse remains sparse. Rather than indicating actual behavioral outcomes, the results suggest that AI-related perceptions primarily manifest as discursive emotional reactions within AI-saturated digital environments. The study contributes to digital mental health and human-AI interaction research by demonstrating how large-scale user-generated discourse can reveal psychologically meaningful patterns of emotional expression associated with perceived AI presence.
title: Psychological decoupling in responses to AI: emotional reactivity and behavioral discourse in digital environments

abstract: Humanity is witnessing what Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, has termed the “tsunami of intelligence.” The development of large language models (LLMs), led by Anthropic and OpenAI, is based on “scaling laws,” which state that intelligence improves exponentially simply by increasing data and computing resources. Dario Amodei likens this process to a chemical reaction, arguing that when materials (data and computing power) exceed a certain threshold, the ability to think and code “emerges.” This optimistic functionalism, grounded in the empirical fact that AI is already producing results on par with human experts, has fostered a strong trend within academia to treat AI as de facto AGI (Artificial General Intelligence). However, the fundamental and philosophical question of whether these achievements mark the birth of a “complete, autonomous intelligence” or are merely the result of a sophisticated combination of the vast data accumulated by humanity remains unresolved. I argue that the advent of AGI (Artificial General Intelligence), as claimed by Dario Amodei of Anthropic and others, is not the birth of actual autonomous intelligence, but rather an “epistemological illusion” regarding the high-resolution computational outputs generated by “Infinite Scale Knowledge Combination (ISKC: Infinite Scale Knowledge Combination), rather than the birth of true, autonomous intelligence. Furthermore, the AI models currently perceived by the AI industry as the emergence of intelligence will converge not into intelligence, but into AGK (Artificial General Knowledge), which is essentially the ‘final evolved form of a calculator.’ [Please refer to the paper for related details.] In summary, all AI models in the current AI industry—including those from Entropic and OpenAI—are not achieving the emergence of intelligence through the law of scaling. Instead, they are constructing a space for the K-Manifold (Knowledge Manifold) (the geometric form of AGK) (the mechanism that constitutes intelligence). Even if they claim that all their AI models will be continuously updated over the coming years through the law of scale to reach AGI, this would merely represent a further enhanced level of AGK (Artificial General Knowledge): Artificial General Knowledge (a core concept and the antithesis of AGI). Therefore, this is not the emergence of knowledge but rather Epistemic Capitulation (a state in which humans abandon critical thinking), and since it has breached the Epistemic Event Horizon (the critical point beyond which verification becomes impossible), humans will be led to believe that AGI has been achieved. The “theory of intelligence emergence” based on the Law of Scaling, as proposed by Dario Amodei of Entropic, may be a misconception; consequently, current models are not converging toward intelligence but are instead becoming highly advanced AGKs that expand and combine infinitely. At this point, I would like to state this clearly. I am convinced that AGI/ASI will emerge in the not-too-distant future. However, the true civilizational transition to genuine AGI/ASI will not be achieved merely by adhering to the current Law of Scale, but rather through Artificial Synthetic Knowledge (ASK), Physical Grounding, and Biological Synthesis. Crucially, current AI models will serve as the most essential baseline foundation for this impending leap, and pouring capital into drastically densifying the current computing matrix is an essential teleological prerequisite for maturing this technology into a standardized baseline commodity utility layer. Therefore, the global AI industry must aggressively expand and further accelerate macro-scale infrastructure investment and research without hesitation. Ultimately, the birth of the first generation of true AGI and its subsequent rapid expansion into ASI will entail a multi-layered evolutionary framework rooted in bio-physical integration, and this top-level paradigm shift is already underway through the synergistic frameworks of xAI (Grok), Neuralink, and advanced robotics. I look forward to hearing your insightful and diverse perspectives.
title: The Tsunami of Emergence: The Infinite Interpolator
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: PROMETHEUS NEEDS AN OPERATING SYSTEM: Why Jeff Bezos’ $6.2B Vision Requires the CollectiveOS Anti-Scarcity Stack 1. Introduction: The Limits of Promethean Thinking The mythological Prometheus stole fire from the gods to empower humanity, an act of rebellion that catalyzed the dawn of civilization. In late 2025, Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon and Blue Origin, invoked this Titan’s name for his latest and perhaps most ambitious venture: Project Prometheus.1 With an initial funding commitment of $6.2 billion—one of the largest seed rounds in industrial history—and a mandate to revolutionize "heavy industry" through artificial intelligence, Bezos has positioned this initiative as the engine that will finally drive humanity’s industrial base off the surface of the Earth.3 It is a vision of staggering scale, aiming to transform the cosmos into a manufacturing zone so that Earth can be rezoned for "residential and light industry," effectively turning the planet into a protected garden while the machinery of production migrates to the void.5 However, the Promethean myth carries a warning that the project’s architects seem to have overlooked. Prometheus gave humanity the tool (fire), but he did not provide the system to manage it. He provided the energy source but not the governance structure, the environmental safeguards, or the regenerative loops necessary to prevent that fire from consuming its users. Bezos’ Project Prometheus suffers from an identical architectural flaw. It is a masterclass in industrial logic applied to a biological vacuum. It focuses entirely on the "fire"—nuclear propulsion, autonomous manufacturing, robotic assembly, and supply chain optimization—while assuming that the "civilization"—the water cycles, the food systems, the microbial governance, and the ethical guardrails—will largely take care of themselves, or worse, can be imported from Earth via supply chain logistics.6 This assumption is not merely optimistic; it is fatal. The transition from terrestrial industry to off-world habitation is not a linear scaling problem; it is a phase change. On Earth, industry operates within a pre-existing biosphere that provides free air, water filtration, and waste decomposition. In the vacuum of space or the desolation of the lunar surface, none of these services exist. A factory in orbit cannot simply "emit" waste; it must metabolize it. A habitat on the Moon cannot "draw" water; it must molecularly reconstitute it. This white paper posits that the missing "civilization layer" for Project Prometheus has already been architected, governed, and published. In August 2025, months prior to the public unveiling of Bezos’ initiative, the CollectiveOS Anti-Scarcity Stack was released to the world via Zenodo and secured within cryptographic Proof Vaults.7 This stack, encompassing the Aqua Pillar (atmospheric water harvesting), the Food Cube (bio-upcycling), FarmOS (swarm agriculture), and GATA PRIME (algorithmic governance), provides the specific bio-digital operating system required to sustain life and industry in hostile environments.8 By conducting a rigorous gap analysis between the stated goals of Project Prometheus and the capabilities of the CollectiveOS, this report demonstrates that Bezos’ $6.2 billion investment, while necessary, is insufficient. It builds the rocket, but not the world. To succeed, Project Prometheus must integrate the Post-Promethean architecture—specifically the circular biological loops and zero-trust governance frameworks of the CollectiveOS—to transform from a remote industrial outpost into a viable extension of human civilization. 2. The Prometheus Doctrine: Industrial Logic in a Biological Void 2.1 The Infrastructure Emperor and the $6.2 Billion Signal Jeff Bezos does not build products; he builds substrates. His career is a testament to the power of creating the foundational layers upon which other economies function. Amazon was not merely a bookstore; it was the substrate for global digital commerce. Amazon Web Services (AWS) was not merely a server farm; it was the substrate for the modern internet. Blue Origin is not merely a rocket company; it is the substrate for orbital mobility.9 Project Prometheus represents the fourth pillar in this "Infrastructure Emperor" doctrine: the substrate for off-world heavy industry.4 The magnitude of the capital injection—$6.2 billion—signals that this is not an exploratory probe but a foundational stake in the ground.9 In the venture capital ecosystem, such a sum is unprecedented for a seed round, dwarfing the $2 billion raised by competitors like Thinking Machines Lab.3 This capital is being deployed to assemble a "Physical Intelligence" powerhouse, poaching nearly 100 top-tier researchers from OpenAI, DeepMind, Meta, and Google to solve the problems of robotics and industrial automation rather than generative text.9 The strategic intent is explicit and consistent with Bezos’ decades-long rhetoric. He views Earth as a finite system threatened by energy stasis and pollution. His solution is not degrowth, but spatial expansion: moving energy-intensive mining, smelting, and manufacturing to orbit, where solar energy is continuous and pollution does not degrade a biosphere.5 Project Prometheus is the software layer designed to run this hardware vision. It aims to build the "brain" that will control the robotic arms, the smelters, and the transport ships that will construct this orbital industrial complex.6 2.2 The Vik Bajaj Factor: A Biological anomaly? A critical, often overlooked nuance in the Prometheus leadership structure is the appointment of Vik Bajaj as co-CEO.14 Bajaj is not a traditional industrialist or a pure software engineer; he is a physicist and chemist with a profound background in life sciences. As a former executive at Google X (The Moonshot Factory) and the co-founder of Verily (Alphabet’s life sciences arm), Bajaj has spent his career at the intersection of biology, data, and complex systems.3 His presence at the helm of an "industrial AI" company suggests a latent recognition within Prometheus that physics and chemistry are the true bottlenecks of off-world expansion, not just code. Bajaj’s expertise in "scientific computing" and "real-world experimentation" aligns with the project's goal to move beyond text-based Large Language Models (LLMs) toward AI that understands the physical laws of nature.2 However, despite this biological leadership, the public roadmap of Project Prometheus remains stubbornly industrial. It speaks of "aerospace," "automotive," and "manufacturing efficiency".1 It does not speak of "metabolism," "homeostasis," or "ecosystem services." This disconnect—between a biologically-literate CEO and an industrially-focused mandate—creates a strategic tension. It implies that Prometheus wants to be a complex adaptive system but is currently architected as a linear optimization engine. This is exactly the gap that the CollectiveOS is designed to fill. 2.3 The Geopolitics of Orbit: The Tortoise and the Hare To understand the urgency of Project Prometheus, one must contextualize it within the broader "New Space Race." This is not a race between nations, but between arch-architects: Jeff Bezos (Blue Origin/Prometheus) and Elon Musk (SpaceX). Analysts have characterized this dynamic as the "Tortoise and the Hare".17 The Hare (Musk/SpaceX): Driven by an existential urgency to make humanity multi-planetary (Mars), operating with extreme speed, risk tolerance, and vertical integration. SpaceX funds its ambitions through Starlink revenue and operates on a philosophy of "move fast and break things".17 The Tortoise (Bezos/Blue Origin/Prometheus): Driven by a vision of preserving Earth by moving industry off it. Operating under the motto Gradatim Ferociter (Step by Step, Ferociously), Bezos relies on personal wealth and patient, methodical infrastructure building.10 Project Prometheus is the "turbocharger" for the Tortoise. It is an attempt to inject the speed of AI-driven iteration into the methodical pace of Blue Origin’s hardware development. By using AI to simulate, test, and optimize manufacturing processes in silico before cutting metal, Bezos aims to close the gap with SpaceX’s hardware-rich iteration cycles.19 However, while SpaceX focuses on the vehicle (Starship), Prometheus focuses on the destination (the factory). Musk wants to get you there; Bezos wants to give you a job when you arrive. The flaw in both visions is the lack of a habitat. Neither the Starship nor the Orbital Factory contains the inherent biological logic to sustain human life indefinitely without massive, fragile supply chains from Earth. 2.4 The Fatal Gap: Fire Without Water The Prometheus architecture, as publicly outlined, rests on four industrial pillars: Energy Mastery: Nuclear thermal propulsion and high-energy orbital power systems.20 Orbital Industry: Autonomous manufacturing nodes for processing regolith and asteroid materials.21 Lunar Resource Chains: Extraction of lunar ice and metals for ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilization).22 Space Logistics: A unified transport layer for heavy lift.17 This is a blueprint for a mine, a refinery, and a shipyard. abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.
title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration

abstract: Sim-to-real research pursues physics fidelity as a primary objective: simulators are judged by how closely they reproduce real-world contact dynamics. For governance benchmarking of LLM-driven robots, where the simulator demonstrates that an admission/policy/contract/audit pipeline behaves correctly, contact fidelity at object handoffs (grasp, carry, place) becomes a liability: contact-force integration noise injects audit-chain divergence that is structurally unrelated to the governance property under test. We propose bounded-fidelity sim-as-demo-stage, a design pattern that suppresses contact physics within explicitly bracketed handoff envelopes while preserving full dynamics elsewhere. The construction uses MuJoCo's mocap-body primitive driven by a 220-line Python adapter that the governance bridge invokes via structured intents. We formalise audit-chain stability as byte-equality of the hashed event log across replays and identify two structural envelope properties that imply it. Across N=1000 replays per posture, the mocap variant produces one distinct audit-chain hash (1000/1000 byte-identical; Wilson 95% CI [0.997, 1.000]); the contact-force baseline produces 584 distinct hashes (993/1000 diverged; CI [0.987, 0.998]). A timestep sweep (1, 2, 5, 10 ms) shows the divergence is structural, not a tuning artefact: it stays at 0.985 at every timestep. Envelope-edge timing jitter (+/-10 simulation steps, 1,400 replays) produces 0 divergence, and audit chains remain byte-equal across K in {1, 2, 3} sequentially handed-off objects (1,500 replays) with sub-linear per-pick-and-place overhead. The pattern gives benchmark designers audit-chain reproducibility at near-zero engineering cost; we also map where it is harmful (sim-to-real validation, policy training, contact-rich tasks) so it is not mis-deployed.
title: Bounded-Fidelity Sim-as-Demo-Stage: Mocap Handoff for Governance Benchmarks

abstract: World models provide computational representations of environmental states, transitions, and potential outcomes. However, a world model may contain internal inconsistencies, inaccurate state estimates, incorrect transition predictions, or assumptions that no longer correspond to the environment. Diagnosing these problems is therefore essential for maintaining reliable world representations. Existing research has investigated model-based diagnosis, multi-agent fault diagnosis, self-correction, and collaborative reasoning, but these research directions do not, by themselves, establish a unified framework in which self-diagnosis and mutual diagnosis are adaptively selected as complementary operating modes within a world-model architecture. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Models (WSMM) framework, a conceptual architecture that combines world-model-based state representation with a higher-level self-and-mutual modeling principle. WSMM distinguishes two diagnostic modes. In self-diagnosis, an individual world model examines its own state estimates, transition predictions, internal constraints, and accumulated discrepancies. In mutual diagnosis, multiple world models examine one another's predictions, compare their representations, and investigate inconsistencies that cannot be adequately resolved through isolated analysis. A diagnostic controller dynamically selects between these modes according to uncertainty, prediction error, disagreement, diagnostic confidence, task risk, computational cost, and the expected value of additional evidence. The framework formalizes world-state estimation, diagnostic discrepancy, mode selection, cross-model evidence integration, and model updating. It also introduces a distinction between diagnosing the state of the external world and diagnosing the internal reliability of the model representing that world. This distinction is important because an apparent environmental anomaly may originate from a faulty model, incomplete observations, an incorrect transition assumption, or a genuine change in the environment. The proposed framework is independent of any particular model architecture and does not require large language models. It can be implemented using predictive state-space models, robotics models, simulation systems, scientific models, or heterogeneous computational representations. Finally, the paper develops research questions, testable hypotheses, evaluation metrics, baseline comparisons, and a reproducible experimental design. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated; its principal contribution is a formal research direction for adaptive switching between individual and cross-model diagnosis in world-model systems.
title: World Self-and-Mutual Models: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis for World-State Understanding and Model Reliability
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: This article explores the latest advancements in organic synthesis, detailing methodologies that are transforming the discovery of complex molecules for biomedical applications. It begins with foundational strategies, such as retrosynthetic analysis, a logical approach for deconstructing target molecules to plan efficient synthetic routes. The text then delves into modern paradigms like molecular editing, or skeletal editing, which enables precise, atom-level modifications of molecular frameworks, inspired by CRISPR gene editing. A significant focus is placed on late-stage functionalization (LSF), a transformative strategy for directly modifying complex molecules like drug candidates without requiring de novo synthesis, thereby accelerating structure-activity relationship studies. The article emphasizes a shift toward sustainability and efficiency. It covers C-H activation, which bypasses traditional pre-functionalization steps, and green chemistry approaches that utilize metal-free conditions and bio-based solvents to reduce waste and toxicity. Biocatalysis and chemoenzymatic synthesis are highlighted for their ability to combine the selectivity of enzymes with the versatility of chemical synthesis, enabling access to stereochemically complex architectures under mild conditions. Innovative activation methods like photobiocatalysis and light-activated aryne generation are presented as tools for accessing novel reaction pathways. Furthermore, the integration of technology is a central theme. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) platforms for rapid reaction screening, AI-driven algorithms for reaction optimization, and automated synthesis platforms using mobile robots and LLMs are shown to dramatically accelerate the research and development pipeline. The article also discusses the importance of robust evaluation frameworks, including multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA) for assessing the 'greenness' of synthetic routes and validation strategies for new methodologies. Collectively, these advancements provide a powerful toolkit for overcoming challenges in selectivity and yield, enabling more efficient and sustainable synthesis of complex, biologically active compounds. Source: https://www.orgsynthchem.com/posts/innovative-organic-synthesis-methods-for-complex-molecule-discovery-in-drug-development
title: Innovative Organic Synthesis Methods for Complex Molecule Discovery in Drug Development
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: We organize the research needs around three connected challenges: AI-assisted problem formulation and structural representation; scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains; and closed-loop adaptation in dynamic, uncertain, and multi-objective environments. Two requirements cut across all three challenges: structure-aware integration of optimization, learning, and simulation; and operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability. In the latter, information, tasks, and decision authority are allocated among domain experts, operators, AI assistants and agents, optimizers, and simulators according to risk and context (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Industrial optimization begins before a solver is selected. Relevant information is distributed across data systems, engineering documents, regulations, and expert practice. These sources differ in timing, vocabulary, and reliability. Model formulation requires identification of the decisions, objectives, constraints, uncertainties, and couplings that define the operational problem. Translating an agreed description into equations is only one part of that task.Methods for constraint acquisition can infer candidate rules from examples and expert queries (Bessiere et al., 2017), while decision-focused approaches can optimize predictive models for downstream decision quality (Donti et al., 2017;Wilder et al., 2019). Rules inferred from data or text remain provisional until they are checked against actual operations. Each candidate rule requires verification of its provenance, scope, conflicts with other rules, and operational consequences before it enters a decision model. Human skills, decision rights, and handoff responsibilities may themselves be part of the modeled structure, particularly when tasks can move between people and automated components (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents can mediate between informal descriptions and formal optimization models. They can propose formulations, generate solver code, and assign modeling or verification tasks to specialized components (Zhang et al., 2024a;Xiao et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2026). Recent work that combines LLM-based extraction with reusable modeling graphs and expert-defined templates illustrates a more controlled division of responsibility (Li et al., 2026). These outputs remain candidate models. Solver execution can expose coding errors or infeasibility, but it cannot establish semantic completeness or show that an omitted business rule is inconsequential.A traceable modeling loop records how constraints are acquired and classified, who validates them, how uncertainty and problem structure are represented, and when operational change triggers model revision. If the resulting problem is infeasible, the algorithm needs to identify the conflicting assumptions and return either an interpretable relaxation or a safe recovery action. Evaluation then turns on downstream decision performance under missing or changing information; fluent model generation alone is insufficient.The computational burden of large industrial optimization problems arises from both problem size and coordination across resources, organizations, and time scales. Machines, workforce capabilities, energy supply, inventory, and transport capacity are coupled through shared constraints, but their influence on system performance is unequal and state dependent. A disruption can shift the bottleneck from equipment to technicians, spare parts, storage, or transport. Algorithms need representations and sensitivity measures that identify the binding couplings and detect when those relationships change.In distributed scheduling, job-to-factory assignment and within-factory sequencing are interdependent (Naderi and Ruiz, 2010). Across a supply chain, procurement, production, inventory, and delivery decisions are made over different planning horizons. Solving these stages separately can shift costs, delays, or emissions downstream; even under restricted assumptions, integrated production-inventory-delivery models are computationally demanding (Gen et al., 2008;Li et al., 2017). Coordination also involves organizations, human planners, and AI agents that hold different information and decision rights. Recent supply-chain research on agentic AI accordingly treats human-agent roles and organizational constraints as design choices rather than assuming full autonomy (Trifone et al., 2026).Decomposition and mathematical programming can exploit sparsity and explicit constraint structure, while evolutionary algorithms and large-neighborhood search can explore difficult discrete and nonconvex search spaces (Yu and Gen, 2010;Pisinger and Ropke, 2010). A central design question is how to balance global exploration with local improvement. Global moves reallocate orders, capacity, and supply-chain flows; local moves refine sequences, routes, and maintenance schedules. Learned components may select neighborhoods, warm starts, decompositions, or algorithm configurations. Their value depends on preserving global consistency while reducing end-to-end decision time and resource use. A learned policy may improve one subproblem yet render another infeasible when cross-stage constraints are omitted, represented too coarsely, or invalidated by a disruption. Learned guidance also needs to recognize when a fixed decomposition is no longer valid.Multiple objectives introduce an additional tension between computational efficiency and decision effectiveness. Efficiency concerns whether an algorithm returns an answer before the decision deadline. Effectiveness covers feasibility, solution-set quality and diversity, and alignment with decision-maker preferences (Deb et al., 2002;Zhang et al., 2024b). Automated program search can generate heuristics and search rules, including variants for multi-objective optimization (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2025). Their performance remains uncertain when the evaluation function overlooks cross-stage couplings. Evaluation should establish whether local gains persist once supply-chain interactions are accounted for and whether a globally consistent plan can be produced on time.Demand, resource availability, prices, and customer priorities change over different time scales. Parameter uncertainty, observed disruptions, distribution shift, and structural change each call for a different response. Repeatedly running a static optimizer after every event does not by itself create a closed-loop strategy.A closed-loop algorithm links state estimation and prediction to model revision, optimization, execution, and feedback. Robust planning and reactive rescheduling play complementary roles and can be coordinated through rolling-horizon optimization, online learning, dynamic optimization, and calibrated simulation. Full regeneration may improve the objective value but increase schedule nervousness; local repair preserves stability but can lock in a poor global allocation (Vieira et al., 2003;Blackburn et al., 1986). Reinforcement learning can represent delayed consequences, but exploration in industrial systems must respect constraints during training and deployment. A high expected return does not establish acceptable tail risk or recoverability (García and Fernández, 2015;Wachi et al., 2024). Recent dynamic-scheduling work shows how a formal supervisor can restrict reinforcement learning to a safe, non-blocking operating space and support rapid recovery after disruptions (Wang et al., 2026).Digital twins are useful for stress testing only if their models remain valid under the disruptions that drive decisions (Tao et al., 2019). Emerging architectures connect digital twins, multiple agents, online multi-objective optimization, and human-robot collaboration (Huang et al., 2026). These combinations strengthen the case for a closed loop, but they also increase the number of interfaces whose state, latency, and failure modes need monitoring.Priorities assigned to cost, service, sustainability, resilience, and workload may also change during a disruption. Adaptation therefore requires more than repeated static Pareto optimization. The algorithm needs to choose among continuing or repairing the current plan, re-optimizing, updating the model, and escalating the decision to a human decision-maker. Task and decision authority may also need to shift as risk, AI confidence, human workload, and time pressure change. Evaluation needs to report feasibility under distributional and structural shifts, tail-risk and recovery metrics, and operational gains net of excessive plan changes.Hybrid algorithmic architectures are justified only when their components perform distinct, necessary functions, their interfaces can be validated, and the integrated method outperforms a strong but simpler baseline (Fan et al., 2026;Wiberg et al., 2026). Learning can estimate uncertain states or surrogate models and select search controls when equivalent information is unavailable within the operational deadline. Mathematical and constraint programming can enforce explicit feasibility logic and provide bounds. Evolutionary algorithms are useful for discrete, nonconvex, black-box, or preference-sensitive search, whereas simulation represents behavior that is difficult to express analytically.The interfaces between components deserve equal scrutiny because they govern information exchange, uncertainty propagation, and failure detection. A learned initialization may accelerate a solver yet fail under distribution shift. Likewise, a high-fidelity simulation may consume the computation needed for adequate stress testing. Ablation studies need to test both individual contributions and failures at component interfaces under the same operational budget.A learning-based or generative component may propose a formulation or heuristic; a solver, simulator, or explicit checker can then test it. The inclusion of every added component should be justified by a verifiable improvement in decision quality. This division of responsibility is especially important for LLM-based agents, whose ability to orchestrate tools does not remove the need for formal checks and controlled access to operational systems.Operational reliability depends on how an algorithm interacts with enterprise data flows, shop-floor execution systems, and human decision-makers. Stale state information, interface mismatches, human overrides, and execution deviations can all change the optimization problem. Monitoring, rollback, reoptimization, escalation, and revalidation are consequently part of the algorithm lifecycle.The appropriate unit of analysis is the hybrid decision team rather than the AI component in isolation.Its performance depends on how information, tasks, and authority are distributed among operators, managers, AI agents, optimization solvers, and organizational units. Human participants can contribute tacit knowledge and handle exceptions, but poor handoffs or unclear authority can delay responses and obscure accountability. Experimental evidence from AI-assisted production indicates that team organization affects failure recovery through the frequency and quality of communication (Krzywdzinski et al., 2026). Semantic models for dynamic work sharing offer one way to represent changing human and artificial roles, although their contribution must ultimately be tested through team and system outcomes (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Accordingly, evaluation should include communication quality, handoff latency, calibrated reliance, intervention workload, recovery performance, and operational outcomes alongside conventional algorithmic metrics. Explanations need separate scrutiny: in a job-shop scheduling experiment, brief AI rationales increased behavioral reliance without necessarily improving understanding (Saßmannshausen et al., 2026). Trust, reliance, and decision correctness are distinct measures.Claims of improvement require comparison against competitive optimization, learning, and engineering baselines under matched end-to-end resource budgets. Those budgets include data preparation, model development, computation, simulation, and human effort. Experiments need to vary coupling strength, constraint tightness, disruption severity, distribution shift, and decision deadlines rather than instance size alone. Studies should also report prediction quality, optimization quality, and operational value separately. Optimization quality includes feasibility, optimality gap, regret, and Pareto-front approximation quality; operational value includes plan stability, service performance, recovery time, and integration effort.Fluent formulations and executable code do not establish correctness. Grounded in solver functions, LLM interfaces can nevertheless support infeasibility diagnosis, sensitivity analysis, and what-if or why-not queries (Chen et al., 2025). High-consequence decisions still require traceable constraints, validated alternatives, controlled system access, and explicit human authority over rollback and escalation.The three challenges span problem formulation and structural representation, scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains, and closed-loop adaptation. Success depends on a faithful operational model, coordination of coupled decisions within the available time, and revision of those decisions without sacrificing feasibility or stability. Structure-aware integration determines whether the algorithmic components work together; operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability determine whether gains at one stage translate into system-level performance.Prediction accuracy, average reward, isolated benchmark gains, and the addition of another AI component provide incomplete evidence of progress. The stronger standard is better decision quality under realistic constraints, coupling, and change, together with communication and authority arrangements that support timely intervention and recovery. Ultimately, an industrial AI algorithm needs to solve the right problem within the decision deadline and continue to produce feasible, stable, and controllable decisions as operating conditions change.
title: Artificial intelligence algorithms for complex industrial optimization

abstract: The ability to reason has been a salient characteristic of human intelligence, and there is a critical need for verifiable reasoning in AI systems. Main Takeaways * Reasoning has always been seen as a core characteristic of human intelligence. Reasoning is used to derive new information from given base knowledge; this new information is guaranteed correct when sound formal reasoning is used, otherwise it is merely plausible. * AI research has led to a range of automated reasoning techniques. These reasoning techniques have given rise to AI algorithms and systems, including SAT, SMT, and constraints solvers as well as probabilistic graphical models, all of which play a key role in critical real-world applications. * While large pre-trained systems (such as LLMs) have made impressive advancements in their reasoning capabilities, more research is needed to guarantee correctness and depth of the reasoning performed by them; such guarantees are particularly important for autonomously operating AI agents Context & History Reasoning is a core component of human intelligence. From the dawn of humanity, abductive reasoning has been used to predict danger and inductive reasoning made it possible to learn regularities governing the world. Beginning in Ancient Greece, deductive reasoning techniques were developed to draw valid conclusions that follow logically from premises known to be true. The development of reasoning methods with such a priori guarantees was a key factor in the advancement of modern science, mathematics, and engineering; notably, according to philosophers such as Charles Sanders Peirce, the interplay between abduction, deduction, and induction forms the basis of the scientific method and hence all modern science. Attempts to mechanize logical reasoning can be traced back to 13th-century philosopher Ramon Lull and lie at the heart of the concept of computation. Probabilistic reasoning and inference have also profoundly impacted reasoning, often relying on the celebrated theorem by Thomas Bayes on inverse probability that also forms the basis for many machine learning and statistics approaches. Finally, the evaluation of correct (sound) reasoning lies at the heart of most quantitative assessments of human cognition. Not surprisingly, reasoning has been central to the AI enterprise. Indeed, the earliest research in AI – from Logic Theorist onwards [1] – had a strong focus on reasoning [2]. Since the 1960s, AI has also embraced probabilistic reasoning and models, initially for medical diagnosis [3]. Since then, the reasoning tasks addressed in AI research have covered the gamut from planning and temporal reasoning to diagnosis and explanation. While early AI has paid attention to both plausible reasoning (case-based, analogical, qualitative) and sound formal reasoning with guarantees (logical, probabilistic, constraint-based), over the years, the focus has shifted more towards reasoning with formal guarantees. There are good reasons for this when designing AI systems and techniques that compensate for human limitations and weaknesses since reasoning with guarantees is challenging for humans. This has led to practically impactful applications of AI systems such as SAT, SMT, and constraints solvers, including the verification of correctness properties of computer hardware and software, the safety of communications protocols, the design of new proteins, and, more recently, the robustness of neural networks against adversarial attacks. It has also resulted in probabilistic graphical models [4, 5], which are powerful modeling and inference tools that have found their way into numerous applications of reasoning in medicine, robotics, and beyond. Current State & Trends The emergence of the Internet and the associated technology that made it possible to capture the human digital footprint at scale, as well as the leaps in computing power, have made possible novel approaches to learning bottom up from data. Of particular interest are large pre-trained models, such as LLMs, that have shown surprising abilities in plausible reasoning. Unlike the earlier research on reasoning in AI, LLMs have focused on plausible reasoning patterns as they emerge automatically after large-scale training on petabyte corpora. While the results have been quite remarkable so far, the reasoning in this context has been of the “plausible” variety with no guarantees. Meanwhile, sound formal reasoning techniques remain key to important and impactful applications of cuttingedge AI technology for the verification of computer hardware and software, as well as for real-world planning and resource allocation problems. They are also increasingly recognized as a crucial basis for the formal verification of machine learning techniques such as neural networks, e.g., in the context of local robustness against adversarial attacks [6]. Significant research activity takes place in these areas, focusing on improving various types of reasoning algorithms (notably with respect to their computational complexity), leveraging learning within sound formal reasoning, and combining reasoning and learning techniques [7, 8]. Research Challenges Bringing some of the rigorous a priori or post hoc guarantees back into plausible reasoning patterns turbocharged by the pre-trained models has become an active and promising area of research – especially where AI systems need to work autonomously in safety-critical domains. Research on so-called “large reasoning models” as well as on neurosymbolic approaches is addressing these challenges. Furthermore, even though formal reasoning with correctness guarantees is currently considerably less in vogue than the use of generative AI techniques for plausible reasoning, formidable and essential challenges also remain in that area. In this context, the combination of machine learning techniques with formal reasoning techniques holds considerable promise for economically and socially valuable breakthroughs, notably in the area of AI safety and transparency. The questions and challenges we face range from the philosophical: * What exactly is “reasoning”? to the practical: * Can LLM ‘reasoning’ be trusted? and include: What does the future hold for the advancement and role of symbolic reasoning? * To what extent can LLMs or other generative models reproduce or replace symbolic reasoning? * To what degree will symbolic reasoning be necessary or sufficient to overcome the current limitations of LLMs? * How well can AI reasoning, especially LLM ‘reasoning,’ be explained and understood? * How can computers better understand and simulate human reasoning? * What is the role of collaborative reasoning between humans and computers? * How best can LLMs and symbolic reasoning be integrated into “neurosymbolic reasoning”? * Are further breakthroughs, beyond both LLMs and traditional symbolic reasoning, required to achieve AGIlevel reasoning? * What forms of reasoning can best support humans when dealing with various challenges, e.g., in medical, scientific, engineering, and legal domains? Community Opinion The AAAI community appears to strongly agree on the importance of reasoning in AI systems. In our community survey, slightly over 55% of the respondents chose to answer specific questions related to the topic of reasoning. Of these, 79% indicated that the topic of reasoning is relevant to their research (with 44.7% marking it as “very relevant”). Of the properties required for referring to a process as reasoning, 77.5% of the survey participants marked “Knowledge can be incorporated”, 72.5% “Explanations can be provided,” and 56.9% “Involves multiple steps to arrive at a conclusion”. Interestingly, merely 37.4% indicated “Guaranteed correctness of inference results/outcomes”, and only 23.7% that “A formal system and solver is used,” which reflects the recent focus on informal, plausible reasoning, likely in the context of generative AI methods. This suggests that an effort may be warranted to better communicate the importance and success of formal, sound reasoning techniques. Finally, 44.7% of respondents agreed that “Reasoning involves a search process.” There was broad agreement among survey participants that focusing reasoning research in AI on humanlevel reasoning is valuable (41.6%) or even essential (47%); similarly, a focus on domain-specific reasoning abilities was seen by 49.6% of respondents as valuable, and by 42.8% as essential. This clearly reflects the importance attributed to a research focus on reasoning. The community also sees an exciting potential of synergy offered by logical and probabilistic models of reasoning that were developed in AI prior to large pre-trained models. This is clearly reflected in the fact that 76.9% of survey participants marked the integration of learning and reasoning approaches as very important (6 or 7 on a scale of 7); interestingly, the percentage of respondents that considered Explainability and verifiability as very important was similarly high (at 71.7%). Finally, 61.8% of survey participants estimated the minimal percentage of symbolic AI techniques required for reaching human-level reasoning to be at least 50% (with 24.8% estimating it at 75% or more, compared to 38.2% estimating it at 25% or below). What remains unclear is the degree to which AI researchers and practitioners realize that decidedly superhuman levels of reasoning are required for and displayed in the prominent and successful applications of formal AI reasoning techniques for scientific and mathematical discovery and engineering applications, as well as in AI safety. 1.
