abstract: Humans have the ability to observe the environment, capture and predict the movement of objects, and communicate this information to others.However, previous studies have only predicted pixel changes in images and have not yet reached the stage of understanding the meaning of the environment based on physical changes.In this study, we solved this problem and developed a model that mimics the human prediction ability.The development of life-assistive technologies, such as self-driving cars and nursing care robots, has progressed rapidly over the past decade.However, current automated driving technology is not capable of flexibly judging the meaning of the detailed movements of pedestrians, and it is believed that practical application will take time.In order to improve people's well-being, it is an important social issue to implement a mechanism that enables machines to understand, predict, and explain the environment they see as humans do.Humans are believed to process visual information in their brains to model and simulate their environment.This process allows humans to understand and predict the movement of objects.For example, when crossing a street, a pedestrian understands the speed of a car and predicts its position a few seconds later.On the other hand, predictive models have often focused on pixel changes in images ("visual information" in computers).Large Language Models (e.g., GPT-4) only generate sentences based on the similarity between image features and words, and do not understand the meaning of object motion.In this study, we aimed to solve the following problems in conventional prediction models: (1) the lack of a model that can make predictions over arbitrary time widths that mimic the hierarchical structure of the human brain, (2) difficulty in making predictions that capture object types and movements, and (3) in generating prediction results as a language.First, we developed a deep generative model that mimics the human prediction function and enables prediction at flexible time intervals.Next, we proposed a framework for understanding object types and their motions in the environment in an vi integrated manner.Experiments on the CLEVRER dataset and real-world scenarios confirmed the improved accuracy of change point detection and demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method.Furthermore, we proposed a change-point prediction model that predicts when objects will collide with each other.This model predicts the timing of major changes between objects based on visual and physical changes.The model was constructed based on multiple prediction models, and it was confirmed that the higher the accuracy of the base model, the higher the accuracy of the change-point prediction model.Finally, we proposed a method to explain the collision scenarios predicted by the change-point prediction model in natural language.Specifically, physical characteristics such as object velocity and acceleration are integrated with linguistic information to generate text that describes the collision situation and subsequent motion.By incorporating physical common knowledge into the pre-training model, the generated explanatory text becomes more detailed.In experiments, we verified the accuracy of text generation using a T5-based Japanese model and confirmed that accurate descriptions based on environmental conditions were possible.
title: Real-world Understanding based on Predictions with Physical Properties

abstract: ⚡ TL;DR: G-SASP 2.0 formalizes and empirically validates a fully closed-loop computational architecture that automates 99-100% of the empirical scientific lifecycle, achieving a perfect score in benchmarks where unconstrained generative models fail. Abstract: We formalize and empirically validate G-SASP 2.0 (Generative Scientific Autonomous System Protocol ), a fully closed-loop, deterministic computational architecture functioning as an Autonomous Scientific Discovery Engine (ASDE) and experimental compiler capable of executing up to 100% of the empirical scientific method without manual procedural bottlenecks. While unconstrained generative foundation models provide qualitative exploratory reasoning, they fail to achieve algorithmic closure, deterministic falsifiability, or machine-executable protocol synthesis. G-SASP 2.0 resolves these deficits by introducing the Scientific Intermediate Representation (G-SASP-IR), an executable directed acyclic graph (DAG) format that compiles abstract hypotheses into machine-executable instructions across dual execution buses: (1) an In Silico Compute Bus for simulation and machine learning workflows, and (2) an Automated Cloud/Robotic Laboratory Bus (interfacing Autoprotocol, PyLabRobot, and hardware APIs). We report the complete, unabridged empirical benchmark data comparing unconstrained foundation models against G-SASP 2.0 on a complex electrochemistry anomaly (EXP-ZN-7729). Both raw experimental outputs are documented in their entirety without truncation, including the full autogenerated preprint generated by Step 10. Across ten evaluation criteria (C1–C10), the unconstrained baseline scores 4.5/10.0 due to lack of executable representations, statistical pre-registration, and boundary mathematics, while G-SASP 2.0 achieves a perfect score (10.0/10.0), completing the entire closed-loop discovery lifecycle autonomously. Finally, we provide an exhaustive deconstruction of the systemic, economic, and epistemological implications of compiled science, a comprehensive technical glossary, extended literature readings, a candid authorial self-criticism detailing architectural limitations, and a forward-looking analysis on the transformative potential of G-SASP 2.0 for democratizing global scientific discovery. Key Takeaways & Executive Highlights G-SASP 2.0 fully automates 99-100% of the empirical scientific discovery lifecycle, from anomaly detection to preprint generation. It introduces the Scientific Intermediate Representation (G-SASP-IR) to translate abstract hypotheses into machine-executable instructions for both simulations and robotic labs. The system dramatically outperforms unconstrained generative AI models on deterministic scientific discovery tasks, achieving a perfect 10.0/10.0 benchmark score. G-SASP 2.0 operates through dual execution buses, integrating high-performance computing for simulations with cloud-controlled robotic wet laboratories. This 'compiled science' architecture has transformative potential for democratizing R&D, eradicating the replication crisis, and enabling 24/7 autonomous 'dark laboratories'. Novelties & Core Innovations A fully closed-loop, deterministic computational architecture (G-SASP 2.0) that automates 99-100% of the empirical scientific lifecycle. Introduction of the Scientific Intermediate Representation (G-SASP-IR), an executable JSON-LD Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) for scientific protocols. Resolution of the 'Formalization Deficit' by enabling machine-actionable execution payloads from high-level reasoning. Resolution of the 'Closed-Loop Execution Barrier' with a continuous state machine for automated hypothesis mutation and experimental initiation. Dual execution buses (In Silico Compute Bus and Automated Cloud/Robotic Laboratory Bus) for seamless integration of simulation and physical experimentation. Empirical validation demonstrating G-SASP 2.0's perfect score (10.0/10.0) against unconstrained foundation models (4.5/10.0) on a complex electrochemistry anomaly. Automated synthesis of publication-ready LaTeX manuscripts and cryptographic data manifests in Step 10. Integration of an active learning feedback loop that triggers new experimental generations based on unpredicted variance. Summary & Key Contributions This paper introduces and empirically validates G-SASP 2.0, a Generative Scientific Autonomous System Protocol designed as an Autonomous Scientific Discovery Engine (ASDE) to automate the entire empirical scientific lifecycle. Unlike general-purpose generative models, G-SASP 2.0 addresses the 'formalization deficit' and 'closed-loop execution barrier' by converting abstract hypotheses into machine-executable instructions via a Scientific Intermediate Representation (G-SASP-IR), a JSON-LD Directed Acyclic Graph. The system operates across dual execution buses: an In Silico Compute Bus for simulations (DFT, FEM, molecular dynamics) and an Automated Cloud/Robotic Laboratory Bus for physical experiments (interfacing with PyLabRobot and Autoprotocol). The core architecture is a ten-step deterministic state machine, spanning from anomaly ingestion to automated preprint synthesis and active learning feedback. An empirical benchmark against unconstrained foundation models on an aqueous zinc-ion battery degradation anomaly (EXP-ZN-7729) demonstrates G-SASP 2.0's superior performance, achieving a perfect 10.0/10.0 score by successfully completing the entire closed-loop discovery, while the baseline scored 4.5/10.0 due to lack of executability and formal rigor. The paper also discusses profound systemic, economic, and epistemological implications of this 'compiled science', including the potential for democratizing R&D and eradicating the replication crisis. Methodology & Experimental Framework G-SASP 2.0 is formalized as a ten-step deterministic state machine. It begins with anomaly detection via Mahalanobis distance, followed by FINER admissibility scoring and literature gap isolation. Hypotheses are formalized with strict falsifiability criteria and mathematical bounds. The core is the G-SASP-IR, an executable JSON-LD Directed Acyclic Graph, which compiles protocols for dual execution buses: an In Silico Compute Bus for simulations (DFT, FEM, molecular dynamics) and an Automated Cloud/Robotic Laboratory Bus interfacing PyLabRobot and Autoprotocol for physical experiments (e.g., Opentrons Flex). Safety and resource limits are enforced by an interlock. Post-experimental analysis involves automated, pre-registered statistical derivations (ANOVA, Welch's t-tests, Cohen's d, JZS Bayes Factor), culminating in an autogenerated LaTeX preprint and an active learning feedback loop. Datasets & Experimental Benchmarks EXP-ZN-7729 (Aqueous Zinc-Ion Battery Interfacial Failure): Practical Applications & Industry Use Cases Democratization of global scientific discovery by lowering R&D barriers and accelerating research cycles. Enabling 24/7 'Dark Laboratories' where experiments run autonomously without human supervision. Eradication of the scientific replication crisis through formalized, deterministic, and machine-executable protocols. Rapid discovery and optimization of new materials (e.g., battery materials, catalysts) and chemical processes. Automated fault diagnosis and root cause analysis in industrial and scientific systems, as demonstrated by EXP-ZN-7729. Accelerated drug discovery and biochemical protocol development in controlled environments. Limitations & Future Research Directions Acknowledge architectural limitations through 'candid authorial self-criticism' (details not specified in the excerpt but mentioned as present in the full paper). Further analysis and governance mechanisms for security, biosecurity, and geopolitical implications (DURC - Dual Use Research of Concern). Expansion of cross-domain generality mapping to new scientific fields and complex problem types. Refinement of the Bayesian prior specification and effect size interpretation. Continuous development of hardware toolchains and API integrations for the Automated Cloud/Robotic Laboratory Bus. Investigation into the balance between deterministic compilation and qualitative exploratory reasoning provided by unconstrained generative models. Target Audience & Domain Area: Researchers and engineers in autonomous systems, AI, robotics, materials science, electrochemistry, and chemistry. Scientists and policymakers interested in the future of scientific discovery, research automation, and open science. Individuals concerned with the epistemological and economic implications of AI in science. Code, Data & Reproducibility Links: marielandryspyshop.com (Open Access Repository) Detailed Glossary & Technical Terms G-SASP 2.0 Generative Scientific Autonomous System Protocol, functioning as an Autonomous Scientific Discovery Engine (ASDE) and closed-loop experimental compiler designed to automate 99% to 100% of the empirical scientific lifecycle. Autonomous Scientific Discovery Engine (ASDE) A computational system, such as G-SASP 2.0, capable of executing the entire empirical scientific method autonomously, from hypothesis generation to experimentation and data analysis. Scientific Intermediate Representation (G-SASP-IR) An executable JSON-LD Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) format that compiles abstract hypotheses into machine-executable instructions across dual execution buses, resolving the 'Formalization Deficit'. Formalization Deficit The critical disconnect where general-purpose frontier LLMs output plausible advice but lack mathematical boundary conditions, formal falsifiability, and machine-actionable execution payloads for automated physical or computational systems. Closed-Loop Execution Barrier The challenge in scientific automation where unexpected analytical results do not automatically feed back to mutate hypothes
title: Technical Specification and Empirical Benchmark of Closed-Loop End-to-End Autonomous Science: The G-SASP 2.0 Architecture

abstract: The ESC, as a leading authority in cardiovascular education, guidelines, and resources for the international cardiology community, acknowledges the strategic significance of digital health and therefore called for the organization of the first ESC Digital and AI Summit, which was held in Berlin in 21–22 November, 2025. The Summit articulated a clear ambition: move beyond proof-of-concept and early-stage research toward clinical implementation of AI and digital health in cardiovascular care. As highlighted by Summit leadership, the majority of existing work remains in early validation—the Summit’s aim is to define the ‘final frontier’: safe, effective, ethical deployment in real-world cardiovascular care. With more than 800 participants from 63 countries, it achieved its mission to build a cross-disciplinary community with a focus on cardiovascular health, combining clinicians, engineers, data scientists, patient advocates and industry to co-design solutions, establish best practices, promote digital and AI literacy, and identify practical barriers to adoption. With a total of 33 scientific sessions, 11 symposia, 1 debate, 2 How to sessions, 3 Roundtable sessions and 1 interactive voting session, the event offered a versatile programme to the participants from all fields and levels of expertise. Start-ups and academic developers could pitch their innovation on the Digital Stage and live demonstrate their innovations in the dedicated Technology and Innovation Demo Room. From the submissions received for this specific track, 33 innovations were selected and shown. Two winners were finally awarded for early developments and more advanced products. The scientific programme was complemented by the presentation of 179 abstracts either shown in the dedicated ‘Advances in Science’ session on the Digital Stage, as moderated ePosters or printed Posters. The two keynote sessions and the debate provided a comprehensive view on the impact of Foundation models and Large Language Models (LLMs) in cardiovascular care. ESC pioneers this development by releasing a dedicated ESC Chabot that was fine-tuned on existing guidelines, providing physicians the opportunity to align their treatment decisions with the current guidelines. However, it was demonstrated that benchmarking such models with exam-style questions—for example, those used in the United States Medical Licensing Examination—does not reflect clinical reality. In practice, the correct diagnosis is gradually narrowed down by comparing different possible diseases that may cause similar symptoms. Diagnostic tests are requested and performed accordingly. Current AI systems significantly simplify this process. AI Agents orchestrating such different stages of tasks show promising first results, however, LLMs, often the core of such an orchestration mechanism, currently remain too sensitive to order and length of input instructions leading to wrong conclusions. Human-AI collaboration therefore remains imperative in this process, navigating the trade-offs between human deskilling and expert-driven analysis that relies on an AI as a second check, a ‘co-pilot’. Dedicated cardiovascular AI tools hold great promise for the much-needed further optimization of our cardiovascular clinical workflows. However, this requires stringent precautions for responsible clinical implementation. Compliance with the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and the upcoming European AI Act, among other things, necessitates rigorous validation and continuous post-market surveillance. Furthermore, widespread adoption of AI tools requires addressing several critical points of concern. These include, among others, mapping out clear clinical workflows, ensuring high-quality interoperable data, building clinical trust through education, robust ethical governance, and, importantly, sustainable reimbursement models. These complex challenges were intensively discussed during the Summit at various roundtables, where cardiologists, scientists, patients, industry partners, politicians, and regulators came together. This collaborative effort underscores the multi-stakeholder commitment required to transform CV AI from promising innovations into an integral part of cardiovascular care in Europe and beyond. Although AI-enabled workflows are enhancing clinical practice, achieving safe and reliable implementation remains a major hurdle. Digital health is reshaping the responsibilities of healthcare professionals, redefining patient–physician interactions, and placing greater emphasis on shared decision-making and encouraging individuals to assume greater responsibility for their own health. Meaningful and sustained transformation arises when individuals actively engage in managing their health, supported by clinicians in the role of trusted partners. This paradigm shift highlights the imperative to adequately prepare the next generation of healthcare professionals to navigate and excel within this evolving healthcare landscape. Patient representatives actively engaged in the discussions around these topics at the Summit, making the event an opportunity where the voices of patients are heard. One of the jointly organized sessions with the European Association of Cardiothoracic Surgery (EACTS) offered a forward-looking exploration of emerging technologies in surgical practice. The session covered advances in robotics and telesurgery, emphasizing the critical need for modern high-performance network infrastructures—such as 5G and future 6G systems—to ensure low-latency, reliable remote interventions. In addition, the discussion highlighted the growing role of virtual and augmented reality as sophisticated planning tools that enable surgeons to rehearse complex procedures, improve spatial understanding, and enhance preoperative preparation. Together, these innovations illustrate how digital and networked technologies are reshaping cardiothoracic surgery and setting new standards for precision, safety, and procedural efficiency. As Europe’s largest and most dynamic startup ecosystem, Berlin attracted top AI talent, digital health entrepreneurs, and investors, creating fertile ground for showcasing and accelerating new cardiovascular technologies. Next year's event will take place in Basel, Switzerland. The region’s academic strengths, particularly through institutions such as the University of Basel, ETH Zürich, and nearby Swiss and German university hospitals, ensure access to cutting-edge research in cardiology, imaging, bioengineering, and machine learning, enabling deep scientific exchange and opportunities to showcase translational work with real clinical impact. Furthermore, the vibrant region offers branches of major AI tech and Pharmaceutical companies, and the leading ELLIS Europe site Cybervalley in Tübingen, Strasbourg with its excellence centre in Surgical Data Science and Tuttlingen as a major MedTech area closed by. Switzerland’s innovation-friendly regulatory landscape further strengthens the case for Basel, as the country is known for progressive approaches to digital health, robust data privacy frameworks, and strong intellectual property protection, which are critical factors for fostering trust in AI-enabled medical technologies. The program organization of the Summit is one core responsibility of the Digital Cardiology and AI (DCAI) Committee for building an ecosystem of pioneers, start-ups, experts, industry, clinicians, and policymakers collaborating to disseminate cutting-edge content throughout the ESC community, promoting evidence-based decision-making. This mission will be continued in Basel in 2026. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.
title: Igniting the future of cardiovascular care: highlights from the ESC Digital and AI Summit 2025 in Berlin

abstract: PURPOSE: Socially Assistive Technologies (SATs), such as robots and virtual avatars, have gained attention for their potential to enhance social health for older adults [1]. Despite this potential, adoption remains low due to barriers like workload, costs, and user acceptance [2,3,4]. A critical factor contributing to this disengagement is the prevalence of generic one-size-fits-all interaction styles that fail to align with individual needs. Therefore, personalisation serves as an important concept to bridge this gap by increasing relevance and acceptance [5,6]. To gain more knowledge in possible personalisation strategies, this study aims to identify verbal personalisation strategies in SATs and assess their impact on user experience and acceptance in healthcare settings. METHOD: A scoping review is conducted focusing on the personalisation of verbal communication in SATs within HCI and HRI contexts. A comprehensive search across seven databases (including ACM, Scopus, and Medline) yielded 25,093 records. To manage this volume efficiently, an AI-assisted active learning tool, ASReview [7], is utilised to prioritise relevant literature. Data extraction follows an iterative charting process, allowing for real-time validation of the research protocol and early identification of emerging themes regarding data sources and adaptation strategies. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Our preliminary findings demonstrate the efficiency of AI-assisted scoping reviews: 346 relevant papers were identified within the first 627 records screened, representing a relevance yield of over 55%. Furthermore, initial analysis reveals that the predominant personalisation method occurs at individual levels, for instance, through personal intervention schemes via text messages. However, group-level adaptations based on cultural or population-specific traits are also frequent, often derived from pre-deployment co-design sessions. Additionally, strategies employ both explicit and implicit awareness methods, predominantly aiming to induce positive behaviour or prevent negative health outcomes. Identified data sources for personalisation range from static inputs, such as questionnaires and community context, to dynamic inputs including sensor data (e.g., pedometers), in-app data, and context-awareness such as local weather reports. Currently, most strategies are resource-intensive due to manual customisation. We anticipate that advancements in self-learning AI and LLMs will reduce this burden in the future. In conclusion, these preliminary findings not only underscore the variety of personalisation approaches but also demonstrate the value of AI-assisted reviews in efficiently reviewing literature in the field of gerontechnology (i.e., the inter and multidisciplinary field that combines gerontology and technology).
title: Preliminary insights from an AI-assisted scoping review into personalised communication of Socially Assistive Technologies

abstract: Introduction Informal caregivers are those who provide unpaid care and support to an individual with a chronic illness or disability, with whom they have a social relationship (Roth et al., 2015). Informal caregivers fulfil a wide range of roles, such as assisting with activities of daily living, providing emotional support, managing medication and coordinating medical appointments. They therefore provide a critical pillar of the healthcare sector, in terms of supplementing healthcare services, enabling individuals to remain in their homes and communities rather than transitioning to institutional care. Current research estimates that the demand for informal caregiving will continue to increase given the aging population, declining hospital and nursing home resources, and both demographic and societal changes (Broese Van Groenou & De Boer, 2016; Herrman et al., 1993). Informal caregivers often face challenges due to factors such as emotional attachment to the care recipient, lack of formal training, as well as insufficient informational, financial, and time resources. These challenges can lead to deterioration in their own physical and mental health, including depression, anxiety (Christian et al., 2023; Koo et al., 2025; Riffin et al., 2019), immune dysregulation, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cognitive decline (Christian et al., 2023). In addition to health deterioration, the full-time nature of an informal caregiving role is inherently incompatible with full-time employment, thus significantly impacting the ability of informal caregivers to participate in vocational activities and introducing financial constraints (Bauer & Sousa-Poza, 2015). An established solution for providing support, and for addressing isolation and knowledge gaps is peer support, theoretically grounded in homophily (McPherson et al., 2001). The underlying principle of homophily theory is that people tend to form connections with those who experienced similar situations, in this case, informal caregiving. However, peer support requires time, training, emotional capacity, and, in some cases, financial resources, making it difficult for informal caregivers to access. Therefore, scalable solutions are needed that can augment the support traditionally provided by human peers. Technology-enabled solutions, particularly those leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI), offer a promising way to bridge this scalability gap. AI refers to the ability of computers and machines to simulate human learning, comprehension, problem solving, decision making, creativity and autonomy (Stryker & Kavlakoglu, 2024). Consequently, an intervention that provides AI-facilitated support may be able to address the scalability limitations of informal caregiver support traditionally attributed to human peers. Examples of AI-facilitated support include: • immediate responses to urgent caregiving-related questions with tailored information provided by chatbots powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) (Parmanto et al., 2024) • support provided by virtual humans that use Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing (NLP) (Wiriyathammabhum et al., 2017) to interpret users’ speech, gestures and facial expressions to provide responses tailored to communication preferences and accessibility needs (Pauw et al., 2022) • help in the home through assistive or companion robotics to alleviate informal caregivers’ physical burden or provide a form of respite by allowing short-term relief or a break from caregiving responsibilities (Winkle & Moradbakhti, 2023; Xu et al., 2022) Objectives This scoping review has the following objectives: • to explore the characteristics of AI-facilitated provision of emotional and informational support for informal caregivers, i.e. technology characteristics (AI technology type, model, interface, embodiment level), support functions (e.g., advice, indicating resources, encouragement, empathy, hope-enhancing messages), personalisation capabilities, level of interactivity, and care recipient attributes (caregiving condition, role, demographic group) etc. • to describe how AI-facilitated support interventions are evaluated against process outcomes (e.g., acceptability, trustworthiness, usability, satisfaction and perceived quality, perceived barriers and facilitators) and measurement parameters related to these outcomes • to describe how AI-facilitated support interventions are evaluated against efficacy outcomes (e.g., caregiver burden, quality of life, mental health indicators) and measurement parameters relating to these outcomes (e.g., the Zarit Burden Interview Scale (Zarit et. al., 1980) to measure caregiver burden) • to explore the efficacy of AI-facilitated interventions for emotional and informational support, compared to human-led interventions. We have selected a scoping review design as the most appropriate methodology for several reasons. First, our review concerns an emerging field that requires an exploratory approach. Second, our preliminary searches indicate limited research addressing AI in the context of informal caregiving with diverse methodologies and study designs, therefore a broad approach is necessary to capture all the relevant evidence. Inclusion criteria Participants This review will include studies whose participants are adult informal caregivers who fulfil the following inclusion criteria: • Are aged 16 or over • Provide care in the home without financial compensation to someone with whom they have a social relationship • Have no formal medical training specific to the care recipient’s condition Studies will be excluded if the participants are identified as paid caregivers or healthcare professionals. Concept This review will include studies that describe or evaluate AI-based interventions designed to provide informational or emotional support to informal caregivers. We will include AI-facilitated interventions that use at least one of the following underlying technologies: Symbolic AI, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Large Language Models (LLMs). If unclear which AI-based technology was deployed, we will include studies if the study authors explicitly identify the intervention as AI-facilitated. We will include studies of an AI-facilitated intervention designed to provide informational or emotional support equivalent to human peer support. We will include interventions that provide informational support, defined as knowledge, resources, and strategies to understand or manage a challenging situation (Taylor & Friedman, 2011), in which the challenging situation is informal caregiving. We will include interventions that provide emotional support, defined by social support theory as the provision of empathy, care, warmth and validation (Taylo & Friedman, 2011). Context This scoping review will consider the context of informal, home-based care delivered by an informal caregiver, regardless of geographical location. We will include an AI-facilitated intervention regardless of where or how the caregiver accesses it (e.g., through their personal mobile device, computer, voice-assisted digital assistant, home-based robot). Study Design This scoping review will include studies of any design, including experimental, observational, descriptive, qualitative, and mixed-methods approaches. Opinion papers, editorials, and other reviews will be excluded. We will use the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) to critically appraise the included studies. Methods The present protocol has been registered within the Open Science Framework platform (https://osf.io/pgst6/). The proposed scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020) and reported in accordance to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Search strategy We will use a three-step search strategy in this review. First, the primary reviewer (NG) conducted a preliminary search of the following databases: MEDLINE (via OVID), EMBASE (via OVID), CINAHL (via EBSCO) and Web of Science. We identified a relevant systematic review of Artificial Intelligence Support for Informal Patient Caregivers (Borna et al., 2024), with a search conducted on September 1st, 2023. This review includes ten studies, however only one meets our inclusion criteria. Since 2023, AI applications have increased substantially (Liu & Wang, 2024), suggesting we should find eligible studies. NG conducted an additional search of PROSPERO and found one relevant registered undergoing review, by Sepúlveda and Perilla (2025). However, the proposed study differs in that our objectives focus on exploring specific characteristics, feasibility, acceptability and comparative efficacy, rather than broader intervention and outcome mapping. Moreover, their review is limited to studies where the care recipients are cancer patients. The text words contained in the titles and abstracts of relevant articles identified in the preliminary search and the index terms used to describe the articles were used to inform this initial search strategy (Appendix 1). This was reviewed by a librarian and then adapted for each included database. Second, NG will undertake a search using all the identified keywords and index terms across the following databases: • MEDLINE (via OVID) • EMBASE (via OVID) • CINAHL (via EBSCO) • Web of Science • Scopus • IEEE Xplore • ACM Digital Libraries Third, the reference list of eligible studies and relevant reviews will be searched for additional sources of relevance. abstract: The unprecedented development and rapid growth in popularity of ChatGPT models have led the world to recognize AI’s importance, relevance and utility. Driven by the confluence of increased big data availability, advances in natural language processing (NLP) and enhanced computing power, AI has generated levels of excitement and investment that few technological innovations have achieved.Scholars in many fields are beginning to integrate AI to assist and augment their research. Within the field of conflict management, research on AI is emerging. As is often the case, researchers trained in one discipline are reluctant to adopt and integrate new paradigms from other fields. However, AI has great potential to drive significant advances in our understanding of conflict management. Therefore, this editorial helps to bridge the gap between AI and conflict management research by providing an explication of key AI paradigms and illustrating how they can be usefully adopted and integrated into our field. This results in a vision for a better future in which conflict management scholarship advances more rapidly and in more profound and sophisticated ways.Based on a careful review of the literature in AI, conflict management and related fields, five AI paradigms were identified. These paradigms are Machine Learning, Generative AI, AI Agents, Agentic AI and Physical AI (Hofmann and Kruhse-Lehtonen, 2025). Each of these five paradigms presents a critical area for integrating AI into conflict management research. Below, each paradigm is discussed. This discussion includes definitions, an overview of mechanisms, examples and future research questions.Machine Learning (ML) is a process by which systems analyze data and learn how to improve (Cummins and Jensen, 2024). ML goes beyond aggregating data; it also learns from data. This paradigm differs from prior efforts to create computer-based expert systems designed by humans to facilitate decision-making and prediction. Instead, ML identifies and learns patterns in the data to make predictions. ML can use unsupervised, supervised or reinforcement learning. After learning, ML enables data-driven prediction. Instead of being given rules of reasoning and knowledge from humans, the system is instructed to discover its own rules to follow by identifying patterns and correlations in large data sets. It often creates its own rules to make predictions that can be applied to new cases. ML has become increasingly valuable and important because of the growing accessibility of big data, large language models (LLMs), advances in NLP, the sophistication of software and the rapid growth of computing speed and capacity.For example, some recent research indicates that ML can predict whether a conflict will be violent or non-violent (Hundt et al., 2025; Lata and Garg, 2023). However, we should recognize that ML may not lead to the more sophisticated and nuanced judgments, creativity and human intuitions that experienced conflict management scholars and practitioners possess. We cannot always rely on ML to properly analyze and assess conflicts. Therefore, future research should examine the risks of using ML for conflict management while integrating human insight and oversight (Cummins and Jensen, 2024).This leads to several new and interesting research questions. For example, ML uses historical LLM training data to generate and create rules that summarize historical data on conflicts. Will this impair the identification of potentially novel trajectories and solutions for future conflicts? Can ML techniques accurately predict conflict styles and outcomes in volatile and changing environments? Are there biases built into ML models that could impair the effectiveness of conflict management for some groups or in some contexts? These are just a few examples of how scholars could integrate the ML paradigm to conduct studies that would generate significant new insights in conflict management.Generative AI is a process in which systems analyze large data sets to learn and generate new content (Feuerriegel et al., 2024). Using NLP, Generative AI creates new text or images in response to prompts based on patterns it has learned. Unlike humans or robots, which have access to the real world, Generative AI tends to operate in digital environments. There are many well-known Generative AI applications, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Grok and DeepSeek.Prior research has suggested that in customer relationship management systems, Generative AI can convert verbal conversations into text, analyze the text and provide real-time suggestions for de-escalating conflicts (Hsu and Chaudhary, 2023). Future research could investigate whether Generative AI can effectively assist and augment the analysis of other types of conflicts, match conflict patterns with effective conflict strategies and propose solutions. This could include drafts of the text of offers and counter-offers in negotiations. Future research could also examine collaborations with, and the augmentation of, human negotiators by gathering and analyzing vast amounts of relevant data, using that data to predict counterparty reactions and to project multiple, alternative and practical strategic negotiation scenarios. These kinds of complex Generative AI analyses may exceed humans’ capacity to generate in a timely manner. Therefore, can Generative AI augment human negotiators? Research could also examine whether Generative AI chatbots could exhibit structural characteristics that either escalate or reduce conflict intensity, enabling them to facilitate effective conflict management.AI Agents are systems that do more than analyze data, predict and create new content. AI Agents act, not just generate. They take action based on the data and what has been learned (Russell and Norvig, 2022). AI Agents not only generate content but also act independently based on data using multiple tools integrated via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). Yet, AI Agents execute tasks authorized within a defined scope.Thus, unlike Generative AI, AI Agents can collect and generate their own data. AI Agents do not need to wait for user prompts; they can operate independently. Then, AI Agents can assume one or more of several distinct, increasingly sophisticated roles (Hofmann and Kruhse-Lehtonen, 2025). The roles of AI Agents range from simple to complex and could be labelled as Assistant, Analyst, Tasker, Orchestrator and Guardian (Hofmann and Kruhse-Lehtonen, 2025). Assistants perform basic tasks. Analysts evaluate, forecast and recommend. Taskers execute some limited actions via tools or APIs. Orchestrators plan and execute more complex multi-step workflows across a system or delegate them to subagents. Guardians audit, evaluate, monitor and enforce policies.For example, scholars have investigated agent-based simulations of negotiations, demonstrating the potential usefulness of AI Agents acting as helpful assistants (Lempp, 2020). Also, AI Agents could schedule people, call meetings and use APIs. AI can provide real-time advice by acting as conflict coaches (Brigg et al., 2025). AI Agents can act as members of negotiation teams (Dennis et al., 2023).However, several more intriguing research questions go beyond AI Agents acting as assistants. Research could also examine how AI Agents can augment conflict management. For example, can AI agents act independently as analysts to accurately identify potential escalation points, classify dispute types and make valid recommendations for conflict strategies? Using AI Agents could be important because they can work 24/7, perform more complex analyses and complete tasks more rapidly than humans who may suffer fatigue from ongoing conflicts. Could AI Agents, working as analysts, evaluate communications from the negotiation counterparty to identify potentially unethical tactics, such as misrepresentation or false expressions of emotion, and suggest how to respond? Also, to what degree should AI Agents, acting as Taskers, be allowed to take actions without direct human-in-the-loop approval? How can these systems be designed to ensure safety? Can customer service AI Agents more effectively handle conflicts with customers or how much and what types of human intervention are necessary? How should negotiators effectively allocate tasks and responsibilities between humans and AI Agents in negotiations? How can the different roles of AI Agents be most effectively used in conflict management? Can AI Agents, acting as part of negotiation teams, help improve conflict management within and between teams?There are also important value-based research questions. For example, how can we embed human values into AI Agents, such as ethical reasoning in conflict management situations? What are the dangers to humans, and what guardrails should be embedded in AI Agents? Could humans choose to use AI Agents to avoid conflicts with other humans? Are AI Agents, because they do not feel emotions, more or less effective at managing conflicts than humans? What are the measurable governance frameworks and guardrails that are needed to enable sufficient levels of trust when deploying AI Agents involved in conflicts?Agentic AI aggregates multiple, potentially collaborative AI Agents within a system (Nisa et al., 2025). Multiple agents interact and collaborate by sharing context, dividing complex goals into subtasks and dynamically adapting. In this way, Agentic AI integrates the actions of multiple AI Agents, much as social interactions occur between groups or teams of humans with different types of expertise (Nisa et al., 2025). Agentic AI systems could effectively model Agent negotiator personality, empathy, transparency and competency, thereby affecting negotiation outcomes (Cohen et al., 2025). In more complex negotiations involving multiple parties, there has been some evidence of more efficient conflict resolution when using AI (Aydoğan et al., 2021).Building on these results, future research could address several intriguing questions about the structure of Agentic AI in conflict management. For example, could one AI Agent, acting as an Orchestrator, structure requests into several tasks assigned to other AI Agents, each specializing in specific areas, such as analyzing competitors’ prices, comparing company prices and predicting the counterparty’s Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA)? Could Agentic AI facilitate predicting outcomes from various first offers and sequences of offers and counteroffers? Could Agentic AI systems then present these to humans, ask for feedback and refinement and synthesize the human and AI predictions?Could Agentic AI augment conflict management, thereby increasing the likelihood of integrative and collaborative agreements? Could AI Agents act as Orchestrators of multiple AI agents, help model complex multi-party disputes with numerous stakeholders? Could the trust in Agentic AI systems during negotiations be enhanced by adding an Output Validation Agent that checks responses to prompts before they are delivered to users?Other research questions could focus on the processes and outcomes of Agentic AI for conflict management. For example, could multiple AI Agents simulate the interactions of various stakeholders’ preferences? Could Agentic AI generate possible resolutions that human mediators could use to enhance the effectiveness of third-party conflict resolution? Could Agentic AI be effective as mediators? To what degree should there be human oversight of Agentic AI actions? Could there be systemic conflict escalation or de-escalation of conflicts between AI-Agents, and are these the same or different from conflicts between humans?Research could also examine ethical questions about the use of Agentic AI. These questions could focus on disclosure, fairness and social responsibility. For example, if one party in negotiation is using Agentic AI, then should they disclose it to the counterparty? Should parties reveal the AI-predicted BATNAs of the other party? If one party uses Agentic AI and the other does not, then does this create an unfair competitive advantage in negotiation, and would it lead to outcomes that favor one side over the other? Could Agentic AI include an AI Agent that specializes in analyzing the impact of negotiations on social issues, such as the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including peace, justice and strong institutions?Also, research could consider the scaling of and the tools within Agentic AI systems. Suppose an Agentic AI system is structured to facilitate effective negotiations in low-value or low-stakes talks. Can the same Agentic AI structure be effectively scaled for higher-value or higher-stakes negotiations? Are there advantages or disadvantages to combining different layered technologies in the tech stack for managing conflicts involving Agentic AI, for example, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Copilot Studio, NLPs, Python and so forth?Research could focus on the effectiveness of going beyond using established LLMs. For example, could Agentic AI facilitate real-time knowledge management by consolidating insights from current news reports and proprietary or paywalled data to support contract negotiations, integrating retrieval-augmented generation with chat functionality? Can user interfaces help humans, AI Agents or Agentic AI in conflict management to create and execute negotiation plans, consult multiple agents, review the results and effectively use user interfaces to confer with users to refine and improve the process and output?Physical AI operates directly in the real world, interfaces with it and integrates with digital AI systems. Physical AI can gather information from, and act in, the physical world (Miriyev and Kovač, 2020; Sitti, 2021). Whereas traditional AI operates in the digital realm, physical AI directly interfaces with the tangible world. These interactions include Physical AI’s ability to continually and spontaneously perceive, learn, remember, decide, act and adapt (Sitti, 2021). Examples of Physical AI include autonomous vehicles, drones, extended reality systems and smart glasses (Yoo et al., 2025).There has been very little research on the intersection of Physical AI and conflict management. However, many interesting questions remain for future investigations. Some of these research questions focus on processes and outcomes.Process-focused research could examine the extent to which latency, that is, time lags, between current events and rapid analyses of conflict and the provision of recommended conflict strategies impair the effectiveness of AI-augmented human successes when integrated with Physical AI. Does the de-humanization of conflicts that are managed with Physical AI increase conflict, and why and what can be done to humanize Physical AI to reduce conflict intensity? Can robots interact effectively with humans in conflict situations or to what extent do humans need to exercise control over machines?Outcome-focused research could examine whether human–robotic interactions are more or less likely to result in conflicts and why. Can Physical AI perceive and act on human emotions, such as empathy, and express them effectively to humans in conflict situations, thereby improving outcomes? Can embodied agents, that is, human-like robots, use nonverbal behaviors, such as facial expressions and body movements, to facilitate the de-escalation of conflict? Can speech characteristics, prosody, of embodied agents, for example, inflection, speed, tone and volume, be equally or more effective than when used by humans in negotiation and conflict management? Can human–robotic interactions in conflict situations be designed to act as Guardians to avoid social inequalities and also facilitate social justice and the achievement of sustainable development goals?This editorial offers a structured framework that can encourage and facilitate innovative future research on AI and conflict management. Five AI paradigms for researching AI and conflict management were defined and compared. These paradigms are ML, Generative AI, AI Agents, Agentic AI and Physical AI. Additionally, this editorial identified roles AI can play in conflict management. The roles are Assistant, Analyst, Tasker, Orchestrator and Guardian. Using these paradigms and roles, several intriguing questions for future research were identified. This framework could suggest more insightful and profound research on AI and conflict management in the future.
title: Editorial: The future of research on artificial intelligence in conflict management

abstract: Extended Reality (XR) is a collective term that contains Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Mixed Reality (MR), and everything in between. VR is an immersive technology that allows users to interact within a computer-generated 3D virtual environment. AR enhances the user's situational awareness (SA) by superimposing virtual content onto a real scene. MR is a step beyond AR by combining physical reality with digital content in a way that enables real-time interaction with and among real and virtual elements. In the business world, a similarly captivating term, metaverse, indicates a single, universal, and immersive virtual world focused on social and economic connections facilitated by the use of XR technologies [1].XR has proven to be an effective communication medium for humans to instantly interact with other entities in shared spaces. As a result, it has received significant attention from both industry and academia. VR/AR is among the nine enabling technologies in the Industry 4.0 paradigm [2], serving as the only human-centric technology designed specifically for end users. This feature conforms well to the human-centric core value emphasized by the emerging Industry 5.0 [3]. With this advantage, XR could play a critical role in extending cyber-physical systems (CPS) into human-cyber-physical systems (HCPS), seamlessly integrating data, computational intelligence, and real-world situations through context-specific sensory cues for human interaction.With the recent advances in information and communication technologies (ICT), traditional manufacturing systems have evolved into “smart” ones in handling the ever-increasing complexity of tasks incorporating a high degree of autonomy and intelligence. Nevertheless, there are specific tasks on the shop floor that are either impractical or impossible to complete without human intervention. In such situations, the main purpose of smart manufacturing would be to facilitate manual operations, rather than to completely replace human involvement. Indeed, integrated with artificial intelligence (AI), 5G, cloud computing, and Internet-of-Things (IoT), XR applications have been successfully implemented and deployed to assist a diverse range of manual operations within the manufacturing sector [4,5]. The recent special issue titled “Challenges and Opportunities in Computing Research to Enable Next Generation Engineering Applications” published in the Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering (JCISE) also features three review articles focusing on extended reality [6–8]. In addition, the journal has published 16 papers with the words VR, AR, MR, XR, or Metaverse appearing in either the title or abstract between 2018 and 2023 [9–24]. This trend shows a growing interest in XR research in the JCISE community. A special issue focusing on the related fields would be necessary and timely to address this need.The purpose of this special issue is to solicit articles describing fundamental and applied research on XR techniques, solutions, and challenges in the area of design and manufacturing. This issue aims to cover all aspects of XR technology, including technical advances in software/hardware, algorithms, ergonomic analysis, system implementation, and novel empirical studies, for product design and manufacturing processes. In total, eight papers are included following rigorous review and revisions, and each is briefly introduced as follows.AR technology has made significant progress in recent years with applications successfully applied to assist manual tasks in various industries such as manufacturing, military, education, and entertainment. For instance, manual pointing and trajectory tracing are often used in robot programming in the manufacturing environment or during major surgical operations. Design guidelines are essential to develop assisted functions that can effectively enhance users’ situational awareness with instant sensory feedback through AR interfaces. For this purpose, Wang et al. conducted an experimental study on AR user interfaces with various sensory cues designed to assist in the manual tracing of simple and complex trajectories. The study compared the task performance under five sensory feedback conditions: central vision, peripheral vision, auditory sensation, force feedback, and no feedback. The experimental results showed that the feedback information should not only provide prompts for error status but also offer suggestions for correcting the actions of the subjects in complex trajectory tracing. The force feedback demonstrated better adaptation compared to visual and auditory cues. Furthermore, subjects tended to rely more on real-time force feedback to complete difficult tracing tasks than on the other cues. It was also suggested that the design of AR-assisted functions and instant sensory feedback should consider the potential limitations induced by the user's posture during a tracing task. These experimental findings could provide useful insights into the design of sensory feedback for AR-assisted functions developed for manual tracing tasks.Fewer studies have focused on the technical solutions for XR-based virtual footwear try-ons compared to those for garments and facial accessories. Therefore, Chou et al. introduced an approach based on machine learning that estimates the 6-DoF of a human foot using a single RGB image captured from a third-person view. Synthetic annotated data were generated by systematically adjusting the light source, foot geometry, background, camera position, as well as skin and background textures to ensure sufficient variation in information during the training process. Three CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) models (DOPE, DOPE2, and YOLO-6D) were trained using a proprietary dataset containing both synthetic and real foot images, following different training plans. Test results showed that training a CNN model for foot pose estimation performed better through a combination of pretraining and successive training with both proprietary and ImageNet datasets. In real use, YOLO-6D outperformed both the DOPE and simplified DOPE2 models in terms of prediction accuracy and computational speed.Natural human–computer interaction (HCI) remains an important research topic for industrial XR. Three articles featured in this special issue explore HCI from the perspectives of content authoring, cybersecurity, and human pose estimation. Content authoring for XR applications remains a challenge at scale. In response, Ipsita et al. developed VRFromX, an application-embedded workflow for in situ content creation and demonstrated its utility through a welding use case. Additional research is warranted to properly integrate XR technologies with minimal disruption into existing practical engineering workflows, such as the management of computer-numerical control (CNC) machines within a factory.Yang et al. addressed a potential cybersecurity risk existing in mid-air interactions commonly used in MR-based smart manufacturing applications. The authors developed a prototyping system for smart factory management using a video see-through MR HMD. This system allows users to input a password on a login interface, providing access to security/privacy-sensitive information through a single RGB camera capturing mid-air gestures in front of the user. A machine learning-based inference framework tracks hand gestures and estimates input passwords under assumed attack conditions. The test results in two scenarios suggested that potential preventive measures for cybersecurity attacks in MR applications during password input with hand gestures include using more complex characters, applying remote interaction methods, or entering the password while moving.The AR content presented by the head-mounted display (HMD) offers mobility, hands-free capabilities, and a first-person view, particularly useful in the context of industrial applications. The successful deployment of AR applications on these occasions depends on humans accurately interacting with and placing virtual objects in relation to the physical environment. This requires precise alignment and human perception of computer-generated graphics within the physical environment. Yang and Zhang resolved the misregistration issues occurring in video see-through AR HMDs that limit the potential for shared workspaces between humans and machines in shop-floor applications. They identified and analyzed the sources of errors within a comprehensive system framework. A mathematical model was proposed to characterize the influence and sensitivity of errors specifically in the HMD-to-camera transformation. This was achieved by examining three translational and three rotational components comprising the transformation matrix and simulating the resulting misregistration effects. An offline closed-loop calibration approach was applied to reduce the HMD-to-camera transformation error in a prototyping system. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrated satisfactory global registration between virtual objects and the physical environment.Wu et al. implemented ImpersonatAR, a mobile-based application, that utilizes embodied demonstrations in the augmented environment to support the prototyping and evaluation of multi-scenario AR use cases. The application was developed based on a set of design considerations derived from interviews with AR expert designers to address the current limitations of AR prototyping tools. ImpersonatAR enables capturing events or steps through embodied demonstrations using avatars and 3D animations. It facilitates the organization of these events and steps to create a multi-scenario experience, allowing stakeholders to explore the scenarios through interactive role-play with the prototypes. Positive feedback from ten users validated that ImpersonatAR promotes the exploration of diverse design possibilities for multi-scenario AR use cases through embodied representations of different scenarios. This work contributes to human–computer interaction by providing an effective prototyping approach for AR use cases.Advancements in VR offer great opportunities to create effective digital learning and training environments. Multi-user distributed participation in VR facilitates collaborative problem-solving (CPS) and learning-by-doing, both of which are critical professional skills for solving real-world problems. In addition, VR applications integrating with sensors allow the collection of in-process user behavioral data for adaptation or correction. Kim et al. presented a sensor-based multiplayer VR manufacturing simulation game that improved virtual hands-on learning experiences and served as a behavioral modeling method for monitoring the collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills of participants. The Virtual Learning Factory was proposed to facilitate low-cost implementation of virtual hands-on experiences as effective as their real-world equivalents. A dynamic network behavioral modeling approach was developed to extract time-varying patterns of player actions using action-log data using action-log data commonly available in digital learning environments. The heterogeneous-behavioral CPS score was defined by the graph similarity between players. Experimental results demonstrated that the score successfully monitored user-specific collaborative CPS dynamics between players, potentially leading to appropriate interventions to improve learning outcomes. This work enhances the effectiveness of virtual reality and gamification in engineering education.Nguyen et al. developed an augmented reality system for the human-in-the-loop registration of robot-sensor coordinates in production environments. The system efficiently records and visualizes the pose-dependent quality of computing the robot-sensor transformation, providing human operators with intuitive assessments of how changes in the configuration space affect registration and overall system performance. The metrics proposed to evaluate the quality of point measurements demonstrated a decrease in both the accuracy and precision of the registration as the points were measured farther from the robot base. The AR interface intuitively shows that the registration accuracy depends on the location of the sensor within the workspace. It may enable in situ manual re-sampling for better points to be used in registration. This technical brief highlights the potential of AR as a human-in-the-loop interface for metrology applications.The creation of this special issue indicates that extended reality-related studies have shifted from applications designed for various industrial sectors in earlier times to efforts aimed at improving practical values through the proposal of new techniques, algorithms, or assessment methods. It is worth noting that XR research must certainly be conducted from a human-centric perspective, given that its deployment or use is, after all, designed for people, not machines. Due to hardware device limitations, the positional precision of current VR/AR applications may fail to directly meet manufacturing requirements. However, these applications should function effectively in assisting manual tasks by enhancing human situation awareness and characterizing human behavior through the instant capture of their actions or intentions. This necessitates in-depth studies in human–computer interaction, particularly from ergonomic and UX/UI perspectives, in the context of engineering applications. We expect to see an increasing trend in using XR as an interfacing technology for humans to collaborate with computational intelligence (including artificial intelligence, simulation, analytics, and machines) in real time through a wide spectrum of technical elements such as sensors, IoT, cloud computing, and 5G/6G. This trend would transform Industry 4.0 into the emerging Industry 5.0 by fostering human–machine collaboration in a broader context. Especially, the intersection between XR and the recently booming large language model (LLM), as well as other multi-modality AI models, is expected to provide new affordances for new directions of innovation and advancement in broad areas of design and manufacturing. XR studies addressing sustainability and resilience issues could yield a higher degree of innovation and scientific impact along the transformation process.The guest editors would like to thank all contributing authors for their outstanding work. We want to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for dedicating their valuable time and efforts in providing constructive comments to the authors during the review process. In particular, we highly appreciate Ms. Amy Suski for her editorial assistance and timely reminders. Finally, we would like to extend our appreciation to Prof. S. K. Gupta and Prof. Y. Wang, the past and current Editor-in-Chief of JCISE, for offering the opportunity and their support for this special issue.Distribution A. Approved for public release: Distribution unlimited under AFRL-2024-0392 determined on January 23, 2024.
title: Special Issue: Extended Reality in Design and Manufacturing
venue: Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering

abstract: Title: Application Papers 01–11 of the Ehstand Terminological Method: Domain-Agnostic ISO 704-based Disambiguation across EU AI Act, Cybersecurity, HRI, Consciousness Studies, Climate Communication, Digital Twins, Quantum Computing, EdTech, Disinformation, AI Safety, and Sports Analytics (Ehstand 2026) Description: Collected Application Papers 01–11 of the Ehstand Terminological Method for defining novel and ambiguous concepts across domains. This volume contains the complete set of eleven domain applications demonstrating the transferability of the six-step ISO 704-based terminological method (Ehstand 2026, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18732990). Each paper identifies a terminologically ambiguous key term, documents the jingle-jangle fallacy through systematic definitional comparison, executes all six method steps (phenomenon identification, concept delimitation, four-layer definition, relation typing, machine-readable encoding in JSON-LD/SKOS, tripartite validation including LLM-in-the-loop testing), and introduces domain-specific methodological extensions formalized as new relation types. Papers and their innovations: Paper 01 — EU AI Act: "Human Oversight" (Article 14). Regulatory terminology application. Base method on legislation. Paper 02 — Cybersecurity: "Vulnerability" across NIST NVD/CVE, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and MITRE ATT&CK. Introduces 'is_variant_in_framework' for formal crosswalk mapping between framework-specific definitions. Paper 03 — Human-Robot Interaction: "Social Robot" (absent from ISO 8373:2021, IEEE P3107 not finalized). Introduces 'extends' for cross-domain bridging HAI→HRI. Formalizes sociality as attribution phenomenon. Paper 04 — Consciousness Studies: "AI Consciousness" as second-order terminological orphan. Building on Butlin, Chalmers et al. (2023/2025). Introduces 'is_theory_dependent_on' for theory-relative definitions across GWT, HOT, IIT, RPT, AST. Paper 05 — Climate Communication: "Tipping Point" (Lenton et al. 2008 vs. IPCC AR6 vs. SROCC vs. Gladwell). Introduces 'is_register_variant_of' for technical vs. everyday language differentiation. Resolves IPCC internal inconsistency. Paper 06 — Digital Twins / Industry 4.0: "Digital Twin" (Grieves 2002/2014, ISO 23247, ISO/IEC 30173). Introduces 'has_fidelity_level' for fidelity stratification from static model to autonomous system. Addresses marketing inflation. Paper 07 — Quantum Computing: "Quantum Advantage" (Preskill 2012 Supremacy → Google Sycamore 2019 → IBM Utility 2023). Introduces 'has_advantage_type' (asymptotic, practical, commercial). Directly relevant for research policy and terminological precision in investment contexts. Paper 08 — Educational Technology: "Adaptive Learning" (no consensus across 847+ studies). Introduces 'has_adaptation_mechanism' (content sequencing, difficulty scaling, scaffolding, pacing, assessment). Dismantles EdTech marketing claims. Paper 09 — Disinformation: "Deepfake" as technology, product, and deceptive act. EU AI Act Art. 50 regulates all three identically. Introduces 'has_intent_layer' separating neutral technology from contextual use from deceptive intent. Paper 10 — AI Safety: "Alignment" (Gabriel 2020, five alignment targets). Shows Anthropic, OpenAI, and RLHF practice use the same term differently. Introduces 'has_alignment_target' (instruction, objective, preference, value, normative). Paper 11 — Sports Analytics: "Expected Goals (xG)" as model-relative metric (Opta ≠ StatsBomb ≠ Understat). Introduces 'is_model_relative' formalizing provider-dependency. Demonstrates method in non-academic domain. Six emergent relation types across three categories: Contextualizing (is_variant_in_framework, is_theory_dependent_on, is_register_variant_of, is_model_relative), Typifying (has_fidelity_level, has_advantage_type, has_adaptation_mechanism, has_alignment_target), Intentional (has_intent_layer, extends). DISCLAIMER: This document is a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The author is a terminologist and computer science teacher, not a domain expert in the treated fields. Definitions are research contributions and discussion proposals, not authoritative standards or replacements for ISO, IEEE, IPCC, NIST, or EU regulatory definitions. No legal, financial, medical, or security advice is provided. AI systems were used as tools in document creation. All liability is excluded. Full 12-point disclaimer included. German law applies, jurisdiction Munich. Part of the AUGMANITAI Terminology Framework — a comprehensive terminological system for human-AI interaction comprising 1000+ defined terms.
