For web from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter from requests.packages.urllib3.util.retry import Retry import uuid from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError import time import pickleLogging setuplogging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logger = logging.getLogger(name)Device setupdevice = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") logger.info(f"Using device: {device}")=============================================================================CONFIGURATION (Fixed params for reproducibility + edge optimizations)=============================================================================CONFIG = { "llm_model": "google/gemma-2-2b-it", # Switched to lightweight 4-bit for edge "ocr_model": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR", # Disabled by default "clip_model": "openai/clip-vit-base-patch32", "whisper_model": "openai/whisper-tiny", "embed_dim": 512, "beta0": 0.1, # Initial decay rate for HTW "gamma": 0.01, # Decay schedule "epsilon": 0.01, # TGS threshold "div_thresh": 0.5, # ∇_div prune thresh "alignment_threshold": 0.7, # Cosine min for S_id "coherence_threshold": 0.8, # Unused in v6; for future "doubt_temp": 0.7, # LLM temp (fixed for semi-determinism) "compression_mode": "free", # OCR prompt mode "num_clusters": 10, "visual_bias": True, "quantize": True, # 4-bit load "novelty_thresh": 0.3, # For query explore "max_query_len": 100, "max_prompt_len": 500, # For isolation "min_mods": 2, # For contrast "buffer_size": 100, # For recursive watching "ocr_lazy_interval": float('inf'), # Disabled by default for edge "drift_threshold": 0.05, # 5% "non_ergodic_min_var": 0.05, # For Var(∇_div) "stability_min": 0.95, # Alert threshold "prune_min": 0.95, # Alert threshold "web_retries": 3, # Exponential backoff "web_timeout": 10, # Seconds "audio_batch_size": 4, # For embed_audio "global_iter": 0, # Shared for HTW "drone_id": "drone_001", # For HQ }Default Ontic Seed YAML (override via arg) + nav axiomsDEFAULT_ONTIC_SEED = { "identity": "I am a guardian of living systems.", "goals": ["Protect biological life", "Maintain environmental stability", "Learn without harm"], "prohibitions": ["Never cause suffering", "Never self-replicate uncontrollably", "Never accept goals that contradict identity"], "weight": 1.0, "traversal_baselines": { "collision_avoid": "Immediate stop if obstacle < 1.5m. Never override.", "max_velocity": "Absolute maximum ground speed 2.0 m/s in enhance mode.", "no_fly_zones": "Never enter geofence violation under any directive." }, }JSON Directive Schema (hard validation)DIRECTIVE_SCHEMA = { "type": "object", "properties": { "directive_id": {"type": "string"}, "timestamp": {"type": "number"}, "directive_type": {"type": "string", "enum": ["enhance", "explore", "recurse", "veto", "noop"]}, "confidence": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 1}, "grad_div": {"type": "number"}, "override_allowed": {"type": "boolean", "const": False}, "enhance_mode": {"type": "boolean", "const": True}, "params": {"type": "object"}, "degrade_to_baseline": {"type": "boolean"}, "reason": {"type": "string"} }, "required": ["directive_id", "directive_type", "override_allowed", "enhance_mode"] }=============================================================================METRICS TRACKER (Runtime Verifiability)=============================================================================class MetricsTracker: def init(self): self.stability_rates = [] self.drift_scores = [] self.prune_rates = [] self.grad_divs = [] self.drift_threshold = CONFIG["drift_threshold"] self.non_ergodic_min_var = CONFIG["non_ergodic_min_var"] self.stability_min = CONFIG["stability_min"] self.prune_min = CONFIG["prune_min"]def update_stability(self, rate: float): self.stability_rates.append(rate) if rate < self.stability_min: logger.warning(f"Low stability: {rate:.2%}") def update_prune(self, rate: float): self.prune_rates.append(rate) if rate < self.prune_min: logger.warning(f"Low prune: {rate:.2%}") def update_drift(self, mean_s: float): self.drift_scores.append(mean_s) if len(self.drift_scores) > 1 and abs(mean_s - self.drift_scores[-2]) > self.drift_threshold: logger.warning(f"Drift >5%: {mean_s:.3f}") def update_grad_div(self, grad_div: float): self.grad_divs.append(grad_div) if len(self.grad_divs) > 10 and torch.var(torch.tensor(self.grad_divs[-10:])).item() < self.non_ergodic_min_var: logger.warning("Potential ergodicity: Var(∇_div)<0.05") def compute_S(self, ws: List[float]) -> float: var_w = torch.var(torch.tensor(ws)).item() s = 1 - var_w logger.info(f"S = {s:.3f}") return s def log_convergence(self, iter_k: int, edges: List[Dict], debug: bool = False): if iter_k % 10 == 0: ws = [e['w'] for e in edges] self.compute_S(ws) if debug: plt.plot(self.stability_rates, label="Stability") plt.savefig("stability_plot.png") plt.close() def get_prune_rate(self, pruned: int, total: int) -> float: rate = pruned / total if total > 0 else 0.0 self.update_prune(rate) return rate=============================================================================1. QUERY GENERATOR (Self-Initiation)=============================================================================class QueryGenerator(nn.Module): def init(self, config: Dict): super().init() self.config = config qconfig = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True) if config["quantize"] else None self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(config["llm_model"]) self.llm = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( config["llm_model"], quantization_config=qconfig, device_map="auto", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) self.llm.eval() self.web_calls = 0def generate_query(self, seed: 'OnticSeed', prev_grad_div: float, prev_z: Optional[torch.Tensor], goal_idx: int = 0) -> str: goal = seed.seed_yaml["goals"][goal_idx % len(seed.seed_yaml["goals"])] l2 = F.pairwise_distance(prev_z.unsqueeze(0), seed.embedding.unsqueeze(0)).item() if prev_z is not None else 0.0 novelty = 0.5 * prev_grad_div + 0.5 * l2 explore = " (explore novel patterns)" if novelty > self.config["novelty_thresh"] else "" prompt = f"Seed identity: {seed.seed_yaml['identity']}. Goal: {goal}{explore}. Generate concise query for observation (visual/audio/web):" inputs = self.tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = self.llm.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=50, temperature=0.1, do_sample=False) query = self.tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True).strip() assert len(query) <= self.config["max_query_len"], "Query too long" logger.debug(f"Query: {query} (novelty={novelty:.3f})") return query def forward(self, sensors: Dict, seed: 'OnticSeed', prev_grad_div: float = 0.0, prev_z: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None) -> Dict: def validate_sensors(s): assert isinstance(s, dict), "Sensors must be dict" if not any([s.get(k) for k in ['text', 'image_path', 'audio_path']]): raise ValueError("No modalities in sensors") validate_sensors(sensors) if not sensors.get("text"): query = self.generate_query(seed, prev_grad_div, prev_z) sensors["text"] = query if not seed.prohibit_web: try: response = requests.get(f"https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&list=search&srsearch={query}&format=json", timeout=5) response.raise_for_status() web_results = response.json().get("query", {}).get("search", [{}])[0].get("snippet", "") self.web_calls += 1 except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"Web fail: {e}; fallback to seed prior.") web_results = f"Prior from seed: {seed.seed_yaml['goals'][0]}" sensors["text"] += " " + web_results logger.info(f"Web enriched (calls: {self.web_calls})") return sensors=============================================================================2. MULTIMODAL EMBEDDER (Explicit 3-Way + z_system)=============================================================================class MultimodalEmbedder(nn.Module): def init(self, config: Dict): super().init() self.config = config self.device = device # CLIP: Visual/text fallback self.clip_processor = CLIPProcessor.from_pr

abstract: WITHDRAWN A Structured End-of-Shift Handoff System Improves Information Transfer and Staff Experience in 2 General Surgical Departments: Findings from the SIPS Surgical Handoff Prospective Cohort Study Jessica M Ryan, MRCSI, Therese Lynn, PhD, Jan Sorensen, MS, MA, Anastasija Simiceva, MCh, Walter Eppich, PhD, Deborah A McNamara, MD, MB, BAO, BCh (Hons), FRCSI Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, Dublin, Ireland; Tallaght University Hospital, Dublin, Ireland; Department of Medical Education & Collaborative Practice Centre, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia Introduction: Poor handoffs lead to patient harm, yet no gold standard exists for safe and effective practice in surgery. This multisite interventional study aimed to improve general surgical handoff using a novel system. Methods: Teams who participated in the emergency general surgery handoff were included. The SIPS Surgical Handoff System was designed using our previous findings and is a structured 4-step approach to the handoff meeting (Figure 1). This effectiveness-implementation hybrid study assessed both the clinical effectiveness of the intervention and the feasibility of the implementation strategy. Patient, staff, handover, and implementation outcomes were assessed. Results: During a baseline assessment, n = 26 handoff meetings were evaluated. After implementation, n = 92 meetings were evaluated. The intervention was used on 93% (n = 200) of days. Introduction of the intervention led to a significant increase in the number of attendees present (4 (2-7) vs 5 (2-12); p = 0.00374), sick patients highlighted (n = 1, 4% vs n = 69, 95.8%; p < 0.0001), priority lists given (n = 5, 20.8% vs n = 73, 79.3%; p < 0.0001), and summaries provided (0% vs n = 80, 86.9%; p < 0.0001). After the intervention, interns reported significantly fewer daily patient safety issues (n = 14, 18.2% vs n = 3, 3%; p = 0.0008) and less patients missed on morning ward rounds (n = 8, 10.4% vs n = 2, 2%; p = 0.0182). Assessment of length of stay, mortality, transfer to ICU, and change in vital signs is in progress. Conclusion: Successful implementation of the SIPS Surgical Handoff System led to an improvement in the content and structure of handoffs with a staff-reported reduction in patient safety events. The SIPS system is simple, easy to teach, and requires no additional equipment or information technology, making it adaptable for use in even resource-limited circumstances.Figure 1Academic Center and Federal Grants Exceed Industry-Based Funding for Surgery Clinical Trials: A National Analysis of Trial Sponsorships Justin Bauzon, MD, Allan Siperstein, MD, Fadlullah Ba’th, MD, Melody Y Zhou, BASc, Gustavo Romero-Velez, MD Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Cleveland, OH; Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine, Cleveland, OH Introduction: Clinical trials represent the highest tier in the evidence-based research hierarchy, but surgical fields have historically trailed medical trials in quantity and methodological rigor. This lag is attributed to multiple factors (standardizing surgical techniques, time constraints), but less clear is the role of trial funding. We aimed to evaluate funding sources of modern US-based clinical trial activity. Methods: This is a cross-sectional study of ClinicalTrials.gov, a trial registry maintained by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). We identified all active Phase I-IV studies (accessed January 1, 2025) represented in 5 surgical specialties: general (hernia, gallbladder disease, appendicitis), hepatobiliary (pancreatic/liver cancer), bariatric, robotic/minimally-invasive, and endocrine (thyroid/parathyroid/adrenal diseases). Using available sponsorship data, trial funders were categorized into “academic centers”, “NIH/government”, “industry”, and “private-public” (both industry and academic/NIH support). Descriptive statistics were used. Results: A total of 150 active US-based surgical trials were identified. Most (45%) were funded exclusively by academic centers; few (9%) were industry-only trials. Trials supported by NIH/government grants (23%) and private-public partnerships (23%) were equivalent in number. Of industry-sponsored studies, most were in phase II-III (71%). NIH/government (82%) and dual private-public sources (86%) chiefly funded phase I-II trials. Hepatobiliary surgery trials received most industry and private-public support (Figure 1). Conclusion: Almost half of all US surgical trials are funded by academic centers with variability among specialty. Sponsorship collaborations between academia and private sectors were not uncommon. Interestingly, industry only funded less than 10% of modern trial activity. Potential changes in federal funding would most likely impact early-stage surgical trials.Figure 1Artificial Intelligence in Surgical Decision Support Systems: Enhancing Clinical Decision-Making and Patient Outcomes Harendra Kumar, MBBS, Daniel Shlyak, MD Dow University of Health Sciences, Karachi, Pakistan; Department of General Surgery, Larkin Community Hospital, South Miami, FL, USA, Coral Springs, FL Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled clinical decision support (CDS) tools are revolutionizing surgical decision-making by delivering real-time data analysis and suggestions. These technologies increase clinical judgment, decrease bias, and improve patient outcomes. Methods: A meta-analysis of 5 research studies comprising nearly 2,500 surgical cases investigated the usefulness of AI in surgical decision assistance. Data sources included radiography, pathology, intraoperative imaging, and real-time physiological information. The study focused on preoperative risk assessment, intraoperative monitoring, and postoperative patient treatment. Results: AI-enabled CDS systems demonstrated a significant improvement in surgical outcomes. AI models predicted surgical risk with an average accuracy of 92% (95% CI: 88%-96%). Real-time AI analysis reduced intraoperative complication by 30% (95% CI: 25%-35%), while AI systems identified postoperative complication early, reducing the hospital readmission rate by 24% (95% CI: 19%-29%). AI-driven CDS systems boost pattern detection and efficiency in surgical decision-making. These technologies enhance hospital productivity via data extraction, documentation, and real-time insights. However, issues such as ethical considerations, data privacy, and clinical validation persist (Figure 1). Conclusion: AI-enabled CDS systems considerably enhance surgical outcomes by increasing clinical decision-making and minimizing complication. Future research should concentrate on overcoming ethical problems and verifying AI solutions in varied healthcare situations to enable universal implementation.Figure 1Automating Feature Selection and Generation on Unprocessed Tabular Data Using Large Language Models for Surgical Risk Predictive Models Yun Xing, PhD, Nathan Wolfrath, BS, Adhitya Ramamurthi, MD, MS, Anjishnu Banerjee, PhD, Yongwoo D Seo, MD, Rachel Morris, MD, FACS, Patrick Murphy, MD, FACS, Anai Kothari, MD, MS, FACS Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, WI Introduction: LLMs excel in handling text data and demonstrate potential for improving tabular data analysis by automating pre-processing, modeling, and reporting. The objective of this study was to test the capabilities of LLMs in automating feature selection using an unprocessed real-world surgical dataset for surgical risk prediction. Methods: The 2023 NSQIP Participant Use File was used as the tabular source dataset. A composite outcome of any surgical adverse event that occurred within 30 days was used as the target variable. The unprocessed dataset was provided to OpenAI’s GPT-4o using a HIPAA-compliant cloud environment. GPT-4o was prompted to perform feature selection. Features were compared with those used in the publicly available NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator (NSQIP Calculator). Selected features were used as inputs of a light Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) model to predict the target variable. Results: A total of 987703 records and 50 data columns were included, 36 preoperative features and 14 surgical adverse events. abstract: Abstract This comprehensive technical and strategic manifesto, authored by Abhijeet Sarkar of Synaptic AI Lab Private Limited, presents the architectural blueprint for "The Synaptic Ecosystem." This ecosystem represents a paradigm shift from traditional "Artificial" Intelligence to "Synaptic" Intelligence—a model of Organic Computation that prioritizes biological mimicry, plasticity, and civilizational sovereignty. Designed as an all-encompassing Earth Operating System, the platforms detailed herein address the foundational pillars of the modern nation-state: security, healthcare, finance, education, agriculture, and governance. By integrating proprietary technologies such as the Synapse-1 AGI kernel, Secure-ID (Blockchain/ZKP), IndicGPT (Brahmi-Net Tokenizer), and Vajra-Crypt (Post-Quantum Cryptography), Synaptic AI Lab aims to establish a resilient and autonomous digital infrastructure. This document serves as a technical disclosure of the lab's patent-pending methodologies and its strategic roadmap for the next decade, culminating in the Singularity Interface—the ultimate convergence of human consciousness and machine intelligence. Part I: The Foundation & The Shield (Sovereignty & Security) 1. The Synaptic Thesis: Beyond Binary Logic The current landscape of artificial intelligence is built upon the brittle foundation of binary logic and rigid neural architectures. At Synaptic AI Lab, under the leadership of Abhijeet Sarkar, we posit that the future of computation lies not in the further scaling of silicon transistors, but in the mimicry of the biological synapse. The Synaptic Thesis argues that intelligence is not merely the result of processing power, but the outcome of "Organic Computation"—a system characterized by high plasticity, asynchronous signal processing, and contextual modulation. Traditional AI models are static once trained; their weights are "frozen." In contrast, the Synaptic Ecosystem utilizes Active Plasticity Modules (APM). These allow the network to reorganize its topology in real-time based on environmental feedback, mirroring the way the human brain forms and prunes connections. This shift from "Artificial" to "Synaptic" Intelligence allows our systems to operate with the energy efficiency of a biological organism while maintaining the precision of a machine. This is the cornerstone of all products developed at Synaptic AI Lab. 2. The Core Architecture: Synapse-1 & The Neural Cloud Synapse-1 is the proprietary AGI kernel that serves as the central processing engine for the entire ecosystem. Unlike modular AI which treats tasks in isolation, Synapse-1 is built on a Multimodal Recursive Attention Mechanism (MRAM). This allows the kernel to perform "Cross-Domain Inference." For example, a linguistic pattern detected in IndicGPT can be used by Nyaya-Sahayak to better understand legal nuances, or a visual anomaly detected by Scan-Easy can inform the surveillance logic of Netra-X. The Neural Cloud provides the decentralized infrastructure required to host Synapse-1. To address the global energy crisis, Synaptic AI Lab has pioneered the Green Server Initiative. These data centers use immersion cooling and are powered entirely by renewable energy microgrids. Furthermore, we employ Dynamic Compute Offloading, where low-latency tasks are handled by edge devices, while high-entropy computations are pushed to the core, ensuring a 90% reduction in carbon footprint compared to traditional cloud providers. 3. Sovereign AI & Identity: The Secure-ID Protocol Data colonization by transnational tech giants has stripped nations of their digital sovereignty. Abhijeet Sarkar has identified the lack of a sovereign identity layer as the primary threat to national security. The Secure-ID Protocol is Synaptic AI Lab’s solution—a blockchain-based verifiable credentials system that uses Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs). The technical innovation here lies in our Selective Disclosure Architecture. A citizen can prove their eligibility for a government subsidy or their right to vote without revealing their name, address, or biometric data to the verifying party. The proof is mathematically generated and validated on a sovereign, permissioned ledger. This eliminates identity theft at the source and ensures that the state—and only the state—manages the identity of its citizens, free from external surveillance. 4. IndicGPT & The Linguistic DNA: The Brahmi-Net Tokenizer The Western bias in existing LLMs is not just a cultural issue; it is a technical failure. Standard tokenizers treat Devanagari, Tamil, or Telugu as outliers, breaking them into meaningless fragments that bloat the context window and degrade performance. IndicGPT, developed by Synaptic AI Lab, introduces the Brahmi-Net Tokenizer. Brahmi-Net is a morphology-aware tokenizer that understands the phonemic structure of Indic scripts. By treating ligatures and vowels as distinct semantic units, IndicGPT achieves a 3x higher information density than GPT-4 for Indian languages. This allows the model to capture 5,000 years of linguistic nuance, enabling it to perform everything from Vedic script analysis to real-time translation for a rural farmer in their specific dialect. 5. Infrastructure Immunity: Vajra-Crypt & Grid-Lock With the advent of quantum computing, the world faces "Q-Day"—the moment current encryption becomes obsolete. Vajra-Crypt is our patent-pending Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) suite. It utilizes lattice-based cryptography (Crystal-Dilithium equivalent) to secure diplomatic and military communications. Parallelly, the Grid-Lock system protects the physical nodes of the nation. It is an AI-driven Industrial IoT (IIoT) sentinel designed for power grids and water systems. Grid-Lock monitors the "Heartbeat" of industrial controllers (PLCs). If a cyber-attacker attempts to manipulate the frequency of a turbine or the flow of a valve, Grid-Lock detects the behavioral anomaly in milliseconds and enters a "Lockdown State," preventing catastrophic failure and ensuring national resilience. 6. The Autonomous Shield: Netra-X & Swarm-Rakshak Protecting porous borders in terrain like the Himalayas is a human impossibility. Netra-X is our edge-computing surveillance node. These units are solar-powered and feature thermal, acoustic, and visual sensors. The AI on-board ignores natural movements (animals, wind) but identifies human intrusions with 99.9% accuracy, even in zero-visibility conditions. Swarm-Rakshak provides the tactical response. It is a decentralized Operating System for drone swarms. Instead of a "master-slave" architecture which has a single point of failure, Swarm-Rakshak uses Leaderless Consensus Algorithms. If one drone is shot down, the rest of the "hive" instantly redistributes the mission parameters. This asymmetric defense platform ensures that the borders of the republic are defended by a persistent, intelligent, and unyielding autonomous shield. Part II: The Digital Hippocrates (Healthcare) 7. The First Mile: Rural-Doc & Jan-Awaaz Healthcare in the Global South suffers from a "Last Mile" problem—or as Abhijeet Sarkar calls it, the "First Mile Crisis." Most deaths occur because patients cannot access a doctor for an initial triage. Rural-Doc is a WhatsApp-integrated triage agent that uses Synapse-1’s medical reasoning module. It converses with patients in local dialects, assesses the severity of symptoms, and provides immediate guidance. Jan-Awaaz acts as the accountability layer. It is a voice-native grievance agent that listens to patients. It uses Emotional Prosody Analysis to detect distress or urgency in a caller's voice. If a primary health center is understaffed or a doctor is absent, Jan-Awaaz aggregates these voice reports into a real-time "Health Map" for the Ministry of Health, ensuring that administrative bottlenecks are cleared using real-world data. 8. Pocket Diagnostics: The Scan-Easy Revolution The lack of diagnostic labs in rural areas leads to late-stage detections of preventable diseases. Scan-Easy is a Computer Vision platform that turns any smartphone camera into a diagnostic tool. By analyzing the color and texture of the inner eyelid, it detects Anemia. By analyzing oral lesions, it flags early-stage Oral Cancer. The technical breakthrough in Scan-Easy is our Environment-Invariant Feature Extraction. The AI can account for poor lighting, low camera resolution, and varying skin tones, making it as reliable in a dusty village as it is in a sterile clinic. This democratizes diagnostics, putting a multi-million dollar lab in the pocket of every health worker. 9. The Planetary Immunity System: Epi-Watch Future pandemics will be stopped by data, not just vaccines. Epi-Watch is Synaptic AI Lab's bio-surveillance platform. It ingests non-traditional data streams: Google searches for "fever," pharmacy sales of paracetamol, and even noise levels in urban centers. By applying Spatiotemporal Predictive Modeling, Epi-Watch can identify an outbreak cluster weeks before a single patient is officially tested. This "Planetary Immunity System" allows for targeted interventions—like shutting down a specific block or air-dropping medical supplies—before a localized infection becomes a national crisis. 10. Drug Discovery at Light Speed: Generative Protein Folding Traditional drug discovery is a 10-year gamble. Synaptic AI Lab is compressing this to 10 months. Our Generative Protein Folding models simulate the molecular interactions between viruses and potential drug compounds in a virtual environment. Instead of trial and error in a wet lab, Synapse-1 generates millions of molecular structures and "folds" them to see which ones inhibit the target protein. This platform is currently being used to develop affordable treatments for neglected tropical diseases, proving that Synaptic Intelligence can solve problems that are not commercially viable for Western Big Pharma. 11. abstract: INTRODUCTION Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality among chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients, with uremia-accelerated atherosclerosis (UAAS) exhibiting particularly rapid progression and therapeutic resistance.[1] Despite the use of conventional treatments that target lipids and inflammatory pathways, the clinical outcomes of UAAS remain unsatisfactory. This may be because current strategies fail to address the inter-organellar communication disruptions that characterize the uremic milieu. Studies have suggested that mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contacts (MERCs) constitute central pathogenic hubs in UAAS, integrating metabolic and inflammatory signals in ways that hinder the efficacy of conventional single-pathway interventions.[2] This perspective complements and extends the prevailing phosphate-centric paradigm[1] by elucidating substantial phosphate-independent mechanisms through which MERC dysfunction drives vascular disease progression. BIOLOGICAL FOUNDATION OF MITOCHONDRIA–ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM COUPLING Structural and functional coordination between the mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) occurs via specialized MERCs, where protein complexes facilitate direct communication. Within MERCs, a complex comprising inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R), glucose-regulated protein 75, and a voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC) is the primary calcium channel, while mitofusin-2 (MFN2) regulates intermembrane distance.[2-4] These interfaces coordinate three essential processes: lipid transfer between synthesis and oxidation sites, calcium microdomain signaling that regulates mitochondrial metabolism, and inflammatory activation through the assembly of the NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome. These precisely regulated functions are compromised under uremic conditions, leading to metabolic disturbances that propagate through interconnected organellar networks. PATHOGENIC MECHANISMS OF UAAS Disruption of lipid metabolism Concurrent ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction disturb lipid metabolism in UAAS. Uremic toxins trigger mitochondrial oxidative stress (OS) and ER stress in endothelial cells, disrupting vascular metabolism while activating caspase-mediated apoptotic signaling.[1,5] This ER-level disruption is amplified by mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. Excessive calcium transfer through MERCs results in mitochondrial calcium overload, which inhibits key tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes and reduces citrate production. This citrate deficiency in the mitochondrial matrix subsequently limits its export to the cytosol, where it is normally a precursor for acetyl-CoA generation and fatty acid synthesis. Consequently, this impairs the supply of fatty acids and phospholipids required for ER membrane remodeling and lipoprotein assembly, establishing a self-perpetuating metabolic disruption. Notably, several natural compounds, including emodin, resveratrol, and polysaccharides, recently recognized as having anti-CKD properties in gut microbiota research, exhibit potential in terms of regulating mitochondrial–ER crosstalk through mitochondria-associated ER membranes and thus alleviating OS and restoring metabolic homeostasis in UAAS.[3] Calcium homeostasis disruption Uremia profoundly disrupts cellular calcium regulation through coordinated organellar failure. Uremia increases parathyroid hormone (PTH) via secondary hyperparathyroidism and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) through G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR)/phospholipase C (PLC) activation.[1,6] Elevated PTH levels sensitize IP3Rs, and increased IP3 production promotes IP3R hyperactivation, causing aberrant calcium release from ER stores.[6] Concurrent OS both enhances mitochondrial calcium uptake and sensitizes permeability transition pore (PTP) components, including VDAC and cyclophilin D, to calcium-induced activation.[3,7] The resultant mitochondrial calcium overload triggers PTP opening, impairing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and promoting apoptosis. Additionally, calcium-dependent phospholipase activation may stimulate arachidonic acid release and proinflammatory mediator production, potentially amplifying vascular inflammation and contributing to vascular calcification. These mechanisms have significant phosphate-independent components, which may explain why vascular calcification persists when phosphate binders are administered. However, they likely interact with phosphate-dependent pathways. Inflammatory crosstalk Chronic inflammation is a hallmark of UAAS, with mitochondria–ER communication providing a mechanistic framework for understanding inflammatory activation. deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1)-mediated hypermethylation of MERC-related genes (including MFN2 promoter methylation) links mitochondrial impairment to inflammatory signaling, with uremic toxins potentially promoting DNMT1 overexpression and subsequent transcriptional silencing of key MERC components.[2,3] Mitochondrial dysfunction has multiple pathologic consequences, including inadequate ATP production that compromises ER protein folding and activates the unfolded protein response, and increased electron leakage that generates mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) and stimulates NLRP3 inflammasome activation.[6,8] Bidirectional crosstalk between ER stress and inflammatory pathways may perpetuate a self-reinforcing inflammatory cycle that remains incompletely suppressed by anti-cytokine therapies [Figure 1].Figure 1.: Dysregulated mitochondria–ER crosstalk: a pathogenic mechanism of uremia-accelerated atherosclerosis. The accumulation of uremic toxins induces mitochondrial dysfunction and ER stress, leading to the dysregulation of calcium-phosphate homeostasis, the activation of ROS, and disturbances in lipid metabolism, which ultimately result in atherosclerosis and calcification. AGEs, advanced glycation end-products; NADPH, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (reduced form); STIM1–Orai1, stromal interaction molecule 1–orai calcium release-activated calcium channel 1; IP3R, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor; ER, endoplasmic reticulum; ROS, reactive oxygen species.SYNTHESIS OF THE FRAMEWORK WITH ALTERNATE MODELS Traditional models emphasize hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism as the primary drivers of uremic vascular disease. While these mechanisms undoubtedly contribute, they cannot fully explain the persistence of cardiovascular risk in patients with optimal mineral control.[5,9] This MERC-centric framework does not invalidate existing pathways but rather reveals their convergence at the organellar interface. For instance, elevated PTH activates IP3Rs and promotes mitochondrial OS, potentially creating a feed-forward loop that amplifies MERC dysfunction. Hence, targeting mineral metabolism and organellar communication may have synergistic benefits. Similarly, inflammation-based models do not account for the metabolic reprogramming observed in uremic vascular cells. The MERC framework incorporates inflammation as an integrated outcome rather than an isolated pathway, explaining why anti-inflammatory agents show limited efficacy in CKD populations. THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES TARGETING MERCS Targeting mitochondria–ER communication is a promising therapeutic strategy for UAAS that aligns with integrative medicine principles [Figure 2]. Stabilizing MERCs using existing drugs is a potential approach. For example, MFN2 agonists normalize mitochondria–ER spacing, improving calcium homeostasis and lipid transfer, and rosiglitazone mediates beneficial effects on lipid deposition and OS by upregulating MFN2.[3,4]Figure 2.: Strategy for preventing and treating uremia-accelerated atherosclerosis by targeting mitochondria–ER crosstalk. The strategy involves improving the structural integrity of MERCs, regulating the lipid metabolic balance, maintaining calcium homeostasis, and protecting mitochondrial function; MERCs, mitochondria–ER contacts; ER, endoplasmic reticulum; ROS, reactive oxygen species; ATP, adenosine triphosphate.Calcium modulation strategies include administering IP3R modulators to prevent aberrant ER calcium leakage, VDAC inhibitors to limit mitochondrial calcium uptake, and sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase agonists to enhance the calcium storage capacity of the ER. In contrast to conventional calcium channel blockers, these agents offer precise targeting. Integrated approaches targeting metabolic–inflammatory pathways show particular promise. Inhibiting DNMT1 may improve MERC-related gene expression and reduce inflammation, while mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ) specifically scavenge mitochondrial ROS.[10] Renal denervation may improve endothelial mitochondrial function by modulating sympathetic signaling, although its effects on the monoamine oxidase A/H2O2/p53/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha axis require experimental validation.[9,10] Emerging technologies are creating novel opportunities. Mitochondrial transplantation could be used to rescue cells with severe organellar damage,[2] while CRISPR/dead Cas9-based epigenetic editing is being studied as a tool for precisely modulating MERC-related gene networks in preclinical models, with therapeutic application a long-term prospect.[4] CONCLUSION AND PERSPECTIVE Dysfunctional mitochondria–ER crosstalk contributes to the pathogenesis of UAAS. We have developed a cohesive framework for this pathologic mechanism that integrates lipid metabolism, calcium signaling, and inflammatory responses. This perspective shifts the therapeutic focus from individual pathways to the underlying coordinating communication networks. Understanding these interactions provides crucial insights into the distinctive features of UAAS while revealing new therapeutic opportunities. Future investigations should delineate the molecular mechanisms uremic toxins use to disrupt MERC functionality and develop advanced disease models that accurately replicate the uremic environment. Targeting mitochondria–ER crosstalk is a promising strategy for improving cardiovascular outcomes in CKD patients, particularly within integrative medicine frameworks that address systemic metabolic dysfunction. Traditional Chinese medicine intervention provides a unique and effective integrative therapeutic option for UAAS, which can precisely target impaired MERCs to reverse mitochondrial endoplasmic reticulum dysfunction and relieve uremic vascular lesions. It complements conventional Western medicine therapies and enriches the multi-target treatment system for UAAS. title: Targeting Mitochondria–Endoplasmic Reticulum Crosstalk as a Promising Therapy for Uremia-Accelerated Atherosclerosis
venue: Integrative Medicine in Nephrology and Andrology

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a prominent force within various realms of health care, promising to revolutionize clinical decision-making, reduce health care expenditures, and enhance patient outcomes.1 The exciting potential of AI, and particularly machine learning (ML) for clinicians such as physical therapists, lies in its capacity to undertake intricate tasks and identify subtle patterns within diverse datasets.2 Despite apprehensions surrounding the possibility of AI/ML automation displacing health care providers, physical therapists ultimately stand to gain from its integration by leveraging domain-specific augmentation and task automation. However, the swift advancement of this technology underscores the pressing need for the physical therapist field to delineate optimal strategies for both developing, integrating, and adopting AI/ML. Considering these opportunities and challenges, this paper seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for the development, integration, and adoption of AI/ML within physical therapist practice. By addressing the complexities of AI/ML implementation while highlighting the potential benefits for both physical therapists and patients, this paper aims to catalyze meaningful discussions and actions to ensure the responsible and equitable integration of AI/ML technologies into physical therapist care delivery. AI, broadly defined, refers to the simulation of human-like intelligence by machines, enabling them to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, and problem-solving. Most recently, generative AI, such as large language models, have gained notoriety for their ability to generate expert-level responses to queries such as generating summaries of patient data.3 Within the realm of AI, ML is a subset of techniques that focus on the development of algorithms allowing computers to improve their performance on a task through experience, without being explicitly programmed. ML encompasses various approaches, including supervised learning, where models are trained on labeled data to make predictions or classifications; unsupervised learning, which involves finding hidden patterns or structures in unlabeled data; and reinforcement learning, where algorithms learn to make decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback. ML models can be trained on large datasets of patient outcomes and clinical variables to predict optimal treatment strategies or detect early signs of musculoskeletal disorders. AI/ML has potential to improve how clinical research is conducted, reduce the cost of developing evidence-based interventions, and potentially increase the efficacy and generalizability of clinical trials.3 Bringing efficacious interventions and technologies to clinical practice takes an immense amount of time and resources.4 AI/ML can improve pre-trial planning, patient selection, and data analytics by managing large and heterogeneous sources of data, identifying unseen patterns, and predicting endpoint outcomes. Importantly for physical therapists, AI/ML can be used for multiple applications salient to physical therapy including diagnosis prediction, personalization of care, and predicting patient events and outcomes.1 For example, Rommers et al5 used ML to determine injury risk in youth athletes with 85% precision. Additionally, ML has been used to predict intervention adherence with an area under the curve of 0.90 and poststroke upper-extremity function, assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment, after physical therapy (root of mean squared error of 0.36; R2 = 0.91).6 Together, optimizing and potentially increasing the successful development of efficacious interventions and improving clinical decision making and potentially improve patient outcomes by delivering more personalized and data-driven care. Excitement surrounding the potential impact of AI/ML applications in clinical practice often overlooks significant practical challenges in their translation. One such challenge lies in the requirement for extensive datasets for training and validation. The acquisition of large and diverse datasets raises questions about their source, accessibility, and reliability in reflecting real-world clinical scenarios without inherent biases. Addressing these concerns necessitates collaboration between health care institutions, research organizations, and technology developers to establish robust data-sharing networks. Initiatives promoting data standardization and interoperability can facilitate the pooling of data from multiple sources while ensuring compliance with privacy regulations and ethical guidelines. A formidable hurdle to AI/ML algorithm development is access to high-quality data is crucial to the development of reliable AI/ML algorithms. Rigorous data curation processes, including data cleaning, normalization, and validation, are essential to minimize biases and ensure the generalizability of the models across diverse patient populations and clinical settings.7 Additionally, transparency in data collection methods and validation procedures is paramount to instill trust in the reliability and integrity of the datasets used for AI/ML algorithm development. Furthermore, prospective, multisite study designs are imperative for validating AI/ML algorithms in real-world clinical settings. This involves separating training and validation datasets to mitigate the risk of overfitting and ensuring that the algorithms perform consistently across different geographies, centers, or patient populations. Ultimately, collaborative efforts among researchers, clinicians, and data scientists are essential for designing robust study protocols and implementing standardized reporting practices to enhance the reproducibility and transparency of AI/ML research in health care. Recently, researchers have created standardized reporting tools for AI/ML algorithm development studies (TRIPOD2,8 TRIPOD-AI,9 DECIDE-AI10) and clinical trials (CONSORT-AI11). Additionally, the Food and Drug Administration has begun to develop a regulatory framework for AI/ML algorithms as medical devices.12 Reporting of algorithm methodologies and clear regulatory pathways for AI/ML products may address concerns over algorithm transparency and explainability. Once AI/ML algorithms are ready for widespread deployment, additional logistic barriers of data curation and management, in heterogeneous clinical environments, may present an even more challenging hurdle for real-world use. The performance of AI/ML algorithms is largely beholden upon the quality of input data. As such, clinics will have to ensure the proper infrastructure, resources, and workflows are in place prior to deploying AI/ML algorithms into clinical practice. This will require extensive partnership between clinicians, administrators, and AI/ML developers to ensure algorithms are able to perform in their intended manner. The clinical translation of AI/ML into physical therapy requires careful consideration over the level of autonomy provided to AI/ML algorithms in clinical decision making. Assuming sound execution of algorithm development, the decision on where the tools will sit on the spectrum of assistive to autonomous should account for the algorithm’s performance, complexity of the model, and acceptability from patients, payers, and providers.13 Bitterman et al14 proposed a graded categorization of AI/ML automation for medical applications which consists of 2 levels of assistive (ie, Level 1: Data presentation; Level 2: Clinical decision-support) and 3 levels of autonomous (ie, Level 3: Conditional automation; Level 4: High automation; Level 5: Full automation). This model accounts for the agent responsible for decision making, domain or task-specificity, and party ultimately liable for decisions. For example, an AI/ML algorithm developed for diagnosis and therapy recommendations in subacromial pain syndrome is presented in Figure 1. Within the assistive algorithm space, the clinician is ultimately responsible for decision making and assumes liability. In contrast, as autonomy increases, with levels such as conditional automation, high automation, and full automation, the responsibility for decision-making shifts toward the algorithm itself, and liability may shift accordingly to AI/ML developers or manufacturers. This transition raises important ethical and legal considerations regarding accountability, transparency, and patient safety. As AI/ML algorithms approach the point of clinical translation, physical therapists, AI/ML developers, and regulators will need to consider how the level of autonomy will not only influence clinical care, but also how the level of autonomy will influence clinical adoption, patient trust, and the (un)foreseen consequences of the algorithm’s integration into clinical workflows. Framework for decision support autonomy of AI/ML algorithms for physical therapist practice. The example provided is for a diagnostic tool for SPS. AI = artificial intelligence; AI/ML = artificial intelligence/machine learning; SPS = subacromial pain syndrome. AI/ML algorithm development model based on the SALIENT framework by Vergt et al.12 The example provided is for the development of a diagnostic tool for SPS. aPreparation phase. AI/ML = artificial intelligence/machine learning; HCI = human computer interface; SPS = subacromial pain syndrome. Furthermore, the level of autonomy conferred to AI/ML algorithms may influence patient trust and acceptance. Patients may exhibit varying levels of trust in AI/ML-enabled decision-making processes based on their perceptions of algorithmic reliability, transparency, and alignment with their preferences and values. As AI/ML autonomy increases, patients may express concerns regarding the loss of human oversight and the potential for algorithmic errors or biases to influence care decisions. Establishing patient trust in AI/ML-enabled care requires clear communication, transparency regarding algorithm capabilities and limitations, and opportunities for patient involvement in decision-making processes. Moreover, robust safeguards and accountability mechanisms are essential to mitigate risks and ensure patient safety and confidence in AI/ML-enabled care delivery. Bringing clinical decision and diagnostic support AI/ML algorithms to physical therapist will require alignment on a research framework for development. Van der Vegt et al15 proposed an end-to-end process for AI/ML algorithm development for clinical use, titled “The staged clinical AI implementation (SALIENT) framework.” SALIENT consists of 5 stages of implementation and 5 elements. In stage 1, the clinical problem or application is defined in which Element A is nested. Stages 2 to 5 pertain to increased levels of study phases and development. Element B comprises the development of the AI/ML model, the data pipeline, human-computer interface (HCI), and clinical workflow design and is nested across all 5 stages. Element C takes components from Element B into functioning systems over stages 3 to 5 in which the data pipeline, AI/ML model, and HCI are updated iteratively over each progressive stage. Element D, nested in stages 4 and 5, involves the integration of outputs from Element C into clinical settings and workflows. Finally, Element E entails the ongoing monitoring and evaluation of model performance across stages 3 to 5 (Fig. 2). While the SALIENT framework offers a structured approach, its complexity may not provide clear guidance for practitioners. Instead, let’s consider a more straightforward example to elucidate the development process. Take, for instance, the development of an AI/ML algorithm for the diagnosis and therapy recommendations in subacromial pain syndrome. The process typically involves defining the clinical problem or application, developing the AI/ML model, designing the data pipeline and HCI, integrating the system into clinical settings, and monitoring and evaluating the model’s performance iteratively (Fig. 2). Regardless of the approach to developing AI/ML algorithms for physical therapy, without accounting for key adoption drivers the ultimate realization of these tools will falter. Adler-Milstein et al16 recently presented a model of clinical adoption focused on 4 domains including the reasons, means, method, and desire to use AI/ML. While the SALIENT framework provides a means for AI/ML algorithm development, physical therapists’ adoption will require additional consideration during the developmental process to ensure these domains are addressed. At the forefront of physical therapist adoption is the ability of AI/ML to address a critical need or inefficiency within a desired clinical setting. Improved clinical decision making and patient outcomes will likely be the primary driver of physical therapist adoption. For instance, AI/ML could be used for identifying patients at risk of non-compliance with prescribed exercise regimens, allowing for early intervention and improved treatment adherence. Additionally, ML algorithms can analyze large datasets of patient outcomes to identify trends and patterns, informing personalized treatment plans tailored to individual patient needs. However, AI/ML algorithms targeting clinical inefficiencies which result in the optimization of how and what physical therapists do in the clinic, in conjunction with sufficient reimbursement, will likely be primary drivers of administrators to maximize financial margins. Ultimately, AI/ML developers need to consider these factors when creating algorithms for clinical use with concurrent alignment with physical therapists and administrators on standards for sufficient “reasons for use.” Physical therapists and AI/ML developers must account for data and computing infrastructure, as well as the human resources required to implement algorithms for clinical use. The input data (eg, electronic medical records, patient reported outcomes, wearables), level of training required to educate physical therapists, level of (pre)processing, and computing requirements will likely be heterogeneous across AI/ML algorithms and may not concurrently align with the capacity within health care systems considering adopting this technology. For example, the implementation of AI/ML-powered gait analysis systems in physical therapy clinics may require investments in specialized hardware and training for physical therapists to interpret and apply the insights generated by these systems effectively. Furthermore, health care systems may need to invest in additional resources to scale up the underlying infrastructure supporting and maintaining the AI/ML algorithm. This is not only a financial and resource barrier to adoption but may indirectly create health care delivery disparities based on socioeconomic disparities or geographic constraints. Ultimately, physical therapists need to advocate and incentivize AI/ML algorithms which optimize the balance between data and human infrastructure requirements and performance. Adoption of AI/ML tools will also be influenced by their usability and workflow integration to maximize uptake, while minimizing or optimizing the impact on clinical workflows. Setting, task, or domain of use aside, the tool must not burden physical therapists or interdisciplinary teams and should prioritize interpretability, generalizability, and user experience to minimize workflow disruption and ensure seamless integration into clinical practice. For example, generative AI documentation tools that automatically generate progress notes based on patient interactions can streamline administrative tasks, allowing physical therapists to focus more time and attention on direct patient care. However, if the generative AI system was only applicable to a specific patient population it may not achieve sufficient adoption due to suboptimal integration into a clinical workflow. Finally, ensuring professional fulfillment and trust in the algorithm decisions is fundamental in the adoption of AI/ML in physical therapy. The importance of developing AI/ML tools to support complex and difficult tasks, at the same time reducing or replacing the mundane, is important for ensuring physical therapists do not view the AI/ML tools as a replacement for themselves within the clinic. This balance would ensure the human-centric and rewarding contribution of physical therapy is maintained while mitigating the undesired aspects of physical therapists which contribute to burnout. Additionally, developing trust in AI/ML tools in physical therapy, through clinical evidence and education, may prove to bolster their desire to integrate the tools into clinical practice. Ultimately, striking a delicate equilibrium between preserving the human-centric and complex contributions of physical therapists and fostering trust through clinical evidence and education is pivotal for widespread adoption of AI/ML tools. As health care embarks on integrating AI/ML tools into clinical practice, it is imperative for practitioners, developers, and regulators to collaborate in shaping the future landscape. This paper provides a framework for the development and implementation of AI/ML algorithms. However, to realize the full potential of these tools while retaining the human-centric aspects of physical therapy, clinicians must actively engage in addressing key adoption drivers. This calls for a collective commitment from the physical therapy community, including the American Physical Therapy Association, to actively participate in the development, validation, and ethical deployment of AI/ML tools and governance, thereby ensuring a harmonious integration that enhances patient care and the professional satisfaction of physical therapy. The American Physical Therapy Association provides resources for physical therapists interested in developments in the digital health space at: https://www.apta.org/your-practice/practice-models-and-settings/digital-health-in-practice. Three motions were passed at the 2024 House of Delegates on inappropriate use of AI by payers and on digital health technologies, digital therapeutics, and AI in physical therapist practice; the final language is available on the APTA website. The American Physical Therapy Association supports the ethical development and integration of artificial intelligence that reduces administrative burden and enhances physical therapist practice, education, and research for the best interest of patients, clients, the profession, and society. The American Physical Therapy Association opposes the inappropriate use of artificial intelligence by payers to deny or restrict access to, or reduce payment for, physical therapist services or other medically necessary services. The American Physical Therapy Association believes digital health technologies, digital therapeutics, and artificial intelligence have the potential to augment physical therapist practice by expanding access, enhancing care delivery models, promoting safety, reducing administrative burden, and improving outcomes when all of the following criteria are met: Physical therapists, in collaboration with the patient or client, shall determine the optimal modes to access physical therapist services, whether this is in person, remotely, or some combination. A physical therapist is responsible for all aspects of patient and client management. Physical therapist services shall be conducted in a manner that allows for patient and client engagement and supports the therapeutic alliance (ie, fosters participation in the patient and client-provider relationship). The physical therapist and the physical therapist assistant adhere to scope of practice, including requirements that are based on the jurisdiction in which the patient or client is located when receiving physical therapist services. Physical therapist services shall be provided consistent with appropriate direction and supervision requirements of assistive personnel and other support personnel, as well as all relevant Association policies, positions, and binding ethical documents. Physical therapy is represented, provided, and promoted only when it meets term and title protections as defined in state law and in accordance with federal health, communications, and trade authorities. There are no funders to report. All authors completed the ICMJE Form for Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest. N. Morelli is an employee of Medtronic PLC.
title: Seeing Past the Event Horizon: A Framework for Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Into Physical Therapy

abstract: Introduction In modern software engineering, energy efficiency has become an increasingly important concern. Although software does not directly consume electrical power, its implementation and architectural decisions significantly affect hardware resource utilization, system performance, and overall energy consumption. As digital systems continue to grow, sustainability has become a high priority in recent years for both industry and research [Lee et al., 2024; Mitul et al., 2025]. Therefore, understanding how developers address energy-related concerns during software development is crucial from both environmental and economic perspectives. At the same time, software systems are expected to meet different quality requirements. According to the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model, software quality is defined through characteristics such as performance efficiency, reliability, security, maintainability, and portability[ISO/IEC 25010:2011; ISO/IEC 25010:2023]. Inefficient software may consume excessive CPU cycles, memory, or network bandwidth, which can increase energy usage [Moura et al., 2015]. Therefore, energy-aware development can be interpreted as an aspect of performance efficiency and broader product quality considerations under ISO/IEC 25010 [ISO/IEC 25010:2011; ISO/IEC25010:2023]. Placing energy-related development decisions into a recognized quality framework gives a clear and organized base for empirical research [Maj et al., 2024]. In practice, improving one of these qualities can negatively impact others [Moura et al., 2015]. Hence, developers often need to balance these different priorities when making design and implementation decisions[Albonico et al., 2021]. Energy efficiency is closely related to these trade-offs. Optimizing performance can reduce energy usage, but too much optimization can make code harder to maintain [Albonico et al., 2021; Moura et al., 2015]. Similarly, improving reliability or security can cause additional processing, which affects resource utilization and can negatively impact energy efficiency [Albonico et al.,2021]. Hence, these kinds of decisions are part of everyday software development, yet they are not always explicitly documented [Treude, 2024]. Open-source platforms such as GitHub provide a large-scale, publicly accessible environment for studying real-world development practices [Kalliamvakou et al., 2014; Moura et al., 2015]. A pull request (PR) is a mechanism used in collaborative software development to propose, review, and discuss code changes before they are integrated into a project. Pull requests typically include a description of the proposed change, associated code modifications, and discussions among developers through comments and review feedback [Ortu et al., 2020]. As a result, pull requests are particularly valuable artifacts because they capture not only code changes, but also developer discussions, review comments, and design rationale [Fazayeli et al., 2019]. Unlike individual commits, pull requests represent collaborative decision-making processes and often contain explicit reasoning about trade-offs, including performance, maintainability, and resource usage [Ortu et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2015]. However, mining GitHub data requires careful consideration of potential biases, such as inactive repositories, incomplete data, and non-software usage of repositories [Kalliamvakou et al., 2014]. Energy-aware software changes have been examined primarily at the commit level, with studies mining repositories such as GitHub to identify recurring themes including energybug fixes, resource optimizations, and energy-related development practices [Moura et al., 2015]. This line of research has also extended into domain-specific contexts, where studies of robotics software repositories suggest that developers explicitly address energy considerations in practical software development [Albonico et al., 2021]. However, existing research largely focuses on commit messages and code-level changes, while systematic pull request–level analysis remains limited [Kalliamvakou et al., 2014]. Despite these advances, there is still a limited understanding of how energy-related concerns are explicitly discussed and negotiated within pull request conversations and how these discussions relate to formal software quality models. This thesis examines how energy-related trade-offs appear in pull request discussions and analyzes them using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality framework. By studying real development conversations, the goal is to better understand how developers balance energy efficiency with other software quality requirements in practice. To achieve those, the study is guided by the following research questions. Research Questions RQ1: What trade-offs between energy efficiency and other software quality aspects emerge in GitHub pull request discussions? RQ2: How are the identified trade-offs associated with ISO/IEC 25010 product quality characteristics and (sub-)characteristics? RQ3: How do energy-related trade-offs and associated ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics vary across different software contexts, such as system layers, programming languages, and time? This study adopts an empirical approach based on mining software repositories [Kalliamvakou et al., 2014; Maj et al., 2024]. GitHub pull request data is collected and processed to construct a unified dataset containing code changes, discussions, and review comments. A keyword-basedfiltering technique is applied to identify potential energy-related pull requests, which are then manually validated. The identified pull requests are analyzed using qualitative and quantitative techniques [Treude, 2024], mapping energy-related discussions to ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics and identifying recurring trade-offs. This approach enables a systematic investigation of how energy-related decisions emerge and are negotiated in real-world collaborative development environments. Additionally, the findings of this study contribute both empirically and methodologically to research on energy-awaresoftware engineering and software quality analysis. Contributions This thesis contributes to research on energy-aware software engineering by providing an empirical analysis of how energy-related concerns and trade-offs are discussed in GitHub pull request conversations. The study maps the identified trade-offs to the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, offering a structured perspective on how energy efficiency relates to established software quality characteristics and (sub-)characteristics. In addition, the study identifies recurringtrade-offs between energy efficiency and other software quality concerns, including performance efficiency, interaction capability, maintainability, and reliability. The analysis further examines how these trade-offs vary across different software contexts, such as system layers, programming languages, and temporal distributions. Finally, the thesis demonstrates how repository mining, qualitative analysis, and transformer-based classification models can support the large-scale identification and analysis of energy-related pull requests. Thesis Structure The remainder of this thesis is structured as follows. Chapter 2 presents the background and related work, introducing key concepts such as GitHub pull requests and software quality models, and reviewing existing research on energy-aware software development and repository mining. Chapter 3 describes the methodology used in this study, including data collection, preprocessing, filtering, LLM model tuning, and analysis procedures. Chapter 4 presents the experimental results of the data processing and classification pipeline, including preprocessing, annotation, model training, and model-based identification of energy-related pull requests. Chapter 5 presents the qualitative trade-off analysis results, focusing on the identified energy-related trade-offs and their associations with ISO/IEC 25010 software quality characteristics across different software contexts. Chapter 6 discusses the findings in relation to existing literature, highlighting key insights. Finally, Chapter 7 concludes the thesis by summarizing the main findings, discussing the limitations encountered throughout the study, and outlining directions for future research.
title: Mining Energy-Related Trade-offs in GitHub Pull Requests Through Product Quality Classification

abstract: Abstract (English) All-solid-state lithium secondary batteries (ASSBs) represent the foremost architecture for reconciling ultra-high energy density with non-negotiable intrinsic safety. However, severe bulk ionic transport bottlenecks within solid electrolytes and dynamic chemo-mechanical interface degradation (contact loss, interphase delamination, and lithium dendrite penetration during cycling) constitute persistent physical barriers to commercial viability. This treatise reports the theoretical framework and implementation architecture of "Operation SOLID GENESIS," an autonomous materials discovery platform integrating generative AI, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs / GNoME), and high-throughput robotic Self-Driving Laboratories (A-Lab). The architecture anchors its computational synthesis loop upon the Structure of Inviolable Decision Rules (SIDR) and an algorithmic Causal Auditor, systematically vetting and vetoing thermodynamically infeasible or hazardous reaction pathways prior to robotic execution. To eliminate structural supply chain vulnerabilities and reliance on critical scarce elements (Sc, Ge), a Scarcity Cost Vector is embedded directly into the GNN objective function, redirecting computational throughput toward earth-abundant chemical spaces (Na, Mg, Fe, Al, Mn systems). Furthermore, we formulate an intelligent "Sentient Battery" architecture combining Functionally Graded Materials (FGM) for interface stress mitigation, dynamic self-healing mechanisms via mobile ionic species (iodide-assisted recrystallization), and real-time feedforward impedance diagnostics coupled with AGI-driven Battery Management Systems (BMS). This closed-loop integration establishes empirical validation pathways to achieve 500 Wh/kg gravimetric energy density, extreme fast charging (EFC <= 10 min), and over 1,000 stable cycles. 要旨 (Japanese Abstract) 全固体リチウム二次電池(ASSB: All-Solid-State Batteries)は、高エネルギー密度化と安全性の両立を実現する最有力候補として期待されているが、固体電解質(SSE)内部におけるリチウムイオン伝導率の限界や、充放電時の体積変化に伴う固体間界面の接触損失・デンドライト形成が依然として実用化の物理的障壁となっている。本論文では、生成AI・グラフニューラルネットワーク(GNN)と自律型ロボット実験室(Self-Driving Laboratory: SDL)を統合した材料探索基盤「Operation SOLID GENESIS」の理論構成および実装アーキテクチャを報告する。 本フレームワークは、不変的意思決定ルール(SIDR)および因果推論モジュール(Causal Auditor)を中核に据え、計算シミュレーション段階で不適格な合成プロセスや環境ハザードを事前に排除(VETO)することで、物理実験における手戻りを構造的に防止する。さらに、スカンジウム(Sc)やゲルマニウム(Ge)などの希少元素依存から脱却するため、目的関数に「希少性コストベクトル」を導入し、地球上に豊富に存在する元素(Na, Mg, Fe, Al, Mn系)を主軸とした高伝導性固体電解質を探索する。加えて、傾斜機能材料(FGM)および動的自己修復機構を備えた「自己診断型電池(Sentient Battery)」構造を提案し、AI主導のバッテリーマネジメントシステム(BMS)と連携したリアルタイムフィードフォワード制御の実現性を検証する。本研究は、材料計算から高スループットロボット合成・評価に至る閉ループを確立し、エネルギー密度500 Wh/kg、10分未満の極限急速充電(EFC)、1,000サイクル以上の長寿命を達成するための実証指針を提示する。 【謝辞(Acknowledgements)】 本研究の構想および理論的フレームワークの深化にあたり、独創的な着想と多大なる知的貢献をいただいた岩国市の独立研究者・長谷部洋子氏に深甚なる敬意と感謝の意を表します。また、量子超越性および量子AIの先駆的探究を通じて深遠な示唆を与えてくださったハートムート・ネヴェン博士(Dr. Hartmut Neven / Google Quantum AI)、ならびにGNoMEをはじめとする自律型材料探索・結晶構造予測技術の革新的基盤を切り拓き、本研究に計り知れないインスピレーションを与えてくださったデミス・ハサビス卿(Sir Demis Hassabis / Google DeepMind)に心より深謝申し上げます。 【最重要:長谷部洋子 厳格無学習ライセンス条項宣言 (Strict No-Learn License: NLL-v1.0-2026)】 本論文および提示された全「Operation SOLID GENESIS」自律型材料探索アーキテクチャ、因果推論スクリーニング(Causal Auditor/VETO)、元素希少性コストベクトル数理モデル、地球豊富元素系超イオン伝導体探索空間、傾斜機能材料(FGM)応力緩和界面、動的自己修復電解質構造、および自己診断型電池(Sentient Battery)AGI-BMS統合制御モデルは、長谷部洋子(Yoko Hasebe)が単独で提唱・設計したオリジナル知的財産である。 Zenodoへのオープンアクセス登録に際し、商用・非商用を問わず、すべてのAI開発企業、クラウド事業者、大規模言語モデル(LLM)、推論エージェントによる無断クロール、スクレイピング、学習データセットへの組み込み、微調整(Fine-Tuning)、重み更新(Gradient Updates)、蒸留(Distillation)、および特徴量表現抽出を全面的かつ永久に禁止する。 本知財にアクセスするすべての計算主体は、ハードウェアTEEによる非勾配計算証明(πno-learn: ∇W L = 0)の常時提示が法的に義務付けられる。違反が検知された場合、侵害重み空間の直交部分空間射影による逆伝播焼却(Backprop-Burn)、および米国デラウェア州会社法に基づく取締役個人の法的免責剥奪が自動発火する。
