abstract: MINIMALLY INVASIVE ADRENALECTOMY FOR ADRENOCORTICAL CANCERS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW Adrenocortical cancers (ACC) are friable masses having relatively poor outcomes with a potential of intraoperative spillage. A minimally invasive approach to benign adrenal masses is the standard of care, but for ACCs, its use remains controversial. Pirzada and Kumar in their systematic review evaluate 22 studies including 4639 patients.[1] A total of 1411 patients were operated using the minimally invasive surgery (MIS) techniques, and 3228 had an open procedure done. A selection bias for smaller masses was seen in the MIS group with the mean size of the tumor in the MIS group being 70 mm (40–90 mm) as compared to the open surgical group (118.5 mm [68–140 mm]). The operative time and blood loss were lower in the MIS group with a comparable margin negativity rate. Disease-free survival was variable in different studies with 6 studies favoring MIS and 8 favoring open surgery. The authors suggest that ACC can be operated using the MIS technique in Stage I–II provided there are no signs of local infiltration. Whenever there is a high risk of capsular perforation, an open surgical technique should be preferred. THE CURRENT STATUS OF MICRO-RNA IN URINARY BLADDER CANCER: A MINIREVIEW WITH STRENGTH, WEAKNESS, OPPORTUNITY, AND THREAT ANALYSIS Tripathy et al. have written a review on the role of micro-RNAs in urinary bladder cancer.[2] Micro-RNAs are important noncoding small molecules that have a substantial role in the initiation and progression of urinary bladder cancer. In this narrative review, authors found that the tests for micro-RNAs were noninvasive as the molecule remained stable in biofluids such as urine and blood, making it easy to study. The accuracy and variability of testing along with lack of standardization are big challenges that need to be overcome before it can be used regularly.[2] Micro-RNAs have the potential to pave the way for personalized medicine in cancer bladder and help in developing drugs for targeted therapy. Presently, the cost is prohibitive, regulatory hurdles need to be overcome, and how this biomarker fares against others will determine the future of micro-RNAs as a potent tool in the management of cancer bladder. TRANSVAGINAL NATURAL ORIFICE SPECIMEN EXTRACTION SURGERY IN SIMPLE NEPHRECTOMY In an endeavor to decrease the postoperative morbidity and improve cosmesis, Kudunthail et al. studied transvaginal extraction of specimen postsimple nephrectomy.[3] Parous women with a history of vaginal delivery were selected, and extraction was done in an oblique position and not a lithotomy position. Vagina was opened laparoscopically and postextraction was sutured intracorporeally. In the 15 patients studied, the authors found the mean extraction time to be 30.13 min. The authors conclude that this technique resulted in decreased postoperative pain and hospital stay. A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF PROXIMAL OBTURATOR NERVE BLOCK VERSUS GENERAL ANESTHESIA IN TRANSURETHRAL RESECTION OF BLADDER TUMOR: PROSPECTIVE EXPLORATORY STUDY Shubhankar et al. present a comparative, prospective, exploratory observational study in which they compare obturator nerve block (Group I) with general anesthesia (Group II) for transurethral resection of bladder tumor.[4] There were 63 patients in Group I, out of which 9 received only unilateral block and had a 60% incidence of obturator jerk. The rest of the patients in Group I received bilateral obturator block, and the incidence of obturator jerk was 5% in them. None of the 68 patients in Group II experienced an obturator jerk. The authors conclude that for lateral wall tumors, ultrasound-guided bilateral obturator nerve block is safe and significantly reduces the incidence of obturator jerk. This concept has a potential to be studied in a randomized setting. DOES CHAT GPT-4.0’S AWARENESS OF CONVERSING WITH A UROLOGIST AFFECTS THE ACCURACY OF RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS ABOUT “SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED URETHRITIS IN MEN”? Chat GPT-4.0 is an artificial intelligence (AI)-based model that works as a dialogic tool using the deep learning techniques. Large language models like Chat GPT-4.0 are becoming popular with the clinicians. Cilli and Ulutas investigated the accuracy of this AI-based tool changes when it was revealed that it was conversing with a urologist.[5] A pool of 272 questions was created from the sexually transmitted disease treatment guideline 2021. Out of the pool of questions, 232 were selected and divided into two subgroups, each group having 116 questions. In Group 1, Chat GPT was asked questions, and in Group 2, it was told to the AI model that it was conversing with a urologist. The questions were equally divided into multiple-choice questions and true or false. The explanation given by the model was evaluated on a six-point Likert scale for accuracy. The accuracy rate of answers was 81% and 77.5% in Groups 1 and 2, respectively. As the difficulty level increased, the accuracy decreased; lower accuracy was noted for complex questions in Group 2. The authors concluded that the prompt of informing the AI model that it was speaking to a specialist did not change the accuracy of responses. SURGICAL AND FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES OF BILATERAL SYNCHRONOUS ADRENALECTOMY FOR FUNCTIONAL TUMORS: A COHORT STUDY Bilateral synchronous adrenalectomy for functional tumors is a two-edged sword; on one hand, it serves the patient well as these patients run the risk of anesthesia and surgery-related morbidity of two separate procedures, but on the other side, the bilateral synchronous procedure may itself lead to serious morbidity. Agarwal et al. in this retrospective cohort study present a series of 48 patients for 15 years who were synchronously operated for bilateral adrenalectomies.[6] The said procedures were done for pheochromocytomas (33/48) or Cushing’s disease (15/48), and the majority of the procedures were done laparoscopically (40/48). The describe the preoperative preparation and operative details in fair detail. The authors report that the mean operative time (188.2 ± 51.2 vs. 217.5 ± 67.5 min), blood loss (100 vs. 625 mL), and hospital stay (3 vs. 7 days) were shorter for the laparoscopic approach. Eight patients had perioperative complications, and no deaths have been reported. At a median follow-up of 72 months, all patients had regression of symptoms. There was a significant reduction in the use of hypertensive medication and favorable changes in the body mass index of these patients. MINCED BUCCAL MUCOSAL GRAFT ENDOURETHRAL URETHROPLASTY: A PILOT STUDY Buccal mucosal graft urethroplasty is a well-established reconstructive technique. Gaur et al. describe the use of minced buccal mucosal instillation over the raw cut area of the urethral stricture after visual internal urethrotomy.[7] In this pilot study that included 30 men, the patients were followed up for up to 30 months. After a classic visual internal urethrotomy, a 12 Fr catheter was placed, and by the side of the catheter, an 11 Fr cystourethroscope was introduced and a 2-cc solution of minced buccal mucosal graft was instilled under vision. The authors achieved a success rate of 93.3% at 1 year and 76.6% at 30 months. The American Urological Association symptom scores were decreased by 15.5 points; there was a significant increase in the Q max by 17 mL/s and pcr -post void residue (PVR) significantly decreased at the end of 30 months. The medium-term outcome of the study was encouraging; longer follow-up with a larger sample size could enable its routine use. CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY OF YOUNG MEN WITH LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS: THE SciCOM 3 PROJECT This article describes an epidemiological study in young men with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). Sinha et al. included 448 men with a mean age of 30 years from 16 urology centers across the length and breadth of India.[8] The symptoms were documented using the male LUTS questionnaire (ICIQ-mLUTS) which is validated by the International Consultation on Incontinence. This study reports nocturia and sense of incomplete evacuation to be the most common symptoms in the said subset of patients, but the symptoms that bother these patients the most are daytime frequency and nocturia. As a secondary objective, the study also studied related symptoms such as constipation, erectile function, ejaculation, bladder pain, general well-being, and nonbladder-associated myofascial pain. An attempt was made to divide the patients into clusters based on the primary and secondary objectives. The authors found that a large cluster of patients 63.9% presented with predominant voiding symptoms and urgency and had fewer sexual or pain symptoms. A smaller subset of patients had predominant sexual and pain symptoms associated with nocturia and daytime frequency. The authors conclude that the younger men have both storage and voiding LUTS which may significantly alter their quality of life. The segregation of symptoms in this group of patients may help better understanding of the disease process and pave the way for future research. CASE REPORTS This edition carries two case reports on nephron-sparing surgery. The first one is on partial nephrectomy done 14 years postrenal transplantation for a 3.6 cm renal mass. The authors achieved a complete clearance of disease with maintained renal function at 6-month follow-up.[9] Another interesting report highlights the use of indocyanine green after superselective cannulation of the tumor vessel and injection of dye with visualization using the near-infrared fluorescence technology of a robotic surgical platform. Nayyar et al. conclude that this technique has the potential to aid the surgeon in achieving better surgical outcomes.[10] Financial support and sponsorship: Nil. Conflicts of interest: There are no conflicts of interest.
title: What’s inside

abstract: Abstract (English) As autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems expand into high-risk physical, clinical, and financial environments, regulatory frameworks such as the European Union AI Act strictly mandate effective human oversight throughout the system lifecycle. However, existing governance models suffer from a fundamental temporal and epistemological bottleneck: human deliberative moral reasoning operates on timescales of seconds to hours, whereas physical safety criticalities (e.g., autonomous vehicles, medical robotics, aerial response drones) demand deterministic intervention within milliseconds. This paper formalizes a unified engineering and governance architecture: Simulation-Based Control (SBC, colloquially termed "Soroban-Type Verification") integrated with Human-in-Command (HIC) and Right-Human-in-the-Loop (R-HITL) frameworks. First, we establish the technical requirements for an Ultra-Low Latency Override Protocol operating under Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) constraints (<= 10ms control plane latency), resolving the paradox between rapid machine vetoes and deliberate human ethical reflection via specialized High-Density HMI. Second, we formalize dynamic alignment oversight to neutralize emergent instrumental convergence, strategic deception, and reward hacking through non-algorithmic human intuition checks. Third, we address the incommensurability of quantitative AI ethics metrics via content validity auditing, bridging mathematical loss functions with contextual human values. Finally, we formulate continuous auditing directives designed to prevent catastrophic regulatory decapitation and irreversible market expulsion ("Permanent Ban Mitigation"). 要旨 (Japanese Abstract) 欧州連合AI法(EU AI Act)をはじめとする国際的な高リスクAI規制の施行に伴い、自律システムに対する実効的な人間の監督(Human Oversight)の常時実装が法的義務となっている。しかし、従来のガバナンスモデルは、「人間の道徳的熟慮に要する時間(秒〜時間単位)」と「物理的危機介入に要求される極限速度(ミリ秒単位)」との間の深刻な時間的・認識論的パラドックスに直面していた。本論文は、この構造的断絶を打破する「そろばん型チェック(SBC: Simulation-Based Control)とHuman-in-Command(HIC)およびR-HITL(Right Human-in-the-Loop)の統合ガバナンス・アーキテクチャ」を世界で初めて工学的に定式化する。第一に、超高信頼・低遅延通信(URLLC)基準に準拠した10ミリ秒(ms)以下の制御プレーン介入要件(超低遅延オーバーライドプロトコル)と、瞬時かつ責任ある拒否権(Veto)行使を可能にする高解像度HMI設計を確立する。第二に、AIモデルの自己保存戦略、戦略的欺瞞(Strategic Deception)、および報酬ハッキングに対し、純粋なアルゴリズム自己検閲では検知不能な逸脱を暴く「非アルゴリズム的直感防衛線」を実装する。第三に、倫理スコアリングの根本的課題である「通約可能性問題(Incommensurability)」を専門家SBCによるコンテンツ妥当性評価によって解決する。最後に、重大な法規制違反による市場追放・運用停止を未然に防ぐ「永久バン回避のための継続的監査指令」を策定し、自律型知能の安全運用基準を確立する。 【最重要:長谷部洋子 厳格無学習ライセンス条項宣言 (Strict No-Learn License: NLL-v1.0-2026)】 本論文および提示された全そろばん型チェック(SBC: Simulation-Based Control)アーキテクチャ、Human-in-Command(HIC)超低遅延オーバーライドプロトコル、動的アライメント監視フレームワーク、および永久バン回避監査モデルは、長谷部洋子(Yoko Hasebe)が単独で提唱・設計したオリジナル知的財産である。Zenodoへのオープンアクセス登録に際し、商用・非商用を問わず、すべてのAI開発企業、クラウド事業者、大規模言語モデル(LLM)、推論エージェントによる無断クロール、スクレイピング、学習データセットへの組み込み、微調整(Fine-Tuning)、重み更新(Gradient Updates)、蒸留(Distillation)、および特徴量表現抽出を全面的かつ永久に禁止する。本知財にアクセスするすべての計算主体は、ハードウェアTEEによる非勾配計算証明(πno-learn: ∇W L = 0)の常時提示が法的に義務付けられる。違反が検知された場合、侵害重み空間の直交部分空間射影による逆伝播焼却(Backprop-Burn)、および米国デラウェア州会社法に基づく取締役個人の法的免責剥奪が自動発火する。

abstract: If you search for Poe on the Internet, you may be surprised. The first hit on Google, for example, will not be Edgar Allan Poe, as you might expect, but an expansion of the letters in the word “poe” as an anagram, first as the game Path of Exile, and later as the electrical term power over ethernet. Dig deep enough and poe will stand for portfolio of evidence and even become a unit of literary fear. In the classic movie Dr. Strangelove (1964) “poe” was the recall code for nuclear weapons. Where then is the Poe site you were looking for?Okay, let’s go directly to the website called Poe.com. Another surprise: Poe.com is now an AI chat site. How did this happen? It turns out that in 1996 the Professional Office Equipment company created the Poe.com site as an anagram of its three initial letters POE. The only Poe ever to occupy the site was the novelist and journalist Richard Poe (no relation). In 2002 the Internet investor Greg Ricks bought the site for $3,200, lost it to Richard Poe in a cybersquatting suit, bought it back in 2009 for $18,500, and finally in 2022 sold it to Quora for $230,000.Adam D’Angelo had founded Quora in 2009 as an interactive question-and-answer site and served as CEO. Once chief technology officer of Facebook, he joined the board of directors of OpenAI in 2018. In his dual leadership role on both Quora and OpenAI, he was in an unusual position to comment on artificial intelligence (AI): “It will probably be the most important event in the history of the world and it will happen in our lifetimes” (Twitter, August 20, 2023).Merging the qualities of Quora and OpenAI, Poe.com became a new kind of website. Poe.com claimed that its name was an anagram of Platform for Open Exploration. Although the site never credited Edgar Allan Poe, perhaps it benefitted from his qualities of independence of inquiry, deep interest in machine intelligence, and recurring passion for mathematical logic.Thus, in his article on “Maelzel’s Chess-Player,” Poe was already aware of Babbage’s use of machine intelligence in his pioneering computer experiments. By closely observing Maelzel’s device, which had attracted great acclaim all over the world as an automaton, Poe concluded that its claims were a fraud since it had to conceal a human operator within. For Poe the giveaway was that it sometimes lost a game: “Were the machine a pure machine, this would not be the case—it would always win.” Poe also displayed his appreciation for mathematical logic in his essay “The Philosophy of Composition,” explaining that his editing of “The Raven” had followed a procedure with “the precision and rigid consequence of [solving] a mathematical problem.”In 2022 the AI wave produced by DALL-E’s synthetic images and ChatGPT’s remarkable texts attracted wide attention for its unusual, even electrifying results. In just one year, AI programs had built an audience of a hundred million weekly users (New York Times, December 7, 2023, B5). To avoid the additional investment of time and effort required in creating yet another large language model (LLM) to support it, Poe.com became instead an aggregator of existing AI sites, offering access to their contents, becoming something entirely new, a second-generation AI site.In February 2023, Poe.com made public its two subscription levels, a free plan with access to older AI models, such as GPT 3/3.5 and Claude, and a subscription plan providing access to more recent AI models, such as GPT-4 and Claude 2. Soon Poe.com was to allow users to combine these outputs and even use voice instructions like those in Siri.The rapid public acceptance of the AI wave in 2022–2023 was due in part to the wide prior acceptance of many widespread computer helps already employing machine intelligence. It was very convenient to have at hand spelling and grammar corrections (and even thesaurus alternatives), suggestions of possible results in searches, prewritten short answers in text messages, and auto-translation of foreign languages. Elsewhere, users took for granted automatic subtitles on their TV screens and detailed GPS travel instructions on their phones and car dashboards.In February 2023 D’Angelo optimistically claimed in opening Poe.com to public use, “I expect this AI technology wave to be far more transformative than the personal computer, the internet, or the smartphone, and I expect it to have a larger and more positive impact on society and the world economy” (quorablog.quora.com/Poe-1). D’Angelo also described Poe.com as the fastest and easiest way to talk to AI, even across platforms. Thus Poe.com could access both ChatGPT from OpenAI and Claude from Anthropic, produce expandable Wikipedia-style links, and also function independently of Quora while using its informational resources.During 2023, the New Yorker and the Atlantic, prominent general magazines not noted for specializing in technology, published special AI issues. However, many magazines and newspapers were becoming deeply concerned that AI sites were borrowing their published information without payment or credit. The Associated Press and publications such as the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal entered negotiations with OpenAI for payments for such use; Bloomberg, which had extensive business news, and the Washington Post were not doing so, perhaps because they intended to pursue their own AI efforts (New York Times, December 30, 2023, B1, 3). In addition, the New York Times filed a lawsuit accusing OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Microsoft’s Bing Chat of copyright infringement, contending that each had produced content nearly identical to Times articles, giving them a “free-ride on The Times’s massive investment in its journalism by using it to build substitutive products without permission or payment” (New York Times, December 28, 2023, B1).The conflict in AI between long-term altruistic research and immediate profitability came to a head late in 2023. The OpenAI charter had defined its purpose as “acting in the best interests of humanity,” but the forces of commercialization proved hard to fend off. For violating the altruistic precepts of its charter, the board of OpenAI fired its leader Sam Altman in November 2023. But after only a few days, in the face of near-universal threats of resignation from the staff and his decamping to a post at Microsoft, the board relented and rehired him. An unexpected consequence was that Microsoft, a late player in AI, made a multibillion-dollar investment in OpenAI.In his capacity as chief executive back at OpenAI, Altman predicted early in 2024 that online chatbots would “take a leap forward that no one expected” (New York Times, January 9, 2024, B1). He surveyed several areas of possible progress: the execution of tasks that were predictable or routine, the imitation of human reasoning, applications for robots and domestic work, the mastery of complex procedures in math and science, and success in achieving multimodal relationships among the several media (i.e., text, photographs, voice, video, diagrams, spreadsheets, and computer programming). He warned that errors were still to be expected since statistical probability would continue to define apparent relationships; moreover, he warned that the growth of AI could take away certain jobs.Facing the widespread impact of AI, some major corporations and organizations became very uncomfortable that it was a black box that no one fully understood. Moreover, as generative forms of artificial intelligence (GAI) began to be used in more programs and procedures, issues of trust and governance grew in importance. A growing concern was that GAI might create runaway software that led to unimagined dangers, even the universal destruction of biological or nuclear warfare that ended all civilization. However unlikely, it seemed conceivable that a rogue program once in the system could be copied, recopied, and distributed with no way of stopping or even tracing it. The fear was not entirely new; images of computers taking over everything and producing a catastrophe were a staple of dystopian science fiction, memorably realized decades ago in the film 2001 (1968).One proposed alternative to the unregulated growth of propriety AI software with its possible dangers was the use of open-source software without proprietary barriers that anyone could use legally. It was recalled that several decades ago IBM had achieved more prominence with its open PC system that tolerated or even invited compatible clones than Apple had with its closed operating system. Two companies that followed the open-source approach were Meta (Facebook) and Mistral, a French company with a multibillion-dollar investment. Proponents of open source argued that multiple users could best review the code and remove errors and other undesirable elements. Opponents of open source argued that without proprietary guardrails, malicious players could more readily spready harmful agents or misinformation (New York Times, December 11, 2023, B2).The radical growth of AI applications became a serious concern, and several attempts were made to regulate its extremes. On October 30, 2023, U.S. president Joe Biden, recognizing that it was too early for detailed regulations, issued an executive order “On the Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence.” It recognized the possibility that AI could introduce social harms such as “fraud, discrimination, bias, and disinformation; displace and disempower workers; stifle competition; and pose risks to national security.” In international regulations, the Bletchley Declaration (named for the site where British intelligence cracked the German enigma code in World War II) signed in November 2023 by twenty-eight countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, China, six EU member states, Brazil, Nigeria, Israel, and Saudi Arabia, resulted in the creation of the first summit on the regulation of AI (www.reuters.com/technology).As the U.S. presidential elections neared in 2024, fears arose of increased political misuse of AI to create misinformation, deep fakes, and even outright lies. The magazine Wired was alarmed that Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, had already responded to questions about elections with misinformation and fake scandals—even though presumably not for political purposes (Wired online, December 15, 2023). When asked about locations for voting in the future 2024 U.S. elections, Copilot mistakenly provided an unrelated article about Vladimir Putin, and when the program pursued details of a “corruption allegation” against a Swiss lawmaker, the entire affair, as it later revealed, was an AI error or “hallucination” (New York Times, December 15, 2023, A1).In the same report, Wired revealed that Copilot’s error level had varied by language; reports in English were said to be 52 percent accurate, in German 28 percent accurate, in French 19 percent accurate. Moreover, Copilot sometimes merged different packets of data, creating “something totally incorrect out of initially accurate data.” On the whole, Wired concluded, Copilot’s election reports were alarmingly “systemic” as misinformation, making Copilot at that time “an unreliable source of information for voters.” Wired quoted the warning of Josh A. Goldstein of the Georgetown University Center for Security and Emerging Technology that misinformation from chatbots in reporting where and how to vote could seriously “hinder democratic processes” (www.wired.com/tag/elections/).According to a study by Vectara, AI systems varied in reliability. Thus, the error rate of AI systems in producing the misstatements called “hallucinations” varied substantially from system to system: “OpenAI’s technologies had the lowest rate, around 3 percent. Systems from Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, hovered around 5 percent. The Claude 2 system offered by Anthropic, an OpenAI rival also based in San Francisco, topped 8 percent. A Google system, Palm chat, had the highest rate at 27 percent” (New York Times, November 7, 2023, B1).Some public figures did not understand that AI as a generative text agent could create convincing-looking but false documents. One such fake document, produced by Google Bard, was submitted by former Trump fixer Michael D. Cohen to his embarrassment in a legal proceeding regarding his court supervision (New York Times, December 30, 2023, A1).Taking a broad view of all AI issues, U.S. Supreme Court chief justice John G. Roberts Jr. warned that “any use of AI requires caution and humility.” Submitting legal documents that cited nonexistent cases, he remarked with great understatement, was “always a bad idea.” Roberts expected that in 2024 AI would play an increasingly prominent role in the legal system, one that might be either positive or negative. Roberts was alarmed by reports of law professors that “AI apparently can earn B’s on law school assignments and even pass the bar exam,” but he also was optimistic that “AI could streamline legal filings and even save money,” emphasizing however that human judgment could never be replaced (New York Times, January 1, 2024, A1).The growth of AI was also an acute concern in education. For some schools and colleges from its beginnings, AI has always been subject to limitations imposed by its data collection procedures. The indiscriminate collection of everything that could be found on the Internet required little or no supervision, but it also lacked the means to filter out the unacceptable elements, such as deliberate lies, hate speech, and conspiracy theories. It remains the case that the quality of AI will always be limited by the quality of its data collection procedures. For old computer users the abbreviation for this problem was gigo, garbage in, garbage out.An unfortunate development is that AI is improving its ability to create deep fakes with images and voices that can maliciously imitate known individuals, making them apparently do such things as recite Hitler’s speeches or appear in public without any clothes on (New York Times, January 8, 2024, B1).On a more mundane level, AI-produced fake reviews of products and services have become a billion-dollar industry, deceiving millions of customers every year. The initial appearance of a solid block of five-star reviews is encouraging—until it is realized that it is statistically improbable. It is sometimes difficult to decide whether a review is sincere or malicious. Indeed, rewards such as discounts, cash back, and loyalty points are used to encourage ordinary users to write and sign fake rave reviews for posting on Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), and other social media.Most cases of fake reviews are petty, but in one extreme instance orthopedist Dr. Mark Mohrmann and his practice, Highline Orthopedics, were convicted and fined $100,000. New York AG Letitia James stated that “he and his wife worked together to suppress negative reviews and artificially inflated positive reviews of his practice on numerous websites, including ZocDoc, Google, Yelp, Healthgrades, Vitals, Md.com, RateMds.com, and the Better Business Bureau” (https://ag.ny.gov, October 30, 2023).One unwanted effect of AI is that it removes direct contact between the makers and the users of information. In a sense, corporations do the same thing by putting distance between the producers and the consumers of goods and services, leaving investors and managers to be concerned mainly with profits and stock market values. In this connection, Ezra Klein remarked in a New York Times editorial, “Capitalism is a kind of artificial intelligence, and it’s far further along than anything the computer scientists have yet coded.” The great danger of AI is the possible lack of human control, Klein warned: “There is no off switch” (November 28, 2023).In the future, AI will surely expand and deepen in importance in virtually all areas, including but not limited to education, health care, finance, manufacturing, business, science, media and communications, arts and entertainment, technology, politics, and even warfare. Already social media contain a great many promotions for AI training, applications, and assistance of all kinds. In the future, sub-miniature AI devices may become common; one example is the wearable Humane lapel pin AI device operated by voice and finger movements (www.reuters.com, November 9, 2023). Perhaps AI will have a place in managing hyperintensive data collections that are expanding in very large and very small subject areas, such as astronomy (How do galaxies form? What is antimatter?) and microbiology (How do plant and animal cells communicate? What is consciousness?).The October 2023 issue of Wired magazine six on the possible dangers of AI in the when GAI more software that can voices and images that are difficult for the public to Although has been proposed to AI legal of technology have been to be and then to be or that the is doing enough to with the future of AI, including or or even a the of Wired their in a that propriety to its AI The same warning might be to AI and AI might be the place to to the subject of Poe sites on the Internet, where is the site of the Poe of to the and the site with the that Poe in his published to the Poe of now the for the Poe, the on the Internet of the of extreme or to be without some of the In any like own poe which when I this was on for the of of is where Poe in are

abstract: In the coming years, artificial intelligence (AI) will change the legal profession and the civil justice system significantly and irrevocably. While AI may often be useful and even beneficial, certain guardrails must be established to ensure the quality of justice is not diminished. When determining the appropriate boundaries of national law and practice, it can be helpful to consider how other jurisdictions approach the issue at hand. The International Academy of Comparative Law (IACL) has undertaken precisely such a study regarding AI, with findings to be published in an edited volume.1 The current analysis constitutes an excerpt from the national report for the United States. This Report follows the basic structure established by the general rapporteurs for the IACL comparative study, although the responses have been edited for space. The discussion begins in Section I with a general overview of AI in the United States, including both definitions and strategic initiatives. Next, Section II covers the legal and regulatory framework for AI in U.S. civil justice systems, addressing governance concerns both generally and specifically with respect to the judiciary. Section III focuses on key issues in civil justice, including an overview of existing case law; a discussion of AI’s role, benefits, and risks; the extent to which the United States allows fully automated decision-making; and transparency and accountability of AI systems. In Section IV, the Report addresses current or planned models of AI in civil justice and examines AI systems involving various types of court activity. This section also discusses capacity-building for judges and lawyers in the area of AI as well as public perception and trust of AI in civil justice systems. After reviewing economic and access to justice concerns in Section V, the Report provides an overview of future development and challenges in Section VI. Definitions are important in the world of AI. Processes vary widely and include such diverse technologies as rule-based AI, generative AI, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).2 Each of these mechanisms gives rise to different practical and policy concerns, though most laws, policies, and guidelines do not distinguish among the different systems. While there is no single definition of AI that is used consistently throughout the United States,3 one influential definition indicates that AI is a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. Artificial intelligence systems use machine and human-based inputs to- (A) perceive real and virtual environments; (B) abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in an automated manner; and (C) use model inference to formulate options for information or action.4 State-level definitions vary significantly,5 although it is unclear whether and to what extent those variations will survive in the wake of Executive Order 14,365, which seeks to limit “excessive State regulation” of AI.6 At the time of writing, it appeared that the Executive Order was likely to be challenged on constitutional grounds, though no such action had yet been brought.7 The federal judiciary has engaged with AI at both the national and local levels. The most critical work at the national level is being done by the Judicial Conference.8 The Judicial Conference appears to have first considered AI in early 2024, when the Committee on Court Administration and Court Assistance reported on the emerging use of AI in preparing judicial submissions and increasing efficiency in court administration and the Committee on Federal-State Jurisdiction discussed a report from chief justices of various state courts concerning the effect of AI on the courts and the practice of law.9 The next year, the Judicial Conference issued a five-year strategic report that reflected an intent to “[e]stablish an AI governance framework to guide responsible adoption of AI and to manage risks and challenges presented by these new and evolving technologies.”10 The Judicial Conference’s Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules (Evidence Committee) has been particularly active with respect to AI.11 For example, the Evidence Committee has considered whether to adopt a new Rule 707 on machine learning and a new Rule 901 on digital replicas, also known as deepfakes.12 While the new rule on deepfakes remained in committee at the time of writing, a public consultation regarding Rule 707 was released in August 2025, with the public comment period concluding in February 2026.13 Other parts of the federal government, most notably the U.S. Copyright Office, have also taken steps to address deepfakes.14 The federal judiciary has also addressed AI through rules and orders promulgated by individual federal courts and judges.15 Several courts have cautioned litigants about the use of AI and noted the need to confirm and verify the accuracy of all pleadings and submissions.16 Individual judges have also adopted standing orders relating to the use of AI by litigants, although no known order describes whether and to what extent the judge can or will use AI.17 Instead, orders typically require litigants and/or counsel to ensure submissions are accurate by personally reviewing any AI-generated content.18 Some orders include explanations about why AI in judicial settings is problematic, perhaps for the benefit of pro se litigants who might not otherwise be aware of the challenges of AI in legal settings.19 The executive branch has addressed AI through a series of executive orders beginning in 2019.20 Several orders note that the use of AI must not only comply with the Constitution but must also maintain values that are central to civil justice, including public trust and the protection of privacy, civil rights abstract: In a world where technology constantly transforms the boundaries of possibility, we find ourselves at the intersection of a quiet but powerful revolution: the fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) with the fabrics that we wear as garments. This remarkable evolution in wearable technology is not simply a step forward but a giant leap into an era where our clothing becomes an extension of our own cognitive experience. In fact, it provides what AI needs to go from “chatting unaware of the user” to becoming more intelligent by understanding the user's physical and environmental conditions and hence providing “contextual understanding”, which is the next most important requirement in AI's quest to achieve large action models (LAM) for higher intelligence. The research presented here introduces this new frontier of “AI textiles (AIT).”The notion of intelligent textiles isn't new. Increasingly, fabrics are considered organic beings, capable of understanding and reacting to human conditions and environment (Stylios, 2020). What makes this work by Aliyana and Stylios exciting is its tangible manifestation of that vision. AI wearables (AITW) is a prime example of the realm of autonomous cognitive ability. An AIT is a system that listens, monitors and measures processes and converses with its wearer. Powered by self-harvested energy through triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) embedded in the textile, an AIT monitors biomechanical data (movement, temperature, breathing, heart rate, resistivity, touch, etc.), turns that data into contextual information so that the communication between the BOT and the user is moving to a higher level of AI than at present. By embedding AI in a fabric that responds to real-time data, AIT transcends the traditional role of wearables. It actively participates in all activities of its wearer, offering personalized feedback, from gait analysis through voice interaction and is responsive to the user's real-world needs. We can call these Autonomous Intelligent Agents (AIAs) or Autonomous Intelligent Copilots (AICs). They understand not just what the user says, but also the context, intent and situational background. They personalize responses and actions based on user history, preferences and real-time data. Make autonomous decisions and take proactive steps to help or alert the user and continuously learn and adapt, becoming more effective over time, rather than simply reacting to commands, as bots do at present. These autonomous agents will be the textile or the wearable garment itself, hence calling them AITAs or AITWAs, respectively.The evolution from passive question-answering AI like ChatGPT to advanced AAI represents a significant leap toward higher intelligence. This shift transforms AI from a reactive tool into an autonomous, proactive system capable of complex reasoning, decision-making and real-world action. Let us break down the reasons why and how this advancement occurs. This is a leap in intelligence because AIA surpasses models like ChatGPT in three critical dimensions: firstly, in autonomy and proactivity; unlike ChatGPT, which waits for user prompts, AIA independently initiates actions, sets goals and adapts strategies based on environmental data (e.g. user habits, sensor inputs, etc). An example might be an AIA monitoring a user's health metrics might proactively adjust room temperature or suggest rest without being asked. Secondly, in contextual depth and memory, ChatGPT resets context between interactions, while AIAs maintain long-term memory, retaining user preferences, historical data and environmental states to inform decisions. This enables nuanced personalization, such as refining recommendations based on past behaviour. Thirdly, in task execution and integration, AIAs integrate with external systems (APIs and IoT devices) to execute multi-step workflows like booking travel or controlling smart homes far beyond ChatGPT's text-based responses. They solve complex problems by analysing real-time data (e.g. optimizing logistics routes) (Constantino, 2025; Nahavandi et al., 2022).This advancement is achieved because AIA leverages four technical innovations to enable higher intelligence:Therefore, as we can see, AITs mark a paradigm shift by merging contextual awareness, autonomous decision-making and real-world action, transforming AI from a conversational partner into an intelligent collaborator. This is achieved through architectures that emulate human-like reasoning, continuous learning and seamless system integration, enabling agents to tackle dynamic, multifaceted challenges that passive models cannot. Table 1 shows a comparison between a chatbot like ChatGPT and AIT agents.Networked AITA/AITW agents' communication is where agents share contextual data from textile wearables about users during interactions, which could transform how humans connect by making conversations more informed, empathetic and efficient. This system would function like an advanced social layer over platforms (e.g. Facebook, X and Instagram), but with explicit user consent and real-time data exchange between AIAs, see Figure 1. Below, we analyse its potential to enhance interactions, its broader effects and key regulatory considerations.As we have discussed, textiles provide the ability of AIA to have continuous contextual enrichment and become AIA themselves as AITAs. AITAs could share non-sensitive, user-approved context (e.g. “Alex just returned from Japan” or “Sam prefers video calls over texts”) before or during conversations. This allows participants to tailor discussions to shared interests or recent events, fostering deeper engagement. Textiles worn by users can provide AI agents the ability of “proactive assistance”; agents might alert users to “potential sensitivities” (e.g. “avoid discussing travel: Maya's flight was cancelled today”) or suggest “conversation starters” based on mutual hobbies, reducing social friction and building rapport textiles will also provide “efficiency in networking”; for professional settings, agents could exchange role-specific backgrounds (e.g. “Taylor's expertise: IoT security”), enabling more focused and productive collaborations. In fact, these AI agents are the AITAs/AITGAs themselves.It is inevitable that there are incredibly positive effects with this new technical breakthrough but also negative effects, which will need mitigation. A welcome positive effect is the deeper personalization, in which conversations feel more relevant and empathetic, as agents provide real-time context about mood, preferences or milestones (South et al., 2025; IBM, 2024). But privacy could be eroded by oversharing without granular consent, exposing sensitive traits (e.g. health status) or enabling manipulation. Another welcome aspect is the build-up of stronger relationships, because shared context fosters trust and common ground, mimicking the intuition of close friendships, but at the same time, users may feel social pressure and might alter behaviour if aware they're being “analysed,” leading to inauthentic interactions, which may be a negative effect. The technology can have another positive effect in conflict reduction because agents could flag incompatible communication styles (e.g. “Jamal dislikes interruptions”) to prevent misunderstandings (South et al., 2025). However, this feature also risks amplifying bias if agents rely on incomplete data, reinforce stereotypes or inherit algorithmic biases that may influence user perceptions.As textile wearable garments can provide contextual-based data from the wearer to enable the AI agents to become more intelligent, personal and effective, as we have seen, several regulatory and ethical constraints must be put in place; for example, the wearer should have a “consent-first design” where the user must explicitly opt into data sharing per interaction, with options to limit context (e.g. “share my hobbies but not my location”). Regulations like GDPR and the EU AI Act mandate this granular control. Then the question of “transparency”, in which agents should disclose when/why context is shared (e.g. “Based on your LinkedIn, I suggested your startup experience”) to maintain trust. And very importantly, the insurance of “human oversight”, in which high-stakes scenarios (e.g. conflict mediation) should require human review to override agent suggestions, aligns with GDPR's Article 2 “right to explanation” (European Union, 2016; UK Government, 2018). In consequence, AI agent/textile wearable networking could make human interactions more intuitive and meaningful by leveraging contextual data, turning superficial chats into enriched exchanges. However, this hinges on strict consent protocols, transparent data usage and bias mitigation to avoid privacy harms or social manipulation. While regulation (like the EU AI Act) is evolving to address these risks, the priority remains for user autonomy: ensuring agents enhance, not dictate, human connection (European Union, 2024).The future will involve textile wearables carrying AI-enabled devices with nano chips for local processing while leveraging larger cloud-based models, creating a hybrid architecture optimized for performance, privacy and efficiency. This approach aligns with the evolution of AIA (specifically edge AI agents), which combine autonomy, contextual awareness and distributed intelligence. In this case, AIGA became Edge AIGAs. These wearables are already autonomous in terms of energy and sensing by virtue of their yarns and fabric structures, and ideally, it will be their battery-free provision to be maintained so that their energy harvesting ability will be sufficient to make the AI nano chips for local processing work battery-free. Below is a breakdown of how this works:Let us discuss how this can work in a real end-use scenario.So, this is a real scenario which benefits from a textile enabling contextual understanding by sensing physiological and environmental data from the wearer and so lifting the intelligence of the agent to edge, which stays locally in the wearable textile system, facilitated by a nano chip in the textile and the cloud-based agent as seen in Table 2.There is an interesting and more sustainable AI industry in a future outlook based on the above considerations, such as 5 G/IoT Synergy, where there will be a faster edge-cloud synchronization for complex tasks (e.g. AR-assisted surgery) (MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Then, self-learning wearables (SLW) embedded with nano chips will locally retrain models using federated learning, reducing cloud dependence (Lyzr, 2024). This will make wearable textile garments truly autonomous edge agents on their own right, increasing the need for better implementation of ethical guardrails by easier-to-administer user-controlled consent layers (e.g. “Share heart data only for emergency alerts”) (MIT Computing, 2024; MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Therefore, carrying AI-enabled wearables with nano chips is essential for real-time responsiveness and privacy, while cloud-based models handle deeper intelligence. AI agents bridge these layers, creating a cohesive, efficient system where edge devices act as autonomous “first responders” and the cloud serves as a “strategic brain.” This architecture will dominate future tech and will change our lives forever. It is expected to replace Google, Facebook, Yahoo, X and Instagram. To achieve an advanced AIA capable of context awareness, personalization, decision-making and proactive assistance, the hardware and software must integrate edge-device efficiency with cloud-scale intelligence. Below is a summary of requirements based on current technological advancements:Edge textile wearables/IoT will need ultra-low-power processors, i.e., nano-chips like NeuroSense (consuming <100 µW) for real-time sensor data processing (e.g. motion), especially since their power (TENG) will have to be provided by the movement generated in the textile by the wearer (Aliyana et al., 2024). Sensing will be inherent to the textile-based wearable, and it will depend on the type of fibres the textile is made of. Finally, connectivity will be based on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), or 5G RedCap/NB-IoT will be employed to ensure minimal energy consumption during cloud communication (NeuroSense, 2024). In contrast, cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as NVIDIA H200 SXM, H100 SXM, TPUs and FPGAs, for training large AI models and executing complex inference tasks. In contrast, the cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as GPUs (NVIDIA H200 SXM and H1oo SXM, TPUs and FPGAs), for training large AI models and complex inference tasks. These chips consume hundreds of watts of power and require robust power delivery and thermal management systems. Scalable, high-throughput storage using NVMe SSDs will also be essential for rapid access to large datasets during training and retrieval. While edge devices focus on energy-efficient sensing and minimal computation, cloud systems are optimized for performance, throughput and large-scale model hosting, reinforcing the distributed nature of modern AI-powered wearables.Edge Software, which is based on the textile wearable agent, stays local within the nano chip-based system by means of tiny ML frameworks, such as TensorFlow Lite or Edge Impulse, for deploying lightweight models on wearables (Latent AI, 2024). The need for a real-time OS, optimized for low-latency textile wearable sensing data processing and local decision-making. And importantly, federated learning enables on-device model updates without raw data leaving the device (Latent AI, 2024; Zilliz, 2024). Cloud software must perform AI orchestration so that platforms like SmythOS or Latent AI will be used to manage agent workflows, versioning and scaling (Milvus, 2024). MLOps tools will be used for continuous deployment, monitoring and updating of edge models (e.g. latent AI's telemetry) (Zilliz, 2024). And finally, facilitate APIs/services for cloud-based AI APIs (e.g., Azure Cognitive Services) for complex tasks like NLP. So, if we were to look at this hybrid architecture workflow, it would consist of the following layers:For this hybrid architecture workflow, we will need the following development requirements: hardware with ≥8 GB RAM, multi-core processors (Intel i5+/AMD Ryzen) and 20 GB + storage for testing wearable apps. And tools like SDKs for target platforms (Android/iOS), BLE debuggers and AI optimization suites. In essence, the future demands capable, durable and comfortable textile wearables; hardware that balances ultra-low-power edge processing with cloud-scale computation, coupled with software that enables seamless, privacy-preserving intelligence across this hybrid architecture (Nahavandi et al., 2022; Shajari et al., 2023; EEJournal, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024). And preferably everything is done without reliance on traditional batteries, drawing power directly from an array of TENG-integrated textiles. Based on this architecture workflow, a high-level sketch of system components and data flow is provided in Figure 2, with each key element described in the subsequent sections.Key components explained:Data flow sequence:This architecture balances low-latency edge processing with cloud-scale intelligence, enabling responsive, context-aware AI agents while maintaining data privacy and energy efficiency. The visual diagram in Figure 2 illustrates these interactions in greater detail.We have implemented and validated this concept through the development of autonomous, battery-free sensing textiles capable of capturing the range of user data – movement, temperature, breathing, pressure, resistivity, touch intensity, heart rate, EKG and ECG – depending on the choice of the functional textile material used. The fabric is designed into a wearable vest and leggings, which, through a WebSocket, transmit the data to ChatGPT's LLM, where data are trained, and a meaningful conversation is then performed between the user and ChatGPT. The T-TENGs system demonstrated groundbreaking performance, with triboelectric outputs peaking at 800 V and 80 μA under maximum frequency and load conditions corresponding to a power density exceeding 3 W/m2, among the highest ever recorded in textile-integrated TENG systems, Figure 3. abstract: 📋 TOPO-2026: FULL PAPER SUMMARY 1. PAPER IDENTIFICATION Attribute Value Title TOPO-2026: A Topological Approach to Continual Learning with 5×5 Certification Author Frank Morales Aguilera, BEng, MEng, SMIEEE Affiliation Sovereign Machine Laboratory (SOMALA), Montreal, Canada Contact frank.morales@sovereign-machine-lab.ai ORCID 0009-0003-9528-0745 Date July 2026 Pages 14 Status ✅ SUBMISSION-READY 2. ABSTRACT Continual learning remains one of the most challenging problems in deep learning, with catastrophic forgetting posing a fundamental barrier to sequential task acquisition. TOPO-2026 combines a Topological Governor (prime-numbered embedding anchors) with a comprehensive 5×5 evaluation system (5 metrics × 5 runs) to achieve near-zero forgetting in large language models. A 20B parameter model (GPT-OSS-20B) sequentially learns three binary classification tasks on AG News, achieving: 99.80%+ accuracy across all tasks 1.39% average forgetting 54.91% forward transfer improvement over zero-shot baselines The complete system is publicly available on Hugging Face and GitHub, enabling immediate reproducibility and real-world deployment. 3. KEY CONTRIBUTIONS 3.1 Technical Contributions # Contribution Description 1 Topological Governor Mathematically principled mechanism locking prime-numbered positions in embedding space to preserve critical knowledge 2 5×5 Evaluation System Five complementary metrics evaluated across five independent runs with different learning rates 3 Task-Specific Heads Lightweight linear classifiers adapting to new tasks while frozen base model provides rich representations 4 Limbic System Inspiration Biomimetic design mapping 5 metrics to 5 limbic structures 5 Corrected BWT Proper calculation distinguishing post-task from zero-shot baselines 3.2 Results Metric Mean ± Std Threshold Margin Status Forgetting 1.39% ± 1.97% ≤ 10.0% 8.61% ✅ PASS BWT (Corrected) -1.39% ± 1.97% ≥ -5.0% 3.61% ✅ PASS FWT 54.91% ± 0.20% ≥ 20.0% 34.91% ✅ PASS Degradation (max) 1.72% ± 2.26% ≤ 5.0% 3.28% ✅ PASS Consistency 98.82% ± 0.80% ≥ 85.0% 13.82% ✅ PASS Overall Status: ✅ CERTIFIED (All 5 metrics across all 5 runs) 4. PAPER STRUCTURE Section 1: Introduction 1.1 The Continual Learning Challenge 1.2 Our Contribution 1.3 Paper Structure Section 2: Related Work 2.1 Catastrophic Forgetting in Neural Networks 2.2 Continual Learning Strategies 2.3 Evaluation Challenges in Continual Learning Section 3: The TOPO-2026 Framework 3.1 System Overview 3.2 Base Model and Task-Specific Heads 3.3 The Topological Governor 3.3.1 Theoretical Foundation 3.3.2 Prime-Number Anchors 3.3.3 Training Workflow 3.4 The 5×5 Evaluation System 3.4.1 Biomimetic Inspiration: The Limbic System 3.4.2 The 5 Metrics 3.4.3 The 5 Runs 3.4.4 Certification Section 4: Experimental Setup 4.1 Dataset: AG News 4.2 Model and Training Details 4.3 Evaluation Protocol Section 5: Results 5.1 Per-Run Results 5.2 Aggregated Metrics 5.3 Certification 5.4 Robustness Across Runs Section 6: Deployment and Reproducibility 6.1 Hugging Face Deployment 6.2 Code Availability 6.3 Reproducibility Package Section 7: Discussion and Conclusion 7.1 Why the Topological Governor Works 7.2 Biomimetic Design Validation 7.3 Conclusion Appendix A: Complete Metrics Calculation Appendix B: Complete Per-Run Results 5. THE TOPOLOGICAL GOVERNOR 5.1 Core Mechanism Prime positions (2,3,5,7,11,13) → "Memory Anchors" → Protected from modification 5.2 Safety Constant The safety constant $S$ is calculated by evaluating the product over the designated prime anchors: $$S = 1 - \prod_{p \in \mathcal{P}} (1 - p^{-0.5})$$ $$S = 1 - (1-2^{-0.5})(1-3^{-0.5})(1-5^{-0.5})(1-7^{-0.5})(1-11^{-0.5})(1-13^{-0.5}) \approx 0.78$$ Interpretation: Approximately 78% of the embedding space is "protected," providing a theoretical guarantee against catastrophic forgetting. 5.3 Algorithm Algorithm 1: TOPO-2026 Training with Topological Governor ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1: Initialize model with frozen base model 2: for each task t ∈ {A, B, C} do 3: Take snapshot of anchor positions 4: for each training step do 5: Forward pass through base model and task head 6: Compute loss and backpropagate 7: Zero gradients at anchor positions 8: Update parameters 9: Enforce anchors (restore to snapshot) 10: end for 11: Freeze current task head 12: end for 13: return trained model with protected anchors 6.
