In order to engineer chemical knowledge, chemists are often required to challenge their understanding of chemistry and thinking processes, which may help improve the structure of chemical knowledge.Knowledge engineering in chemistry dates from the development of expert systems that emulated the thinking process of analytical and organic chemists. Since then, many different expert systems employing rather limited knowledge bases have been developed, solving problems in retrosynthesis, analytical chemistry, chemical risk assessment, etc. However, toward the end of the 20th century, the AI winters slowed down the development of expert systems for chemistry. At the same time, the increasing complexity of chemical research, alongside the limitations of the available computing tools, made it difficult for many chemistry expert systems to keep pace.In the past two decades, the semantic web, the popularization of object-oriented programming, and the increase in computational power have revitalized knowledge engineering. Knowledge formalization through ontologies has become commonplace, triggering the subsequent development of knowledge graphs and cognitive software agents. These tools enable the possibility of interoperability, enabling the representation of more complex systems, inference capabilities, and the synthesis of new knowledge.This Account introduces the history, the core principles of KE, and its applications within the broad realm of chemical research and engineering. In this regard, we first discuss how chemical knowledge is formalized and how a chemist's cognition can be emulated with the help of reasoning algorithms. Following this, we discuss various applications of knowledge graph and agent technology used to solve problems in chemistry related to molecular engineering, chemical mechanisms, multiscale modeling, automation of calculations and experiments, and chemist-machine interactions. These developments are discussed in the context of a universal and dynamic knowledge ecosystem, referred to as The World Avatar (TWA).
title: Knowledge Engineering in Chemistry: From Expert Systems to Agents of Creation

abstract: The Internet has evolved by progressively expanding what humanity connects: first computers, then people, and later billions of devices through the Internet of Things (IoT). While IoT succeeded in digitizing perception at scale, it also exposed fundamental limitations, including fragmentation, weak security, limited autonomy, and poor long-term sustainability. Today, advances in edge hardware, sensing, connectivity, and artificial intelligence enable a new phase: the Internet of Physical AI Agents. Unlike IoT devices that primarily sense and report, Physical AI Agents perceive, reason, and act in real time, operating autonomously and cooperatively across safety-critical domains such as disaster response, healthcare, industrial automation, and mobility. However, embedding fast-evolving AI capabilities into long-lived physical infrastructure introduces new architectural risks, particularly around interoperability, lifecycle management, and premature ossification. This article revisits lessons from IoT and Internet evolution, and articulates design principles for building resilient, evolvable, and trustworthy agentic systems. We present an architectural blueprint encompassing agentic identity, secure agent-to-agent communication, semantic interoperability, policy-governed runtimes, and observability-driven governance. We argue that treating evolution, trust, and interoperability as first-class requirements is essential to avoid hard-coding today's assumptions into tomorrow's intelligent infrastructure, and to prevent the high technical and economic cost of getting it wrong.
title: The Internet of Physical AI Agents: Interoperability, Longevity, and the Cost of Getting It Wrong

abstract: Abstract Recycling industries face distinct digitalization challenges compared to conventional manufacturing due to highly variable material inputs, heterogeneous and legacy equipment, frequent reconfiguration of process lines, and increasing regulatory and sustainability requirements. Although large volumes of operational data are generated across recycling plants, this data is often fragmented, inconsistently structured, and weakly contextualized, limiting reuse across manufacturing operations, analytics, and enterprise systems. The lack of shared semantics constitutes a major barrier to scalable digital transformation. This paper presents an architectural approach that addresses these challenges by implementing the ISA-95 (IEC 62264) equipment standard, implemented using a ThingWorx/Kepware technology stack. Kepware acts as the industrial connectivity and normalization layer, aggregating real-time data from control systems. ThingWorx consumes data from kepware and applies ISA-95 object models through reusable templates and information structures to represent assets, operational states, material flows, and performance indicators in a standardized manner across sites. This decouples data producers from data consumers and enables applications such as performance monitoring, material yield analysis, maintenance analytics, and regulatory reporting to be developed without additional point-to-point integrations. By grounding the data layer in ISA-95 semantics and operationalizing it through ThingWorx and Kepware, the proposed architecture enables semantic interoperability by design, supporting cross-site comparability, scalable analytics, and data-driven decision-making for sustainable digitalization in recycling industries. Furthermore, it enables Furter design of Agentic AI.
title: Implementing a Semantic Data Layer in Recycling Industry Towards Agentic AI
venue: IFIP advances in information and communication technology

abstract: The rapid emergence of autonomous AI agents is transforming artificial intelligence from isolated model inference into distributed systems of reasoning, communication, and action. This paper develops the vision of the Internet of Agentic AI (IoAI): an open ecosystem in which heterogeneous agents discover one another, negotiate responsibilities, exchange context, invoke tools, and execute workflows across cloud, edge, device, organizational, and cyber-physical environments. We synthesize foundations from single-agent agentic AI, multi-agent systems, distributed computing, communication networks, game theory, and security engineering to characterize the architectures and mechanisms required for scalable agent ecosystems. The paper examines agent deployment models, workflow lifecycles, communication protocols, interoperability layers, resource-management challenges, and trust architectures, with case studies in adaptive manufacturing and distributed operational coordination. The resulting framework highlights the central research challenges of controlled emergence, semantic interoperability, secure identity, incentive-compatible coordination, resource-aware orchestration, and governance for large-scale networks of autonomous agents.
title: The Internet of Agentic AI: Communication, Coordination, and Collective Intelligence at Scale

abstract: Within Industry 4.0, more applications include multi-agent systems and integrated software agents in the newly developed solutions, as they can provide a valuable contribution to the manufacturing processes. This makes it important to create a digital representation of those virtual assets, similar to how this is done for physical ones. The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) has been designed for just this purpose - to create models of assets, containing all the relevant information. Currently, this is standard for physical assets, however, it could be of value to extend it beyond. We propose the usage of the AAS for creating information models of software agents and suggest a generic approach to apply the AAS meta-model to ensure semantic interoperability between them. For this purpose, we outline a structure and a set of specific submodels to group agent attributes, which can provide a description of all relevant information for a given task. We provide two examples of concrete agents and outline how this approach will be further validated within future use cases.
title: Modelling Agents in Industry 4.0 Applications Using Asset Administration Shell
venue: International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART)

abstract: Abstract Background: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into regulatory toxicology systematic reviews introduces severe methodological risks, including automation bias, stochastic rounding of critical dose values (the tokenization trap), and attention decay over long documents (lost-in-the-middle effects). Standard exploratory AI agents fail to meet regulatory standards because they lack semantic grounding and deterministic operational constraints. Objective: This protocol specifies the design, deployment, and dynamic validation of a local, dual-agent "cognitive RAIL" engineered to restrict language models entirely to deterministic syntactic processing, separating machine text harvesting from human semantic judgment. Methods: The pipeline implements lossless coordinate-based document ingestion with dynamic vertical line-height grouping, a compiler-level Finite-State Machine (FSM) compiling a Prefix Trie for logit-masked JSON schema enforcement, and non-generative programmatic logic firewalls (enforceLogic) conducting study-design coherence checks. The entire workflow is operationalized locally on consumer-grade hardware to safeguard data sovereignty. Results: Analytical derivations and baseline telemetry verify schema-constrained decoding limits at the hardware layer, achieving zero conversational deviation. In-production monitoring executes daily companion back-testing to dynamically track pipeline decay using four unified telemetry metrics: Normalized Extraction Precision (E_p), Logic Drift Rate (L_d), Audit Velocity Ratio (A_v), and Spatial Parsing Precision (S_p). Implications for Evidence-Based Toxicology: This open-source protocol establishes an active, continuous e-validation lifecycle that replaces traditional static software testing. By providing an auditable, local-first evidence-synthesis engine, the framework reduces reviewer fatigue and accelerates review velocity without surrendering the essential critical skepticism required for regulatory decision-making.
title: Procedural Specification and Dynamic e-Validation of a Dual-Agent Cognitive RAIL as Exoskeleton for Evidence Synthesis
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Agentic AI represents a transformative evolution in artificial intelligence systems, characterized by autonomous decision-making and goal-oriented behavior. These systems demonstrate enhanced capabilities in complex decision-making scenarios through advanced Agent-to-Agent communication protocols and Multi-Channel Protocols. Integrating cognitive architectures, state management, and execution engines enables sophisticated task handling across enterprise environments. Implementation considerations encompass robust security frameworks, scalable architecture patterns, and optimized performance mechanisms. Future directions point toward advanced learning models and enhanced integration capabilities, promising improved efficiency and reduced operational complexity in real-world applications. The incorporation of meta-learning capabilities and semantic interoperability frameworks further enhances system adaptability, while dynamic protocol adaptation mechanisms ensure seamless integration across diverse enterprise ecosystems. These advancements, coupled with sophisticated error recovery and resource optimization techniques, position agentic AI as a cornerstone technology for next-generation enterprise automation and intelligent system deployment.
title: Demystifying Agentic AI: Technical Architecture, Integrations, and Real-World Applications
venue: Technix International Journal for Engineering Research

abstract: The increasing availability of digital documentation in cultural heritage has amplified the need for interoperable systems capable of integrating heterogeneous data and supporting risk-informed conservation strategies. In the field of Disaster Risk Management (DRM), the application of structured methodologies—such as the ICCROM-CCI ABC Method—is often hindered by fragmented data sources, inconsistent terminology, and limited interoperability across institutions. This study presents a semantic workflow for the harmonization, enrichment, and integration of cultural heritage risk assessment data within a CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model (CIDOC-CRM)-compliant environment. The proposed system is structured as an Extract–Transform–Load (ETL) pipeline that converts heterogeneous assessment records into interoperable semantic knowledge graphs. The workflow combines controlled vocabularies, project-specific thesauri for risk agents and heritage typologies, and formal ontology mapping implemented through the Mapping Memory Manager (3M) and executed with the X3ML engine. The resulting data are deployed within a ResearchSpace environment, enabling semantic querying, cross-dataset exploration, and integration with external knowledge infrastructures. The workflow was applied to a dataset comprising 295 cultural heritage sites in the municipality of Ravenna (Italy). The transformation process generated a CIDOC-CRM-compliant knowledge graph containing 134,611 RDF triples and 18,954 entities, integrating information on cultural assets, risk scenarios, actors, documentary resources, and quantitative risk assessments. Through the adoption of persistent identifiers and semantic mappings, the workflow also supports interoperability with external cultural heritage resources, including ArCo and GeoNames, facilitating the contextualization and enrichment of local risk assessment data. By transforming fragmented assessment records into structured and interoperable knowledge, the proposed workflow contributes to bridging semantic and information gaps in cultural heritage risk management. The study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating risk assessment data within an ontology-based semantic infrastructure and highlights its potential to support data integration, semantic interoperability, knowledge reuse, and future decision-support applications for preventive conservation and territorial risk management.
title: Semantic Integration and Automation of Cultural Heritage Risk Data: A CIDOC-CRM Workflow for Decision Support at the Territorial Scale

abstract: The interoperability of devices from distinct brands on the Internet of Things (IoT) domain is still an open issue. The main reason is that pioneer companies always deliberately neglected to deploy devices able to interoperate with competitors products. The key factors that may invert such a trend derive, on one hand, from the abstraction of communication protocols that facilitates the migration from vertical to horizontal paradigms and, on the other hand, from the introduction of common and shared ontologies encoding devices specifications. The Semantic Web, with all its layers, can be considered the main framework for delivering ontologies, and by virtue of its features, it is surely the ideal means for providing shared knowledge. In this paper we present a framework that instantiates cognitive agents operating in IoT context, endowed with meta-reasoning in the Semantic Web. The framework, called SW-Caspar, is also provided with a module that performs semi-automatic ontology learning from sentences expressed in natural language; such a learning process generates a conceptual space reflecting the domain of discourse with an instance of a novel foundational ontology called Linguistic Oriented Davidsonian Ontology (LODO), whose main feature is to increase the deepness of reasoning without compromising linguistic-related features. LODO is inspired by the First-Order Logic Davidsonian notation and is serialized in OWL 2. Well-known examples derived from the theory of logical reasoning and a case-study applied to automation on health scenarios are also provided.
title: Towards ontological interoperability of cognitive IoT agents based on natural language processing¶
A Knowledge-Based Diagnostic Framework for Cross-Standard Conceptual Divergences in Industrial Reference Data

abstract: Presently, a range of technologies aimed at facilitating the development of digital twins within industrial contexts are under active research, development, and field-testing. A primary objective of employing digital twins is to ensure the digital, organized availability of online and offline data concerning the physical counterpart in question. However, the semantics of the presented data are typically dispersed across various heterogeneous documents and other sources. Moreover, the implementation of this knowledge within the digital twin paradigm necessitates the verifiability and traceability of the knowledge. This hinders the interoperability of digital twins and methodologies built on top of digital twin technology. In this paper, a digital twin architecture for knowledge extraction, persistence, and application is proposed. In this architecture, semantic web technologies are employed to structure heterogeneous online and offline data into a knowledge graph. This graph is stored in the digital twin and is further utilized in graph-based retrieval augmented generation with large language models as an accessible interface to access information on the shop floor, thereby enhancing industrial decision making.
title: An Architecture for Industrial Knowledge Management in Digital Twins Utilizing Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation

abstract: In future, demand response scenarios, a multitude of different types of resources are potentially to be used, e.g. electric vehicles, flexible residential loads and battery storage systems. In order to solve the problem of real-time communication of data among the various resources, it is likely to be using different communication protocols. An aggregator utilizing several types of resources is faced with a problem of semantic interoperability. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a testbed consisting of a microgrid model integrated with several controllers communicating with industrial grade protocols for demand response, including IEC 61850, OpenChargePoint protocol (OCPP), OpenADR and UDP.
title: Real-time Co-simulation Design of Micro-grid and Information Communication System Based on Multi-agent System
venue: Power System and Green Energy Conference (PSGEC)

abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is transforming enterprise metadata management from rule-based automation to goal-directed systems capable of discovering, interpreting, connecting, and governing metadata across heterogeneous data estates. This review evaluates how autonomous agents can facilitate metadata discovery, sensitive-data classification, semantic enrichment, lineage reconstruction, enterprise catalog maintenance, and stewardship, while maintaining accountability to established data-governance frameworks. A structured integrative review of DOI-verified peer-reviewed literature connects three typically distinct research streams: enterprise metadata and data catalogs, knowledge graphs and provenance, and large-language-model-based autonomous agents. The synthesis indicates that the most effective near-term approach is policy-constrained orchestration, where specialized agents propose metadata changes, ground decisions in catalogs and knowledge graphs, preserve evidence, and escalate significant actions to stewards. DAMA-oriented management domains provide the operational model for ownership, quality, architecture, metadata, and governance, while Saudi Arabia's NDMO context elevates requirements for classification, traceability, control evidence, and institutional accountability. The review introduces an auditable agentic metadata architecture and an autonomy-assurance loop. It concludes that enterprise value relies on provenance-preserving execution, confidence-aware escalation, semantic interoperability, human override, measurable metadata quality, and governance controls that recognize agent actions as auditable events rather than invisible automation.
title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Metadata Management and Enterprise Data Catalogues: Automating Metadata Discovery, Classification, Semantic Enrichment, Data Lineage and Stewardship under DAMA and NDMO Frameworks
venue: Global Academic Journal of Economics and Business

abstract: Description The Next Earth develops a civilization-scale research framework for governing a world in which intelligence is no longer concentrated exclusively in human individuals or centralized institutions, but increasingly distributed across governments, organizations, artificial intelligence systems, autonomous agents, knowledge networks, and social infrastructures. The central question of this work is not whether a single artificial intelligence will someday govern the planet. It is a broader and more immediate question: How can a civilization maintain coherence, legitimacy, human sovereignty, and the capacity for correction when many different intelligent agents operate simultaneously across institutions, jurisdictions, infrastructures, and timescales? The framework begins from the observation that modern states are already multi-agent systems. Governments are composed of ministries, courts, regulators, municipalities, markets, civil-society organizations, technical infrastructures, experts, databases, and increasingly AI-mediated decision systems. These actors possess different information, objectives, incentives, update cycles, authorities, and interpretations of reality. Artificial intelligence does not eliminate this complexity. It amplifies it. Even when institutions deploy the same underlying AI model, different datasets, prompts, legal mandates, organizational cultures, objectives, and temporal horizons can produce functionally different agents. The result is what this work describes as Multi-Agent State Intelligence. Under this model, the primary governance challenge is not simply machine intelligence. It is coordinated intelligence. A civilization may possess extremely capable AI systems while remaining institutionally fragmented, semantically inconsistent, politically illegitimate, or unable to correct collective error. The framework therefore proposes a foundational distinction: The opposite of safe intelligence is not necessarily powerful intelligence. It is uncoordinated intelligence. The Next Earth develops this idea through thirty research axes organized across ten major domains, including multi-agent state intelligence, cooperative intelligence, semantic interoperability, institutional coordination, temporal governance, human sovereignty, AI-assisted policy systems, planetary coherence, civilizational memory, and re-origin capacity. A major concept within the framework is Cooperative Intelligence. Cooperative Intelligence describes the capacity of heterogeneous human and artificial agents to exchange information, coordinate action, identify disagreement, preserve useful diversity, and correct collective error without requiring complete uniformity. This leads to one of the central principles of the work: Coherence ≠ Uniformity Healthy governance does not require all agents to think alike. In fact, excessive uniformity can create systemic fragility. If every institution relies on the same model, the same data assumptions, the same optimization logic, and the same interpretation of risk, a single shared error may propagate across the entire governance system. The objective is therefore not cognitive homogenization. It is coordinated diversity. The framework introduces an expanded Cooperative Intelligence Index as a candidate systems model. Cooperative Intelligence can be understood as increasing with: semantic interoperability, institutional interoperability, incentive compatibility, verification capacity, and correction capacity, while decreasing with: semantic drift, goal conflict, coordination latency, and unresolved institutional divergence. The purpose of this model is not to establish a final mathematical law. It is to provide a comparative language for analyzing whether increasingly complex governance systems are developing coordination capacity faster than coordination complexity. This distinction becomes increasingly important as the number of intelligent agents grows. More agents do not necessarily reduce stability. Additional agents may provide specialization, redundancy, criticism, diversity, and distributed expertise. Instability emerges when coordination complexity grows faster than the system’s ability to communicate, verify, negotiate, and repair disagreement. The framework therefore emphasizes: Coordination ComplexityversusCoordination Capacity as a central relationship in multi-agent governance. The work also develops the concept of Semantic Interoperability. Government agencies and AI systems require shared definitions, legal references, data standards, evidentiary protocols, policy states, and communication interfaces in order to cooperate. However, semantic interoperability must not become ideological uniformity. A shared semantic protocol is not the same as a shared political belief. The Next Earth therefore distinguishes between: Shared Meaning Infrastructure and Meaning Monopoly. Governance systems must be able to understand one another without requiring citizens, institutions, or artificial agents to adopt identical values or interpretations. Pluralism remains a structural requirement of legitimate governance. Another major concern is Temporal Governance Mismatch. Artificial systems may update in seconds. Administrative processes may take months. Legislation may take years. Institutional culture may take decades to change. This creates a governance ratio in which the speed of technological change may exceed the speed of institutional adaptation. When this mismatch becomes too large, regulations, accountability mechanisms, and organizational procedures may become structurally outdated before they can respond. The Next Earth therefore treats temporal coordination as a governance problem in its own right. The framework further develops a Multi-Agent Policy Architecture. This architecture separates several functional layers: Human Authority and Rights Semantic Interoperability Agent Coordination Policy Simulation Institutional Execution Monitoring Audit Appeal Rollback and Civilizational Learning The inclusion of audit, appeal, and rollback is essential. Cooperation alone does not produce legitimate governance. A group of highly coordinated systems can still pursue harmful goals. This leads to another central principle: Cooperative Intelligence ≠ Legitimate Governance Legitimate governance additionally requires: human rights, political authorization, accountability, contestability, transparency, proportionality, and mechanisms for correction. Artificial intelligence may support governance without automatically acquiring political sovereignty. Technical capability does not generate democratic legitimacy. Prediction accuracy does not create moral authority. Optimization power does not create the right to define collective values. Human Sovereignty is therefore treated as a structural constraint rather than an optional design preference. Within this framework, human sovereignty does not mean rejecting artificial intelligence. It means ensuring that increasingly powerful AI-mediated institutions remain subordinate to legitimate human rights, constitutional boundaries, public accountability, and mechanisms of refusal and revision. The work also examines governance entropy. Multi-agent systems can become unstable through: semantic drift, conflicting optimization objectives, data incompatibility, institutional rivalry, delayed feedback, local optimization, automation bias, centralization, model monoculture, and responsibility diffusion. Governance stability is therefore modeled as a dynamic balance between cooperative capacity, policy coherence, correction capacity, entropy, and institutional lock-in. A stable civilization is not one that never disagrees. It is one that can survive disagreement without losing the ability to coordinate, revise, and continue. At the planetary scale, The Next Earth extends these principles beyond individual states. Problems involving climate, pandemics, artificial intelligence, financial networks, migration, digital infrastructure, scientific collaboration, and planetary risk already cross national boundaries. However, planetary coordination does not require a single planetary government or a centralized artificial intelligence. The framework instead explores polycentric governance: multiple centers of legitimate authority connected through shared protocols, negotiated standards, distributed monitoring, and mechanisms for cooperation across scales. Planetary coherence therefore means enough interoperability to cooperate on shared problems while preserving institutional, cultural, and political diversity. The work also introduces the idea of civilizational memory. Governance systems require mechanisms for preserving: past decisions, failed experiments, institutional lessons, model assumptions, policy revisions, minority objections, and reasons for previous changes. Without such memory, future institutions may repeat old failures without understanding why earlier systems were abandoned. This connects governance to intergenerational handoff. The goal of The Next Earth is not to design a permanent political order for future generations. It is to preserve the conditions under which future generations can redesign inherited systems. This leads to the concept of Re-Origin Capacity: the ability of a civilization to restart, reconstruct, decentralize, revise, or replace systems when inherited structures become inadequate. The deepest measure of civilizational maturity may therefore not be the ability to create a perfectly stable order. It may be the ability to remain governable while preserving the right to change that order. The Next Earth does not assume that AGI already exists, nor does it predict the inevitable emergence of a unified planetary intelligence. AGI, autonomous agents, and advanced machine governance are
title: The Next Earth A Civilization-Scale Architecture for Multi-Agent Governance, Cooperative Intelligence, Human Sovereignty, and Planetary Coherence
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: The ACM Multimedia 2025 Industry Program presents a comprehensive overview of how multimodal AI is revolutionizing real-world applications. The program features contributions from over twenty industry leaders, covering a spectrum of domains from content creation and distribution to healthcare, manufacturing, and foundational technology. Keynotes by leaders from NEC and Google DeepMind address critical challenges in business transformation and media integrity, respectively. A dedicated seminar from Google explores advancements in video codecs like AV2 and the development of next-generation quality metrics using Large Language Models (LLMs). The program also includes twelve expert talks and seven demonstrations that showcase practical innovations, such as LLM-driven recommendation systems at Meta, generative AI for industrial optimization by Mitsubishi Electric, and a Siemens-developed protocol for semantic interoperability in manufacturing. These components collectively highlight the profound societal and industrial impact of multimedia research and bridge the gap between academic theory and real-world deployment.
title: An Innovative Industry Program on Multimedia in A New AI Era
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

abstract: The deep integration of the digital economy and artificial intelligence has accelerated the transition of accounting systems from informatization and automation toward intelligence and multimodal processing. Traditional accounting systems are mainly designed for structured data, and therefore show limited ability to parse unstructured documents, images, audio, and video, as well as insufficient integration between business and financial data. This study designs a multimodal intelligent accounting system based on large language models, computer vision, speech recognition, knowledge graphs, intelligent agents, and data governance theory. A full-chain architecture of “perceptionunderstanding-reasoning-decision-making-interaction” is constructed, covering heterogeneous data ingestion, cross-modal alignment, semantic interoperability, conversational interaction, workflow automation, security control, and efficiency evaluation. The system treats OCR, ASR, and RPA as downstream tool plugins coordinated by a domain-specific LLM agent. It also considers the engineering requirements of secure wireless data transmission, electromagnetic-compatible terminal environments, and reliable networked accounting infrastructures. The proposed architecture provides theoretical and practical support for improving accounting efficiency, financial risk control, decision support, and enterprise digital transformation.
title: Research on the Architecture Design and Efficiency Evaluation of Multimodal Intelligent Accounting Systeme

abstract: The powerful generative capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) has instigated a paradigm shift in recommendation. However, existing generative models (e.g., OneRec) operate as implicit predictors, critically lacking the capacity for explicit and controllable reasoning—a key advantage of LLMs. To bridge this gap, we propose OneRec-Think, a unified framework that seamlessly integrates dialogue, reasoning, and personalized recommendation. OneRec-Think incorporates: (1) Itemic Alignment: cross-modal Item-Textual Alignment for semantic grounding; (2) Reasoning Activation: Reasoning Scaffolding to activate LLM reasoning within the recommendation context; and (3) Reasoning Enhancement, where we design a recommendation-specific reward function that accounts for the multi-validity nature of user preferences. Experiments across public benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, our proposed "Think-Ahead" architecture enables effective industrial deployment, achieving a 0.159% gain in APP Stay Time and validating the practical efficacy of the model's explicit reasoning capability.
title: OneRec-Think: In-Text Reasoning for Generative Recommendation
Architectural perspectives on GenAI-driven software testing systems: A systematic literature review

abstract: Standardizing nursing care plan data from electronic health records is critical for interoperability and large-scale research but is often hindered by the heterogeneity of local terminologies. This study evaluates an optimized Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using large language models to map local care plan problems, goals, and interventions from two health systems to standardized nursing terminologies. We compared multiple prompt engineering techniques. Structured Prompts combined with Few-Shot Learning achieved the highest performance, with moderate accuracy (45-70%). Although full automation remains out of reach, this approach reduced human workload and supports scalable, human-in-the-loop semantic interoperability of nursing data.
title: Using Prompt Engineering to Optimize a RAG Pipeline for EHR-Nursing Data Standardization
venue: Studies in health technology and informatics

abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) integrates cyber-physical systems, edge-cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and advanced connectivity to enable intelligent, data-driven operations across manufacturing, energy, transportation, and healthcare. The convergence of Operational Technology (OT) and Information Technology (IT), together with pervasive AI-driven automation, complicates meeting the joint requirements of performance, adaptability, and security (PAS). This survey adopts an explicitly AI-centric view of PAS and reviews IIoT research spanning deep reinforcement learning (DRL), multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), digital twins (DTs), federated and collaborative learning, graph neural networks (GNNs), blockchain-assisted analytics, and lightweight and post-quantum cryptography. The reviewed approaches are analyzed across device, edge, fog, cloud, and application layers under industrial constraints such as latency, reliability, resource limits, safety requirements, and regulatory compliance. A PAS-centric taxonomy is introduced that links technique families to deployment layers and application domains, and recurring trade-offs among PAS dimensions are summarized. Open challenges are identified in multi-objective optimization, semantic interoperability, lifecycle validation, and governance, with directions outlined toward secure and sustainable Industry 5.0 IIoT ecosystems.
title: Performance, Adaptability, and Security in AI-Driven IIoT: A Survey
Event-state knowledge graph-enhanced GraphRAG for order-driven 3D printing supply chain configuration

abstract: Large language models can interpret user requests plausibly yet fail to produce actions that satisfy structural constraints. We study this problem in Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) combat, where player intent must be grounded in the current game state and translated into well-formed commands for Avrae, a Discord-based D&D automation system. We fine-tune a 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 8B model with Low-Rank Adaptation on 256 curated FIREBALL-derived examples and compare it with zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting. On 25 held-out interactions, the model achieves 56% semantic grounding accuracy and 48% strict command validity. Results suggest that parameter-efficient adaptation improves grounding, while formatting, argument, and reference errors remain common.
title: Grounding Player Intent in Game Commands: A Study of Compact Language Model Adaptation
venue: ACM International Conference on Intelligent Virtual Agents (IVA)

abstract: Offsite construction (OSC) requires an integrated design and delivery system. Reusing prior OSC knowledge is paramount to the success of new OSC projects. However, a gap remains in managing and reusing this knowledge across the broader industry. The challenge lies in the fragmented nature of project-based organisations with isolated knowledge systems, which often lack integration and advanced capabilities for knowledge-based collaboration. This paper proposes a novel framework that leverages cutting-edge knowledge-based methods and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to create a container-based knowledge system (CBKS) that can enhance knowledge capture and reuse towards collaborative OSC. Specifically, the semantic web stack is adopted to construct multimodal knowledge containers for both human users and AI agents. In addition, GPT-4o, a large language model (LLM), is embedded into the knowledge system for better knowledge querying, matching and retrieving. By using this framework, constructed modular knowledge units can integrate product, process and organisation factors to address specific OSC problems. To evaluate the technical feasibility of the proposed framework, a prototype is developed and illustrated through a modular connection design. This illustrative case study demonstrates how knowledge is captured for product representation under manufacturing and assembly constraints, enabling its reuse in different projects. Moreover, the usefulness of GPT-4o for enhancing this process is also tested.
title: Enhancing Knowledge Capture and Reuse for Offsite Construction Through A Container-Based Knowledge Approach

abstract: This thesis presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of Nora, an AI generative co-pilot developed to support the construction and refinement of bowtie diagrams in the field of industrial risk management. Bowtie diagrams are structured graphical models that illustrate how specific threats can lead to an undesired top event and, subsequently, to potential consequences, while also showing the preventive and mitigative barriers in place to control both threats and consequences. The work was conducted at Beawre Digital S.L., a technology start-up dedicated to digital risk automation and continuous risk management for the construction industry. Traditional bowtie tools are effective for visualization but require extensive manual effort, limiting knowledge reuse and scalability. Nora addresses these limitations by combining large language models (LLMs), embeddings, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) into a single interactive assistant that communicates through natural language and updates diagrams dynamically. The system was re-architected from a slow, error-prone prototype into a scalable, production-ready service. With this new approach, task or intent classification and context retrieval occur simultaneously, followed by real-time response streaming and persistent "smart view" storage in Azure Blob Storage. A multi-agent orchestration layer separates classification, generation, and validation tasks, ensuring linguistic consistency and robust recovery from errors. In parallel, a weighted embedding framework allows semantic comparison of bowtie diagrams, supporting knowledge reuse across projects. The entire pipeline is deployed securely through GitLab CI/CD, Docker, and Kubernetes for automated scalability. The empirical evaluation compared the improved and initial versions of Nora across three dimensions: correctness, latency, and cost. The results show significant improvements: mean latency decreased fivefold; correctness improved from 59% to over 93%; and cost per request was reduced by up to 70%. Statistical testing confirmed that these improvements were both reliable and significant. These advances stem from concurrent processing, structured and extensive prompt engineering, and asynchronous embedding computations. Conclusively, the thesis demonstrates that generative AI can operate reliably within structured industrial frameworks when supported by modular orchestration, validation, and semantic grounding. Nora thus represents a novel blend of conversational AI and formal safety methodologies that supports Beawre's vision of continuous, data-driven risk management. Future research will focus on multi-agent coordination, enhanced data governance, and the transition toward hosting and fine-tuning an in-house language model to ensure long-term independence and scalability.
title: Generative AI co-pilot for dynamic bowtie diagrams in construction risk management
venue: UPCommons institutional repository (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)

abstract: This volume highlights computational frameworks and knowledge representation methods used to convert raw and unstructured data into meaningful, contextual, and actionable intelligence. It emphasizes knowledge graph engineering, semantic web models, reasoning algorithms, cognitive computing frameworks, inference mechanisms, and multi-agent cooperative decision systems. Research exploring hybrid symbolic–neural intelligence architectures, explainable machine reasoning, domain-specific knowledge encoding, and semantic interpretation is encouraged. Real-world deployment in sectors such as healthcare diagnostics, enterprise knowledge systems, smart governance, manufacturing automation, and environmental intelligence is particularly relevant. The goal is to advance systematic and interpretable intelligent system development guided by structured knowledge design.
title: ADVANCES IN INFORMATION AND KNOWLEDGE-ENGINEERING: FROM DATA TO INTELLIGENT SYSTEMS VOLUME 6 2026 S1007B1

abstract: Autonomous driving is experiencing a paradigm shift from solely pursuing technical autonomy to building systems that align with human intentions, preferences, and trust. However, traditional autonomous vehicles are still designed as automated "tools'' which are optimized for perception, planning, and control, however lack the ability to interpret natural human communication or adapt to personalized driving styles. This mismatch hampers user acceptance and limits the deployment of autonomy.This dissertation introduces Human-Autonomy Teaming (HAT) as a new paradigm and demonstrates that recent advances in Foundation Models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Language Models (VLMs), provide the missing capabilities needed to realize this paradigm in autonomous driving. This work systematically proposes, develops, benchmarks, and validates this new paradigm. The dissertation begins by formalizing the conceptual framework of HAT for autonomous driving, integrating autonomy foundations, human foundations, core teaming processes, and closed-loop feedback. To situate HAT within broader research progress, the dissertation provides the first unified survey of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for autonomous driving, covering perception, reasoning, planning, control, benchmarks, and emerging industry applications. Building on the human foundation, the work introduces VLM-DC, a semantic grounding and data collection ecosystem that aligns scene understanding and data collection with human relevance. Through two different architectures, the system identifies semantically meaningful driving scenes, reduces redundancy, and constructs personalized data distributions for different kinds of vehicles that support human-aligned autonomy. On the autonomy side, the dissertation presents ViLaD, a vision-language diffusion generative planning model that produces both quick and accurate driving decisions. By replacing autoregressive generation with parallel masked denoising, ViLaD improves robustness, inference efficiency, and the expressiveness needed to support collaborative decision processes.The dissertation then validates the HAT paradigm through teaming behaviors in simulation. The Receive, Reason, React (RRR) framework demonstrates that LLMs can serve as the core teaming engine in simulation, interpreting natural language instructions and generating context-aware driving policies. To evaluate such agents, the dissertation introduces LaMPilot, the first benchmark designed for instruction-following and reasoning in autonomous driving through a "code as policy'' strategy. Building on these foundations, the dissertation conducts extensive real-world field experiments to demonstrate HAT-enabled autonomy. The Talk2Drive framework shows that cloud-based LLMs can interpret diverse natural language commands, reason over driving context, and personalize vehicle behavior through memory, significantly reducing driver takeovers. To overcome network-latency limitations, this work further presents the first on-board VLM-based personalized motion control system, achieving low-latency collaboration with a RAG-enhanced memory module and reducing takeovers by 76.9% in real driving tests.Together, these contributions present a comprehensive demonstration of moving pure automation toward true HAT, providing conceptual foundations, comprehensive reviews, technical foundations, simulation verification, and real-world validation. This dissertation demonstrates how foundation models can enable autonomous vehicles that communicate, reason, adapt, and collaborate, building the next generation of safe, trustworthy, and personalized autonomous vehicles.
title: Foundation Models for Human-Autonomy Teaming in Autonomous Vehicles

abstract: Critical Infrastructure (CI) operators increasingly face systemic challenges due to interdependencies between physical and digital domains, heterogeneous data, delayed threat detection, and limited predictive capabilities. The ATLANTIS project addresses these barriers by delivering an integrated, modular framework for enhanced situational awareness, cross-sector data fusion, proactive response, and secure data processing. It leverages a combination of Digital Twin models, semantic reasoning, and cognitive decision intelligence to support real-time, cross-CI risk management. This chapter presents the ATLANTIS architecture, focusing on its key components: the Digital Twin paradigm for CI modelling; SAFER for event correlation and situational picture generation; semantic integration strategies; cognitive decision support tools; and AI-agent systems for dynamic mitigation. The solution prioritizes interoperability among diverse systems and intelligent automation to effectively address complex cyber-physical threats. The chapter concludes by outlining ATLANTIS's contributions to CI resilience, including its decision-intelligence approach, semantic interoperability through STIX/TAXII and ontologies, and LLM-driven agentic AI for coordinated risk response. Policy and regulatory alignment are also discussed, with attention to GDPR-compliant AI, data sharing, and standardization. Future work will enhance scalability, trust, and explainability, and pursue operational validation in real-world settings to support broader deployment across CI domains.
title: Enhancing Critical Infrastructure Resilience Through a Decision Intelligence Distributed Situational Picture and Incidents Mitigation

abstract: The exponential growth of data streaming from edge devices, IoT sensors, and transactional systems has rendered traditional Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) pipelines obsolete for real-time analytics. These conventional, rule-based pipelines struggle with dynamic workloads, unpredictable system failures, and the semantic heterogeneity of cross-industry data. This paper proposes a unified, AI-driven framework for optimizing real-time ETL pipelines deployed on cloud infrastructure. The framework integrates three core components: (1) a predictive auto-scaling engine utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to forecast workload volatility and dynamically allocate cloud resources, minimizing latency and cost; (2) a self-healing fault tolerance mechanism powered by reinforcement learning (RL) that proactively identifies anomalous node behaviour and orchestrates failover strategies without human intervention; and (3) a semantic interoperability layer employing graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models (LLMs) to map disparate data schemas (e.g., HL7 for healthcare, X12 for finance, and OPC-UA for manufacturing) into a unified, query-able format. We evaluate the proposed framework using a simulated multi-cloud environment with mixed-industry streaming datasets. Results demonstrate a 42% reduction in ETL latency during demand spikes, a 99.99% uptime through predictive self-healing, and a 95% reduction in manual schema-mapping efforts. This unified approach establishes a new paradigm for resilient, efficient, and interoperable real-time data processing across industry verticals.
title: AI-driven optimization of real-time ETL pipelines in cloud infrastructure: A unified framework for predictive scaling, fault tolerance and cross-industry data interoperability
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

abstract: Qualitative coding is an essential methodological tool in qualitative research. Although various tools exist to support manual qualitative coding, the process remains highly resource-intensive, requiring significant time and expertise. It is further complicated by inconsistent reporting of coding protocols, differing interpretations of inter-coder reliability metrics, and difficulties in achieving conceptual agreement among coders – all of which contribute to the broader replication crisis in science. Meanwhile, large language models have demonstrated remarkable abilities to understand context across diverse tasks and are increasingly applied to information and, in combination with semantic web technologies, knowledge extraction. In this work, we define qualitative coding process as a knowledge base construction task and propose an ontology-mediated approach to automating qualitative coding, formalising key aspects of the methodology and reliability assessment using semantic web standards. We evaluate the reliability of this approach through a concrete implementation and case study, finding that qualitative coding can benefit substantially from AI-driven automation – especially when the underlying coding ontology is well-defined and domain-relevant constraints are explicitly codified.
title: Qualitative Coding in the Age of AI:An Ontology-Driven Approach

abstract: This thesis addresses the challenge of automating documentary compliance checking within Ghana’s upstream petroleum industry, focusing on the area of local content and participation governed by the Petroleum (Local Con-tent and Local Participation) Regulations, 2013 (LI 2204) as amended by LI 2435. The research seeks to contribute to maximizing the beneﬁts of Ghana’s petroleum resources while mitigating the resource curse by ensuring compliance with local content and participation regulations as provided for in LI 2204 and its amendment. To achieve this, the study leverages Semantic Web technologies, speciﬁcally the W3C standards RDF, OWL,SHACL, and SPARQL, to represent, validate, and reason with legal knowledge relevant to the domain. The research demonstrates that Semantic Web technologies are highly eﬀective in automating documentary compliance checking, particularly through the use of SHACL-SPARQL for legal reasoning. While OWL provides foundational expressivity and interoperability, SHACL-SPARQL proves more capable of handling the inferencing required for compliance checks, including temporal and aggregate functionalities. The study also highlights the scalability and eﬃciency of SHACL-SPARQL, supported by recent research showing its superiority over other automated reasoning tools in the legal domain. A key contribution of this work is the development of a computational artifact, which comprises a three-module OWL ontology, SHACL-SPARQL rules, and SHACL shapes, evaluated using competence questions (CQs)and the O2 evaluative framework (Gangemi et al., 2005) through a web application. The web app collects data based on the Annual Local Content Plan, which is the main compliance ﬁling document used by the Ghana Petroleum Commission to ensure compliance with local content and participation regulations, and, using the computational artifact, assesses it against the chosen regulations upon which the CQs are based, thereby answering the CQs. The artifact successfully identiﬁes compliance and non-compliance with the selected regulations, streamlining the process for both companies and the Petroleum Commission. The research underscores the importance of complementing traditional databases with knowledge bases (ontologies) to enhance interoperability, explainability, and eﬃciency in compliance checking. The ﬁndings have practical implications for Ghana’s petroleum sector, as evidenced by ongoing discussions with the Petroleum Commission to scale up the web application for industrial use. Additionally, the research pro-vides a tool that is accessibility-friendly for the manipulation and implementation of Semantic Web technologies, i.e., the development of ontologies, writing and executing SHACL rules and shapes, for blind individuals as an ancillary beneﬁt. Future work will extend the formalization to cover all provisions of LI 2204, Act 919, and relevant parts of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana, while incorporating LegalDocML for legislative encoding. Additionally, the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) with Semantic Web technologies is proposed to address free-text sections in compliance documents. This research represents a pioneering eﬀort in applying advanced Semantic Web technologies to real-world legal compliance challenges, oﬀering a scalable and eﬃcient solution for Ghana’s upstream petroleum industry and potentially other regulatory domains.
title: Automating documentary regulatory compliance in the upstream petroleum sector of Ghana with particular focus on the area of local content and participation
To Share or Not to Share: Orchestrating Trustworthy Data in Global Value Chains

abstract: Interoperability is a central challenge in modern materials science as scientific workflows increasingly need to integrate heterogeneous computational methods, experimental infrastructures, data platforms, and AI‐assisted systems. This perspective presents interoperability concepts from European digitalization initiatives in materials science namely, Platform MaterialDigital, NFDI‐MatWerk, and MaterialsCommons, which focus on workflow management systems (WfMSs), semantic representations, and knowledge graph technologies, while relating these developments to the broader landscape of materials informatics. Since various WfMSs address different requirements, interoperable abstraction layers such as the Python Workflow Definition are needed and enable workflows to be exchanged between systems while preserving reproducibility. Beyond technical interoperability, the review highlights the growing importance of semantic interoperability through ontology‐driven frameworks, including atomRDF, the Abstract Workflow Language, and semantikon. These approaches enrich workflows with machine‐readable semantic annotations, provenance information, and Resource Description Framework‐based knowledge graphs, enabling workflows to become semantically transparent and reusable scientific objects. The growing importance of semantically annotated workflows for the integration of computational and experimental workflows within Materials Acceleration Platforms and the emerging role of large language models and AI‐assisted workflow orchestration are also emphasized. Together, these developments outline a multilayered interoperability ecosystem that combines workflow execution, semantic reasoning, provenance tracking, and AI‐driven scientific automation within unified materials research infrastructures.
title: Toward Full Interoperability in Materials Science: Integrating Workflows With Knowledge Graphs

abstract: This thesis investigates the development of Digital Twins (DTs), virtual representations of physical systems that support predictive monitoring, optimization, and lifecycle management. DTs rely on the integration of diverse software components, particularly Simulation Models (SiMs), yet current development practices face significant challenges in integrating, understanding, and orchestrating these heterogeneous elements. The research aims to address these challenges by applying Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) principles to facilitate the systematic, scalable, and robust development of DTs. Research Motivation and Framework The study begins by identifying the need for a more structured engineering approach to DT development. Although DTs are widely recognized as a key enabler for Industry 4.0, their implementation often relies on ad-hoc, domain-specific, and tool-dependent solutions. These fragmented practices hinder reuse, semantic interoperability, and cross-domain scalability. The research focuses on three dimensions of DTs: 1.Virtual Environment (VE) : representing the digital mirror of the physical system through executable models. 2.Digital Data : connecting and contextualizing information flows. 3.Services : enabling interaction and orchestration between components. The work is structured around five research questions (RQs) addressing (1) current practices, (2) tool support, (3) integration methods, (4) semantic interoperability, and (5) orchestration modeling. Empirical Research: DT Development Practices (RQ1)An empirical study involving 19 practitioners from academia and industry revealed diverse understandings of DTs but a shared agreement on their fundamental components: Physical Entity (PE), Virtual Entity (VE), data, connections, and purpose. The VE, composed mainly of SiMs, emerged as the most critical and complex element due to its executable and dynamic nature. Findings indicate a lack of standardized methodologies for integration and orchestration. Most practitioners develop custom or in-house tools, frequently adopting a multi-tool strategy combining several simulation and integration environments. While standards like FMI (Functional Mock-up Interface) are widely used, they often fail to support many required simulation engines. This underscores the need for flexible integration frameworks. Practitioners also highlighted issues of semantic interoperability, ensuring shared understanding across models, and SiM reusability, both linked to poor documentation and inconsistent metadata. Finally, orchestration practices were found to be domain-specific, lacking formalism and flexibility, motivating the need for a more systematic orchestration framework. Tooling Experimentation: Evaluating Open-Source Support (RQ2)The second part of the research assessed open-source (OS) tools for DT development, focusing on integration and orchestration support. A taxonomy of six essential features was developed to evaluate these tools objectively. This taxonomy provides a structured framework to assess capabilities such as interface generation, orchestration mechanisms, and semantic interoperability. Results showed that none of the evaluated tools (TwinOps, ThingsBoard, and Ptolemy II) fully supported all essential features. In particular:•Interface Generation was insufficiently supported, forcing developers to manually create interfaces for integrating heterogeneous SiMs.•Semantic Interoperability was poorly handled, with limited mechanisms for ensuring data consistency. •Orchestration capabilities were present but limited, especially for hybrid simulations combining different time semantics. These findings motivated the development of new MDE-based methods to fill these gaps. Model-Driven Support for Integration and Orchestration The thesis introduces three complementary model-driven methods designed to enhance DT development: 1. Interface Generation Method (Chapter 4, RQ3)A model-driven interface generation approach was proposed to simplify the functional integration of heterogeneous behavioral models. Three concepts were defined:•Common Interface (CI): an abstract interface independent of any simulation engine. •Model Interface Description (MID) and Formalism Interface Description (FID): model-specific descriptions supporting automated interface generation. These concepts standardize how SiMs communicate, enabling functional interoperability across different platforms and engines. The approach significantly reduces manual coding, promotes reuse, and ensures consistency in data exchange. 2. Metamodel for Simulation Model Comprehension (Chapter 5, RQ4)To address semantic interoperability and reusability, a metamodel-based approach was developed for systematically documenting SiMs. The metamodel captures metadata such as:•Data formats and units (for compatibility),•Scope and limitations (for substitutability),•Versioning and evolution history. This structure enables knowledge transfer, facilitates SiM reuse, and allows developers to detect semantic inconsistencies across components. The method includes a collaborative assimilation process aligned with natural cognitive workflows. Future extensions envision integrating semantic web technologies (e.g., RDF) and AI-driven assistants (LLMs) to automate documentation and evolution management. 3. OrchTwin and LOTTS: Language-Oriented Orchestration (Chapter 6, RQ5)The final contribution introduces OrchTwin, a language-oriented model-driven framework that formalizes DT orchestration. It is implemented in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL) called LOTTS (Language for Orchestrating Twin-based Systems).LOTTS allows defining orchestration workflows through four structured views: 1.Component Description 2.Communication Definition 3.Execution Specification4.Deployment Allocation It enables model-to-code transformations, automatically generating executable code from high-level orchestration models. LOTTS embeds metadata constraints (e.g., units, formats, validity checks), ensuring semantic consistency and improving integration between heterogeneous SiMs. The approach supports modular and iterative DT development, reducing implementation effort and increasing maintainability. Contributions to Digital Twin Engineering The thesis makes three major contributions: 1.A Taxonomy for Evaluating DT Tools A reproducible framework for assessing integration and orchestration capabilities in DT tooling, guiding future tool development and benchmarking. 2.Model-Driven Methods for DT Integration The combination of interface generation and metamodeling methods provides a systematic approach to achieving functional and semantic interoperability among heterogeneous components. 3.OrchTwin Framework and LOTTS DSLA complete orchestration solution that bridges the design–implementation gap through model-driven automation, offering scalability, reusability, and formal consistency across DT development phases. Collectively, these contributions demonstrate how MDE can address complexity in DT engineering, establishing formal connections between conceptual models and operational systems. Future Work The thesis identifies several promising research directions:•Extending the evaluation taxonomy to include consistency management and verification mechanisms. •AI-assisted development for automatic definition and interpretation of DT artifacts. •Automated reasoning in the metamodel to support SiM evolution and validation. •Expanding OrchTwin to integrate microservice-based architectures, enhancing modularity and scalability. •Large-scale industrial validation to test applicability across diverse domains. •Performance evaluation and optimization to improve scalability and adoption in production contexts. Conclusion This research provides a comprehensive methodological framework for Digital Twin development, emphasizing integration, semantic interoperability, and orchestration. By uniting empirical insights with model-driven techniques, the thesis contributes to the foundation of systematic, reusable, and automated DT engineering. The proposed approaches, interface generation, SiM metamodeling, and the OrchTwin framework, collectively advance the state of practice from ad-hoc development toward formalized and automated DT engineering. Through the integration of MDE principles, the thesis establishes a clear path toward scalable, consistent, and maintainable digital twin systems, paving the way for future research and industrial adoption.
title: A Model Orchestra in Digital Twins:A Model-Driven Approach to Integration and Orchestration

abstract: Abstract The representation and exploitation of semantics has been gaining popularity in recent research, as exemplified by the uptake of large language models in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and knowledge graphs (KGs) in the Semantic Web. Although KGs are already employed in manufacturing to integrate and standardize domain knowledge, the generation and application of corresponding KG embeddings as lean feature representations of graph elements have yet to be extensively explored in this domain. Existing KGs in manufacturing often focus on top-level domain knowledge and thus ignore domain dynamics, or they lack interconnectedness, i.e., nodes primarily represent non-contextual data values with single adjacent edges, such as sensor measurements. Consequently, context-dependent KG embedding algorithms are either restricted to non-dynamic use cases or cannot be applied at all due to the given KG characteristics. Therefore, this work provides an overview of state-of-the-art KG embedding methods and their functionalities, identifying the lack of dynamic embedding formalisms and application scenarios as the key obstacles that hinder their implementation in manufacturing. Accordingly, we introduce an approach for dynamizing existing KG embeddings based on local embedding reconstructions. Furthermore, we address the utilization of KG embeddings in the Horizon2020 project Teaming.AI ( www.teamingai-project.eu .) focusing on their respective benefits.
title: Leveraging Semantic Representations via Knowledge Graph Embeddings

abstract: This contribution reflects on the long-term development of the Mittelhochdeutsche Begriffsdatenbank (MHDBDB), one of the oldest Digital Humanities projects in the German-speaking world, as a case study in modeling medieval meaning under changing technological conditions. Starting from the premise that modeling meaning is a central task of Digital Humanities, the paper traces how different technological paradigms—from early database systems to Semantic Web infrastructures—have shaped, constrained, and at times obscured access to the data itself. Particular attention is paid to the challenges arising from highly interconnected RDF-based models, including issues of scalability, maintainability, and human readability within small research teams. The contribution argues that increasing technical complexity does not necessarily lead to better knowledge production. Instead, long-term usability depends on factors such as transparency, maintainability, and the ability of domain experts to understand and actively work with their own data. Against this background, the recent transformation of the MHDBDB towards a TEI-based, human-readable data structure is presented as a strategic shift toward greater autonomy. This includes not only independence from proprietary systems and heavy infrastructure, but also a reconfiguration of workflows that foreground interpretability and sustainability. A further focus lies on the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into the redevelopment process. Rather than relying on automation, the project employs controlled, expert-driven workflows, including prompt-based reconstruction, iterative validation, and human review at every stage. The case of the MHDBDB demonstrates that what endures across technological change is not a specific data model, but a set of principles: the need to model meaning explicitly, the central role of human expertise, and the responsibility inherent in every act of modeling. Ultimately, the paper argues for a more cautious, reflective approach to digital infrastructures—one that prioritizes clarity, control, and sustainability over maximal complexity.
title: HALF A CENTURY OF MODELING MEDIEVAL MEANING. What Endures When Technologies Change?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Despite intensified recycling efforts, global material consumption has more than tripled over the past five decades, while the global circularity rate has declined. This widening gap reveals that incremental improvements are insufficient and that a transition toward circular economy must be structural. This transition is constrained by fragmented data ecosystems, limited transparency among stakeholders, and conventional digital twin architectures that struggle to represent the dynamic, multi-loop nature of circular supply networks. To address these challenges, this position paper discusses a conceptual Federated Digital Twin framework that integrates federated system architectures to protect data sovereignty, intelligent agents to enable real-time negotiation and synchronization, and knowledge graphs to ensure semantic interoperability across distributed actors. The framework serves as a decision-support backbone for circular manufacturing, aiming for a coordinated management and systemic coherence of value-retention strategies and production planning for circular supply chains.
title: Federated digital twins for intelligent decision-making in circular supply networks

abstract: Execution Governance 6.0 (EG6) proposes Governed Effect Grounding as a candidate research-architecture layer for consequential effect authorization. It addresses a specific operational question: when an authorization decision depends on claims about the external world, are those claims correctly and reconstructably bound to the exact referents, properties, sources or procedures, semantic mappings, temporal conditions, uncertainty treatment, and evidence dependencies on which the proposed effect actually depends? EG6 is cumulative rather than substitutive. It does not replace the Execution Governance Six Conditions, EG3 commitment integrity, EG4 fabric integrity, or EG5 regime integrity. Canonical Execution Governance already requires Live-Context Integrity and Sufficient Verifiable Proof. The candidate EG6 contribution is therefore narrower: making profile-relative, effect-dispositive grounding dependencies first-class, version-pinned, completeness-checked, commitment-bound, and independently reconstructable at effect commitment. The paper introduces six candidate Grounding Integrity properties: Referent Binding Integrity; Source & Procedure Integrity; Semantic Mapping Integrity; Temporal Applicability Integrity; Uncertainty-Bounded Interpretation; and Grounding Witness Closure. It also presents a candidate formal kernel, an incremental-obligation separability criterion, a synthetic referent-misbinding counterexample, a grounding-failure taxonomy, a minimal reference profile, machine-readable JSON artifacts, conformance and attack vectors, an EG5–EG6 handoff rule, and staged evidence gates for executable, formal, reproducible, and independently reconstructable validation. The prior-art boundary is deliberately explicit. EG6 does not claim invention of grounding, semantic grounding, provenance, attribute association, continuous authorization, sensor semantics, metrological traceability, data-quality vocabularies, context attestation, authorization evidence, or semantic interoperability. Instead, the research hypothesis is whether dependency-complete, effect-dispositive, commit-time grounding closure creates an independently falsifiable operational obligation not already fully specified by a named lower-layer implementation or profile. The architecture is intentionally cross-domain. Potential profiles include agentic AI, cyber-physical and autonomous systems, industrial control, payments and digital assets, healthcare, and public or institutional infrastructure. Version: Research Architecture v0.1.5Date: 30 August 2026Status: Independent research and pre-standardization candidate. This publication is not a standard, certification scheme, legal determination, production-safety assurance claim, proof of governance completeness, or novelty/patentability opinion.
title: Execution Governance 6.0: Governed Effect Grounding
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Enterprise data analysis is emerging as a distinct frontier for autonomous agents. Compared with general-purpose interaction and software engineering, it operates in an open, ambiguous, and continuously evolving environment. These characteristics call for a data-agent architecture that treats semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class system concerns. To this end, we introduce QwenPaw-Data, an agentic data system designed for enterprise intelligent data analysis. QwenPaw-Data consolidates heterogeneous assets from warehouses, dashboards, documents, interaction logs, and historical tasks into reusable, governable, and evolvable analysis assets, then turns natural-language requests into end-to-end analytical workflows spanning data understanding, retrieval, analysis, report generation, and decision support. Its architecture decomposes the problem into three collaborative subsystems: DataBridge provides trustworthy semantic grounding through interconnected metadata, knowledge, and trace graphs; Skill-Hub codifies expert analytical methodology into reusable and verifiable skills; and Host materializes these evidence and method assets into controllable, artifact-centric runtime execution. Across these subsystems, semantics, methods, traces, and feedback are continuously deposited back into the system, forming a self-evolving asset flywheel. Experiments on public benchmarks and real-world industrial BI workloads show that QwenPaw-Data improves both verifiable data access capability and higher-level analytical quality, offering a practical foundation for reliable, traceable, and continuously improving enterprise data agents.
title: QwenPaw-Data: Bridging Facts, Methodology, and Execution for Autonomous Enterprise Data Analytics
Features and Capabilities of a Blockchain-Based Ridesharing Enhanced with Semantics
venue: Communications in computer and information science

title: Metadata schema for virtual sensors in digital twin-enabled building systems using Brick schema

abstract: Knowledge Organization (KO) has historically been used to structure biological knowledge, from taxonomy to ontologies. This becomes increasingly challenging as life sciences evolve into a data-intensive domain. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has enabled knowledge organization systems (KOSs) to assume active roles in computational workflows rather than serve as passive repositories. This thematic review examines the evolution of KOSs in AI-augmented biological research by situating them within scientific paradigmatic and epistemological shifts. By synthesizing foundational theories from library and information science, philosophy of science, and biological systematics, we propose the Knowledge Organization Analysis Framework (KOAF) to capture bio-KOSs’ developments across functional sophistication, automation degree in system construction, and reasoning and inference capability. Representative empirical studies show that bio-KOSs enable semantic interoperability and data integration, while also contributing to hypothesis generation and reasoning. We argue that advanced bio-KOSs increasingly function as epistemic agents in scientific discovery. This transformation marks KOSs as theoretical frameworks shaping scientific inquiry through AI-KO convergence and highlights the need for future research on accountability, epistemic integrity, and scientific trustworthiness in AI-driven knowledge discovery.
title: Knowledge Organization in AI-Era Biological Sciences: A Thematic Review

abstract: The study is devoted to the analysis of the problems of coordination of interaction of subsystems in distributed automated production control systems (DAPCS). The work is aimed at finding effective methods and architectural solutions that ensure the coordinated functioning of territorially and functionally distributed components of the system in the context of dynamically changing production scenarios. The article provides a retrospective analysis of the evolution of approaches to organizing interaction in DAPCS, tracing the path from centralized monolithic architectures to modern flexible decentralized systems based on a service-oriented approach and multi-agent technologies. The key requirements for coordination mechanisms in DAPCS are systematized, including ensuring semantic interoperability, supporting dynamic reconfiguration of the link structure, taking into account real-time constraints, decentralized decision-making under uncertainty. The advantages and disadvantages of the basic architectural styles of interaction organization — canonical, event-oriented and service — are analyzed. Promising approaches to the construction of adaptive coordination mechanisms based on the multi-agent approach, the development of ontological models for representing knowledge about processes and resources, and the dynamic formation of coalitions of service agents for business process tasks are considered.
