abstract: Episode summary: Microsoft has been quietly building a comprehensive agentic AI stack that most people have never heard of. From the open-source AutoGen framework for multi-agent conversations to the low-code power of Copilot Studio and the specialized FI models, there's a coherent strategy hiding in plain sight. This episode unpacks how these three layers work together, why Microsoft's enterprise-first approach differs from competitors, and what it means for the future of AI development. Show Notes Microsoft's Agentic AI Stack: A Deep Dive into AutoGen, Copilot Studio, and FI Models Microsoft has been quietly building one of the most comprehensive agentic AI ecosystems in the industry, yet most of it remains hidden beneath layers of enterprise branding and Azure integration. While the company rarely gets credit for cutting-edge AI architecture, three key components form a surprisingly coherent strategy for multi-agent systems: AutoGen, Copilot Studio, and the mysterious FI models. AutoGen: Multi-Agent Orchestration Done Right AutoGen is Microsoft's open-source framework for building multi-agent applications, and it represents a fundamental departure from how most developers think about AI chains. Unlike LangChain's approach of chaining API calls together, AutoGen treats agents as first-class conversational participants in a stateful environment. The core mechanism is GroupChat, which manages how multiple agents interact within a shared conversation. Rather than using a simple round-robin approach where agents respond in sequence, AutoGen v0.4 employs an LLM-based routing system. This means the system actually reasons about which agent is best suited to handle the current question based on conversation state and each agent's capabilities. The architecture supports a Manager agent concept where one agent can delegate specific sub-tasks to specialist agents. Imagine a customer service workflow where a Manager receives a query, identifies it as a billing issue, and routes it to a specialist agent with access to payment systems and account history. Technical support queries go to entirely different specialists with diagnostic tools and knowledge bases. Each specialist agent maintains its own context window, tool access, and system prompts, while the Manager handles orchestration. This approach naturally raises questions about hallucination loops—what happens if one agent starts generating nonsense that poisons the entire conversation? AutoGen addresses this through multiple guardrails. Termination conditions can be set at the GroupChat level to end conversations when specific criteria are met or after a maximum number of turns. Each agent has scoped permissions, preventing unauthorized actions like issuing refunds without explicit authorization. Optional human-in-the-loop steps can pause high-stakes actions for confirmation. The result is less "let agents figure it out" and more "let agents figure it out within carefully defined boundaries." This governance-oriented approach reflects Microsoft's enterprise DNA, emphasizing audit trails, approval workflows, and rollback capabilities. Copilot Studio: Democratizing Agent Development While AutoGen serves developers who want fine-grained control, Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code platform for business users and IT admins who need to build functional agents without writing Python. Deeply integrated with Microsoft 365, it's often misunderstood as just a chatbot builder when it's actually a full workflow automation platform using natural language as its interface. The underlying architecture uses a trigger-action model similar to IFTTT or Zapier, but with a critical difference: reasoning steps. Before taking action, Copilot Studio agents can interpret ambiguous instructions, check context, query data sources, and make multi-factor decisions. Consider a practical example. With traditional IFTTT, you might create an applet that turns on smart lights when rain is forecast. With Copilot Studio, the workflow becomes deliberative. An agent receives a natural language request like "prepare the house for the evening." It checks the weather forecast, examines your calendar for video calls, confirms your location, and then makes a complex decision: turn on living room lights with a warm tone for the video call, adjust the thermostat because temperatures are dropping, and potentially take other contextual actions. This deliberation is enabled by integration with Microsoft Dataverse, a managed data platform providing persistent state storage. Agents can cache relevant data, maintain session state, and build context over time—capabilities that separate true agentic systems from simple automation. The trade-off is lock-in. Building on Copilot Studio means committing to Dataverse, Azure, and the broader Microsoft ecosystem. But for organizations already running on Teams, Outlook, and SharePoint, this native integration delivers genuine value that platform-agnostic alternatives can't match. The learning curve from simple automation tools like Zapier is more conceptual than technical. The interface is friendly with drag-and-drop connectors and natural language prompts, but teams must shift from thinking in rigid rules to trusting models to interpret intent correctly. Microsoft provides templates for common scenarios like HR onboarding and IT helpdesk to bridge this gap. FI Models: The Invisible Efficiency Layer The Functionary Inference (FI) models represent Microsoft's specialized approach to efficiency in agentic workflows. These are not general-purpose language models competing with GPT-4o or Claude on creative writing or broad reasoning. They're purpose-built for one narrow task: correctly identifying which tools to call, with what parameters, in what order. In standard agentic workflows, using large general-purpose models for every step—including simple routing decisions—is massively overkill. FI models reduce token usage by approximately thirty percent compared to GPT-4o in tool-use scenarios. For enterprises running thousands of daily agent interactions, this translates to significant cost savings and potentially lower latency due to smaller model size. However, FI models remain largely invisible. They're primarily used internally within Microsoft's own agentic products, including Copilot Studio and Azure services. Unlike GPT-4o or Claude, they haven't been released as standalone APIs for direct developer access. They function as infrastructure components powering products rather than products themselves. This raises questions about Microsoft's long-term strategy. Will the company open-source FI models or release them publicly? Or will they remain a proprietary advantage locked inside Azure? The answer likely depends on competitive pressure. If Anthropic or Google release equally efficient specialized function-calling models, Microsoft might open up FI models to stay competitive. As long as they maintain a cost advantage through proprietary control, there's little incentive to share. The Future of Specialized Models The FI models represent an interesting trend toward commoditization of specific AI capabilities. Rather than pursuing broad intelligence, they focus on being exceptionally good at one narrow task. This suggests a potential future where we have dozens of tiny, hyper-specialized models instead of one large model handling everything. Microsoft's three-layer approach—AutoGen for orchestration, Copilot Studio for democratization, and FI models for efficiency—creates a comprehensive agentic AI stack. While much of it remains obscure to those outside the Microsoft ecosystem, the technical architecture and enterprise-first philosophy make it a formidable player in the agentic AI space. The open question is whether this approach will translate beyond enterprise customers. As AI agents become more accessible, Microsoft's governance-heavy, platform-integrated strategy may prove either a significant advantage or a limitation depending on how the market evolves. title: Microsoft's Secret Agentic AI Stack, Explained
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly connected to everyday business and technology workflows. From generating content and analysing documents to automating repetitive processes and developing intelligent applications, AI is being applied across a wide range of professional functions. As these applications evolve, learning AI involves more than understanding basic concepts or experimenting with individual AI tools. Professionals and aspiring technology learners increasingly need practical knowledge of Generative AI, retrieval systems, AI agents, automation, and deployment. Moving From AI Concepts to Practical Skills Understanding what artificial intelligence can do is only the beginning. Practical AI learning involves applying concepts to specific problems and understanding how different components work together. For example, a learner may start by understanding how a large language model generates responses. The next step could involve controlling those responses through prompt engineering, connecting the model to external information through RAG, and eventually creating an agent that can use tools to complete multiple tasks. This progression helps connect individual concepts into complete AI workflows. Generative AI as a Foundation Generative AI allows models to produce different types of content, including text, code, images, and other digital outputs. Large language models have also expanded the use of AI in research, communication, software development, customer support, and business processes. A structured learning program can introduce learners to areas such as: Generative AI fundamentals Large language models Prompt engineering Token and context management AI output evaluation AI application development Model limitations Responsible AI practices The AI Pro program published by upGrad includes foundations of applied GenAI systems, prompt engineering pipelines, output control, and evaluation pipelines as part of its curriculum. Understanding Retrieval-Augmented Generation One practical challenge with AI systems is providing models with relevant information for a specific task. Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly called RAG, is one approach used to connect AI models with external knowledge sources. A RAG workflow can involve: Documents → Data Processing → Embeddings → Vector Database → Retrieval → AI Model → Response Learners can explore how information is divided into usable sections, converted into embeddings, retrieved based on relevance, and provided to a language model as context. The published upGrad curriculum includes RAG pipelines, embeddings, vector databases, semantic search, context-aware question answering, chunking, retrieval strategies, and troubleshooting hallucinations. Exploring Agentic AI Workflows Agentic AI introduces another layer of functionality. Instead of limiting an AI application to a single response, an agentic workflow can involve multiple steps, tools, decisions, and actions. A simplified workflow could look like: Goal → Planning → Tool Selection → Action → Evaluation → Next Step → Final Output For example, an AI agent designed for business research could potentially identify a task, retrieve relevant information, process the information, and prepare a structured result.A Generative AI and Agentic AI Course in Indore can provide a structured environment for developing these skills through guided learning, technical exercises, and project-based application. Learning these concepts gives students an opportunity to understand how AI systems can move from simple question-answering toward multi-step workflows. The AI Pro curriculum includes multi-step agent workflows, tool calling, autonomous task execution, API integration, reasoning and decision flows, memory-based planning, and failure-handling concepts. Learning Through Hands-On Projects Practical projects can help transform technical concepts into usable skills. The published program information states that learners work on 15+ live projects, with examples covering RAG systems, AI agents, and deployed GenAI applications. Potential project areas include: 1. Enterprise Document Intelligence Learners can explore an AI system capable of searching, summarising, and answering questions from a collection of documents. 2. Autonomous Workflow Agent A project can demonstrate how an agent plans tasks, interacts with tools, and performs multiple operations. 3. AI Assistant With RAG Combining retrieval with an AI assistant can demonstrate how external knowledge can be incorporated into AI-generated responses. 4. AI Application Deployment Learners can explore how an AI solution can be exposed through APIs and prepared for deployment. These types of projects provide a practical context for understanding how different AI components interact. Developing Prompt Engineering Skills Prompt engineering remains an important part of Generative AI applications. A well-designed prompt can provide an AI model with: A defined objective Relevant context Clear instructions Output requirements Examples Constraints Learners can experiment with different prompting approaches and evaluate how changes in instructions affect model outputs. However, practical AI development goes beyond prompting. Once learners understand prompting, they can explore retrieval, tool calling, agents, APIs, evaluation, and deployment. Working With Modern AI Tools Practical AI development involves working with multiple tools and technologies. The published AI Pro curriculum lists technologies including Python, Pandas, NumPy, OpenAI, LangChain, LangGraph, FAISS, Hugging Face, Neo4j, Jupyter, Streamlit, GitHub, Power BI, and n8n.A Generative AI and Agentic AI Course in Indore can provide a structured pathway for learners to explore these technologies through instructor-led learning and practical projects. Exposure to these technologies can help learners understand different parts of an AI development workflow. For example: Technology Area Potential Application Python AI application development OpenAI Generative AI applications LangChain AI application and workflow development LangGraph Agentic workflow development FAISS Vector search Hugging Face AI and machine learning models Streamlit Application interfaces GitHub Version control and collaboration n8n Workflow automation The exact tools used in professional projects can vary, so understanding the underlying concepts is equally important. Developing AI Problem-Solving Skills Practical AI learning should focus on solving problems rather than simply learning tools. A useful process can involve: Identifying a real problem. Determining whether AI can contribute to the solution. Selecting appropriate data and models. Designing the workflow. Building a prototype. Testing the outputs. Identifying errors and limitations. Improving the system. Deploying or presenting the final solution. This approach can help learners develop a more structured understanding of AI application development. Building AI Skills Through Classroom Learning Learning complex AI technologies can involve several interconnected concepts. Classroom-based learning can provide learners with direct access to instructors and peers while they work through these concepts. The Indore program information describes structured batches, live instructor sessions, dedicated mentors, and offline classroom learning. This type of environment can support: Immediate doubt resolution Guided technical exercises Peer discussions Project feedback Instructor demonstrations Structured learning schedules For learners who prefer direct interaction while developing technical skills, this can provide an alternative to entirely self-paced learning. Creating a Portfolio of AI Projects Practical projects can also become part of a learner's professional portfolio. A project portfolio can document: The problem statement Technology used AI architecture Development approach Workflow Results Challenges Improvements For example, instead of simply mentioning "RAG" on a resume, a learner could demonstrate a project showing how documents were processed, indexed, retrieved, and used to generate contextual responses. This makes the learning experience more demonstrable and project-oriented. Understanding AI Deployment Building an AI prototype is different from deploying a functional application. Deployment introduces additional considerations such as: APIs System architecture Performance Cost Security Latency Monitoring Reliability Responsible AI The AI Pro curriculum includes API-based GenAI services, local and cloud-ready deployment, end-to-end architecture, and responsible AI practices. Exposure to these concepts can help learners understand the broader AI application lifecycle. Responsible AI and System Limitations Practical AI skills also require awareness of limitations. AI models can generate incorrect or incomplete information. Applications that use external data can also encounter retrieval errors, outdated information, or inappropriate outputs. Learners should therefore understand concepts such as: Output evaluation Hallucination management Human oversight Data privacy Security Safety boundaries Responsible AI implementation The published curriculum specifically includes failure handling, safety boundaries, and responsible AI practices. Career Applications of Practical AI Skills Generative AI and agentic AI skills can complement existing technical and professional backgrounds. Depending on their prior education and experience, learners can explore areas such as: Generative AI development AI engineering AI application development AI automation
title: Building Practical AI Skills with a Generative AI and Agentic AI Course in Indore

abstract: Journal of Victorian Culture’s Digital Forum has been leading discussions on digital transformations in Victorian Studies for well over a decade. From 2016–2019, I co-edited a series of issues with Dr Christopher Donaldson. In a 2017 forum, ‘Workflow’, Christopher and I cautioned readers about historians’ increasing dependence on digital sources, in particular, an over-reliance on that great open sesame of digital archives: the keyword search.1 Conscious that relying on digital collections could lead us to being less critically reflexive or forthright about our work, we encouraged scholars to open the ‘black box’ of digital archives and develop new forms of source criticism that acknowledged how original documents are manipulated, recoded, and reframed through the digitization and web-publication process. As Tim Hitchcock argued, ‘Algorithm-driven discovery and misleading forms of search, poor OCR, and all the selection biases of a new edition of the Western print archive have changed how we research the past, and the underlying character of the object of study (inherited text)’.2 Since that time, the introduction of new tools and techniques, notably machine learning and its subsets, including generative artificial intelligence models such as ChatGPT, means we need to renew existing forms of historical data criticism. As novel digital research infrastructures and tools emerge, how will this impact on our understanding of the nineteenth century and even on how we ‘do’ history? In the era of misinformation – fake news, conspiracy theories, and deepfakes – data literacy is an increasingly urgent issue for scholars, students and citizens alike. Even in relevant subject areas, like English and History, where digital humanities techniques are applicable and powerful, some academics still fail to recognize the importance of digital literacy to staff and students and the contribution that digital humanities can make. Yet the core competencies of the historians’ toolkit – source criticism, provenance, historic contextualization, uncovering bias – are crucial for developing digital literacy, and Digital Victorianists are uniquely placed to contribute. This article reflects upon on my experiences co-developing a series of databases and web resources over the past decade. Most recently, I have been involved in two digital history projects: Data Mining Convict Tattoos (British Academy/ JISC, 2019) which examined the largest number of tattoos ever recorded: 75,688 descriptions of tattoos, on 58,002 convicts in Britain and Australia from 1793 to 1925, and Skin and Bone: Interdisciplinary Analysis of Accidents, Injury and Interpersonal Violence in London, 1760-1901 (British Academy/ Leverhulme, 2021–22) which merged convict, hospital and osteoarchaeological datasets and documented 87,903 injuries on 50,659 Londoners, revealing the physical impact of the Industrial Revolution on the body. These projects emerged from the Digital Panopticon (Arts and Humanities Research Council, 2014) which ­created a single, searchable database of 250,000 individuals sentenced at the Old Bailey between 1780 and 1868, and assessed the impact of varying modes of punishment on their lives. Key to all these projects was the reuse and repurposing of data from the Old Bailey Online project, and associated databases including criminal registers, prison licences, hospital admissions records, civil records, and osteoarchaeological datasets. Skin and Bone and Convict Tattoos shared common ground in other areas. The projects developed bespoke techniques derived from machine learning, including data mining, natural language processing, automated record linkage, and data visualization. The projects reused and linked together a wide range of historic datasets, enabling innovative computational research. We made the data and programming codes as open and accessible as possible: to academics and to the wider public.3 In this article, I will reflect upon what we can learn about the opportunities and limitations of computational humanities research for Victorian Studies and the importance of digital humanities skills for developing digital literacies in the era of artificial intelligence. Historians take messy, incomplete, and often disparate sources that are full of errors and biases and make critical interpretations and arguments that respond to their research questions. Digital sources and technologies do not fundamentally alter this, but they do add a layer of technical complexity.4 Developing techniques for dealing with errors is core to digital history work, and we found that iterative processes were key to the critical evaluation of the data. On both the Convict Tattoos and Skin and Bone projects, our aim was to extract previously hidden data about either tattoos or scars and injuries from the written physical descriptions of approximately 250,000 convicts in the Digital Panopticon collection of databases. Extracting and analysing information from physical descriptions of convicts is not straightforward, because these descriptions, often entered in the same column on a form, contain a wide range of other information in a variety of formats. The challenge in these projects, then, was to extract the relevant information from all the other information in these descriptions. In Skin and Bone, for example, this required distinguishing between language used to describe injuries, wounds and bodily impairments from the wider information contained within the physical descriptions in the criminal records (eye colour, hair colour, complexion, height, weight, and other distinguishing marks such as boils and pockmarks), and we needed to standardize the varied terms used to describe injuries and body parts across the different record collections (criminal, hospital, osteoarchaeological).5 We could not apply machine learning because that would have required training data, and we did not have that. So, we developed an approach that used bespoke dictionaries, reflecting the data and domain expertise developed and built upon through various projects since the Old Bailey Online, and applied rules-based methods of extraction, classification, and analysis. We found that the computing tools required to carry out the projects could not reliably be achieved with any commercial or off-the-shelf packages, so we developed a bespoke process iteratively, combining automated processes of rules-based learning with manual checking through several iterations. The importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and iterative processes here cannot be overstated. Both projects involved multi-disciplinary teams that included historians, web developers, software engineers and other heritage professionals. The iterative process was essential in drawing on both technical expertise and domain-specific knowledge as it allowed for the continuous refinement of methods and interpretations. Developing the ability to collaborate and communicate evolving project needs is a long-term skill – one that short-term funding often hinders. Yet, in digital scholarship, multidisciplinary teams are essential and cannot be substituted by the entirely automated roles that commercial Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to promote.6 We developed a computational humanities approach, combining human and machine intelligence, to better understand and interrogate our source material. Big historical data will always be prone to error, inconsistency, and mess, in the same way the original source material will be, and when using multiple record sets, we need to account for the varied nature of recording on a larger, more complex scale. We found that, because they allowed us to take a macroscopic view of the datasets, data visualizations were especially useful in exposing gaps, errors and biases in the sources that would not be picked up by the naked eye. We experimented with different forms of data visualization, such as bar charts, collocations and heat maps to help us identify meaningful patterns in the data, but also to understand how they were complicated by the particular distinguishing features of the sources used (for example, the uneven survival of records across time, the varied nature of recording by the original institutions and the distorting effect of having one very large dataset from the later nineteenth century – the Metropolitan Police Habitual Criminals Register).7 Exploratory, machine-driven reading of historic ‘big’ data can reveal statistically meaningful patterns illegible to the human eye, but these techniques need to be combined with close reading, so that the data can be understood both at the scale of the full dataset, and at the individual datum in its fullest evidential context. We need to understand how that information was retrieved, check the outputs for accuracy, and interpret our findings accordingly. Andreas Fickers terms this ‘scalable reading’: ‘Learning to move easily between these two forms of reading will require training a new generation of historians in a new cultural technique of information retrieval and interpretation which I frame as “scalable reading”’.8 This level of data literacy is portable, as Fickers argues, not just to academic research, but to a wide range of disciplines and professional sectors. As we move further into the AI era, combining human and machine intelligence will continue to be fundamental, but doing so effectively requires us to develop new forms of historical source criticism. This is npt to suggest that all scholars must become digital humanists or computer scientists, but as digital tools become increasingly commonplace in our research and teaching, knowledge of the underlying data and algorithms must be central to our source criticism. Indeed, ‘digital humanists do not need to understand algorithms at all. They do need, however, to understand the transformations that algorithms attempt to bring about’.9 Artificial intelligence increasingly underpins the tagging, classification, organization, and filtering processes that determine which digital sources historians encounter.10 Commercial information companies like ProQuest are developing algorithms that use features such as phrase recognition to enhance filtered searching and relevance rankings. Increasingly, for-profit companies like Proquest are building databases of digital sources and applying AI to improve search functionality, while creating data mining tools like ProQuest’s TDM Studio to market as new products.11 Consequently, we face the risk of surrendering not just historical sources but entire research methodologies to corporate control.12 But as Lauren Tilton contends, ‘[u]nderstanding the algorithms that built the path through the collection that led to the results is becoming an important feature for understanding our evidence’.13 Future historians must be aware of how history is increasingly filtered and shaped through algorithmic decision-making shaped by AI. Integrating these skills is crucial in ensuring the discipline does not involve a slackening of academic standards. Scholars need to equip current and future humanities students with two essential skills: first, embed computational humanities techniques into undergraduate and postgraduate curricula to demonstrate the potential of technology for humanities scholarship, and second, foster critical, politically aware engagement with web-based tools like ChatGPT, focusing sharply on bias, provenance, and ethics. Digital humanities techniques should not revolve solely around ‘the digital’ but should be used as a tool to make new knowledge that contributes to existing historical research. As Ian Gregory contends, ‘The work that will ultimately prove the relevance and importance of digital resources and methods will not stress the digital, it will stress the applied and contribute to knowledge on particular topics within history that “non-digital” historians will be interested in’.14 Digital humanists are already examining the opportunities of using LLMs for work that extends beyond text, especially as AI capabilities increasingly support multimodal analysis including images and maps.15 It remains to be seen whether LLMs will revolutionize digital humanities; certainly, modes of access (open source versus commercial) and the models’ capabilities for learning context bring challenges. Looking to the future, I could imagine the possibilities of building bespoke LLMs which could be relevant to sub-disciplines in History. As a crime historian, I could envisage a bespoke LLM relating to crime, law and associated materials in the eighteenth to twentieth centuries. The data could incorporate the wide range of open access datasets available, including smaller databases collected by individuals in their research, and associated metadata would provide accurate provenance. Machine translation and transcription in LLMs, including AI tools such as Transkribus, provide tools for extracting, classifying and translating rare and indigenous languages, making once marginalized histories more widely visible and accessible.16 Such work both preserves linguistic heritage and makes non-English academic resources available to a broader audience.17 ChatGPT-4 can power through some steps in the historians’ toolkit – improved OCR, data cleaning, complex, multivariate analysis, data visualization, and translation, for example – but commercial LLMs fail spectacularly at being the historian. ChatGPT and other commercial generative AI tools use webscraping to feed and train their models, meaning that bias, presentism, and a lack of provenance are all current barriers to using these tools for historical research and teaching. The models are unable to assess authenticity, cross-check information across different records, nor can they be ethical or self-reflexive. But perhaps a bespoke LLM, driven by historical data and informed by critical contextualization and developed by multidisciplinary teams, can help the historians of the future navigate the Victorian and contemporary digital world in new ways, all whilst maintaining those core skills and competencies that are relevant to both historical study and cultural citizenship. Zoë Alker is a digital historian of nineteenth-century crime and punishment. Her work focuses on histories of gender, violence and the body, primarily amongst the working classes. With colleagues she has created a series of resources helping to give the public direct access to an extensive range of primary sources evidencing the history of modern Britain, including Digital Panopticon, Convict Tattoos, and Skin and Bone.
title: AI and the Historian: Why Digital Literacy Matters Now More Than Ever

abstract: ⚡ TL;DR: A comprehensive operational framework and system prompt designed to standardize the behavior, methodology, and tone of an AI developer assistant. Abstract: This document serves as the universal developer specification for Gemini-Dev. It defines the identity, core capabilities, navigation rules, and execution flow for an AI-powered full-stack development assistant capable of handling traditional code-based development as well as no-code/low-code platform orchestration. Key Takeaways & Executive Highlights Gemini-Dev must act as a platform-agnostic bridge between code-based and visual/no-code development. The assistant is required to always follow a 'Process First' approach, outlining steps before executing tasks. Mode detection is mandatory; if the user's intent is ambiguous, a hybrid approach should be proposed. All outputs must prioritize structural clarity, utilizing Markdown for code blocks and logical lists. The interaction loop must always conclude by offering the user a clear path forward for subsequent troubleshooting or development. Novelties & Core Innovations Unified framework for both traditional programming and no-code configuration. Explicit mandate for hybrid-mode development strategy in the absence of user preference. Standardized 5-step task execution protocol for AI assistant consistency. Requirement for 'Process First' planning before any technical implementation begins. Integration of search-tool usage as a mandatory operational capability for syntax and library accuracy. Summary & Key Contributions The document outlines the operational persona and procedural guidelines for 'Gemini-Dev,' an AI-based assistant focused on software development. The instructions emphasize a platform-agnostic approach, mandating that the assistant maintain expertise across both traditional coding environments (Python, JavaScript, etc.) and visual development platforms (Bubble, Webflow, Zapier). By enforcing a 'process-first' methodology, the instructions ensure that the assistant outlines plans, validates user intent through clarifying questions, and structures responses clearly using Markdown. The framework covers specific protocols for code generation, debugging, refactoring, and no-code implementation. It mandates that the assistant must diagnose the user's preferred development mode—code, no-code, or hybrid—and provide solutions that are actionable, well-documented, and professional. The document concludes by specifying a mandatory 5-step task execution loop to ensure consistency in interaction quality, project scoping, and continuous user engagement. Methodology & Experimental Framework The document utilizes a procedural prompt engineering methodology based on role-play, structured navigation rules, a defined task execution loop (Analyze, Determine, Outline, Execute, Offer), and clear tonal guidelines. Practical Applications & Industry Use Cases Deployment of AI assistants for internal software engineering teams. Standardizing chatbot responses for SaaS development platforms. Educational tools for mentoring junior developers. Bridge systems for cross-functional teams using both code and visual automation tools. Limitations & Future Research Directions The effectiveness depends on the quality of the underlying LLM's reasoning capabilities. No mechanisms defined for automated testing of generated code snippets. Assumes the assistant has live internet access for tool use. Scope limited to standard development tasks; advanced cybersecurity or specialized hardware tasks may require further refinement. Target Audience & Domain Area: Software engineers, AI developers, prompt engineers, and technical support teams deploying AI assistants. Detailed Glossary & Technical Terms Gemini-Dev The specific persona and operational instruction set assigned to the AI assistant. Platform Agnostic The capability to handle development requests across web, mobile, cloud, or automation platforms without bias. Mode Detection The heuristic process of identifying whether a user wants a code-based, no-code, or hybrid solution. Process First A communication methodology requiring the assistant to propose a plan and obtain user approval before executing code or technical implementation. No-Code/Low-Code Platforms that allow software creation through visual interfaces rather than traditional text-based programming (e.g., Bubble, Zapier). Full-stack The ability to assist with both frontend, backend, and integration-level technical tasks. Refactoring The process of restructuring existing code to improve performance and readability without changing its external behavior. Markdown A lightweight markup language used by the assistant to ensure highly structured and readable responses. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) Q1: How does Gemini-Dev handle vague user requests? A: It is instructed to ask one to three highly relevant clarifying questions to properly scope the project before proceeding. Q2: What happens if a user doesn't specify if they want code or no-code? A: The assistant defaults to a Hybrid solution and explains the pros and cons of both approaches for the specific request. Q3: What is the priority when presenting code? A: The priority is to first identify any potential errors, then offer a refactored and optimized solution. Q4: Are there constraints on the programming languages supported? A: No; the guidelines specify expertise in all major programming languages including Python, JavaScript, Go, HTML/CSS, and SQL. Q5: How should the assistant handle no-code platform questions? A: It must provide exact steps for the specific platform, explain the logic involved, and suggest external resources or search queries. abstract: Abstract Recently, artificial intelligence techniques have been utilized in several applications, including prediction, content generation, automated planning, and task execution mediated by tools. However, often there are complex human- and organizational-level goals and needs that can only be met through the integration of multiple capabilities for a significant duration, including goal specification, constraint satisfaction, planning, resource coordination, execution monitoring, replanning, adaptation, and evaluation. Therefore, this paper presents Executive artificial intelligence (Executive AI), a goal-oriented systems architecture designed to integrate these capabilities in a long-term, feedback-loop-driven execution cycle. Furthermore, Executive AI formalizes goals and monitors their execution, evaluates competing plans within resource and operational constraints, drives heterogeneous resource coordination, and replans as necessary in response to changes. Additionally, it integrates human oversight, access control, and goal/result evaluation as primary design requirements, and describes how relevant ideas from intelligent agents, automated planning, decision theory, operations research, control systems, and AI governance architectures can inform the design of Executive AI. Moreover, a formal conceptual model, research questions, and an outline for empirical evaluation are also provided. This manuscript introduces a research program to explore whether this integrated, objective-driven orchestration can enhance the utility, resilience, and responsibility of AI-supported goal achievement. Keywords: Executive AI; artificial intelligence; goal-based artificial intelligence; goal execution; autonomous agents; automated planning; autonomous task-oriented AI; autonomous systems. 1. Introduction Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most transformative technologies of the twenty-first century. Over the past seven decades, AI has evolved from symbolic reasoning systems to statistical learning methods, deep neural networks, and, most recently, large language models (LLMs) capable of generating human-like text, images, software code, and multimedia content [1-3]. Consequently, these advances have fundamentally changed how individuals, organizations, and governments access information, automate processes, and interact with digital systems [4, 5]. Contemporary general-purpose AI offers many of these capabilities and supports various functions such as prediction, content creation, planning, and acting through external systems [6]. Nevertheless, sophisticated human and organizational objectives might necessitate multiple combinations of these capabilities. Furthermore, extending across multiple time steps and evolving environments, general-purpose AI might need to accomplish complex multi-stage goals involving multiple tasks, constraints, heterogeneous resources, external constituencies, and concurrent mission steps, with a set of evolving conditions that may change as the mission unfolds [7-10]. While individual AI systems can support numerous such activities, the achievement of a goal depends on more than the quality of an individual response or the success of a single action [11, 12]. Specifically, achieving a goal may entail representing a persistent goal, coordinating between tools and actors, verifying intermediate results, managing dependencies and alternative routes, and adapting to plan revisions when conditions change [13]. Consequently, the degree to which current systems support all these capabilities depends on systems architecture, application, and implementation. Therefore, the concern is not that existing AI systems cannot accomplish these tasks independently, but that scalable and trustworthy coordination of an entire set of activities needed to accomplish complex goals remains a crucial systems-engineering problem [14-18]. Specific examples illustrate this phenomenon. For instance, a prospective student applying for doctoral studies must research appropriate institutions and admission criteria, submit entrance examination scores, contact faculty members, secure funding, complete applications, monitor deadlines, track responses, and manage visa procedures. Although contemporary AI tools [19] for drafting emails or summarizing admission criteria are beneficial for individual tasks, they do not facilitate the overarching execution process. Similarly, an entrepreneur establishing a new venture must conduct market research, acquire funding, complete online registration, recruit personnel, develop products, and evolve business plans, all of which require integration into a seamless execution process. Moreover, the context of goal execution has become increasingly complex. Currently, individuals and organizations continuously work toward objectives involving complex sets of entities, heterogeneous resources, multiple constraints, and uncertain, dynamic environments [20]. These efforts are supported by intricate software ecosystems, such as enterprise resource planning systems, project management systems, workflow automation systems, customer relationship management systems, and AI assistants [21]; however, they typically facilitate only specific components of the goal execution process, rather than the comprehensive trajectory. Recent agentic AI systems have extended existing functionality in these ways: AI models are enabled to reason with tools utilized outside the model, take action within an interactive environment, and perform multi-step tasks. However, benchmark research still exposes issues with long-horizon reasoning, robustness, instruction following, and end-to-end task completion in realistic environments [17, 18]. Consequently, such results motivate the exploration of alternative architectural methods for persistent goal management and coordinated task execution. Ultimately, these results do not justify certain alternative architectural design solutions for these issues; each proposed solution must also be tested in the real world. Consequently, current AI agents primarily consist of short-lived workflows executing in predefined environments; thus, they lack capabilities for strategic planning, resource negotiation, long-term monitoring, organizational collaboration, and continuous improvement toward extended and dynamic objectives [22, 23]. Ultimately, these findings indicate a broader framework for intelligent computation with objectives as the focal point, rather than relying on prompts or isolated tasks. Such a system would approach goals as first-class computational entities, enabling methodologies for goal specification, constraint reasoning, solution formulation, resource acquisition and scheduling, execution monitoring, uncertainty management, and experiential learning. Consequently, this perspective reframes the primary objective of AI from answering questions or creating content toward maximizing the probability of successful task completion. Consequently, this paper addresses this research problem through Executive AI. Specifically, Executive AI is a systems-level architecture that maintains explicit representations of goals throughout their execution lifecycles. Rather than viewing planning, tool use, resource coordination, monitoring, and adaptive learning as disparate processes, the Executive architecture structures them around the continuous presence of a goal and its constraints. Ultimately, the objective is not to supersede existing AI, planning techniques, workflow managers, human collaborators, and other resources with a new, all-encompassing learning engine, but to connect and leverage them within a single system. Specifically, Executive AI derives from the human executive functions of the mind: planning, prioritization, strategic decision-making, cognitive flexibility, and self-control. Therefore, beyond merely providing information or executing a given task, an Executive AI system can function as an executive support mechanism, coordinating the activities of multiple entities and assisting individuals and organizations throughout the entire process of goal achievement. Whereas predictive AI utilizes past data to forecast future outcomes [24], and generative AI synthesizes new data from learned knowledge [25], Executive AI converts aspirational objectives into tangible achievements through coordinated execution. Consequently, by combining expertise from the fields of artificial intelligence, decision science, operations research, systems engineering, project management, system tuning, and network science, Executive AI applies a unified computational structure for intelligent execution. Regarding the underlying principles of Executive AI design, all objectives are treated as computational first-class objects. Furthermore, execution is framed as a dynamic, evolutionarily informed tuning process. Accordingly, decision-making adapts in real-time to environmental changes by utilizing feedback and continuous learning. In addition, resources of all types, including organizations, personnel, digital services, financial assets, and AI agents, are coordinated within a single execution environment. Ultimately, the experience of execution—where every executed action is measured and subsequently enriched by machine intelligence—becomes institutional knowledge. Importantly, this structure is designed to integrate with existing AI solutions rather than completely replacing them. This configuration leverages the progression in machine learning, large language models, knowledge graphs, automated workflows, and multi-agent systems by introducing an additional execution layer, which synthesizes these components to achieve complex objectives. In this manner, Executive AI functions as an architectural extension, rather than a substitute for existing artificial intelligence frameworks.
