abstract: Artificial intelligence-augmented additive manufacturing (AI2AM) represents a transformative frontier in digital fabrication, where artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded not as a peripheral tool, but as a central framework driving intelligent, adaptive, and autonomous additive manufacturing (AM) systems. The objective of this Roadmap is to present a comprehensive vision of the state-of-the-art developments in AI2AM while charting the future trajectory of this rapidly emerging field. As AM applications continue to expand across diverse sectors, conventional design and control strategies face growing limitations in scalability, quality assurance, and material complexity. AI uses tools like computer vision, generative design, and large language models to help solve problems in scalability, quality assurance, and material complexity, allowing for real-time defect detection, digital twin integration, and closed-loop process control. This roadmap brings together leading contributions from twenty internationally recognized research groups by uniting perspectives from materials science, computer science, robotics, and manufacturing. This work aims to create a cohesive framework for advancing AI2AM as a multidisciplinary science. The ultimate intent of this work is to establish a foundation for coordinated research and innovation in AI-powered AM and to serve as a strategic entry point for future breakthroughs in autonomous and sustainable production.
title: Roadmap on Artiﬁcial Intelligence-Augmented Additive Manufacturing

abstract: This dataset contains the complete coding tables underlying a structured review of how the literature on automated fibre placement and automated tape laying connects manufacturing constraints, the deviations they give rise to, the structural consequences of those deviations, and feedback into the design problem. Two independent layers are provided. The prevalence layer records six implementation indicators and five causal links for a corpus of 167 publications, of which full texts were obtained for 147; proportions are accompanied by assumption-free bounds rather than confidence intervals, because full-text availability was non-random. The mechanism-and-effect layer is a purposively assembled matrix of 91 comparisons extracted from 44 publications, coded by effect class, reference state, direction of comparison, response level, deviation type and origin, fidelity level and the provenance of each reported value. The dataset also contains the screening log for 814 publications, the frozen analytical set of 476, the pilot validation blocks that established the accuracy of coding from bibliographic records, the claim ledger mapping every generalising statement onto the identifiers of the comparisons that support it, the discrepancy register, the metric harmonisation map, the comparison-direction adjudication, the gap-test log, a changelog of two corrections made after the data freeze, and an audit trail from which every numerical value reported in the article can be recomputed. The dataset is entirely in English: identifiers, codes, flags, numerical fields, column names and all free-text provenance, adjudication and interpretation fields. A README with a per-file catalogue and a column glossary is included. Provenance of the values. Every numerical value and every classification in these tables was extracted and verified by the author from the primary sources. A large language model was used only to move information already present in bibliographic records into the fields of the extraction sheet and to assemble comparative tables from fields that had already been coded. No effect class, reference state, comparison direction, fidelity level or numerical magnitude was assigned by a model, and no inclusion decision was made by a model. The accuracy of the dataset does not depend on any tool other than the author's verification against the primary sources.
title: Coding dataset for a structured review of automated layup constraints, manufacturing deviations and structural response in curvilinearly reinforced composite structures

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integral to managing manufacturing quality. Techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision are employed for tasks like defect detection, quality forecasting, process surveillance, fault diagnosis, and process enhancement. Recently, large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and knowledge-graph strategies have introduced innovative methods for utilizing engineering documents and other unstructured manufacturing data in quality assessments. This review analyzes peer-reviewed studies published between January 2021 and September 2026, categorizing the literature by the quality function AI supports rather than by specific algorithms. It explores six domains: automated inspection and defect detection, predictive quality, process monitoring and anomaly detection, explainable AI and diagnosis, quality knowledge management, and integrated decision support. The findings suggest a gradual broadening of AI's functional role, evolving from merely detecting and predicting isolated quality outcomes to interpreting diverse information, aiding diagnosis, supporting engineering decisions, and starting to coordinate quality-related tasks. The review also highlights ongoing challenges related to data quality, rare failures, model drift, explainability, interoperability, industrial validation, and human oversight. Industrial evidence is more mature in inspection, predictive quality, and selected monitoring applications, whereas generative and agentic methods remain at an earlier stage of industrial validation.
title: Artificial Intelligence in Manufacturing Quality: Applications, Challenges, and Emerging Research Directions
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

abstract: The selection of the most suitable architectural pattern for Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) applications within the Industry 4.0 paradigm presents a critical challenge, as organizations grapple with a variety of contexts, sophisticated architecture, complex deployment, stringent performance requirements, and evolving security concerns. This thesis develops and validates a transparent, LLM-based approach and a decision framework for pattern selection. The approach formalizes decision rules that are used to select appropriate IIoT architecture for a provided use-case. Evidence was assembled through a qualitative synthesis of approximately 5,000 publications that were programmatically collected, deduplicated, ranked for relevance, and mined for key metrics describing pattern attributes and reported contexts. Domain experts in IoT were asked in a survey to subsequently specify use-case descriptions and decide how much weight to give each evaluation criterion, which were predefined. This expert mapping constitutes the ground truth that instantiates the theoretical model within the decision framework. A large language model (LLM) was deployed as a tool for context specialization, transforming generic architectural knowledge into case-specific recommendation. Conditioned on the expert-validated pattern–use-case mapping, the model in-gests previously unseen architecture/use-case descriptions and returns a rank-ordered set of suitable architectural patterns with accompanying rationales. The LLM operationalizes and generalizes expert knowledge to novel contexts. The findings indicate that pattern suitability is highly context specific, and that a structured, data-driven approach significantly enhances decision confidence. By formalizing pattern–usecase mappings and incorporating expert judgments, the research delivers a twofold contribution. On the one hand, it establishes a approach for making sense of IIoT architectural choices. On the other hand, it provides a practical, data-driven approach that system architects can apply immediately. The primary users of this approach are system architects, solution engineers, and industrial IT decision makers in manufacturing and industry related sectors. The secondary users include researchers and lecturers who can employ the model as a teaching and benchmarking instrument. Future studies might look at systems that adjust in real-time and examine their pros and cons across different industrial settings.
title: An LLM-based approach to maximize the :effectiveness of Industrial Internet of :Things implementations through the :selection of architecture

abstract: This paper presents a scalable and modular pipeline architecture engineered for real-time big data analytics, focusing on the integration of distributed large language models with advanced resource orchestration techniques. The system uses technologies such as parallel task division, adaptive scheduling, and mathematical foundation optimization to meet the needs of high throughput and low latency processing. Efficiency-driven algorithms enable the pipeline to dynamically allocate computing resources based on real-time workload fluctuations to balance node utilization and reduce end-to-end latency. The adaptive sharding mechanism accurately extracts data from IoT sensor feeds and financial transaction logs to ensure robust load distribution and traffic bursts. Micro-batch scheduling and pipelining across GPU clusters support parallel processing, while hybrid checkpointing and fault recovery protocols ensure that the system recovers quickly in the event of a failure or anomaly. A series of experiments were conducted on a production-scale cluster consisting of multiple GPU-enabled nodes to quantitatively evaluate the performance. The study compares the proposed system with traditional MapReduce, Spark streaming, and non-adaptive LLM inference baselines. The pipeline still has excellent latency and throughput performance even when the number of nodes and data increases. It achieved up to 2.4x throughput and 41% less job latency compared to the best performance baseline. This shows that its adaptive scaling and load balancing functions are effective. A comprehensive scalability evaluation shows that the coordination overhead remains small as the architecture scales horizontally. Smart manufacturing, autonomous system analysis, and real-time financial monitoring are all areas where the modular framework has broad applications. This research pushes the state-of-the-art in big data processing by combining LLM-driven semantic analysis with robust systems engineering. This provides a practical and reliable blueprint for the next generation of real-time data intelligence solutions.
title: A scalable pipeline for real-time big data analytics using LLM-based methods

abstract: The transition to Circular Manufacturing (CM) demands interoperable coordination of heterogeneous Product, Process, and Resource (PPR) data across organizational boundaries and shopfloor systems. Existing semantic technologies for interoperable knowledge representation, such as ontologies and the Asset Administration Shell (AAS), remain passive data carriers decoupled from data integration and operation, while shopfloor orchestration approaches lack grounding in interoperable data standards, leaving a critical gap between structured lifecycle knowledge and closed-loop manufacturing decisions. To resolve this isolation, this paper proposes the Agentic Active AAS (A 4 S), a neural-symbolic architecture that unifies representation, integration, and orchestration within a single framework. A 4 S makes three core contributions. First, A 4 S extends the AAS standard (IEC 63278) from a passive interface to a proactive interoperability layer by leveraging Large Language Models (LLM), which implement the well-known concept of “Active AAS” or “Type3 AAS”. A graph-like recursive encoding of AAS instances is proposed to preserve the strict parent-child topology of AAS shells, submodels, and submodel elements as a symbolic graph traversable by LLM retrieval. Building on this representation, a suite of AAS tools is formalized as the LLM-agent’s bounded action space, enabling the agent to dynamically construct, query, and manipulate AAS instances. Second, A 4 S introduces Agentic Operation Delegation, which abstracts heterogeneous shopfloor operation interfaces into unified AAS operation schemas and mathematically bounds the LLM’s token generation through schema-constrained decoding. Third, building upon the Active AAS layer, an LLM-based Multi-Agent System (LMAS) is developed, in which the Orchestrator Agent and specialized sub-agents interact through the unified AAS substrate. This simultaneously enables automatic creation of Digital Product Passports (DPP) for cross-organizational value chain exchange and intra-enterprise PPR integration for CM operations. The proposed approach is evaluated in a battery remanufacturing scenario with a dynamic system environment. Experimental results show that A 4 S achieves over 95% success rate in complex multi-step shopfloor orchestration tasks, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art LMAS approaches across all model scales. Notably, open-source models (e.g., Qwen3.6–35B) under A 4 S surpass large proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 in orchestration tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed neural-symbolic constraints. For DPP generation, A 4 S-GPT5.2 achieves 90% success rate, where tool execution correctness reaches 100%. These results highlight that A 4 S effectively enables more robust orchestration in the constrained CM environment. The code is released at https://github.com/quickhdsdc/aas-mcp-server.git .
title: Agentic active Asset Administration Shell for circular manufacturing

abstract: Anomaly detection is crucial in maintaining the safety, reliability, and optimal performance of complex systems across diverse domains, such as industrial manufacturing, cybersecurity, and autonomous systems. While conventional methods typically handle single data modalities, recently, there has been an increase in the application of multimodal detection in dynamic real-world environments. This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent research at the intersection of agentic artificial intelligence and large language-based multimodal anomaly detection. We systematically analyze and categorize existing studies based on the agent architecture, reasoning capabilities, tool integration, and modality scope. The main contribution of this work is a novel taxonomy that unifies agentic and multimodal anomaly detection methods, alongside benchmark datasets, evaluation methods, key challenges, and mitigation strategies. Furthermore, we identify major open issues, including data alignment, scalability, reliability, explainability, and evaluation standardization. Finally, we outline future research directions, with a particular emphasis on trustworthy autonomous agents, efficient multimodal fusion, human-in-the-loop systems, and real-world deployment in safety-critical applications.
title: Agentic and LLM-Based Multimodal Anomaly Detection: Architectures, Challenges, and Prospects

abstract: The paper proposes a two-stage pipeline for producing Process Flow Diagrams and Piping & Instrumentation Diagrams for chemicals that have no public process documentation.Stage one is a multi-agent web-navigation layer: a meta-agent decomposes a query, routes subtasks to ve sub-agents (image, scholar, patent, wiki, web insights) by cosine similarity between the subtask embedding and a written capability description, orders them with a DAG, and aggregates their outputs, with an iterative feedback loop involving human experts, a "Gold-LLM-as-a-Judge" and a "Reward-Model-as-Judge" (section Agentic Web Navigation Framework).Stage two turns that text into an ontological knowledge graph -sliding-window chunking with contextual pre xes, LLM-based NER and relation extraction, entity merging by cosine plus Levenshtein, hierarchical Leiden communities, top-K community retrieval -and answers queries over it (section Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation).Evaluation covers 1,020 chemicals for knowledge-base construction, 50 held out for generation, and a 6,000-pair ODQA set (section Datasets), scored by the NVIDIA Nemotron-4-340B-Reward model on Helpfulness, Correctness, Coherence, Complexity, and Verbosity, plus BLEU/ROUGE-N/ROUGE-L (section Results and Additional Experiments).The engineering is real, and the write-up of the architecture is careful.My problem is with what the evidence is asked to carry.
title: Review of: "Accelerating Manufacturing Scale-Up from Material Discovery Using Agentic Web Navigation and Retrieval-Augmented AI for Process Engineering Schematics Design"
A Survey on Agentic AI: Applications, Challenges and Evaluation Frameworks
venue: Lecture notes in networks and systems

abstract: The rapid transition from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 has significantly increased the complexity of manufacturing systems while accelerating the development and deployment of smart and sustainable materials in advanced industrial applications. These emerging materials require intelligent decision-making approaches that integrate data, advanced analytics, optimization, digital twins, and human expertise throughout their design, production, monitoring, and lifecycle management. Although artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, and mathematical optimization have independently advanced intelligent manufacturing, their isolated application often limits adaptability, explainability, and resilience. This study presents a systematic literature review of Decision Intelligence (DI) in collaborative intelligent manufacturing following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology, synthesizing evidence from 140 peer-reviewed publications. The review comprehensively examines the evolution of Decision Intelligence, core enabling technologies, layered architectures, industrial applications, human-centered decision-making, implementation challenges, and emerging research trends. The findings indicate that effective Decision Intelligence requires the seamless integration of artificial intelligence, optimization, digital twins, knowledge graphs, explainable AI, and Human-in-the-Loop AI within a unified decision ecosystem that combines computational intelligence with human judgment. The proposed framework and research roadmap provide valuable theoretical insights and practical guidance for developing resilient, explainable, and human-centric Decision Intelligence systems that support the realization of Industry 5.0 manufacturing for smart and sustainable materials.
title: Decision Intelligence in Collaborative Intelligent Manufacturing of smart and sustainable materials: A Comprehensive Review of Artificial Intelligence, Optimization, Digital Twins, and Human-Centered Decision-Making
venue: Journal of Sustainable Smart Materials and Structural Systems

abstract: The rapid digital transformation in society, driven by Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing, necessitates effective AI education for engineering and technical personnel. Despite the growing prevalence of AI tools like Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT), adoption in developing countries remains uneven, hindered by limited awareness, infrastructural challenges, and ethical concerns. This study aims to assess the readiness and needs of students and teachers in Russia and Armenia regarding AI integration in education. A survey method was employed, involving over 500 participants from universities in both countries. The results reveal increasing AI usage, particularly among students, but also highlight gaps in awareness, infrastructure, and ethical understanding. These findings point to the need for targeted AI literacy programs, improved infrastructure, and ethical guidelines to facilitate responsible AI integration. Future research should explore long-term trends and culturally specific factors influencing AI adoption to support sustainable educational development in the context of Industry 4.0.
title: AI in Education for Smart Manufacturing: Assessing the Readiness and Needs of Students and Teachers in Developing Countries

abstract: Machine learning has become a transformative force in VLSI design and semiconductor manufacturing. This study provides a critical review of state-of-the-art ML approaches from across the digital IC design flow (from HLS, via RTL PPA prediction, to logic synthesis, placement, routing, verification, DFT, and test), and major semiconductor manufacturing domains, such as lithography, etch modeling, metrology, defect classification, yield prediction, and equipment health monitoring. This study provides comparative insights, cross-domain analysis, and taxonomy-driven organization for ML methods such as supervised learning, GNNs, RL, AutoML, generative AI, PINNs, and LLM-based approaches. There is the bottlenecksdomain shift, data scarcity, compute cost, and explainability identified -and put forward a future roadmap that includes hybrid physics-ML modeling, industrial-scale datasets, explainable models, and ML-driven digital twins. This systematic synthesis shows that ML is transforming EDA workflows and making next-generation semiconductor manufacturing intelligence achievable.
title: Intelligent Silicon: A Systematic Study of Machine Learning for Optimization and Automation in Vlsi Design and Manufacturing
venue: Global Conference on Wireless and Optical Technologies (GCWOT)

abstract: Customer-experience (CX) programs collect large volumes of free-text survey verbatims, and those verbatims routinely carry personal data: names of sales and service staff, e-mail addresses, phone numbers, site locations, and order or serial identifiers. Before such text can enter global analytics it must be anonymized, and many organizations still do this by hand. This paper reports a comparative evaluation, conducted in a multinational manufacturing group, of three families of text anonymization: regular-expression and dictionary rules, named-entity-recognition (NER) pipelines built on Presidio-style detectors and spaCy models, and prompt-driven large language models (LLMs) accessed through Azure OpenAI (GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4). On a labeled sample of 2,000 business-to-business survey verbatims in English, German, Spanish, Portuguese and Chinese containing 3,089 annotated personal-data spans, we measure entity-level precision, recall and F1, per-language robustness, sentiment preservation, cost per thousand records, latency and auditability. Rules achieved the highest precision on pattern entities but recalled only 41% of person names; NER degraded sharply outside English and on identifiers; GPT-4 delivered the best single-method F1 (0.88) at roughly twenty times the inference cost of GPT-3.5-Turbo. A hybrid pipeline (rules and NER first, LLM span extraction second, confidence-based routing to human review) reached an F1 of 0.94 before and 0.97 after review, while sending 7.2% of records to reviewers and cutting manual anonymization effort by about 83% per survey wave. We describe the pipeline's integration with data classification and identity-based access control, and derive governance guardrails for generative models in privacy-critical data flows
title: LLM-Assisted Anonymization of Customer Experience Data: A Comparative Study of Rule-Based, NER, and Generative Approaches
venue: International Journal of Research and Applied Innovations

abstract: Recently, digital twins (DTs) have been increasingly used in manufacturing for predictive maintenance, adaptive control, and system-level optimization. The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to control machine operations through DTs is rapidly expanding as AI can identify complex patterns and make adaptive decisions on the fly. However, the scarcity of high-quality time-series data remains a critical bottleneck for training AI systems. Moreover, the use of unverified AI control strategies directly on live machines poses significant safety and reliability risks. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a data-driven surrogate framework, which serves as a virtual replica of the physical machine for safe experimentation. A conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) was employed to generate realistic time-series data for manufacturing processes with Soft-Dynamic Time Warping (soft-DTW) as an additional loss objective. A machine-learning (ML) layer performs anomaly detection and process prediction while a Large Language Model (LLM) interprets system states, explains detected anomalies, and recommends corrective actions. The framework also includes a policy guard module, which validates these recommendations against predefined operational and safety constraints to ensure reliability and rule compliance before execution. The proposed framework is scalable and is validated using multiple surrogates of CNC milling machines and FDM 3D printers. This surrogate-based case study demonstrates that policy-guarded AI integration within a digital twin environment enables safe, reproducible, and scalable research toward intelligent and autonomous manufacturing systems. © 2026 The Authors. Published by ELSEVIER Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0) Peer-review under responsibility of the scientific committee of the NAMRI|SME.
title: Policy-Guarded Explainable ML–LLM Framework for Data-Driven Control in Digital Twin Surrogate

abstract: Manufacturing enterprises increasingly integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) into production processes to enhance efficiency and competitiveness. However, Responsible AI (RAI) practices are often overlooked, leading to potential ethical, legal, and operational risks such as biased decision-making and lack of transparency and trust. Existing maturity models, which evaluate the development stages of systems or practices, primarily address either Industrial AI (IAI) applications or general aspects of RAI. AI sandboxes, as controlled environments for testing and validating AI systems under regulatory supervision, offer a structured approach to assess RAI practices. Yet the frameworks lack a targeted model for determining RAI maturity specifically within manufacturing. To address the gap, this paper introduces a RAI-oriented maturity model adopted to the context of smart manufacturing. The maturity model evaluates AI systems across six key dimensions: Accountability, Fairness, Human-Centricity, Privacy/Security, Sustainability, and Explainability. In particular, this paper delves into the dimension of accountability, exploring its indicators. A structured literature review defines the indicators, and a pairwise comparison determines their relative importance. The model is applied to an industrial case study involving a Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbot for maintenance in the semiconductor industry. Preliminary results demonstrate the model’s practicality and effectiveness, providing actionable insights, i.e. the need for auditing mechanisms, to enhance accountable AI design and deployment in industrial settings.
title: Responsible AI in Manufacturing: The Case of Accountability in AI Systems

abstract: The production industry is experiencing the most radical change ever since the invention of the assembly line due to the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Going beyond conventional automation, AI opens up cognitive possibilities whereby systems can learn on the data and respond to the changing environment and optimize complex tasks on their own. The article is a detailed investigation of the complex nature of AI in the contemporary manufacturing setting. It starts with the definition of the pillars of core technology in the industrial AI that are machine learning, computer vision and the new frontier of Generative AI and Physical AI. The article has then methodically explored the main application applications predictive maintenance, quality control, process optimization, supply chain resilience, human-robot collaboration, and generative design and presented the mechanisms and measurable advantages of each using real-world examples. This is followed by a critical analysis which discusses the major challenges that impede mass adoption which include lack of data infrastructure, talent and culture gap, complication of integration with existing systems, and the black box problem. By combining the findings of the recent industry whitepapers, scholarly work, and surveys across the globe, this article offers a four-pillar how-to guide to successful AI implementation, which focuses on strategic alignment, value-driven use cases, effective data governance, and workforce transformation. Lastly, it envisions the trends of the future such as the emergence of sovereign AI, maturity of context-aware robotics, and essential contribution of AI to enhancing sustainability. The conclusion is that the holistic and human-focused approach is more than just good but the key to manufacturers to reap the full potential of AI and gain a competitive edge in addition to surviving in the age of Industry 4.0.Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Smart Manufacturing, Predictive Maintenance, Quality Control, Supply Chain Optimization, Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC), Generative AI, Digital Twin, Industry 4.0, Implementation Framework, Data Governance, Workforce Upskilling.
title: The AI Revolution in the Manufacturing Environment: A Comprehensive Analysis of Implementation, Impact, and Future Directions
Knowledge Extraction for Commercial Aircraft Process Specification Based on LLM Generation Rules
venue: Lecture notes of the Institute for Computer Sciences, Social Informatics and Telecommunications Engineering

abstract: This experiment examines how different educational interventions affect public perceptions of AI existential risks compared to other global risks like climate change. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions OR one control condition: (1) a conversation with an LLM prompted to educate and persuade about AI existential risks, (2) playing a text-based "AI Safety Game" simulating escalating AI scenarios as the U.S. President, (3) watching 10 minutes of a podcast interview about AI risks (4) engaging in a "Stump the AI" capabilities demonstration game. The final group (5) will be a control group watching an unrelated video about championship ring manufacturing. All participants complete post-intervention questionnaires measuring their concern levels for AI risks versus climate change risks, allowing us to test hypotheses about whether LLM interactions increase AI risk concern, whether the interactive game produces more durable attitude changes, whether LLM persuasiveness varies by prior experience level, and whether focusing on AI risks correspondingly decreases concern for other global risks, like concern for climate change. Participants will also be invited to repeat the survey after six weeks to determine if the effects of the experimental conditions are temporary or not (participants would only be asked to complete page 4,5, and 6 of the survey, skipping the intervention, and demographic questions).
title: How LLM-Based Interventions Shape Public Concern About AI Threats

abstract: With the rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs), significant advancements have emerged in natural language processing, cross-modal reasoning, and complex task planning, heralding a paradigm shift in robotic manipulation. Traditional robotic arm control demands specialized programming and extensive engineering expertise, creating a high barrier to entry. This paper systematically reviews recent advancements in LLM-based zero-code implementation technologies for robotic arms, which enable direct control through natural language and substantially reduce development costs and operational complexity. We establish a clear technical classification framework, analyzing the performance characteristics and applicability of various methods such as direct mapping approaches (SayCan, Code as Policies, ProgPrompt) and feedback-driven architectures (Inner Monologue). We also explore multimodal fusion techniques (RT-2, PaLM-E, VIMA, VoxPoser) and their application across diverse scenarios including education, home services, and manufacturing. Furthermore, we identify key challenges—including natural language parsing accuracy, robustness of multimodal fusion, long-horizon planning, and safety—and propose future research directions aimed at fostering the integration of embodied intelligence with natural language interaction. This study clarifies the research trajectory in this field, offering theoretical support for the broader popularization and deployment of robotic technology.
title: LLM-Based Zero-Code Control for Robotic Arms: Representative Methods, Challenges, and Future Trends
The Idol Factory Multiple Points of Epistemic Failure Across Human-LLM Interaction Systems
CHAIKMAT 4.0 - Commonsense Knowledge and Hybrid Artificial Intelligence for Trusted Flexible Manufacturing

abstract: Scientific experimentation and manufacturing rely on prolonged protocol development and complex, multi-step implementation, which require continuous human expertise for precise execution and decision-making, limiting interpretability and scalability. Here, we introduce human-artificial intelligence (AI) co-embodied intelligence, a new form of physical AI that unites human researchers, agentic AI, and wearable hardware. In this paradigm, humans provide precise execution, while agentic AI contributes contextual reasoning, adaptive planning, and analysis. The wearable interface continuously captures experimentation and manufacturing, facilitating seamless communication between humans and AI. We instantiate this paradigm in a microfabrication cleanroom, leading to the agentic-physical experimentation (APEX) system which understands fabrication procedure with accuracy 51% higher than state-of-the-art multimodal large language models/vision language models (LLMs/VLMs), detects and corrects fabrication errors in real-time, and transfers procedural expertise to novice users. Critically, APEX system enables the co-development of fabrication protocols in cleanrooms, overcoming the incompatibility of elastomeric materials in standard microfabrication processes and enabling previously unattainable fabrication outcomes, as demonstrated by the wafer-scale realization of brain-level soft neural probe capable of single-unit-resolution neural recording. These results establish the human-AI co-embodied intelligence that extends agentic reasoning beyond computation into the physical domain, transforming scientific experimentation and manufacturing into autonomous, traceable, interpretable and scalable processes.
title: Human-AI Co-Embodied Intelligence for Scientific Experimentation and Manufacturing

abstract: The advent of new-generation information and communication technologies, such as Generative AI, Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, Blockchain technology, and artificial intelligence (AI), has led to the emergence of the era of big data in recent years. Digital twin has emerged as one of the most active components in smart manufacturing, garnering significant attention from enterprises, research institutes, and researchers. By creating a digital twin, manufacturers can simulate different scenarios and test various configurations without disrupting the actual production process. This allows for more efficient testing and optimization of production processes, as well as improved quality control and predictive maintenance. Overall, digital twins are an important tool in smart production that can help manufacturers improve efficiency and reduce costs while ensuring high-quality output. In this paper, after reviewing the literature on the subject, in this article, by reviewing the literature, we presented a framework of the digital twin in smart manufacturing, which includes Optimization, Predictive Maintenance, Quality Control, Design, and Simulation, which can be a good guide for future studies.
title: Digital Twin based Smart Manufacturing; From Design to Simulation and Optimization Schema

abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with Digital Twin (DT) technology has emerged as a transformative approach for advancing predictive capabilities in smart manufacturing environments. AI-enhanced digital twins leverage real-time data streams, physics-based models, and machine learning algorithms to create high-fidelity virtual replicas of physical assets, processes, and systems. This paper presents a comprehensive examination of AI-augmented DT frameworks for predictive maintenance, process optimization, and adaptive control in manufacturing. Through an extensive literature survey, we identify prevailing architectures, data integration strategies, and AI methodologies driving predictive smart manufacturing. A mixed-method research design—incorporating case studies, simulation experiments, and field deployments—was employed to evaluate the performance gains and implementation challenges of AI-enhanced DTs. Results demonstrate up to a 30% reduction in unplanned downtime, a 20% improvement in overall equipment effectiveness (OEE), and significant enhancements in supply chain resilience. The findings underscore the critical roles of data quality, semantic interoperability, and adaptive learning models in realizing robust predictive frameworks. We conclude with a discussion of scalability considerations, cybersecurity implications, and future research directions, offering a roadmap for practitioners and researchers aiming to harness AI-driven digital twins for next-generation smart manufacturing.
title: AI-Enhanced Digital Twins in Predictive Smart Manufacturing
venue: World Journal of Future Technologies in Computer Science and Engineering

abstract: The concept of Digital Twin technology has become an important factor in enabling intelligent manufacturing through the creation of dynamic virtual models of physical entities, manufacturing processes, and manufacturing systems. With the use of Digital Twins alongside with AI, IIoT, cloud computing, and cyber-physical systems, manufacturers can monitor their operations in real time, carry out predictive analysis, make autonomous decisions, and optimize the entire process life cycle. This chapter highlights a thorough discussion of digital twins and AI-based smart manufacturing systems from the viewpoint of sustainable mechanical engineering. It reviews the basic concepts and structure of digital twins along with the influence of artificial intelligence, machine learning, predictive maintenance, intelligent process optimization, and quality control in modern manufacturing. This chapter also reviews the applications of digital twins in the context of smart factories, additive manufacturing, robotics, energy management, and supply chain optimization to boost productivity and sustainability in manufacturing. The importance of digital twin technology for resource efficiency, reduction of carbon footprint, circular manufacturing, and net-zero manufacturing processes is also reviewed. This chapter finally discusses the existing challenges associated with data compatibility, cybersecurity, computational intensity, and industrial scalability, along with future perspectives that may include generative AI, edge intelligence, autonomous factories, and human-centric Industry 5.0.
title: DIGITAL TWIN AND AI-DRIVEN SMART MANUFACTURING SYSTEMS

abstract: The manufacturing sector is increasingly adopting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to transition from simple perception to autonomous execution, yet current evaluations fail to reflect the rigorous demands of real-world manufacturing environments. Progress is hindered by data scarcity and a lack of fine-grained domain semantics in existing datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce FORGE. Wefirst construct a high-quality multimodal dataset that combines real-world 2D images and 3D point clouds, annotated with fine-grained domain semantics (e.g., exact model numbers). We then evaluate 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs across three manufacturing tasks, namely workpiece verification, structural surface inspection, and assembly verification, revealing significant performance gaps. Counter to conventional understanding, the bottleneck analysis shows that visual grounding is not the primary limiting factor. Instead, insufficient domain-specific knowledge is the key bottleneck, setting a clear direction for future research. Beyond evaluation, we show that our structured annotations can serve as an actionable training resource: supervised fine-tuning of a compact 3B-parameter model on our data yields up to 90.8% relative improvement in accuracy on held-out manufacturing scenarios, providing preliminary evidence for a practical pathway toward domain-adapted manufacturing MLLMs. The code and datasets are available at https://ai4manufacturing.github.io/forge-web.
title: FORGE: Fine-grained Multimodal Evaluation for Manufacturing Scenarios

abstract: Bearing fault diagnosis faces critical challenges when dataset heterogeneity, operating condition variations, and limited labeled data occur simultaneously in industrial environments. Existing approaches address these issues in isolation and rely on implicit feature alignment, limiting effectiveness under concurrent challenges. This paper proposes a knowledge-guided two-stage transfer learning framework that employs a lightweight GPT-2-style Transformer with causal self-attention for hierarchical feature extraction from vibration signals, establishing explicit pathways where pre-trained encoder weights and fault prototype embeddings serve as knowledge carriers from multi-source pre-training to target adaptation. The framework addresses the dual-shift challenge through multi-source learning for generalizable representations, prototype-based knowledge modulation for target adaptation, and taxonomy-adaptive classification for seamless transfer across heterogeneous fault categories. Experimental validation on four real-world datasets demonstrates 92.61% average accuracy with only 10% labeled target data, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 17.24 percentage points, establishing a practical pathway toward cost-effective predictive maintenance in Industry 4.0 applications.
title: An LLM-based Two-Stage Transformer Framework for Cross-Domain Bearing Fault Diagnosis with Limited Data
venue: IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, the demand for standardized mechanisms that enable seamless, scalable, and context-aware integration of these models in a secure manner is increasing. To meet these requirements, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has come into existence as an open interoperability standard that offers a common language for linking AI models with tools, resources, and external systems. The survey provides a complete overview of the architectural foundations, communication paradigm, client–server model, transport mechanisms, design principles, and primary application areas of MCP, such as enterprise systems, software engineering, healthcare, manufacturing, education, finance, and multi-agent systems. It also reviews the state of the art and research advances, outlining security issues and their mitigation, and evaluates the status of MCP-based implementations. MCP is shown to be a significant factor in improving interoperability, context-aware reasoning, workflow orchestration, and modular integration of AI, while also minimizing the need for proprietary interfaces. Moreover, it pinpoints key areas of research that are needed in the future, such as scalability, security, standardized benchmarking, interoperability, and long-term context management, offering researchers and practitioners working on the creation of next-generation AI systems significant directions for future research.
title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI Systems: A Survey of Architectures and Applications
A comprehensive survey on table question answering: Datasets, methods and future directions

abstract: Digital Twins (DT) facilitate monitoring and reasoning processes in cyber–physical systems. They have progressively gained popularity over the past years because of intense research activity and industrial advancements. Cognitive Twins is a novel concept, recently coined to refer to the involvement of Semantic Web technology in DTs. Recent studies address the relevance of ontologies and knowledge graphs in the context of DTs, in terms of knowledge representation, interoperability and automatic reasoning. However, there is no comprehensive analysis of how semantic technologies, and specifically ontologies, are utilized within DTs. This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) is based on the analysis of 82 research articles, that either propose or benefit from ontologies with respect to DT. The paper uses different analysis perspectives, including a structural analysis based on a reference DT architecture, and an application-specific analysis to specifically address the different domains, such as Manufacturing and Infrastructure. The review also identifies open issues and possible research directions on the usage of ontologies and knowledge graphs in DTs.
title: Ontologies in digital twins: A systematic literature review

abstract: Extended Reality (XR) is a collective term that contains Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Mixed Reality (MR), and everything in between. VR is an immersive technology that allows users to interact within a computer-generated 3D virtual environment. AR enhances the user's situational awareness (SA) by superimposing virtual content onto a real scene. MR is a step beyond AR by combining physical reality with digital content in a way that enables real-time interaction with and among real and virtual elements. In the business world, a similarly captivating term, metaverse, indicates a single, universal, and immersive virtual world focused on social and economic connections facilitated by the use of XR technologies [1].XR has proven to be an effective communication medium for humans to instantly interact with other entities in shared spaces. As a result, it has received significant attention from both industry and academia. VR/AR is among the nine enabling technologies in the Industry 4.0 paradigm [2], serving as the only human-centric technology designed specifically for end users. This feature conforms well to the human-centric core value emphasized by the emerging Industry 5.0 [3]. With this advantage, XR could play a critical role in extending cyber-physical systems (CPS) into human-cyber-physical systems (HCPS), seamlessly integrating data, computational intelligence, and real-world situations through context-specific sensory cues for human interaction.With the recent advances in information and communication technologies (ICT), traditional manufacturing systems have evolved into “smart” ones in handling the ever-increasing complexity of tasks incorporating a high degree of autonomy and intelligence. Nevertheless, there are specific tasks on the shop floor that are either impractical or impossible to complete without human intervention. In such situations, the main purpose of smart manufacturing would be to facilitate manual operations, rather than to completely replace human involvement. Indeed, integrated with artificial intelligence (AI), 5G, cloud computing, and Internet-of-Things (IoT), XR applications have been successfully implemented and deployed to assist a diverse range of manual operations within the manufacturing sector [4,5]. The recent special issue titled “Challenges and Opportunities in Computing Research to Enable Next Generation Engineering Applications” published in the Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering (JCISE) also features three review articles focusing on extended reality [6–8]. In addition, the journal has published 16 papers with the words VR, AR, MR, XR, or Metaverse appearing in either the title or abstract between 2018 and 2023 [9–24]. This trend shows a growing interest in XR research in the JCISE community. A special issue focusing on the related fields would be necessary and timely to address this need.The purpose of this special issue is to solicit articles describing fundamental and applied research on XR techniques, solutions, and challenges in the area of design and manufacturing. This issue aims to cover all aspects of XR technology, including technical advances in software/hardware, algorithms, ergonomic analysis, system implementation, and novel empirical studies, for product design and manufacturing processes. In total, eight papers are included following rigorous review and revisions, and each is briefly introduced as follows.AR technology has made significant progress in recent years with applications successfully applied to assist manual tasks in various industries such as manufacturing, military, education, and entertainment. For instance, manual pointing and trajectory tracing are often used in robot programming in the manufacturing environment or during major surgical operations. Design guidelines are essential to develop assisted functions that can effectively enhance users’ situational awareness with instant sensory feedback through AR interfaces. For this purpose, Wang et al. conducted an experimental study on AR user interfaces with various sensory cues designed to assist in the manual tracing of simple and complex trajectories. The study compared the task performance under five sensory feedback conditions: central vision, peripheral vision, auditory sensation, force feedback, and no feedback. The experimental results showed that the feedback information should not only provide prompts for error status but also offer suggestions for correcting the actions of the subjects in complex trajectory tracing. The force feedback demonstrated better adaptation compared to visual and auditory cues. Furthermore, subjects tended to rely more on real-time force feedback to complete difficult tracing tasks than on the other cues. It was also suggested that the design of AR-assisted functions and instant sensory feedback should consider the potential limitations induced by the user's posture during a tracing task. These experimental findings could provide useful insights into the design of sensory feedback for AR-assisted functions developed for manual tracing tasks.Fewer studies have focused on the technical solutions for XR-based virtual footwear try-ons compared to those for garments and facial accessories. Therefore, Chou et al. introduced an approach based on machine learning that estimates the 6-DoF of a human foot using a single RGB image captured from a third-person view. Synthetic annotated data were generated by systematically adjusting the light source, foot geometry, background, camera position, as well as skin and background textures to ensure sufficient variation in information during the training process. Three CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) models (DOPE, DOPE2, and YOLO-6D) were trained using a proprietary dataset containing both synthetic and real foot images, following different training plans. Test results showed that training a CNN model for foot pose estimation performed better through a combination of pretraining and successive training with both proprietary and ImageNet datasets. In real use, YOLO-6D outperformed both the DOPE and simplified DOPE2 models in terms of prediction accuracy and computational speed.Natural human–computer interaction (HCI) remains an important research topic for industrial XR. Three articles featured in this special issue explore HCI from the perspectives of content authoring, cybersecurity, and human pose estimation. Content authoring for XR applications remains a challenge at scale. In response, Ipsita et al. developed VRFromX, an application-embedded workflow for in situ content creation and demonstrated its utility through a welding use case. Additional research is warranted to properly integrate XR technologies with minimal disruption into existing practical engineering workflows, such as the management of computer-numerical control (CNC) machines within a factory.Yang et al. addressed a potential cybersecurity risk existing in mid-air interactions commonly used in MR-based smart manufacturing applications. The authors developed a prototyping system for smart factory management using a video see-through MR HMD. This system allows users to input a password on a login interface, providing access to security/privacy-sensitive information through a single RGB camera capturing mid-air gestures in front of the user. A machine learning-based inference framework tracks hand gestures and estimates input passwords under assumed attack conditions. The test results in two scenarios suggested that potential preventive measures for cybersecurity attacks in MR applications during password input with hand gestures include using more complex characters, applying remote interaction methods, or entering the password while moving.The AR content presented by the head-mounted display (HMD) offers mobility, hands-free capabilities, and a first-person view, particularly useful in the context of industrial applications. The successful deployment of AR applications on these occasions depends on humans accurately interacting with and placing virtual objects in relation to the physical environment. This requires precise alignment and human perception of computer-generated graphics within the physical environment. Yang and Zhang resolved the misregistration issues occurring in video see-through AR HMDs that limit the potential for shared workspaces between humans and machines in shop-floor applications. They identified and analyzed the sources of errors within a comprehensive system framework. A mathematical model was proposed to characterize the influence and sensitivity of errors specifically in the HMD-to-camera transformation. This was achieved by examining three translational and three rotational components comprising the transformation matrix and simulating the resulting misregistration effects. An offline closed-loop calibration approach was applied to reduce the HMD-to-camera transformation error in a prototyping system. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrated satisfactory global registration between virtual objects and the physical environment.Wu et al. implemented ImpersonatAR, a mobile-based application, that utilizes embodied demonstrations in the augmented environment to support the prototyping and evaluation of multi-scenario AR use cases. The application was developed based on a set of design considerations derived from interviews with AR expert designers to address the current limitations of AR prototyping tools. ImpersonatAR enables capturing events or steps through embodied demonstrations using avatars and 3D animations. It facilitates the organization of these events and steps to create a multi-scenario experience, allowing stakeholders to explore the scenarios through interactive role-play with the prototypes. Positive feedback from ten users validated that ImpersonatAR promotes the exploration of diverse design possibilities for multi-scenario AR use cases through embodied representations of different scenarios. This work contributes to human–computer interaction by providing an effective prototyping approach for AR use cases.Advancements in VR offer great opportunities to create effective digital learning and training environments. Multi-user distributed participation in VR facilitates collaborative problem-solving (CPS) and learning-by-doing, both of which are critical professional skills for solving real-world problems. In addition, VR applications integrating with sensors allow the collection of in-process user behavioral data for adaptation or correction. Kim et al. presented a sensor-based multiplayer VR manufacturing simulation game that improved virtual hands-on learning experiences and served as a behavioral modeling method for monitoring the collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills of participants. The Virtual Learning Factory was proposed to facilitate low-cost implementation of virtual hands-on experiences as effective as their real-world equivalents. A dynamic network behavioral modeling approach was developed to extract time-varying patterns of player actions using action-log data using action-log data commonly available in digital learning environments. The heterogeneous-behavioral CPS score was defined by the graph similarity between players. Experimental results demonstrated that the score successfully monitored user-specific collaborative CPS dynamics between players, potentially leading to appropriate interventions to improve learning outcomes. This work enhances the effectiveness of virtual reality and gamification in engineering education.Nguyen et al. developed an augmented reality system for the human-in-the-loop registration of robot-sensor coordinates in production environments. The system efficiently records and visualizes the pose-dependent quality of computing the robot-sensor transformation, providing human operators with intuitive assessments of how changes in the configuration space affect registration and overall system performance. The metrics proposed to evaluate the quality of point measurements demonstrated a decrease in both the accuracy and precision of the registration as the points were measured farther from the robot base. The AR interface intuitively shows that the registration accuracy depends on the location of the sensor within the workspace. It may enable in situ manual re-sampling for better points to be used in registration. This technical brief highlights the potential of AR as a human-in-the-loop interface for metrology applications.The creation of this special issue indicates that extended reality-related studies have shifted from applications designed for various industrial sectors in earlier times to efforts aimed at improving practical values through the proposal of new techniques, algorithms, or assessment methods. It is worth noting that XR research must certainly be conducted from a human-centric perspective, given that its deployment or use is, after all, designed for people, not machines. Due to hardware device limitations, the positional precision of current VR/AR applications may fail to directly meet manufacturing requirements. However, these applications should function effectively in assisting manual tasks by enhancing human situation awareness and characterizing human behavior through the instant capture of their actions or intentions. This necessitates in-depth studies in human–computer interaction, particularly from ergonomic and UX/UI perspectives, in the context of engineering applications. We expect to see an increasing trend in using XR as an interfacing technology for humans to collaborate with computational intelligence (including artificial intelligence, simulation, analytics, and machines) in real time through a wide spectrum of technical elements such as sensors, IoT, cloud computing, and 5G/6G. This trend would transform Industry 4.0 into the emerging Industry 5.0 by fostering human–machine collaboration in a broader context. Especially, the intersection between XR and the recently booming large language model (LLM), as well as other multi-modality AI models, is expected to provide new affordances for new directions of innovation and advancement in broad areas of design and manufacturing. XR studies addressing sustainability and resilience issues could yield a higher degree of innovation and scientific impact along the transformation process.The guest editors would like to thank all contributing authors for their outstanding work. We want to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for dedicating their valuable time and efforts in providing constructive comments to the authors during the review process. In particular, we highly appreciate Ms. Amy Suski for her editorial assistance and timely reminders. Finally, we would like to extend our appreciation to Prof. S. K. Gupta and Prof. Y. Wang, the past and current Editor-in-Chief of JCISE, for offering the opportunity and their support for this special issue.Distribution A. title: Special Issue: Extended Reality in Design and Manufacturing
venue: Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering

abstract: Metamaterials, renowned for their exceptional mechanical, electromagnetic, and thermal properties, hold transformative potential across diverse applications, yet their design remains constrained by labor‐intensive trial‐and‐error methods and limited data interoperability. Here, we introduce CrossMatAgent—a novel multi‐agent framework that synergistically integrates large language models with state‐of‐the‐art generative AI to revolutionize metamaterial design. By orchestrating a hierarchical team of agents—each specializing in tasks such as pattern analysis, architectural synthesis, prompt engineering, and supervisory feedback—our system leverages the multimodal reasoning of GPT‐4o alongside the generative precision of DALL‐E 3 and a fine‐tuned Stable Diffusion Extra Large (XL) model. This integrated approach automates data augmentation, enhances design fidelity, and produces simulation‐ and 3D printing‐ready metamaterial patterns. Comprehensive evaluations, including Contrastive Language–Image Pre‐training‐based alignment, SHapley Additive exPlanations interpretability analyses, and mechanical simulations under varied load conditions, demonstrate the framework's ability to generate diverse, reproducible, and application‐ready designs. CrossMatAgent thus establishes a scalable, AI‐driven paradigm that bridges the gap between conceptual innovation and practical realization, paving the way for accelerated metamaterial development.
title: CrossMatAgent: AI‐Assisted Design of Manufacturable Metamaterial Patterns via Multi‐Agent Generative Framework
A Survey on Collision Avoidance Algorithms for Multi-robot Systems

abstract: Data-driven tech boosts the semiconductor manufacturing's evolution. This paper reviews advancements in data construction (generative AI), process diagnosis (end-to-end fault tracing), and system optimization (multi-objective balance), forming an intelligent system across the manufacturing chain.
title: Intelligent Semiconductor Manufacturing: Process Optimization and Quality Enhancement Based on Data and Algorithms

abstract: Personalizing product innovation methodologies to align with user needs is essential in China’s rapidly evolving electronic manufacturing industry. Despite this necessity, there remains limited understanding of how advanced technologies can be effectively leveraged to create consumer personas that inform successful product development. The present study examines the impact of the CoPersona methodology, a novel approach that integrates human expertise with Large Language Models (LLMs), on the innovation process within this competitive sector. Through a detailed case study of a mid-sized manufacturer, B.Co, we investigated the use of CoPersona in the design and marketing of a bedside lamp. By analyzing over 38 million posts from the RedNote social network, we examined users’ daily life behaviors in bedroom contexts, leading to the creation of five distinct personas that informed key aspects of the product’s design. By integrating GPT-4 with expert human review, this methodology enabled B.Co to translate consumer pain points into 13 actionable product design directives, achieving a commercial adoption rate of 69.2%. Our findings suggest that the CoPersona methodology enhances the ability to process large datasets while maintaining the critical understanding needed for effective product design. We provide insights into how this hybrid approach can be utilized to personalize product and marketing strategies, offering valuable recommendations for manufacturers aiming to achieve market success through consumer-driven innovation.
title: Copersona: Leveraging LLMs and Expert Collaboration to Understand User Personas Through Social Media Data Analysis

abstract: Abstract Wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) demands both real-time monitoring of process stabi-supervised learning for real-time anomility and defects and offline optimisation of process parameters to guarantee part quality and production efficiency. This review critically surveys recent machine learning (ML) techniques for in situ monitoring and parameter optimisation in WAAM, with an emphasis on the integration of ML and bio-inspired optimisation algorithms. In relation to in-situ monitoring, this review examines the roles of supervised and unsupervised learning, as well as advanced deep-learning architectures—such as generative AI and frequency-informed neural networks—in processing welding current and welding voltage, as well as vision-based, audible, acoustic-emission, and thermal imaging data. Furthermore, this paper surveys the latest developments in bio-inspired optimisation models applied to WAAM, discussing how ML-enabled frameworks can enhance sustainability and efficiency metrics in the offline selection of optimal process parameters. The synthesis of insights at the end of each section establishes a structured framework for practitioners, highlights existing research gaps, and outlines strategic directions for future advancements in ML-driven WAAM monitoring and optimisation.
title: Advances in machine learning for parameters optimisation and in-situ monitoring of wire arc additive manufacturing

abstract: 3D printing or additive manufacturing is a revolutionary technology that enables the creation of physical objects from digital models. However, the quality and accuracy of 3D printing depend on the correctness and efficiency of the G-code, a low-level numerical control programming language that instructs 3D printers how to move and extrude material. Debugging G-code is a challenging task that requires a syntactic and semantic understanding of the G-code format and the geometry of the part to be printed. In this paper, we present the first extensive evaluation of six state-of-the-art foundational large language models (LLMs) for comprehending and debugging G-code files for 3D printing. We design effective prompts to enable pre-trained LLMs to understand and manipulate G-code and test their performance on various aspects of G-code debugging and manipulation, including detection and correction of common errors and the ability to perform geometric transformations. We analyze their strengths and weaknesses for understanding complete G-code files. We also discuss the implications and limitations of using LLMs for G-code comprehension.
title: Towards Foundational AI Models for Additive Manufacturing: Language Models for G-Code Debugging, Manipulation, and Comprehension

abstract: The industrial landscape is being reshaped by agentic AI, which is transforming enterprises, with engineering and manufacturing amongst the domains benefitting the most. Studies project a range of performance improvements based on generative AI and agentic systems of around 15%. For dedicated processes in production studies expect a cost base reduction of up to 40-60% [1,2]. As traditional software business models are under pressure, AI has become the leading category in venture capital and has started to move towards vertical AI solutions. Manufacturing in Q1 2026 ranked among the top 5 investment areas, representing 4% of AI equity deals [3]. Analysts see semantic data infrastructure for AI and agent governance as key future investment areas. Leading consulting companies project an architectural shift in the future manufacturing software stack towards AIOT systems that finally realize the IT/OT convergence. Agentic systems centering around an integrated data layer are predicted to fulfill the promise paying into what is called the "Software-defined Factory." As agentic systems are being piloted in manufacturing, it becomes obvious that the potential of agents does not come from a tactical deployment of individual use cases. Full value realization requires redefining manufacturing end-to-end processes (e.g., maintenance, shopfloor or quality management) with an "AI-first" mindset leveraging information across multiple production environments and value streams. Today, few companies have an integrated approach from product design via value stream and line design to value stream optimization based on a unified digital landscape. Agentic systems could dramatically accelerate the cycle times from product design to value stream operations. Both topics above require a common semantic understanding of information used by agents to ensure maximum quality of agentic outcomes and learning effects across production lines and archetypes. Today's production environments are characterized by a brownfield situation with a highly fragmented IT landscape and limited data integration of production assets. The lack of consistent data integration and comparability across value streams prevents scaling of agentic AI. In addition to consistent curated data, companies see the need for a central orchestration and governance layer for agents to ensure that agents (e.g., from different vendors) operate in a secure, coordinated fashion preventing local optimization and conflicting actions. A common governance frame will become even more relevant once agentic systems get access to the OT / control layer. This will pose additional requirements on cybersecurity, especially in the context of recent agentic misalignment and rogue agent behavior. Ongoing discussions regarding a future Software-defined Factory (SDF) architecture indicate three key elements: An integrated, semantic data layer that serves as a foundation to optimize business value streams. An agentic manufacturing layer where agents operate between MES/ERP and the machine/control level, which requires a common orchestration, governance framework and infrastructure. A flexible connectivity approach that is multi-vendor, maximally data-rich, and cost-effective. Data transformations will be agent-driven benefitting from semantically structured target models. While some research [4] suggests distinct data layers for IT (ERP/MES systems) and operational data on machine level, practitioners begin to discuss a convergence of the data layer representing value streams and the data layers within production lines for operational optimization into a single, unified data layer. One reason for previous, failed attempts of IT/OT convergence was the need for upfront expensive, manual integration efforts. Agents are expected to invert this as they can autonomously read, map, and transform heterogeneous data on demand against a (minimal) predefined semantic data layer. To ensure closed-loop optimization cycles - from product engineering to production engineering to operations and back - the architecture needs to build on existing standards where possible. For Bosch, ontologies need to align with the Bosch Production System as a basis for common semantic layer for production. Finally, the integration of physical AI (humanoids, AGVs) as another form of agent into a next-level automation architecture requires their integration into the above-mentioned data and agent orchestration infrastructure. Agents will enter our factories. The question is how they scale and create maximum economic impact while maintaining a safe and predictable environment. As LLMs and agents will become commodity, semantic understanding of production does not. A software-defined factory needs to provide an architecture to capture, deploy and protect this knowledge. © 2026 The Authors. abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) integrates cyber-physical systems, edge-cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and advanced connectivity to enable intelligent, data-driven operations across manufacturing, energy, transportation, and healthcare. The convergence of Operational Technology (OT) and Information Technology (IT), together with pervasive AI-driven automation, complicates meeting the joint requirements of performance, adaptability, and security (PAS). This survey adopts an explicitly AI-centric view of PAS and reviews IIoT research spanning deep reinforcement learning (DRL), multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), digital twins (DTs), federated and collaborative learning, graph neural networks (GNNs), blockchain-assisted analytics, and lightweight and post-quantum cryptography. The reviewed approaches are analyzed across device, edge, fog, cloud, and application layers under industrial constraints such as latency, reliability, resource limits, safety requirements, and regulatory compliance. A PAS-centric taxonomy is introduced that links technique families to deployment layers and application domains, and recurring trade-offs among PAS dimensions are summarized. Open challenges are identified in multi-objective optimization, semantic interoperability, lifecycle validation, and governance, with directions outlined toward secure and sustainable Industry 5.0 IIoT ecosystems.
title: Performance, Adaptability, and Security in AI-Driven IIoT: A Survey

abstract: Frontier language models solve reasoning problems in a single forward pass that would have been research contributions years ago, yet fail at multi-hour tasks: losing track of earlier decisions, declaring half-finished work done, or drifting from goals. We call this the horizon gap and survey 1,547 arXiv papers (2024-2026) collected via systematic seed harvest with a disclosed 26.8% bleed filter, extended by targeted supplementation. We disambiguate three routinely conflated properties: long-horizon (task property: required steps), long-context (model property: token capacity), and long-term memory (system property: persistence across steps/sessions). We organize the corpus into six categories tracking a long-horizon task's lifecycle -- planning, memory, execution, training, evaluation, and foundations/safety -- crossed with an axis capturing where horizons are carried (within-context, within-task-beyond-context, or cross-task-persistent). Across all categories, we find the same pattern: outcome-only signals grow uninformative as horizons lengthen, and the field's response -- whether process reward models, credit assignment, or trajectory-level diagnostics -- manufactures denser step-level signals. We treat critical and diagnostic literature as first-class threads throughout, arguing that segregating critique from method would routinely split single papers across chapters. We close by naming open measurement problems: decomposing model versus harness capability, managing correlated bias in process-level signals used for both training and evaluation, and whether long-horizon reliability admits general predictive theory.
title: The Horizon Gap: Planning, Memory, Execution, Training, and Evaluation for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
CoCoDisMan: Towards Community Co-Created Distributed Manufacturing Platform

abstract: This study investigates the suitability of an AI-assisted approach for mapping industrial automation variables to OPC UA information models. In industrial environments, variable names and structures vary significantly between different systems, making manual mapping labor-intensive, time-consuming and error prone. A prototype was developed that utilizes embedding based candidate retrieval and Large Language Model (LLM) for mapping decisions. First, an embedding index is created based on the target model, after which the source data is converted into canonical form. Then semantically most similar target nodes are retrieved for every variable and the LLM chooses the most suitable target node or rejects all the candidates. The system also supports manual review for uncertain cases and target collision cases. The prototype was evaluated by comparing zero-shot and few-shot approaches. The results indicate that the few-shot method increases the level of automation and reduces the amount of manual work, but at the same time increases the risk of incorrect mappings. The zero-shot method produces more cautious and reliable results but leaves a larger proportion of cases for manual review. Based on the results, AI-assisted mapping can significantly reduce the amount of manual workload and accelerate the mapping process. However, the approach does not eliminate the need for expert involvement, particularly in cases where multiple source variables correspond to the same target node, or where semantic matching is ambiguous. Therefore, the approach is most suitable for a hybrid model in which AI supports the mapping process and human is responsible for the final validation.
title: AI-Assisted Variable Mapping To OPC UA Information Models : A Study on Embedding-Based Retrieval and LLM-Assisted Decision Making
