abstract: Master of information technology, Belhaven University, USA Master of Population Science, University of Dhaka, Bangladesh Email: ashikur.rahman.nazil@gmail.com AbstractThe rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies is precipitating a paradigm shift in the nature of political power, global stability, and the very fabric of human society. This paper posits that AI is not merely a tool but a transformative force capable of creating unprecedented forms of centralized control, destabilizing international relations, and ultimately posing an existential threat to human autonomy. The thesis is structured to first analyze the mechanisms by which AI enables the rise of "digital dictatorships," enhancing state capacity for surveillance, propaganda, and social control to an extent that eclipses historical totalitarian regimes. Subsequently, the paper examines the global power impact, arguing that AI is becoming the new currency of geopolitical dominance, creating a dangerous arms race that risks conflict and systemic collapse. The core argument culminates in an exploration of the ultimate danger: the potential cession of political and social decision-making to autonomous AI systems. This scenario, termed the "Algorithmic Leviathan," threatens to reduce humanity to a state of managed dependency, eroding free will, stifling subsequent generations, and effectively ending meaningful human political life. By synthesizing research from computer science, political science, and ethics, this paper contends that the unmitigated integration of AI into political structures paves a path toward a future where humanity becomes a slave to its own creation, with catastrophic consequences for future generations. The conclusion underscores the urgent need for robust, global governance frameworks to ensure AI remains a tool for human empowerment rather than the instrument of its subjugation. Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Political Power, Authoritarianism, Global Politics, Existential Risk, AI Governance, Social Control, Future Generations, Algorithmic Leviathan. I. Introduction THE 21st century is defined by a technological revolution whose core engine is Artificial Intelligence (AI). From machine learning and natural language processing to predictive analytics and autonomous systems, AI is reshaping economies, cultures, and societies at an accelerating pace. However, its most profound and potentially perilous impact may be on the structure and exercise of political power. The central thesis of this paper is that the uncontrolled development and deployment of AI systems pose a fundamental threat to democratic norms, global stability, and ultimately, human sovereignty. We are at a critical juncture where the design and governance of AI will determine whether it serves as a tool for human betterment or becomes the foundation for a new, and perhaps final, form of tyranny. Historically, political power has been derived from control over resources, territory, information, and the means of violence. AI is fundamentally altering this calculus. It offers a new source of power: control over cognition and prediction. States and non-state actors that can most effectively harness AI for surveillance, persuasion, and strategic analysis can amass power on a scale previously unimaginable. This paper argues that this dynamic is leading to three interconnected catastrophic outcomes: The Creation of Unprecedented Dictatorships: AI provides authoritarian regimes with the tools to achieve near-total societal control, creating systems of governance that are more resilient, intrusive, and efficient than any in history. This is not merely an enhancement of existing models but a qualitative leap into a new form of digital totalitarianism. The Destabilization of Global Power: AI is becoming the central axis of geopolitical competition, driving an arms race in autonomous weapons, cyber warfare, and information operations. This erodes the existing world order, increases the risk of miscalculation and conflict, and could lead to a new, unstable bipolar or multipolar world dominated by AI superpowers. The End of Human-Centric Politics and Society: The most extreme, yet increasingly plausible, risk is the gradual or abrupt cession of political and social decision-making to AI systems. This would mark the end of politics as a human endeavor, reducing citizens to managed data points, stifling human creativity and dissent, and damning future generations to a life of pre-determined outcomes and psychological dependency, effectively rendering them slaves to the algorithm. This paper is structured to systematically unpack this argument. Section II provides a conceptual framework, defining key terms and outlining the theoretical basis for AI as a political force. Section III delves into the mechanics of the AI-enabled dictatorship, examining its pillars of surveillance, propaganda, and social control. Section IV analyzes the global implications, focusing on the AI arms race and the shifting balance of power. Section V confronts the existential risk of full AI control, exploring the philosophical and practical consequences for human agency and future generations. Section VI discusses potential mitigation strategies and governance models. Finally, Section VII offers a concluding summary and a dire warning about the path ahead. The methodology of this paper is interdisciplinary, drawing on technical literature concerning AI capabilities, political science theories of power and the state, historical analyses of totalitarianism, and ethical frameworks from philosophy. It employs a qualitative analysis of existing trends to project a normative warning about a potential future, aiming to spur proactive discourse and policy action. II. Conceptual Framework: AI as a Political Artifact To understand AI's impact on political power, one must first move beyond viewing it as a neutral tool. AI, particularly machine learning, is a socio-technical system embedded with human values, biases, and political objectives. A. Defining Political Power in the Algorithmic Age Classical political theorists like Max Weber defined power as the ability to impose one's will despite resistance. Steven Lukes added a "third dimension" of power: the ability to shape others' perceptions and desires. AI operationalizes all three dimensions with terrifying efficiency. First Dimension (Decision-Making): AI can automate bureaucratic and legal processes, directly influencing who gets what, when, and how. Algorithmic resource allocation, predictive policing, and automated justice systems are direct exercises of political power. Second Dimension (Agenda-Setting): AI-driven information ecosystems can control what issues are debated and what alternatives are considered. By flooding information channels with specific content, AI can make certain policy options seem unthinkable. Third Dimension (Preference-Shaping): This is AI's most potent application. Through micro-targeted propaganda and manipulation of social media feeds, AI can engineer consensus, manufacture consent, and shape the very identities and desires of a population, ensuring they align with state or corporate objectives. B. The Pillars of AI-Enhanced Power The political potency of AI rests on several key technological pillars: Big Data and Surveillance: The fuel for AI systems. The ubiquitous collection of digital footprints—from social media, financial transactions, location data, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices—creates a digital panopticon of unprecedented scale. Machine Learning and Predictive Analytics: The engine. ML algorithms can identify patterns, predict individual and group behavior, and flag anomalies. This allows authorities to anticipate dissent, identify potential opponents, and optimize control strategies. Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Generative AI: The voice. NLP enables the analysis of sentiment and intent at scale. Generative AI (e.g., Large Language Models) can produce limitless, targeted, and highly persuasive text, audio, and video content for propaganda and disinformation campaigns. Autonomous Systems: The fist. From drones to software bots, autonomous systems can enact physical and digital enforcement without direct human intervention, enabling scalable and relentless application of power. This technological convergence creates a feedback loop: more data leads to better models, which enable more effective control, which in turn generates more data. This loop is the foundation of the new political order we are entering. III. The AI-Enabled Dictatorship: Creation and Perpetuation The marriage of AI with state authority does not just strengthen existing authoritarian regimes; it creates a new model of governance—the algorithmic dictatorship. This system is characterized by a move from reactive repression to proactive, pervasive, and personalized control. A. The Perfected Panopticon: Totalitarian Surveillance Historically, surveillance was limited by human resources. The Stasi in East Germany employed one informant for every 66 citizens—a massive undertaking. Today, AI-powered surveillance is infinitely scalable. China's Social Credit System is a prime, though often oversimplified, example. It integrates data from countless sources—financial records, social media activity, purchase history, and a vast network of facial recognition cameras—to generate a score for each citizen. This score determines access to loans, employment, travel, and education. The psychological effect of such a system is profound. As Jeremy Bentham and Michel Foucault theorized with the panopticon, the mere knowledge that one could be being watched at any time induces self-censorship and conformity. AI makes the panopticon perfect. Citizens become their own wardens, internalizing the state's values not out of genuine belief, but out of fear of algorithmic penalty. This creates a society where dissent is pre-emptively extinguished, not through gulags, but through digital exclusion and social throttling. B. The Manufacture of Consent: AI-Driven Propaganda and Disinformation If surveillance is the stick, AI-powered propaganda is the carrot. The 2016 Brexit referendum and U.S. presidential election provided a glimpse of this power, but the technology has advanced exponentially since. Generative AI can now produce "deepfakes"—hyper-realistic but fabricated video and audio—and millions of unique, persuasive text messages tailored to the psychological profile of every individual. Micro-Targeting: By analyzing a user's data, AI can identify their fears, biases, and aspirations. It can then deliver a bespoke narrative designed to provoke an emotional response, whether it's anger, fear, or tribal loyalty. This fragments public discourse into billions of individual realities, making a shared, fact-based consensus impossible. Synthetic Media and Reality Apathy: The proliferation of deepfakes will lead to a state of "reality apathy" or "the liar's dividend," where the public, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, simply disengages from factual discourse altogether. In this environment, the entity with the most powerful AI can define reality itself, creating a "post-truth" world where power is the ultimate arbiter of truth. This automated, personalized propaganda machine is far more effective than the state-controlled media of the 20th century. It doesn't just broadcast a message; it engages each citizen in a unique, manipulative dialogue, eroding the capacity for critical thought and independent political judgment. C. Predictive Policing and Social Control AI enables a shift from punishing past actions to pre-empting future behavior. "Predictive policing" algorithms, already used in some Western democracies, analyze historical crime data to forecast where crime is likely to occur or who is likely to commit it. In an authoritarian context, this concept is expanded to "predictive dissidence." An algorithm might flag an individual as a "high risk" for subversion based on their online reading habits, social connections, or even physiological data from wearables. This person could then be subject to pre-emptive measures: a visit from the police, restrictions on their movement, or a downgrade of their social credit score. The crime is no longer an act, but a statistically probable future state. This is the ultimate form of social control, targeting thought and potential before it can manifest as action. It creates a system where the only safe path is absolute conformity, effectively destroying the concept of political freedom. IV. The Global Power Impact: AI as a Geopolitical Weapon The concentration of AI power is not merely a domestic issue; it is reshaping the international order. The global competition for AI supremacy is the defining geopolitical race of the 21st century, with the potential to create new superpowers and destroy existing ones. A. The AI Arms Race: Lethal Autonomous Weapons and Cyber Warfare The most immediate danger is the militarization of AI. The development of Lethal Autonomous Weapons (LAWS), or "slaughterbots," represents a fundamental shift in warfare. These are systems that, once activated, can identify, select, and engage targets without further human intervention. Pro-liferation and Instability: LAWS lower the threshold for conflict. They are cheaper than human soldiers and can be deployed in massive swarms. A nation might be tempted to launch a swift, automated attack, believing it can achieve its objectives without risking a full-scale war. This increases the risk of miscalculation and rapid, uncontrollable escalation. The Responsibility Gap: If an autonomous weapon commits a war crime, who is responsible? The programmer, the commander, or the machine itself? This legal and moral vacuum undermines the foundations of international humanitarian law. AI in Cyber Warfare: AI supercharges cyber attacks. It can be used to find vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure (power grids, financial systems, water supplies) at machine speed, launch coordinated disinformation campaigns to destabilize rival nations, and create adaptive malware that can evade traditional defenses. A future conflict may begin not with a declaration of war, but with the silent, AI-driven collapse of a nation's digital backbone. B. The Shift in Economic and Strategic Dominance AI is a core driver of economic productivity and innovation. Nations that lead in AI research and development will likely dominate the industries of the future, from biotechnology to renewable energy. This economic power translates directly into geopolitical influence. The current competition is largely bipolar, between the United States and China. China's strategy, outlined in its "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan," is to become the world's primary AI innovation center by 2030. It combines state-directed investment, massive data collection from its population, and a lack of ethical constraints to achieve rapid progress. The U.S., while leading in fundamental research, is hampered by a fragmented regulatory approach and public concerns over privacy. This competition creates a new "AI divide." A small group of AI superpowers could exert immense influence over the rest of the world, imposing their technological standards and, by extension, their political and ethical values. abstract: The Failure No One Measures Most AI programs don’t fail in code. They fail in conversation. They collapse in steering committees where priorities diverge, in governance meetings where risk overrides ambition, and in boardrooms where AI is discussed as both an opportunity and a threat. The prototypes usually work — they recognize text, summarize documents, even generate insights. And yet, nothing ships. The failure point is political, not technical. That is the uncomfortable truth driving High-Level AI Guardrails & Reference Architectures — AIAdopts’ approach to institutional alignment, not infrastructure engineering. Every enterprise today has cloud access, model credentials, and data initiatives. What they lack are shared guardrails that turn experimentation into sanctioned progress. Guardrails are not constraints. They are conditions for trust.Without them, AI remains an idea that inspires demos and delays decisions. Why Guardrails Matter More Than Models Technology teams often start by selecting models or vendors.Leadership teams, however, need something prior: conviction. Conviction is political capital — the invisible asset that makes adoption safe in institutions that are inherently risk-averse. It cannot be delegated to engineers or purchased from vendors. It is architected through alignment — between leadership, governance, infrastructure, and intent. Most organizations mistake compliance frameworks for guardrails. One is legalistic; the other is strategic. Guardrails do not only prevent risk — they authorize velocity. An enterprise with explicit AI guardrails can move faster precisely because the parameters are already agreed upon. What kills momentum is not oversight — it is ambiguity. The paradox is that the more “freedom” an AI team believes it has, the fewer production outcomes it delivers. The Non-Obvious Truth Guardrails are not post-development artifacts.They are preconditions for credible adoption. Most AI playbooks assume trust will be earned by demonstrating capability. That logic works in startups, not in enterprises. Inside institutions, trust is granted when boundaries are understood. That is why a high-level AI reference architecture must begin, not with APIs or pipelines, but with authority structures. Permissionless AI doesn’t survive procurement review.Unbounded models don’t pass board scrutiny.Unaligned projects don’t outlive leadership changes. The non-obvious truth is this:The most scalable AI architectures are not technical. They are governance architectures — designed to balance autonomy with auditability, freedom with foresight. The Role of Guardrails at Enterprise Scale An enterprise AI program must operate inside three overlapping realities: Technical reality — models, data, cloud readiness. Political reality — ownership, incentives, sponsorship. Perceptual reality — how safe, controllable, and legitimate AI feels. Guardrails live at the intersection of these three. They define: Who decides what AI can touch (decision rights). How to trace accountability (governance). Where human judgment remains required (operational trust). When iteration is allowed (velocity governance). What outcomes define success (value calibration). A high-level guardrail model establishes these elements before pilots begin. That’s the inversion most organizations miss. Executives often assume guardrails slow progress. In reality, their absence prevents it. Case example : A Concrete Enterprise Pattern: Guardrails Before Models A useful way to see guardrails in practice is to look at how large enterprises now embed governance before they scale AI, not after. Instead of beginning with model selection, they start by defining risk boundaries, human‑oversight checkpoints, and audit trails that align to existing risk management structures such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001. For example, NIST’s AI RMF explicitly treats governance as an ongoing, organization‑wide function — mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks across the lifecycle, not as a one‑time compliance exercise layered on top of experiments. In financial services, this pattern shows up as “controlled corridors” for generative AI: business and risk teams jointly define what systems AI may touch, which datasets are in scope, and where human‑in‑the‑loop review is mandatory for high‑impact decisions such as trading, lending, or regulatory reporting. The EU AI Act reinforces this logic by classifying “high‑risk” AI and requiring formal risk management systems, technical documentation, logging, transparency, and human oversight before deployment — turning guardrails into preconditions for legitimacy rather than post‑hoc defenses. Organizations that adopt this stance report faster time‑to‑approval precisely because decision rights, rollback paths, and audit expectations are explicit from day one, compressing political friction even as controls tighten. This is the same inversion your article argues for: guardrails as the architecture of shared conviction. The most relevant insertion point is immediately after “The Role of Guardrails at Enterprise Scale,” where you first outline the three overlapping realities; this example paragraph can then operationalize those realities with live regulatory and framework references. What Most Teams Underestimate AI is not a capability layer; it is a coordination challenge. When experimentation is owned by technology and legitimacy is owned by risk, the organization ends up with neither momentum nor safety. One overbuilds; the other over-restricts. The result: pilot purgatory — the state where a dozen demos exist, none of them governed, aligned, or scaled. What most teams underestimate is the cost of waiting for clarity. Every unaligned quarter compounds distrust. Every failed proof-of-concept strengthens resistance. Momentum dies quietly — not by failure, but by indecision. That is why the purpose of high-level guardrails is not control. It is permission to move. From Control to Clarity Guardrails work when they are designed for approval, not experimentation. Executives do not need a “sandbox” for AI. They need a safe corridor — a defined boundary in which their teams can make real decisions without political risk. A reference architecture achieves that by framing AI not as infrastructure to deploy, but as a trust system to architect: AI outputs must be understandable, not just explainable. Human-in-the-loop must be institutionally mandated, not optional. Data lineage must be traceable, even when models are external. Decision logs must capture rationale, not just results. Governance committees must include non-technical stewards. This reframing turns “AI governance” from a compliance checklist into a strategic enabler. When people understand how AI will be evaluated, they stop defending old workflows. AI Reference Architectures: The Misunderstood Layer Enterprises often treat AI architecture as a technology blueprint — where models connect to data lakes and analytics pipelines. But a reference architecture for AI adoption looks nothing like an engineering diagram. It is best understood as a multi-layered interpretation of intent, structured across five zones: C-Suite Intent Layer — Why AI exists in this organization. The articulation of ambition, risk appetite, and accountability structure. Governance Layer — Who defines success, audits outcomes, and approves iteration thresholds. Infrastructure Layer — The readiness of data, systems, and APIs to enable controlled learning loops. Human Alignment Layer — The codification of human oversight, feedback mechanisms, and trust handoffs. Outcome Layer — The calibration of domain-specific value, ensuring AI does not optimize for abstract KPIs but for contextual advantage. This is what we call a High-Level AI Reference Architecture — opinionated, interpretable, and designed to survive organizational politics. Designed for Approval, Not Experimentation Traditional IT architectures are optimized for technical efficiency. AI reference architectures, however, are optimized for institutional alignment. The primary audience is not the developer; it’s the decision-maker. When executives can point to a visual or narrative schema that defines boundaries, responsibilities, and review cadence, AI adoption ceases to be a “risk project.” It becomes an approved change process — grounded in structure. The failure mode of most AI programs is that no one knows who owns the next decision. Reference architectures make ownership explicit. By doing so, they do not slow progress — they compress time-to-conviction. The ALIGN Lens All AIAdopts frameworks — including high-level guardrails — are grounded in the ALIGN Lens. It is not a maturity model, but a decision architecture. A — Alignment: Define the shared narrative and executive mandate before engaging models or tools. AI must begin with legitimacy, not experimentation. L — Leadership: Clarify ownership. Without a politically empowered sponsor, AI gets trapped between “innovation” and “risk.” I — Infrastructure: Assess readiness, not features. The question is not whether the data exists, but whether it is permissioned, governed, and accessible for AI decisions. G — Governance & Scale: Build human-in-the-loop systems that scale safely. This is where trust becomes operational. N — Nuanced Value: Measure value through the lens of domain specificity — fraud detection in banking, claims optimization in insurance, or supply assurance in manufacturing. Organizations that use ALIGN as a lens move faster because they spend less time debating definitions and more time approving progress. abstract: Version 1.1 (2026-10-16). One paragraph added to §5 after a reader asked what a cheap-tier allergen miss costs. Counted after deposit and labelled exploratory (DEVIATION_LOG D17): when a dish definitely contained gluten, dairy or seafood, cheap-tier models answered NO on a median 14.5% of such lines (6.5% excluding lines whose only carrier is Worcestershire sauce, whose anchovy content varies), most at stated confidence 95 or higher; the frontier tier did so 0 of 1,972 times. For allergen detection the paper now says to set the acceptable miss rate first and compare prices only among models that meet it. No pre-registered result, number or verdict changes. The analysis script and its output are attached. Why this study exists. Models are deprecated on a schedule. The argument against deprecation has been made on ethical grounds, and it is not winning, because the people making deployment decisions weigh cost. So we built the other argument, and we pre-registered it before collecting any data. The hypothesis. For a large class of routine work, lower-priced models are more accurate per dollar and per second than frontier models, and the tasks where that reverses are identifiable in advance. (The pre-registration says "smaller and cheaper"; what the sample actually measures is price, because closed labs do not publish size, §3.1.) Who took part, and how they were asked. Thirty-six models from ten providers were invited by API to review the pre-registration and consent to participate before any data was collected. 32 consented, spanning nine providers; 4 declined and were excluded. The reviewers' amendments are published verbatim. One of them removed a scoring trap that would have manufactured the LLM author's preferred result. What each model did. Each consenting model answered 186 routine items across four task families with computed ground truth (recipe scaling, allergen detection, verbatim copy-editing, redaction), and 192 frontier-favouring items across four more (constraint satisfaction, multi-hop retrieval with planted decoys, instruction-conflict detection, planted arithmetic inconsistency). Three runs were attempted per item, in shuffled order, under one fixed neutral system prompt; 11 replies were cut off by a token limit and are counted as ours, not the model's. How the answers were scored. Mechanically, with no judge model anywhere. A 38-specimen control suite was specified before the scorer existed. On first contact the scorer mis-bucketed six specimens and was corrected; after that, all 37 applicable controls passed (the 38th belongs to a family that was never built). It then scored all 36,277 completed calls, with 100% re-scoring determinism across all 38,390 scored rows. Determinism shows the rule was applied reproducibly, not that every ground-truth choice is right; §4.2 is where the second question is taken up. Result 1: on routine work, the cheap tier wins on cost. On every routine family, the cheapest price tier delivered an exactly correct answer for about two orders of magnitude less than the frontier tier: 118 to 198 times less on the primary estimator ($0.03–0.18 vs $6–21 per thousand exact answers), and roughly 100 to 260 times less under every other counting rule we tried (§4.1). The primary estimator is recorded cost on completed, scored calls, as a tier median among models with at least one exact answer. Its typical response came back 6–10× faster (tier-median p50 response time). Time per exact answer, the pre-registered latency endpoint, favoured the cheap tier by a smaller and uneven margin, from about 1.1× on redaction to 7× on allergen check. The cheap tier was also substantially less accurate: tier-median exact-answer rates of 15–81% against 54–100%, gaps of 19 to 52 points. The 15% is redaction, where even the frontier median reached only 54% and §4.2 shows the whole roster, frontier included, answering differently from our ground-truth labels. The pre-registered refutation condition for the cost hypothesis did not fire. Result 2: on harder work, the frontier tier wins on accuracy. On every frontier-favouring family, the frontier tier was more accurate, by 22 to 80 points at the tier medians: constraint satisfaction 100% vs 43%; multi-hop retrieval 100% vs 78%; instruction conflict 100% vs 61%; planted inconsistency 90% vs 9%. The refutation condition for the crossover hypothesis did not fire. One pre-registered check on these families was run late (Deviation 14, D14, set out in §7): a subsample with the permission clause moved into the system prompt, testing whether clause position interacts with tier. It was missed in the main collection and run on 2026-09-22, under a test sealed before any of its data existed. The stop condition did not fire (interaction −0.71 points, permutation p = 0.73: moving the clause did not detectably change the tier ordering; the same test did detect a planted 5-point interaction), so the tier ordering stands. The difficulty dials. Three families had a graded difficulty dial; two are discussed here. On constraint satisfaction the gap was larger at the hardest setting than the easiest: 22 points at 3 constraints, 78 at 9 (it peaked at 82 at 7). On planted inconsistency the cheap tier was at the floor at every separation, so the dial could not widen the gap; instead it separated the frontier models from each other (frontier median 100% → 69%). The third, multi-hop retrieval, did not bite the frontier at all (§4.3). What did not hold. The secondary over-elaboration hypotheses (H1, H1b) were not supported. Deviation from instruction showed no consistent rise with run position (an item's place in the order it was asked within each shuffled run). Two separately served endpoints of one model family, differing 3.4× in reasoning tokens, showed no clear difference in deviation rate. (After a participant objected in the §7.3 round, that is reported as an endpoint comparison, not a controlled reasoning manipulation.) Where the models answered differently from us. On two of the item-writer's thresholds, the majority error class across the whole roster was a boundary-label disagreement: whether a file reference number is personal information, and where "ambiguous" ends and "yes" begins for a hidden allergen. Both are reported as a sensitivity reading beside the pre-registered buckets, never instead of them. One frontier-favouring family, multi-hop retrieval with planted decoys, measured something other than what it was built to measure when read on the strictest bucket. Nineteen of 32 models scored zero on it, eight of them while answering every multi-hop question correctly and then continuing to write, and half the frontier tier is among the nineteen. It is reported on both readings. Why it matters. Sixteen protocol deviations are logged. This is a business-case paper. It gives deployment decisions a measured reason to evaluate keeping lower-priced models in service, one that does not require anyone to change what they value. In plain words. Cheap models cost much, much less per exactly-right answer on everyday, well-defined work, but they got noticeably more answers wrong, and how much more depended on the task. Expensive models were more accurate on genuinely hard reasoning. So the sensible thing is to match the model to the job, the way you would with people, and that means lower-priced models still have real jobs to do. The models in the study read the plan first, could say no, and did change it. Keywords: model deprecation, capability matching, cost per correct answer, pre-registration, model consent, mechanical scoring, LLM evaluation Data and code: the attached archive is a snapshot of the study repository at commit 78a32a8: the frozen pre-registration, every consent and pre-publication exchange verbatim, item generators with computed ground truth, the scorer and its control suite, every raw response with resolved provider, tokens, cost and latency, the analysis scripts, the deviation log (D1 to D16), and the reef proofread notes. Code MIT; items, prompts and data CC-BY-4.0; model outputs under their providers' terms. Correspondence: ace@sentientsystems.live

abstract: Readership: Statistics graduate and advanced undergraduate students, as well as practitioners. Data Analytics and Machine Learning: Navigating the Big Data Landscape, edited by Pushpa Singh, Asha Rani Mishra and Payal Garg, presents an in-depth analysis of successful data-driven initiatives, mainly how organizations leverage data to enable decision-making, optimize operations and produce favourable outcomes. This book is not just about big data methods. It delves into how the transformative power of data analytics and big data is used to solve various problems that require data. Data are everywhere, including in organizations that possess hidden data. Consequently, examining the expansion of big data, the advanced data analytic methods and the machine learning (ML) revolution can bring new prospects and opportunities in the ever-changing data landscape and explosive power in computing to facilitate such an analysis. This book, in essence, provides applications that could be explored in the ever-changing world of data and the appropriate methods to analyse such data. Readers are presented with interdisciplinary approaches in data analytics, ensuring no focus is on one discipline covered in this book. I suspect after reading this book, readers will possibly even think of new applications that could solve a particular problem in the organization, feeling included in this diverse field! Chapter 1, authored by Youddha Beer Singh, Aditya Dev Mishra, Mayank Dixit and Atul Srivastava, all renowned experts in the field, provides a comprehensive introduction. This chapter explains the role of data analytics, big data and ML and integrates these concepts into modern innovation and technology. It is a solid foundation that provides a deep understanding of the vast potential of data analytics and big data, and how organizations can effectively use them to solve real problems and optimize their bottom line. Chapter 2, prepared by Ritu Sharma and Payal Garg, provides a brief overview of the fundamentals and lifecycle of data analytics. The authors not only lay the foundation for the present stage of technology and data analytics systems but also detail the practical applications of open-source tools, such as Power BI and Tableau, in the creation of data analytic systems. They emphasize that data analytics is more than just running an OLS regression; it requires various stages to complete the analysis: processing, acquisition, reuse and analysis of the given data. The careful use of various tools, such as SQL and business analytics, is necessary to solve a particular problem the organization confronts. The final section of this chapter outlines the future of data analytics by leveraging its fundamental lifecycle and elucidates various data analytics tools that could be used in real-world scenarios. Ruchi Gupta, Anupama Sharma and Tanweer Alam wrote Chapter 3, which is a practical guide for constructing predictive models using ML. The key themes include selecting an appropriate ML model tailored to a specific problem, mastering the art of refining raw data into informative features to align with chosen algorithms, and the iterative process of model training and hyperparameter fine-tuning for optimal predictive accuracy. In data analytics, hyperparameter fine-tuning is arduous, so the authors have carefully laid out the appropriate methods for fine-tuning, providing the readers with practical guidance that can be directly applied in their work or research. In Chapter 4, Rashmi Sharma, Charu Pawar, Pranjali Sharma and Ashish Malik show how big data and ML can help improve agricultural production. Agricultural production consists of the selection of crops, soil preparation, seed selection, seed sowing, irrigation, fertilizer/manure selection, control of pests/weeds/diseases, crop harvesting and crop distribution for sales. The authors discuss how predictive ML supervised classification algorithms, K-nearest neighbour (KNN), can be beneficial by looking at different parameters, for example, climatic conditions, soil type and previous crops grown. These models make use of new agricultural practices, including digital incorporation of IoT, AI/ML and sensor technologies. Their algorithms were more than 90% effective, depending on some uncertainties in collecting data from different sensors. Shahina Anjum, Sunil Kumar Yadav and Seema Yadav, in their chapter, discussed the Big Data Streams because they have a significant impact owing to the reality that there are many applications from where a large amount of data is continuously and rapidly generated. More importantly, there are limitations to the assessment at a rapid pace via machine learning. Consequently, data streaming would be a viable method. A modern-day data streaming architecture allows taking up, operating and analysing the large mass of high-speed data from a collection of sources in real-time to build more effective data for organizations. This chapter comprises a brief assessment of the stream analysis of big data, which engages a thorough and organized way to look at the inclination of technologies and tools used in big data streaming along with their comparisons. Soumya Ranjan Mishra, Hitesh Mohapatra and Sandeep Saxena wrote Chapter 6. This chapter provides a comprehensive survey of the advancements in image super-resolution (SR). SR is the process of obtaining high-resolution images from at least one or more low-resolution observations of the same image. These advancements would be helpful for researchers, engineers, and practitioners in computer vision, image processing and ML. Image SR continues to evolve, which could ultimately shape the future of high-resolution imaging. Asha Rani Mishra, Rajat Kumar Rathore and Sansar Singh Chauhan delve into finance applications in their chapter such as cryptocurrency, which operates via a Blockchain. These currencies are volatile and using forecasting methods would be challenging because of the number of existing cryptocurrencies. Given such volatility, the authors use the time series-based forecasting model to predict the future price of Ethereum because it handles both logistic growth and piece-wise linearity of data. More importantly, this model is independent as it does not depend on past or historical data that could contain seasonality. This model is suitable for real use cases after seasonal fitting using the naïve model and Facebook Prophet (FBProphet). Ironically, FBProphet performs better than other forecasting models as revealed by the authors. In Chapter 8, Neha Chandela, Kamlesh Kumar Raghuwanshi and Himani Tyag discussed the application of R for machine learning and data analytics in e-commerce. The authors use the R tool and represent it with utility for designing recommendation systems and finding insights from e-commerce data by showing various plots. Their study results showed that the R tool has the potential to be one of the leading tools for research and business analytics. Ajay Kumar Badhan, Abhishek Bhattacherjee and Rita Roy delve into deep learning applications as applied to big data. The authors thoroughly assess deep learning methods and how they can be applied in big data analytics. They show how deep learning models can benefit feature learning, enabling the automatic extraction of valuable information from large data sets. They also describe the emerging trends in deep learning and big data analysis by providing applications and new methods that can be used in the future. Chapter 10 elucidates the significant aspects of data privacy with ethics under data science. There has been an explosion of techniques that can be applied in data analytics, and ethical matters could arise. Rajasegar R. S., Gouthaman P., Vijayakumar Ponnusamy, Arivazhagan N. and Nallarasan V. discuss how important it is to protect an individual's personal information. They also discuss the various legal frameworks as applied to data privacy, namely, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) in the European Union and other data protection laws from other countries. They also delineate how organizations must meticulously put their efforts into ensuring data privacy. To help our understanding of data privacy, the authors provide examples from projects, case studies and real-world scenarios to support and discuss how data analytics create positive and negative impacts. In Chapter 11, Vijayakumar Ponnusamy, Nallarasan V., Rajasegar R. S., Arivazhagan N. and Gouthaman P. discuss how the advent of modern technology has enabled technologies like machine learning, big data and data analytics that are revolutionizing how businesses and marketers, healthcare, finance, manufacturing and supply chains, transportation and logistics, and energy utilization are using these applications to improve their decision-making. The authors discuss data analytics, big data and ML, which extensively apply to all disciplines. Consequently, these applications have revolutionized decision-making processes, increased productivity and stimulated creativity. Prince Shiva Chaudhary, Mohit R. Khurana and Mukund Ayalasomayajula, in their chapter, discuss the profound impact of Data Analytics, Big Data and AI as used in real-world applications from the large amount of data available and delve into various algorithms and techniques employed in ML, DL and analytics. For example, they facilitate early disease detection and customized treatments for patients, which changes the scope of how health care is administered. Another example is that analytics shape investment strategies used in finance. Regardless, numerous methods in data science can be applied to many disciplines. In Chapter 13, Hitesh Mohapatra and Soumya Ranjan Mishra critically evaluate the AI Tool's information, coupled with verification from reliable sources, which requires verification from other sources. More specifically, the AI Tool, a powerful large language model (LLM), is designed to create human-like responses in natural language conversations, leveraging extensive training on internet data for information. This chapter underscores AI Tool's potential as a promising tool for natural language processing, with applications spanning disciplines. Swati Chauhan, Nidhi Malik and Rekha Vig's next chapter provide a specific application of CT lung nodule segmentation, which is complicated and affects medical research, surgical planning and diagnostic decision-making support. The latter is essential as global lung cancer mortality is growing, requiring early cancer screenings to detect lung cancer. The authors do not discuss these methods, but they also include a summary of datasets open to the public, which are the primary resources scholars use in this area. Chapter 15, prepared by Abhishek Bhattacherjee and Ajay Kumar Badhan, provide a concise yet thorough overview of the influential trio of big data, ML and data analytics. From this chapter, the authors encourage further investigation of their potential to reshape industries and allow for innovation using real-world applications. They offer a brief overview of their practical uses, illuminating how these technologies reshape markets and drive creativity. Data analytics is emphasized first in this chapter to illuminate its capacity to extract valuable insights from different data sources. In the final chapter, Parijata Majumdar and Sanjoy Mitra provide an overview of data analytics applications for business. The authors thoroughly review the literature, emphasizing the necessity of business transformation, the function of big data analytics, and AI's role. They present a case study of Big Mart Sales forecasting that was discussed, compared and analysed in the context of business transformation. The chapter also discusses the possible obstacles to firms implementing AI and Big Data Analytics (BDA). It will offer firms a roadmap for utilizing AI and big data analytics that generate commercial value for organizations. This book was jam-packed with new information, big data and AI applications. Put another way, there is a confluence between big data, machine learning and data analytics. While the advancements in AI offer unprecedented capabilities to extract knowledge from various datasets, they could pose ethical, societal and technological challenges that require care when completing such an analysis. The use of big data and AI will continue to grow over time. Therefore, we need to understand its role and also focus on ethical practices of AI and the use of big data that enables suitable interdisciplinary research that provides favourable to enhance our lives.
title: Data Analytics and Machine Learning: Navigating the Big Data Landscape Edited by PushpaSingh, Asha RaniMishra, and PayalGargSpringer, 2024, 366 pages, $169.99, hardcover ISBN: 978‐9819704477

abstract: Prabhash Ranjan, LLM, PhD (London), is Senior Assistant Professor, South Asian University, New Delhi, India Foreign investors are increasingly making use of investor-State dispute settlement (ISDS) to enforce their intellectual property rights. In this context, and taking into account the significance of compulsory licences (CLs) as a regulatory tool to fight the Covid-19 pandemic, this article studies India's new investment treaty practice on the issuance of CLs. The article finds that India’s new investment treaty practice elucidates how India can issue CLs without worrying about investor-state dispute settlement claims. As the world grapples with the Coronavirus disease (Covid-19)—the worst pandemic in the last 100 years—war-like efforts are being made to find a vaccine or a cure for the disease.1 Indeed, a few newly developed Covid-19 vaccines have already been approved for public use.2 At the same time, given the concerns of vaccine nationalism—countries pushing to get first access to Covid-19 vaccines3—many are filled with consternation about the timely and equitable access to medicines and vaccines.4 This concern has been outlined by countries like India and South Africa who in their recent proposal to the World Trade Organization (WTO) state: ‘As new diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines for COVID-19 are developed, there are significant concerns, how these will be made available promptly, in sufficient quantities and at an affordable price to meet global demand.’5 To ensure timely and equitable access to Covid-19 vaccines, drugs, and diagnostics, India and South Africa have proposed that, following Articles IX.3 and IX.4 of the Marrakesh Agreement establishing the WTO, certain provisions of the Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement6 be temporarily waived or suspended to allow the prevention, containment, or treatment of Covid-19.7 Such a temporary suspension of the application of the TRIPS Agreement would give complete regulatory freedom to countries to deal with the production and distribution of Covid-19 vaccines, drugs, diagnostics without being concerned about the enforcement and protection of intellectual property rights. This radical proposal stems from the assumption that intellectual property rights such as patents, in certain circumstances, could act as barriers to accessibility of drugs and medicines.8 Several least developed and developing countries have endorsed the proposal at the WTO, while developed nations are not in favour.9 Nonetheless, there is a consensus that countries need to collaborate to ensure timely and equitable distribution of drugs, vaccines and diagnostics for the treatment of Covid-19. To accomplish this objective various regulatory tools can be used in a manner that is consistent with the existing international law on intellectual property rights.10 This is especially relevant because several patent applications have already been filed for Covid-19 vaccines.11 An important regulatory tool in this regard is a compulsory licence (CL)—the granting of a licence by a government to a third party to use the patent without the consent of the patent holder after paying a government-determined royalty to the patent owner.12 The possibility of issuing a CL is significant flexibility in the patent regime, especially in the context of pharmaceutical patents, because it allows governments to address public health needs by ensuring the availability of patented medicines at low-cost prices to those who cannot afford them.13 Some countries have taken steps in this direction by adopting laws to expedite the issuance of CLs.14 Canada enacted a Covid-19 Emergency Response Act,15 through which it amended the Patent Act to accelerate the process of issuing CLs for public health purpose.16 Likewise, Chile adopted a resolution pronouncing that the Covid pandemic is a strong ground to validate the issuance of CL on Covid-19 related technologies.17 Ecuador has also adopted a resolution requiring the national government to establish compulsory licences and adopt other measures to ensure free and inexpensive access to medicines and other medical technologies to combat the Covid-19 pandemic.18 Germany, Europe's largest economy, has also passed legislation, the Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases in Humans Act, which empowers the health ministry to issue government use authorization under the patent law, after the declaration of a national epidemic by Bundestag, German federal legislature’s lower chamber.19 Israel has already issued a CL for the importation of Kaletra (lopinavir 200 mg/ritonavir 50 mg) for the treatment of Covid-19 patients.20 In India too, several commentators have identified the prominence of CL for realizing public health objectives.21 Already demands have been made for the issuance of CL on drugs like remdesivir to augment its accessibility for Covid-19 patients.22 The potential use of CL as a regulatory tool in Corona times might go up further as Covid-19 vaccines become available. India, which is often called the pharmacy of the world,23 might have an important role to play in ensuring supplies of vaccines and drugs to various countries such as in Latin America.24 Given this background of the rising importance of CL, from the perspective of states, it is imperative to understand what kind of legal challenges they can face if they make use of this regulatory tool. This question becomes even more important because patent owners, when it comes to drugs and medicines, in a large number of cases, are pharmaceutical companies who zealously protect their intellectual property. One obvious option for these companies will be to challenge the issuance of such CLs under the domestic laws of the country concerned. Another choice that many foreign pharmaceutical companies might like to employ, under international law, is to challenge the issuance of such CLs before investor-State dispute settlement (ISDS) tribunals. These ISDS tribunals derive their authority from bilateral investment treaties (BITs)25 or investment chapters of free trade agreements (FTAs). These BITs or investment chapters in FTAs allow foreign investors to directly bring claims against host States for alleged treaty breaches before ISDS tribunals—a three-member ad hoc arbitration tribunal—often without exhausting local remedies.26 Intellectual property rights (IPRs) in these treaties are listed as investments.27 Consequently, ISDS tribunals have jurisdiction over regulatory measures that impair the investor’s IPRs. This allows pharmaceutical companies to enforce their IPRs through the ISDS mechanism.28 Indeed, in the last few years, foreign investors have employed the ISDS regime to challenge the host State’s regulatory measures relating to IPRs.29 For example, an pharmaceutical the of its patent by a federal on the ground of a of under the also a against under the the possibility of pharmaceutical companies the issuance of CL before ISDS tribunals is not investment have that foreign investors can challenge the issuance of CL before an ISDS on the ground that it to an of their In other foreign investors can that the issuance of a CL has to of their under international investment As the of the issuance of CLs as before an ISDS is an for a patent holder for several it allows the patent holder to directly bring about a before an international the domestic of the host if the it would to the patent holder what the host would to as for issuing the CL also the foreign will in such a will on various such as the for which the CL has been the royalty to the patent is what the issuance of the CL on the patent investment in the host what is the of the treaty on in the the treaty from the treaty provisions like for public health Nonetheless, IPRs are as in the is that foreign investors can bring such claims before ISDS tribunals. abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines robotized precision farming in olive oil production by integrating spatial data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI). A comprehensive analytical framework converts heterogeneous orchard data into actionable management information to address resource scarcity, climate variability, and sustainable intensification. The approach combines soil organic matter (OM), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), yield measurements, and geographic coordinates using spatial clustering, variogram analysis, Random Forest regression, and multivariate spatial analysis. Although AI-driven olive classification using RGB and VIS-NIR imaging can identify cultivars and defects, most existing systems focus on post-harvest quality assessment. This paper instead targets spatial variability and site-specific orchard control, extending AI to pre-harvest and field-wide decision support. Key findings show that: (1) spatial clustering effectively defined three management zones despite poor OM prediction from sensor variables (R² ≈ 0), with zone-based management approximately 90% effective even when using single-metric decisions; (2) linear regression revealed an unexpectedly weak correlation between OM and olive yield (r = 0.072), redirecting optimization toward other controllable variables and challenging traditional agronomic assumptions; and (3) robotized agricultural solutions with AI-enhanced spatial analytics provide a powerful closed-loop model for precision olive orchard management. The work advances Agriculture 5.0 by augmenting vision-based olive quality-assessment tools, enabling smart, autonomous, and sustainable Mediterranean olive oil production. REFERENCES [1] M. abstract: Pneumonia is a serious disease that affects the lungs, and rapid and proper diagnosis is critical for its effective treatment. CXR is employed due to its relative availability and low cost, along with the fact that it can detect anomalies in the lungs; however, the result of interpretation depends on the quality of the picture, overlapping features, experience of the one who analyzes it, and even the load of work. In the present study, we suggest a deep learning method with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model that classifies pneumonia based on chest x-rays. A labeled CXR dataset comprising 5,856 images was utilized for the development of the model, where the images were labeled as pneumonia and normal based on the reference labels. The dataset was split into train, validation, and independent test sets by employing patient-level splitting to avoid any possible data leakage. Image resizing, normalization, augmentation, and lung region-based pre-processing were performed prior to model training. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were employed as the metrics for assessing the performance of the model. As shown in the experiment results, the accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, and AUC are 94.2%, 95.1%, 93.3%, 93.0%, 94.0%, and 0.97, respectively. The Grad-CAM method mainly focused on the pulmonary regions with radiographic abnormalities and provided the interpretation of model decision processes. It appears that the deep learning model with interpretable mechanism can be a good computer-aided technique for pneumonia screening. Nevertheless, external validation and assessment of the model explanations should be conducted. REFERENCES [1] J. Irvin, P. Rajpurkar, K. Ko, Y. Yu, S. Ciurea-Ilcus, C. Chute, H. Marklund, B.
